"Poland. Business Adventure” 2nd edition gala
Poland
Unknown Publisher

"Poland. Business Adventure” 2nd edition gala
14.09.2026
On 14 September, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Radosław Sikorski inaugurated the gala of the "Poland. Business Adventure” 2nd edition. The event at the Royal Castle in Warsaw was also attended by Director General of the Foreign Service Henryka Mościcka-Dendys and President the Polish Investment and Trade Agency Artur Osuchowski.
Ninety four persons took part in this year’s edition of “Poland. Business Adventure.” Conceived by the MFA, a programme of three-month-long business internships is addressed to the representatives of the Polish diaspora aged 21–35 and carried out in collaboration with the Polish Investment and Trade Agency.
During the gala, Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski stressed that the “Poland. Business Adventure” programme is much more than an opportunity to gain new professional experience.
It is a possibility to make friends with interesting people from all over the world. It is a chance to discover the land of your ancestors, its rich culture, fascinating history, beautiful language, and its achievements
- said Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski.
Participants of “Poland. Business Adventure” not only work during their internships, but also get to know Polish culture and learn the Polish language. This year, they have visited several Polish cities, including Kraków and Gdańsk.
Speaking at the gala, the head of the Polish MFA pointed out that, for some of the internship holders, “Poland. Business Adventure” is just the beginning of their professional careers in Poland.
I am pleased that some of the Polish companies hosting your internships have treated this three-month period as a trial period, which will culminate in the signing of an employment contract
- said Poland’s top diplomat.
Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski also thanked the partner companies that had decided to host internship holders from all over the world and to show them how business is developing in Poland.

Canada in talks to join EU's Erasmus+ exchanges programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:48:08 UTC
22:48:08 KST

Canada is in early talks to join Erasmus+ and possibly Horizon Europe, as Ottawa and Brussels weigh an unprecedented "associate membership" of the EU short of full accession.
Ottawa and Brussels are in talks for Canada to join the Erasmus+ exchange programme, which would let students from both sides study at each other's universities.
EU-Canada relations have rarely been closer, as Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought to build a tighter relationship with the European bloc following the aggressive trade agenda and erratic foreign policy of the second Trump administration.
On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the first "associate member" of the EU, an unprecedented arrangement short of full membership, which remains off the table for Canada since it is not a European country.
While the details of that new status remain unclear, talks are already under way for Canada to join several existing EU programmes, including the flagship Erasmus+ exchange scheme, long hailed as one of the most tangible benefits of European integration.
Canada would be the first non-European country to join the exchange programme, which funds people and organisations to study and train abroad.
"Canadians want to participate in Erasmus+. It will be expensive for them, but they are ready to do that," MEP Javier Moreno Sánchez (Spain/S&D), chair of the European Parliament's delegation to Canada, told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday.
Negotiations are still at an early stage, but there is momentum on both sides of the Atlantic to bring Canada into one of Europe's most successful projects, Euronews understands.
Canada is currently a recognised Erasmus+ partner country, but not an associated one. That means Canadian universities and other entities may join certain Erasmus+ actions, subject to specific eligibility criteria and conditions.
Besides EU member states, six non-EU countries currently take part: North Macedonia, Serbia, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Türkiye. Canada is expected to follow a similar arrangement if an agreement is found.
Moreno hailed the move as a way of strengthening the relationship with tangible benefits for ordinary people. He also said the convention that mutually recognises architects' professional qualifications should be extended to doctors, engineers and professors.
Canada might also join another flagship EU programme, Horizon Europe, which funds research projects. Cooperation there is currently limited to the strands dedicated to global challenges and industrial competitiveness.
"Canadians are the most European people outside of Europe," Moreno said. "If we don't strengthen our relationship with Canada, then with which other country should we do it?"

More than 800 'excess' deaths recorded in France during latest heat wave period
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:45:41 UTC
22:45:41 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
France recorded 817 “excess deaths” between July 27 and Aug. 20 during a period of high temperatures, with at least 751 involving those aged 75 and older, the Health Ministry said Wednesday, according to the Le Monde newspaper.
Sante publique France, the country's national public health agency, said that “this excess all-cause mortality concerns almost exclusively people aged 75 and over, with at least 751 excess deaths.”
It added that “all regions were affected,” except Normandy and Occitanie.
The figure brings the number of excess deaths during heat-wave periods since late May to more than 7,300, according to Sante publique France.
The agency recorded 1,243 excess deaths between July 3 and 22 and 5,764 between June 17 and July 2.
“The final estimate of consolidated excess all-cause mortality for the entire summer, broken down by heat wave, will be presented in the summer assessment produced after the surveillance period,” said Sante publique France.
The agency also recorded 300 deaths during the first heat wave episode of the year, between May 24 and 28.
Its previous assessments were based on preliminary, unconsolidated mortality data.
For the June 17 to July 2 heat wave, those aged 75 and older accounted for about two-thirds of the excess deaths, while they represented three-quarters of the total during July 3 to 22.
Sante publique France concluded that “these impacts highlight the importance of implementing management and prevention measures to reduce the impact of heat on populations, without waiting to observe health impacts.”
France experienced an exceptionally hot summer in 2026, with the season described as the hottest ever recorded in the country, according to data from Meteo-France.

'Starship Troopers' director confirms Donald Trump's space uniforms are Nazi-inspired
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:45:33 UTC
22:45:33 KST

“I don’t know if this president is aware that the movie says these [characters] are fascists without knowing that they’re fascists. That’s the point,” said Paul Verhoeven, the director of 'Starship Troopers' - which was the direct reference cited by Trump when posting about Space Force uniforms.
If the Jackboot fits...
On 6 September, Donald Trump bulk-posted a series of AI-generated images, in which he renamed New Mexico as “New America”, declared the Moon as US territory, and portayed himself as the Green Lantern.
During this AI slop rampage, Trump proposed new uniforms for the United States Space Force – which was established in 2019 during Trump’s first term in office.
The image Trump posted was a design mockup for a new “service dress uniform” that was “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper Uniform.”
Many were quick to point out that this was a curious choice of inspiration, as Starship Troopers is a 1997 sci-fi war movie which is a cautionary tale about the dangers of fascism.
The cult film by Dutch director Paul Verhoeven is about a group of friends who enlist in the military and get swept up in an intergalactic war. Beyond fight against space bugs, Starship Troopers explores themes of misplaced patriotism, colonialism, xenophobia and violence decrying from fascistic rule.
The movie was based on the novel by Robert A. Heinlein, which Verhoeven interpreted as fascistic, nationalistic and in favour of military rule. The director used his film to deconstruct these elements and undermine the themes, using Nazi iconography to further his point. For instance, officer uniforms in Starship Troopers are similar to those worn by the Gestapo...
Verhoeven has gone on the record many times to state that he directed the film in order to turn a “right-wing book” into a film that was a dark satire about the dangers of fascism.
Now, Verhoeven has said that Donald Trump's administration should be aware that the film’s heroes are all "fascists without knowing that they’re fascists”.
“When [the Trump administration] talks about Starship Troopers, they should be aware that it’s based on the style of Leni Riefenstahl," Verhoeven told The Hollywood Reporter - referring to the German filmmaker who was closely associated with the Nazi regime and glorified it through films including 1935's Triumph of the Will.
“I don’t know if this president is aware that the movie says these [characters] are fascists without knowing that they’re fascists. That’s the point,” continued Verhoeven.
Once again, a potent reminder that the Trump administration should really think twice before co-opting cinematic references.
Trump has previously appropriated several pop culture touchstones, including Superman, Hannibal Lecter, Jedis and Spider-Man, and the references have backfired every time – not only by sparking the ire of the original creators and fans, but also for how these hijacked cultural winks display a lack of appreciation or understanding when it comes to the references themselves.
That being said, Verhoeven said that he is used to Starship Troopers’ satirical intent being misread and that the film has been challenging for audiences “because its heroes are, without knowing, Nazis."
"I thought people would understand and laugh about it. But that was not the case,” he added. “I’m a Dutch citizen, and I cannot vote. I’ve been here in this country [US] for 40 years and it’s still difficult for me to understand the political culture here in America.”

Russia to make no agreements with Europe on issues related to its security — Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:45:00 UTC
22:45:00 KST

YEKATERINBURG, September 16. /TASS/. Russia does not intend to enter into any contracts or agreements with the EU on issues of its national security, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the International Youth Festival.
"In areas that affect the security of the state, we will not and do not intend to conclude any contracts or agreements with Europeans," he said.
The foreign minister pointed out that it was Europe that severed relations with Russia, rather than the other way around.
"We are now fully provided with markets and partners, and despite the hybrid war against Russia, everything is going as acceptably and positively as possible given all the circumstances," Lavrov stressed. "When and if any European country wants to resume a serious dialogue, we will first listen to what they have in mind and what they can offer, and then we will decide whether it suits us or not. But there will be no more returns to the embrace that took place at the end of the Soviet Union and in the 1990s."
The International Youth Festival is being held in Yekaterinburg from September 11 to 17 under the slogan "Follow Your Dream." The festival is expected to be attended by 10,000 young leaders from 191 countries: 5,000 from Russia and 5,000 from other countries. The program will include 1,000 teenagers aged 14 to 17.
TASS is the event’s general information partner.

Asian Games Basketball Roundup: China, Japan, South Korea, Iran reach semifinals
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:44:06 CST
22:44:06 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China, Japan, South Korea and Iran advanced to the men's basketball semifinals at the 2026 Asian Games after winning their respective quarterfinals on Wednesday.
China held off Saudi Arabia 87-78 despite forwards Zhu Junlong, Zhao Jiayi and Li Hongquan being sidelined by injuries. China took a 48-39 lead into halftime, but Saudi Arabia fought back to tie the game at 62 at the end of the third quarter.
The fourth quarter remained tight before two free throws from Hu Jinqiu gave China an 83-75 lead with 2:04 remaining. Mohammad Alsuwailem then made a free throw and a layup to cut the deficit to 83-78 with 1:29 left, but consecutive baskets from Cui Yongxi and Liao sealed China's victory.
Liao, who poured in a game-high 30 points, led four Chinese players in double digits, while Yu Jiahao added 16 points and nine rebounds. Muhammad Abdurrahkman led Saudi Arabia with 25 points.
Iran narrowly defeated Bahrain 79-74 to advance to the semifinals. With 10.4 seconds remaining and holding a three-point lead, Iran missed three consecutive free throws, giving Bahrain a final chance to turn the game around.
On Bahrain's last possession, guard Mustafa Rashed missed a three-pointer from the corner. He was then ejected after receiving his second technical foul of the game for disputing the call, ending Bahrain's hopes of a comeback.
In the other two quarterfinals, Lee Hyun-jung scored 28 points and grabbed nine rebounds, while veteran Choi Jun-yong added six points on his return as South Korea routed Jordan 114-80; Host Japan defeated Chinese Taipei 85-78, with Kotetsu Kurokawa scoring 23 points.
The men's basketball semifinals will be staged on Friday, with China facing Japan and South Korea taking on Iran. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: CPEC project helps Pakistani women break barriers, scale new professional heights
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:44:02 CST
22:44:02 KST

by Raheela Nazir
ISLAMABAD, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Wearing a smart navy blue uniform and looking all primed and equipped to operate a massive train, 26-year-old Nida Saleh could barely contain her excitement while mounting herself into a cabin of the Orange Line Metro Train (OLMT).
The metro train is the first modern rail transit system in Pakistan's eastern Lahore city under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), jointly constructed by China Railway Group Corporation and China North Industries Corporation.
"I used to think why I could not get to choose the field of my choice and prove myself in the workplace and challenge traditional gender stereotypes," Saleh said.
"A few years on, here I am working blissfully as Pakistan's first female metro driver." Saleh joined the project as a transport engineer before deciding to take on a more demanding role as a train operator under the guidance of Chinese engineers.
"Initially, my family was concerned, but witnessing my passion for opening a way for other women, my parents were at ease. My main purpose is to bring about social change and improve the well-being of Pakistani women while becoming a source of hope, encouragement and inspiration for other women," she said.
Saleh believed that the journey to become the country's first female metro operator was not possible without the Chinese colleagues who went the extra mile to train her and impart world-class technical knowledge and standard operating procedures.
"The gesture of women's empowerment through the Chinese projects symbolizes the great friendship between Pakistan and China," she said, adding that CPEC projects in Pakistan are not only empowering local women and helping them grow, but also playing a pivotal role in transforming the country's economic landscape.
After Saleh's resounding success, another batch of 10-15 women were trained to enhance women's participation and promote professional independence for them in Pakistan.
"Never in my wildest dreams have I thought of becoming a train driver, said Hijab Aziz, another female train operator.
"I was a bit nervous initially, but thanks to my seniors, Chinese and Pakistani colleagues who taught us the nitty-gritty of train operations and passenger handling," she added.
Aziz takes pride in sharing that she is one of the pioneers. "During my training, I completed my theoretical and practical courses in which we studied safety protocols, passenger safety, fault handling and train operations to become certified train operators," the 25-year-old explained.
"We also learned about pressure handling as we are handling huge locomotives. We have been put through several tests and practice before actually hitting the rail track. This project is first-of-its-kind in providing opportunities to females in such fields," she added.
Being part of Pakistan's public transport system, which is considered the backbone of urban mobility, providing essential services that support economic activity as well as social equity, Aziz said she feels a sense of achievement as she transports people to their workplaces, educational institutes and day-to-day activities.
The OLMT in Lahore developed a new working space for the female segment of society to excel professionally, said Qamar Mehboob, deputy general manager at the OLMT.
"Modern systems do not differentiate between genders, and technology is gender-neutral if mastered. The orange line project is committed to women's empowerment, which will be offering more opportunities for women in various departments, including maintenance and operations in the coming days," he added.
Wang Zhiwen, acting director of operations and maintenance at the OLMT project, said that highly experienced subway drivers from China are involved in teaching Pakistani female train operators according to Chinese standards.
"From theoretical learning to handling emergencies on main lines, female train operators were quite proficient," he said, adding that Chinese supervisors intend to train more female drivers as well as engineers to do maintenance and repair and deal with malfunctions in the future.
The OLMT is catering to more than 260,000 people daily with reduced travel time, having a substantial effect on the lives of people, especially those who could not afford to travel frequently. Considering the high demand for a cheap mode of transportation in Lahore, the capacity of the service is being increased to 500,000 people daily with additional train sets, according to Bilal Akbar Khan, Punjab minister for transport and mass transit.
Many projects under the CPEC and joint ventures between Pakistani and Chinese companies are bringing about socio-economic benefits to Pakistan, transforming the lives of locals, and furthermore, many projects are proving to be game-changers for Pakistani women.
"The Orange Line is one such example where women's participation is being encouraged by creating a conducive environment, making them feel respected, valued and supported, leading to higher job satisfaction and productivity," Khan said.
"Enabling women professionally at workplaces and providing them an appropriate mode of transportation is the country's top priority, and the Chinese people are helping us in this regard," he said.
Sadia Ahmed, an electrical engineer working at the rolling stock department of the OLMT, said that since her recruitment she has excelled in professional skills and learned the latest technology, with the privilege of having a happy and supportive working environment.
"When I joined this company about two years ago, I knew this was exactly what I was looking for -- a chance to jumpstart my career and better future -- build a successful and accomplished life for my family and myself," Ahmed said enthusiastically. ■

China Focus: China's railway construction gains strong momentum as Jan.-Aug. investment rises
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:56 CST
22:43:56 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China's railway construction endeavors maintained solid momentum in the first eight months of 2026, with significant progress made on a number of key projects, the national railway operator said on Wednesday.
Fixed-asset investment in the railway sector totaled 511.8 billion yuan (about 75.68 billion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of the year, up 1.5 percent year on year, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd.
This steady progress in railway construction has helped boost related industries and employment, injecting new momentum into the expansion of domestic demand and stable economic growth, the company said.
A number of key projects have recently made positive progress. For instance, the Wenling-Yuhuan section of the Hangzhou-Shaoxing-Taizhou high-speed railway in east China's Zhejiang Province opened to traffic, putting Yuhuan, a city in southeastern Zhejiang, within 1 hour and 47 minutes of the provincial capital Hangzhou by direct high-speed train.
Construction also advanced on several technically challenging projects.
Railway construction teams have pushed tunnel construction forward in cold and difficult mountain terrain, finished tunnels through complex and risky ground conditions, started building beams on major railway bridges, and begun laying tracks on the country's longest high-speed railway bridge under construction.
The company said it will fully implement the railway construction tasks set out in the outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), coordinate the planning and construction of new lines with the upgrading and capacity expansion of conventional railways, and continue to improve the quality and efficiency of railway investment to support high-quality economic and social development.
China has built the world's largest high-speed railway network. By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
According to the company, the country's operational railway mileage is expected to reach 180,000 km by 2030, with high-speed rail amounting to roughly 60,000 km.
Railway construction boasts a long industrial chain and wide spillover effects, driving demand for steel, cement, construction machinery and equipment manufacturing, while creating local jobs.
In the first seven months of the year, China's railways recorded 2.8 billion passenger trips, up 4.1 percent year on year and a record high for the period. Over the same timeframe, the network carried 14.85 million trips by foreign passengers, a surge of 32.5 percent.
China's railways carried 2.35 billion tonnes of cargo in the first seven months of 2026, rising 0.7 percent from a year earlier, lending solid support to logistics cost cuts and sustained stable economic performance.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. When fully built, the network will cover major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

Kazakhstan to commission at least 8.4 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2035
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:54 CST
22:43:54 KST

ASTANA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Kazakhstan plans to commission at least 8.4 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy capacity by 2035 under its power sector development plan, the country's Ministry of Energy said Wednesday.
Kazakhstan currently operates 170 renewable energy facilities with a combined installed capacity of about 3.8 GW, Vice Minister of Energy Sanzhar Zharkeshov said on the sidelines of the third Regional Central Asian and European Decarbonization Forum in Astana.
To reach its targets of a 15-percent renewable energy share by 2030 and a 50-percent share of alternative and low-carbon energy by 2050, Kazakhstan will continue to hold annual renewable energy auctions and implement major projects with strategic investors, Zharkeshov added. ■

Indonesia vows major investment in disaster response, orders firefighting aircraft
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:42 CST
22:43:42 KST

JAKARTA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said Wednesday that the government would significantly strengthen the country's disaster response capabilities, including expanding its helicopter fleet and acquiring large aircraft for aerial firefighting.
"I am determined to strengthen our mitigation capabilities. The agencies that deal with disasters must be strengthened," Prabowo said during a government talk program, according to the state communications agency.
Prabowo said Indonesia needed hundreds of helicopters for firefighting and other disaster response operations, adding that he had already ordered several large aircraft for water-bombing missions.
The president also warned that corruption in the management of state resources could undermine disaster response capabilities. Citing Indonesia's location along the Pacific "Ring of Fire," he said savings from government spending should be redirected toward more productive programs.
Prabowo said the government had saved more than 300 trillion rupiah (about 17 billion U.S. dollars) during his first year in office, including by cutting ministry spending on anniversary celebrations.
Indonesia has faced widespread forest and land fires this year, particularly in Kalimantan, alongside other natural disasters. ■

Egypt recovers 2,000-year-old golden mummy mask from Switzerland
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:41 CST
22:43:41 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Egypt recovered an ancient golden mummy mask from Switzerland as part of its efforts to retrieve artifacts illegally taken from the country, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said Wednesday.
The Egyptian Embassy in Bern coordinated with Swiss authorities to recover the artifact. Egyptian Ambassador Mohamed Nagm received the mask on behalf of the foreign minister.
The recovery reflects growing cooperation between Egypt and Switzerland in protecting cultural property and combating illegal trafficking of antiquities, the ministry said.
The Embassy of Switzerland in Cairo said the ancient funerary mask dated back to the Ptolemaic period, more than 2,000 years ago.
The return marks another milestone in the longstanding cooperation between Switzerland and Egypt to protect cultural heritage and fight the illicit trafficking of cultural property. Since 2011, Switzerland has returned around 80 cultural objects to Egypt, the embassy added. ■

China to bolster opening up with better legal framework for foreign-related affairs

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:25 CST
22:43:25 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China will further strengthen its foreign-related legal framework over the next five years to improve its "legal toolkit" for relevant affairs, Vice Minister of Justice Wu Yanjun said Wednesday.
The move comes as the country seeks to better support its opening up and manage risks arising from the increasing overseas activities of Chinese citizens and businesses, Wu told a news conference.
Efforts will also be made to guide legal responses to foreign-related civil and commercial disputes and better protect the personal and property rights of Chinese citizens and businesses, Wu said.
China has introduced several sets of regulations in response to practical needs in foreign-related areas this year, including rules on countering foreign long-arm jurisdiction, regulations on industrial and supply-chain security, and rules governing outbound investment.
The rules on countering foreign states' unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction measures, which were issued in April this year, stipulate that the Chinese government has the authority to take countermeasures in response to such actions. The regulations also state that no organization or individual shall enforce or assist in enforcing such unlawful jurisdiction measures.
Under the new rules, Chinese authorities carried out an investigation after the European Commission announced an investigation into Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com's proposed takeover of German retailer Ceconomy in May.
In August, the Ministry of Justice announced that the EU's cross-border investigation constituted unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction, and that no organization or individual may comply with or assist in implementing relevant measures.
In May, citing the same set of rules on countering foreign unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction, the ministry said the EU's probe into Chinese security check company Nuctech constituted unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction.
As some legal experts pointed out, China's efforts in pursuing high-standard opening up require a stable international environment, yet some foreign countries' unlawful extraterritorial jurisdiction measures have brought about serious uncertainties.
Analysts believed that the new regulations also carry direct implications for Chinese companies seeking to safeguard their overseas-related rights and will significantly boost companies' confidence in responding to external bullying.
At Wednesday's media conference, Wu said the ministry has also worked to provide more efficient and higher-quality legal services to Chinese companies and citizens operating overseas.
According to Wu, the ministry will further coordinate legislative work on international judicial assistance in civil and commercial matters, overseas labor cooperation and overseas contracted projects. Measures will also be taken to develop international commercial arbitration centers and support more Chinese law firms and arbitration institutions in expanding their operations overseas.
Moreover, China will play a more constructive role within the framework of international platforms, including the United Nations, in the area of the rule of law and actively participate in international cooperation to combat cross-border crimes such as telecom and online fraud and money laundering, Wu said.
At the same media conference, Jiang Shan, a ministry official in charge of legislative affairs, said the ministry would step up legislation in key areas affecting people's livelihoods and strengthen safeguards for basic work and living conditions.
It will conduct studies on laws and regulations covering oversight of social insurance funds, security of grain reserves, protection of the rights and interests of older people, elderly care services, and food safety, Jiang said. ■

CANBERRA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Australia had a much larger Indigenous population before European arrival, with far greater population losses from colonization than previously thought, new research shows.

====================================================================================================

DR Congo Ebola outbreak remains "uncontrolled" as transmission trends diverge: WHO
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:19 CST
22:43:19 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains "uncontrolled" despite an overall decline in cases and deaths, as the epidemic follows increasingly different trajectories across affected parts of the country, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Wednesday.
"The outbreak remains uncontrolled and increasingly heterogeneous," the WHO Regional Office for Africa said in its latest weekly situation report.
For much of the outbreak, the eastern province of Ituri has been the epicenter of transmission and still accounts for almost 80 percent of confirmed cases. Infections there have been declining since mid-August, helping drive down the national caseload.
"The peak is behind us (in Ituri). We are already on the downward slope," Jean-Jacques Muyembe, a veteran Congolese virologist heading the country's National Institute of Biomedical Research, said late Tuesday in Kinshasa, noting "a clear improvement" in the fight against Ebola in Ituri.
That modest national decline, however, masks what the WHO described as "a pronounced geographic redistribution of transmission." Over the latest three-week period, confirmed cases fell by about 6 percent nationwide, driven largely by a 25-percent drop in Ituri, while cases surged by more than 76 percent in neighboring North Kivu.
North Kivu, the second-most affected province after Ituri, is now moving in the opposite direction. The WHO described a "sharp and sustained increase" there, with the province recording its "highest incidence" since the outbreak began, as the flare-up in North Kivu has been broad-based rather than confined to a few hotspots.
North Kivu now accounts for about one-third of new cases and more than one-third of new deaths nationwide, as its worsening outbreak increasingly offsets the gains made in Ituri, according to the WHO.
Muyembe nevertheless cautioned that progress in some areas did not mean the epidemic was over, as transmission remains uneven and continues to intensify elsewhere. He stressed the need to further strengthen contact tracing and other response measures.
At the same time, researchers are moving closer to results from several experimental vaccines and treatments, as no vaccine or specific therapy has yet been approved for disease caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, the strain behind the current outbreak.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved against Zaire ebolavirus, is being used in the DRC under a compassionate-use framework and research protocols to determine whether it can offer some protection against Bundibugyo ebolavirus. A total of 2,307 health and frontline workers had received the vaccine by Sept. 13, about 20 percent of the targeted group, according to the WHO.
Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said Tuesday that laboratory findings and field observations had provided grounds to investigate possible cross-protection, but stressed that they did not yet amount to proof. Clinical studies are now underway to assess whether the vaccine can reduce infection, severe disease or deaths.
Research on treatments and prevention is also advancing. Mbala said a clinical trial evaluating post-exposure prophylaxis for people at high risk of infection has been moving forward, with an initial analysis potentially available by the end of this month.
Separately, the WHO said 128 people had received investigational treatment or prophylaxis, including 16 confirmed patients and 112 high-risk contacts receiving post-exposure prophylaxis. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial is testing the experimental monoclonal antibody MBP134, remdesivir and their combination in confirmed patients.
"Although the response has been unprecedented in its scale, the epidemic continues to expand," said Olivier le Polain, head of epidemiology and analytics for response at the WHO, Tuesday at a UN briefing in Geneva, warning that the high caseload and wide geographic spread meant it would take "many, many months" to bring the outbreak fully under control.
Muyembe did not give a new deadline for containing the outbreak, saying only that response teams should "do everything possible so that we can celebrate the New Year under better conditions."
The DRC government's latest situation report, with data through Sept. 13, showed that the country had recorded 7,258 confirmed Ebola cases, including 3,510 deaths, across 62 health zones in seven provinces.
The current outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

China overfulfills ozone-depleting substance cut targets as climate efforts intensify
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
21:43:16 CST
22:43:16 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China has overfulfilled its targets to cut ozone-depleting substances under the Kigali Amendment, with its total phase-out amount accounting for more than half of that achieved by developing nations, an ecology and environment official said on Wednesday.
China has phased out about 720,000 tonnes of ozone-depleting substances since joining the Montreal Protocol, which is over half of the total that has been phased out by developing countries worldwide, said Xu Bijiu, vice minister of ecology and environment.
Xu made the remarks at a meeting in Beijing commemorating the 10th anniversary of the adoption of the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, and the 2026 International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer.
The international community adopted the Kigali Amendment under the Montreal Protocol 10 years ago, bringing hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), a non-carbon dioxide greenhouse gas, under the treaty's control. Full implementation of the amendment is expected to avoid 0.5 degrees Celsius of global warming by the end of this century.
China joined the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer in 1991, and accepted the Kigali Amendment in 2021, committing to freezing HFCs production and consumption at baseline levels starting in 2024, followed by gradual reductions as outlined in the amendment.
Since accepting the Kigali Amendment, China has strictly controlled the production and use of HFCs, reducing production by more than 1.185 billion tonnes and cutting use by 759 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent compared with its baseline levels, Xu said.
Over the past year, China's ecology and environment authority has actively advanced compliance actions, improved the whole-chain management system, strictly enforced import and export approval, and promoted green and low-carbon alternatives, he added.
Going forward, China will continue to improve licensing management, enhance regulatory efficiency, accelerate the promotion of alternative technologies, and advance its compliance efforts during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), Xu said. ■

Taiwan’s drone deficit requires attention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:41:10 UTC
22:41:10 KST

There is a Taiwanese proverb that reads, “Do not wait until you are thirsty to dig a well.”
While Western planners focus on China’s visible fleet, Beijing’s ability to mass‑produce automated naval platforms poses a deeper threat — one that upends deterrence by denial and cross‑strait assurance alike.
A leaked transcript from a May 2022 war‑preparedness meeting in Guangdong outlined how commercial maritime technology and military infrastructure are fused under Beijing’s Military‑Civil Fusion strategy to dominate the Pacific by 2027.
Guangdong firms Zhuhai Yunzhou and Jianglong Shipbuilding were reported to be producing dozens of combat‑ready unmanned surface vessels (USVs) monthly, with mobilization capacity far higher. Extrapolated nationally, this points to hundreds of uncrewed vessels per month and a potential inventory of 10,000+ by 2027.
Guangdong emphasizes swarm strike craft, Shanghai’s Jiangnan Shipyard focuses on stealth autonomous corvettes and missile trimarans, while other yards optimize for automated minelayers and anti‑submarine platforms. This framework was exercised in the PLA Eastern Theater Command’s “Justice Mission 2025,” which simulated an integrated maritime blockade reaching Taiwan’s contiguous zone using China coast guard fleets.
Gray‑zone inundation
Beijing’s plan co‑opts its commercial maritime sector, the coast guard and the People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia into strike, blockade and logistics roles. In conflict, thousands of civilian craft fitted with autonomous navigation could serve as radar decoys, explosive boats and sensor nodes. Reinforced roll‑on/roll‑off ferries and cargo ships could move heavy armor without risking crews.
Although allied rules of engagement permit targeting civilian‑flagged vessels supporting warfighting, Beijing’s gambit is political: using uncrewed commercial hulls to pressure allies into firing first at an outwardly “civilian” vanguard.
To anchor this automated force, Beijing relies on BeiDou‑3 for positioning, navigation and timing plus short‑message communications, creating a jam‑resistant over‑the‑horizon backbone. By leveraging cheap, disposable hulls, Beijing aims to degrade the economic and military utility of allied deterrence by punishment, presenting a mass threat too large for traditional retaliatory frameworks to absorb.
Despite scale, Beijing faces operational vulnerabilities. The most severe is a software bottleneck in distributed state estimation and dynamic routing. Real‑time deconfliction for hundreds of autonomous vessels avoiding self‑collision under electronic attack remains an unsolved technical hurdle.
This helps explain the maritime militia anomaly of late 2025 and early 2026. Ship‑tracking telemetry first analyzed by geospatial firm ingeniSPACE showed up to 2,000 civilian fishing vessels ceasing routine fishing on Christmas Day and massing into parallel geometric formations stretching roughly 460 kilometers.
A second operation on Jan. 11, involved 1,400 different vessels forming a 322-km rectangle. Combined, these state‑directed clusters deployed 789 km of floating barriers — enough to cover two‑thirds of Taiwan’s 1,204 km coastline — demonstrating that full national mobilization could achieve multi‑layer encirclement.
Layered defense
In response, Taiwan’s National Security Council shifted in June to intensive tabletop simulations countering a Chinese coast guard “law enforcement” quarantine that weaponizes administrative jurisdiction to choke trade non‑militarily. To counter an automated blockade, a coalition of Pacific allies — Taiwan, the US, Japan and the Philippines — is building a layered defense driven by the cost‑exchange ratio.
A converted Chinese drone boat can cost as little as NT$637,760 (US$20,000), while a traditional US interceptor missile exceeds NT$127.55 million (US$4 million). Shifting from expensive kinetic interceptors toward non‑kinetic area denial and distributed precision aims to break Beijing’s confidence in achieving a rapid fait accompli.
Taiwan’s Asymmetric Swarm Initiative leans on manufacturers like Thunder Tiger and their SeaShark series, integrating Shield AI’s Hivemind autonomy software alongside NCSIST’s Kuai Chi light USV to form GPS‑independent counter‑swarms.
The US deploys the Pentagon’s Replicator initiative and “Hellscape” doctrine to flood the strait with loitering munitions, while using cognitive electronic warfare such as SEWIP Block 3 and DRFM spoofing to alter BeiDou‑3 timestamps and drive Chinese drones off course.
Another classic Taiwanese proverb warns, “Repair the house before it rains.” Yet Taiwan’s structural defense is worsened by a stark production timeline gap. As the CCP actively deploys its own USVs, Taiwan’s planned maritime “drone wall” of 1,320 Kuai Chi attack USVs will not achieve swarm control or mass serial output until 2031, with full production starting in 2028.
Beijing’s runaway production leaves an immediate, dangerous window of maritime operational vulnerability. To neutralize escalating swarm threats affordably, the alliance is fielding next‑generation physical disrupters:
- High‑Power Microwave: Systems like METEOR emit volumetric cones of energy, frying exposed civilian microprocessors on co‑opted hulls. China has already unveiled truck‑mounted HPM weapons such as the Hurricane‑3000, underscoring the drone vs. counter‑drone contest.
- Autonomous Submarines: Operating beneath surface layers, uncrewed submarines can lay smart minefields or fire micro‑torpedoes to break transport hulls.
- Tactical EMPs: Non‑nuclear EMP payloads delivered via cruise missiles could paralyze robotic fleets in assembly ports before deployment.
This defensive wall introduces complex escalatory math. While Beijing’s rapid production signals an aggressive, asymmetric arms race with little regard for regional stability, allied strategy must shift from defending a stagnant status quo to actively arresting China’s creeping expansion. The goal is not to placate a revisionist CCP, but to deny it a pretext for preemptive attack while establishing a hard baseline that halts further territorial or administrative encroachment.
Washington must also provide corporate and security assurances to regional partners. Earlier this year, Japan abandoned strategic ambiguity, reinforcing its Nansei island chain with anti‑ship missile bases to lock down chokepoints.
This operational clarity assures Taipei of allied resolve while signaling to a militarizing Beijing that any further attempts to forcibly rewrite regional reality will incur unacceptable costs. Meanwhile, the Philippines is expanding maritime domain awareness along the Bashi Channel, deploying radar arrays and coastal USVs to counter gray‑zone coercion by the Chinese coast guard and maritime militia in the South China Sea.
Another Taiwanese proverb reminds us that, “A small net can still capture a giant fish.”
While China’s advantage is its capacity to turn commercial shipbuilding into an autonomous weapon of mass production, the allied coalition changes the deterrence calculus by exploiting Beijing’s software integration gaps, holding key chokepoints and shifting the cost‑exchange ratio through HPM, EMP and cognitive electronic warfare.
By building an impenetrable fortress of denial while maintaining clear lines of defensive assurance, the alliance preserves strategic equilibrium in the maritime domain — demonstrating that a CCP automated blockade will fail.

22:40:02 KST

Countries in the Gulf Cooperation Council, whose economies have benefitted massively from natural resources like oil and gas, have been increasingly diversifying their economies beyond the hydrocarbon business.
“In terms of economic strategy, [the GCC countries have] gotten the message that oil is not going to be there for long,” says Adnan Mazarei, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics and former deputy director of the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia department. “They've been aware that the geopolitical landscape is changing. They have a role to play by being a platform for various things in between these two poles: China versus the West.”
To gauge how different industries are developing across the GCC countries, TIME partnered with data firm Statista on a research project aimed at identifying the top-performing 200 companies in Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates based on employee satisfaction, revenue growth in recent years, and sustainability transparency informed by self-reporting.
Methodology: How TIME and Statista Determined Arabia’s Top Companies of 2026
There are varied diversification efforts across the GCC countries. The United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Bahrain have entered into agreements as part of the Trump Administration’s America First Investments to put more money into AI data centers and other technology innovations over the coming years. Saudi Arabia has been interested in becoming a hub where critical minerals are processed. And in the UAE and Saudi Arabia, which lead the region in economic diversification, other growing industries include health services, health tourism, and regular tourism.
Developmental differences in each country have affected which non-oil industries excel. “The most profitable investments are still in energy,” says Mazarei, and an increasing share of their own energy use mix is renewables, which has also been a key part of their diversification strategy. States are investing more in renewable energy and green tech as they consider energy efficiency to meet their enormous electricity needs, and saving oil for exports, says Karen Young, political economist and senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. “There was a lot of inefficient power generation from oil that's being phased out,” she says. “That makes sense from a climate perspective, but also from a cost perspective.” For example, in late 2025, QatarEnergy (no. 1 in the country and no. 6 overall), signed a deal with Samsung C&T to build a 2,000MW solar facility in Dukhan that could supply 750,000 households with energy by 2030.
Banking and finance is the industry most represented on TIME and Statista’s list, with 15.5% of the companies. Bahrain was the first of the GCCs to develop its financial services sector, allowing private equity funds like Investcorp, an investment vehicle that connected Gulf institutions with global business opportunities, to flourish. Places like Abu Dhabi are trying to follow suit. In 2023, Bahrain-headquartered Investcorp spun out Investcorp Capital (no. 84 in the overall list) in an IPO on the Abu Dhabi stock exchange.
Top-ranked First Abu Dhabi Bank’s largest shareholder is the state-owned Mubadala Investment Company. State activity and investment has been behind the expansion of the real estate industry as well as the development of giga-projects. All of these projects are “big business,” Young says, and “the bank sector is doing a lot of lending to these projects.” According to a 2024 McKinsey report, GCC banks tend to be more profitable than their global peers because of a balance of good oil prices, stable domestic deposits, and ambitious public investment programs.
The GCC’s economic development plans have experienced disruptions this year from geopolitical conflicts, and in response, companies have had to pivot their plans. Aluminum Bahrain Alba (no. 1 in country and no. 51 overall), which has long been a driver of the country’s non-oil economy, has had to lower output to protect itself from attack, driving up global prices for the metal and creating supply uncertainties. There’s now new attention on transport and infrastructure in the region. Logistics giant, DP World (no. 2 overall), which has been influential in the region, is now planning on building new shipping ports and boosting its ground transport fleets to accommodate supply chain disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.
Still, economists are projecting that the region will make a recovery starting 2027, as spending in non-oil sectors gains momentum.

British Army moves to restore long-range anti-tank strike
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:39:29 BST
22:39:29 KST

The British Army is moving to restore a beyond-line-of-sight anti-armour capability more than 30 years after Swingfire left service, with MBDA and Thales awarded contracts to explore a new weapon system, Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard has announced.
Speaking at DVD 2026, Pollard said the work would examine technologies for a weapon able to engage armoured targets beyond direct line of sight, improving the ability of British land forces to strike from greater distance while reducing their exposure on the battlefield.
He said: “And thirdly, I can also announce today that we have awarded contracts to MBDA and Thales to explore how we can develop the tech behind a new beyond-line-of-sight anti-armour weapon system, a capability that the British Army has not had since Swingfire, left service over 30 years ago, a capability that can drastically improve the ability of our land forces to strike and survive on the modern battlefield.”
Swingfire was a wire-guided anti-tank missile developed for the British Army and notable for its ability to turn sharply after launch, allowing the firing vehicle to remain concealed while the missile was guided onto a target from another position.
Its withdrawal left the Army without an equivalent long-range ground-launched anti-armour system able to engage targets beyond direct line of sight, with more recent anti-tank weapons generally centred on shorter-range engagements.
The new work with MBDA and Thales forms part of the Army’s wider Recce Strike concept, which is intended to combine surveillance, targeting, drones, armoured vehicles and longer-range weapons into a more connected force.
Pollard described the approach as being built around “better targeting, better battlefield surveillance and more lethal long range fire”, with the aim of improving both the speed and effectiveness of targeting.
The Government is committing more than £19 billion to land warfare capabilities over the next four years, alongside £11 billion for weapons and ammunition.
That includes £190 million for short-range ballistic missiles, £400 million for inexpensive one-way attack drones and weapons, and £220 million for Project Nyx, which is intended to develop armed autonomous aircraft capable of operating alongside Apache attack helicopters.
Another £370 million is being spent on Project Asgard, the digital command-and-control architecture supporting the Army’s Recce Strike model.
Pollard said: “That’s about improving the lethality and delivering against CGS’s 20:40:40 strategy, which has been baked into the Defence Investment Plan. Now, that will be collectively a higher resolution picture of the battlefield and increase the effectiveness and speed of our targeting.”
The new anti-armour work is also being tied directly to lessons from Ukraine, where long-range fires, drones and distributed targeting have changed how armoured forces are detected and engaged.
Pollard said: “Now, these are just three procurements that will not only demonstrate how we’re evolving operationally in response to the lessons from Ukraine, but they’re programmes that demonstrate how we have reformed our procurement processes in response to what we’ve learned from our friends in Ukraine.”
The MBDA and Thales contracts are therefore an early step towards restoring a capability absent from the Army for decades, while fitting into a wider effort to connect reconnaissance and long-range strike more closely across the land force.

‘Iran has agreements with BRICS members for cooperation in various fields’
TEHRAN- Iran’s Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance said at the Supreme Council of the Stock Exchange meeting: At the BRICS summit, we received very good feedback both from the heads of member states and in the meetings held with the countries present at this summit, very useful grounds for cooperation in various economic fields were understood and agreed upon.
According to an IRNA report from the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance, the 318th meeting of the Supreme Council of the Stock Exchange was held under the chairmanship of Seyed Ali Madanizadeh, Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance; in this meeting, while reviewing the capital market situation, items from the agenda were raised and approved.
At the beginning of the meeting, Madanizadeh presented a report on the achievements of the trip to Russia and India and the BRICS economic ministers meeting to the Supreme Council of the Stock Exchange.
The Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, noting that the summary of the news and events of the BRICS summit and the understandings of this meeting have been reflected in the media, said: In these meetings, we received very good feedback both from the heads of BRICS member states and in the meetings held with the countries present at this summit, very useful grounds for cooperation in various economic fields were understood and agreed upon.
Madanizadeh considered the creation of the necessary grounds for interactions with BRICS member banks, including Russian banks, as another achievement of this trip and added: These agreements will definitely be path-breaking for the private sector and the country’s economy.
Ultimately, for Iran, BRICS is more than politics: it is a vast market and network of trade, finance, and transit routes. Iran joined in 2024, but already trades heavily with members—about $23.7 billion in exports and $38.8 billion in imports. The main obstacle is not buyers but payments, banking, insurance, and sanctions. BRICS efforts on local currencies and payment connectivity matter greatly. China dominates Iran’s BRICS trade, so diversification is essential. Iran can also become a North–South transit route. Membership alone is insufficient; real gains require contracts, payments, investment, balanced higher-value trade, and real goods flows.

As Russia attacks Ukraine’s grid, solar offers a path to resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:38:38 UTC
22:38:38 KST

As Russia attacks Ukraine’s grid, solar offers a path to resilience
With help from government incentives, Ukrainian businesses and households are increasingly investing in solar.
Local resident Tetiana Chernyshenko, 55, stands next to solar panels installed on the rooftop of her residential building to mitigate the effects of power outages, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Feb. 19, 2026. (Henry Nicholls / AFP via Getty Images)
This story was produced by Grist and co-published with the Kyiv Independent.
On a spring day earlier this year, 10 men stood on the rooftop of a door manufacturing facility in the central Ukrainian town of Bila Tserkva, surveying the rows of solar panels that surrounded them. Since Russia invaded in 2022, the town has endured repeated attacks, triggering mass power outages. For the factory, which supplies doors to homes and businesses, keeping production going had become extremely challenging.
The outages were particularly brutal in the winter, when limited power supplies led to rolling blackouts across the country.
Some days, the employees burned discarded wood in a fireplace to keep the warehouse warm. The facility has backup generators, but they were expensive to run. Tired of relying on a grid that was being routinely bombarded by Russian missiles, Yaroslav, the facility’s owner, decided to switch to solar earlier this year. Yaroslav requested that the Kyiv Independent use only his first name and withhold details about the facility for fear of Russian retaliation.
Switching to solar energy will "further expand our capacity and be a bit more independent from the general grid," he said. "It will be cheaper, more economical, and more ecological."
In the spring, he contacted Yasno, a Ukrainian electricity and gas supplier owned by Ukraine's largest private energy company DTEK, to install solar panels on his rooftop. Yasno’s clients pay for the panels to be installed, often with the help of a government program that covers some of the installation expenses.
Ukraine created incentives to encourage businesses to switch to renewable energy, like the "Affordable Loans for 5-7-9%" program, which offers loans to purchase solar panels and other equipment. The preferential loans have interest rates of 5, 7, or 9 percent, depending on the type of business, and can cover up to 80 percent of the installation costs.
Yasno will ultimately decide where to station hundreds of solar panels on the warehouse rooftop and install them. The project is one of dozens that the company has undertaken across the country. In the past two years, it has installed solar panels at 117 sites with a combined capacity of 23 megawatts. The company paused its work for the first two years of the war, but resumed operations in the summer of 2024.
Volodymyr Hershtun, a service maintenance manager with Yasno who led the project in Bila Tserkva, said that Ukraine is rapidly developing its renewable energy portfolio in part because the country needs to be resilient as it continues to face a barrage of Russian attacks.
"The enemy is trying to destroy energy infrastructure, and we are building what is very easy to restore," he said. "And those same systems can store electric energy."
Before Russia’s invasion, Ukraine relied on a highly centralized electricity system dominated by nuclear power. More than half of the country’s electricity came from four nuclear power plants, while natural gas and coal generated roughly a quarter of the energy mix.
Renewables made up a small share of the energy portfolio, though the country had been rapidly expanding its solar generation in the years leading up to the war. The surge was driven by the country’s "green tariff" program, which encouraged households and businesses to produce solar and wind power through guaranteed above-market payments for electricity.
Ukrainian law guarantees the tariff until 2030, and lawmakers have described the program as a step toward integrating the country into the European Union’s energy market.
read also
Those government incentives led Ukrainian businesses to install about 8 gigawatts of solar by 2022. But Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure over the past few years have upended that model. Since the invasion, missiles and drones have repeatedly struck power plants, substations, and transmission lines, leaving millions without electricity during the coldest months.
Roughly 30 percent of the installed solar capacity and most of the country’s 36 wind farms in the south were either destroyed, fell under Russian occupation, or are unaccounted for. The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine has also been shut down and under Russian control since the invasion began. Given the legacy of Chornobyl, many Ukrainians live with the fear of another nuclear disaster.
The repeated attacks on the grid have caused prolonged power outages. Parts of Kyiv continue to ration electricity with scheduled power outages that can last for hours. Ukraine’s National Bank has said that Russia’s energy infrastructure attacks this year have worsened the electricity deficit assumptions, raising them from 3 percent to 6 percent.
With the vulnerabilities of relying on large, centralized power stations exposed, Ukraine has begun accelerating its shift toward smaller, distributed sources of electricity that are harder to knock offline. 
In 2025, the Solar Energy Association of Ukraine estimated that 1.5 GW of new solar capacity was built — almost double the prior year's total — and expects 2026 installations to at least match that pace.
"Renewables have become the very obvious choice for Ukraine when the full-scale invasion started and when Russia started deliberately and heavily attacking the energy infrastructure, especially centralized generation facilities," said Anastasia Vereshchynska, the director of the European-Ukrainian Energy Agency, a non-profit that works with energy efficiency and renewable resources in Ukraine.
The investments are likely to help Ukrainians weather brutal winters. Last year, as temperatures dropped to -1 degree Fahrenheit (-17 degrees Celcius), Russia’s bombardments caused widespread electricity and heating outages. Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital, had just half the electricity supply it needed to weather the winter, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared a state of emergency.
In Ukraine, solar panels are a "basic human right."
Volodymyr, a taxi driver in Kyiv who asked that his last name be withheld for safety reasons, told Grist in May that during last winter’s attacks, his apartment building lost power, leaving him and his family without heating and hot water. Fortunately, he said, his apartment faced south and received sunlight most of the day, keeping it relatively warm.
In an attempt to minimize the effects of outages, the building’s management company has since decided to install solar panels on the roof to help keep the boiler turned on and operate the elevators. The installation is part of the 5-7-9% program.
"It’s a cool thing that the government covers at least part of the cost," said Volodymyr. "In emergency cases, during power outages, you could turn to the solar panels. There is no harm to the planet. It’s a good thing."
The need for renewable energy is especially critical in communities closest to the war’s front lines. As Russian forces advance, towns and villages are increasingly cut off from the energy grid as attacks destroy power lines, and the threat to maintenance workers makes repairs difficult or impossible. Some villages, in particular, have become so dangerous that repairs cannot be conducted, leaving residents without electricity and access to the outside world.
In those communities, volunteers and non-governmental organizations have stepped in to install solar panels and battery systems that can power homes and businesses.
Denny Ugorchuk, the founder of Kosmo Tabir, a non-governmental organization that works to help villages access solar energy, said that much of the funding for large projects comes from the help of international partners in the West, while local donations from Ukrainians help fund smaller projects. In one village, solar panels installed at a private residence gave a 50-year-old woman access to online university classes.
In Ukraine, solar panels are a "basic human right," said Ugorchuk. "People should have access to communicate with one another — you can call a doctor, the police, and it helps you feel safe."

US uncovers alleged Russian terrorist group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:38:37 UTC
22:38:37 KST

US prosecutors have charged five individuals – believed to be collaborating with Russian intelligence services – with conspiracy to finance terrorism and plotting a contract killing, Politico reports.
Charges unsealed on the 15th of September state that the network recruited agents to conduct reconnaissance and assassinations within the US, as well as to attack civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are – or are perceived to be – allies of Ukraine. None of the five suspects have been apprehended.
The indictment notes that the group recently approached an individual living in the US, offering payment to surveil and kill a prominent Russian dissident residing there. Two alleged recruiters offered 40,000 dollars to eliminate or “make the target disappear” and discussed hiring another person to carry out the killing.
In another instance, an alleged Russian intelligence agent offered 25,000 dollars for the assassination of a dissident living in Lithuania and subsequently proposed attacking warehouses or electrical substations in countries aiding Ukraine.
The terrorist group is believed to have coordinated operations in the Czech Republic and Lithuania in 2024.
Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg stated that the suspects operated as part of an international network of assassins that extended into the US. He accused the suspects of acting on behalf of the Kremlin.
The charges brought by the US come at a time when European capitals are facing Russian influence operations. Germany clearly indicated that an explosive-laden drone found at Leipzig Airport in August was linked to Moscow. On the 15th of September, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, and a Russian warship fired flares at Danish helicopters.

Kosovo ex-president Thaci jailed for 25 years by Hague court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:37:09 UTC
22:37:09 KST

Kosovo ex-president Thaci jailed for 25 years by Hague court
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Former Kosovo president Hashim Thaci has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a court in The Hague for war crimes committed during the 1998–99 war with Serbia, prompting clashes between his supporters and riot police in the city.
The court is an EU-backed tribunal operating under Kosovan law, and found Thaci (58) guilty of the murder of 96 people, the arbitrary detention of at least 385, and for torturing at least 303 and cruel treatment of at least 49.
The victims were largely political opponents and civilians regarded as collaborators by the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), the ethnic Albanian guerrilla movement he led.
Three other former KLA commanders were also convicted today – Jakup Krasniqi was sentenced to 25 years, Kadri Veseli to 18 and Rexhep Selimi to 13.
All four were cleared of six counts of crimes against humanity, with judges saying prosecutors had not shown the crimes were part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians.
Prosecutors had asked for 45-year sentences. All four men denied the charges and both sides can appeal.
Clashes on the Malieveld
 Dozens of Thaci supporters had gathered on the Malieveld ahead of the verdict, and the protest turned violent shortly after it was read out.
Demonstrators threw stones, branches and flagpoles at police vans and officers, and several climbed onto a police vehicle, news agency ANP reported. Riot police used tear gas and a water cannon to disperse the crowd.
Thaci served as Kosovo’s prime minister and then president between 2008 and 2020, and helped set up the court while foreign minister in 2015.
He resigned in November 2020 to face the charges and has been in custody since. Tens of thousands of people rallied in Pristina in the days before the verdict, where the four men are widely seen as national heroes. Thaci faces a separate trial on witness intimidation charges later this month.

Drivers urged to be cautious of wildlife on the roads as nights draw in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:37:00 UTC
22:37:00 KST

Drivers urged to be cautious of wildlife on the roads as nights draw in
At a time of year when the shortening daylight hours can make driving more hazardous, road users should exercise due care the Transport Board (Transpordiamet) announced.
Drivers should keep in mind wildlife always has the right of way, the authority added, noting fall is also a time of increased wildlife activity and is mating season for some species,
"During periods of increased activity, situations in which wild animals venture onto roads get more frequent, increasing the risk of collisions between vehicles and wildlife. It is consequently important that we as road users remain especially vigilant and take note of wild animals approaching the road. It is also worth keeping in mind that if one wild animal crosses the road, others may follow," said Villu Lükk, head of the board's environmental management unit.
"Wild animals often have established routes they follow, and many of these traverse roadways, hence it being important to pay heed to heed warning signs and cut speeds when necessary," Lükk went on.
"The autumn mating season of moose and red deer increases the movement of wild animals and so also the risk of them getting on the road and getting involved in collisions. If you spot an animal from a distance, you should slow down, brake smoothly and switch your hazard lights on. You should not sound the car horn or try to maneuver around the animal. When startled, a wild animal may behave unpredictably, including turning back across the road to return the way it came," noted Urmas Salmu, project manager of the national hunting society's "Wildlife on Roads" project.
Last year, the Emergency Response Center registered 3,212 reports related to wildlife accidents, a fall on the 3,779 cases reported in 2024.
Road users in Estonia are also warned about stretches of road with a particularly high risk of wildlife by moose warning signs, which drivers should heed and take into account when traveling through the areas they cover. These signs are installed in places where traffic accidents involving wild animals have been known to happen in the past, or where animals have been observed entering the road more frequently.
Since local hunting associations re responsible for removing injured and dead large game animals from roads and therefore know the problem areas well, warning signs are often installed in locations at their proposal-
Starting this week, the Transport Administration has also begun displaying LED-tupe warnings (pictured) after dark on variable-message information boards in areas where wild animals frequently cross roads.
A detailed heat map showing wildlife accident locations is available here.
Another map layer showing large game animals killed on roads last year, as recorded by hunters, is available here. The map provides an overview of the stretches of road with the biggest incidences of accidents involving wildlife.

Ferry runs aground in West Jutland – no injuries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:36:58 UTC
22:36:58 KST

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.
