Blood test shows promise in detecting pancreatic cancer early—a 'Holy Grail' for the field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:34:23 UTC
22:34:23 KST

Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest forms of the disease—because it is so hard to detect, cases are typically caught in the late stages of the disease. A person can live with pancreatic cancer for years and not know because the early symptoms are so subtle as to be absent or negligible. There is no routine screening test, as for breast cancer or colon cancer, and most diagnoses happen only at advanced stages when symptoms such as weight loss, abdominal pain and blood sugar problems become unignorable.
As a result, the five-year survival rate is just 13 percent. A new blood test aims to change that. In results published today in Nature Medicine, scientists show how the blood test, called PAXEON, can accurately detect pancreatic cancer in its early stages, and could even identify precancerous signs, enabling doctors to quickly intervene and treat the disease.
The results come on the heels of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of a drug for pancreatic cancer, called daraxonrasib. The medication is aimed at people with late-stage cancer who have already been through chemotherapy. In a testament to the intractability of this form of cancer, the drug, which is hailed as a breakthrough treatment by experts, improves survival by just half a year compared with chemotherapy alone (13.2 months versus 6.7 months, respectively).
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
About 1,800 people enrolled in an early stage clinical trial to test the efficacy of PAXEON across the U.S., Europe and Asia. The test accurately detected stage 1 and 2 pancreatic cancers approximately 87 percent of the time, with a low rate of false positives. The blood test also identified advanced dysplasia—precancerous conditions in the pancreas—more than 64 percent of the time in people with high-risk pancreatic cysts. Together, the results suggest the test could flag cancer earlier and offer opportunities for clinicians to intervene before the disease has had a chance to spread to other organs.
The blood test screens for three molecular signatures of pancreatic cancer. Researchers then use artificial intelligence to assign a risk score that measures individual risk of cancer. Doctors can use the score to determine whether more investigation or treatment is necessary, particularly in people who have inherited risk of pancreatic cancer or who have had pancreatitis, for example. More advanced clinical trials are needed before this blood test could possibly be used in the clinic, but the results are promising in a disease that is so difficult to manage.
“The earlier we find pancreatic cancer, the greater the chance that meaningful intervention is still possible,” said Ajay Goel, study senior author and chair of Molecular Diagnostics and Experimental Therapeutics at City of Hope, a cancer research and treatment center in California, in a statement.

Russia plans new prison complex in occupied Kherson Oblast among wider prison expansion

Russia plans new prison complex in occupied Kherson Oblast among wider prison expansion
Russian authorities plan to build a new large-scale prison complex in occupied Kherson Oblast as part of a program to construct seven such facilities across Russia and occupied Ukraine by 2035, The Moscow Times reported on Sept. 16, citing a Russian government program.
The new facilities will combine pretrial detention centers with penal colonies of different security levels and will have a combined capacity of more than 20,000 people, according to the The Moscow Times. Of those places, 5,380 are designated for pretrial detainees and 15,120 for prisoners serving sentences.
Apart from occupied Kherson Oblast, Russia plans to build the complexes in Kaluga, Astrakhan, and Tyumen oblasts, Buryatia, and Zabaykalsky Krai, while the first is expected to open in Tatarstan by 2030.
Each facility is expected to cost between 13 billion and 20 billion rubles (around $154 million and $237 million), The Moscow Times reports. Russia's Justice Ministry estimates that concentrating detention centers and penal colonies in the same complexes could reduce the cost of holding prisoners and detainees by 25-30%, allowing the projects to pay for themselves within about a decade.
Russian Justice Minister Konstantin Chuychenko said the facilities would use modern engineering and IT systems, while providing improved working conditions for prison employees and access to work, education, and medical services for inmates.
The new construction plans come as Russia expands its detention infrastructure in occupied Ukrainian territories. A Kyiv Independent investigation found that two new pretrial detention centers in occupied Crimea became part of a system used to unlawfully detain Ukrainian civilians.
Former detainees said civilians were held for months without formal charges, access to lawyers, or contact with their families, and described beatings, electric shocks, denial of medical care, and other abuse. One of the facilities is formally operated by Russia's Federal Penitentiary Service, while the other came under the direct control of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), in March 2026.
Russia has also used occupied Crimea as a hub for detaining civilians seized in occupied Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.
According to estimates by Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, Russia unlawfully holds about 16,000 Ukrainian civilians in about 200 detention sites in Russia and occupied parts of Ukraine. Only a few hundred people have been brought back.

Google agrees biggest carbon-removal deal yet, aims to scale new model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:33:00 UTC
22:33:00 KST

Google agrees biggest carbon-removal deal yet, aims to scale new model
- Google has agreed its largest carbon-removal deal with Terradot for a 200,000ha project in Brazil targeting methane reduction from rice farming and carbon dioxide capture.
- The project aims to generate one million tonnes each of methane-abatement credits by 2030 and carbon-removal credits by 2040, combining both efforts uniquely at scale.
- Terradot plans to expand the model across Brazil and other countries by 2028, with the project offering lower costs though credits remain above the US$100 (S$127) per tonne target price.
AI generated
LONDON – Google has agreed its biggest carbon-removal deal yet, backing a project in Brazil run by developer Terradot that aims to both cut methane emissions from rice farming and capture carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, executives told Reuters.
Spanning more than 200,000ha in the southern state of Rio Grande do Sul, it is the largest enhanced rock-weathering project to date, aiming to accelerate a natural process where certain rocks absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
The initiative, which Google said it hopes will serve as a template for future projects, is the first at such a scale to combine methane abatement and carbon removal, said Randy Spock, the company’s head of carbon removal.
Tackling methane, a ‘super-pollutant’ greenhouse gas that warms the atmosphere more quickly than carbon dioxide, helps slow global warming, but carbon dioxide removal is still needed over time to address centuries of accumulated emissions.
“We need to do both. We do not have the luxury of focusing all of our resources on going after short-lived super-pollutants, or all of our resources purely scaling long-term carbon removal,” Spock said.
The project will generate one million metric tonnes of methane-abatement credits by 2030 and one million tonnes of carbon-removal credits by 2040, generated and verified separately. The carbon-removal portion of the deal is 10 times larger than previous rock-weathering projects.
Rice paddies account for 10-12 per cent of global methane emissions, according to a 2021 assessment by the UN Environment Programme. Accelerating action on methane is expected to be central to the COP31 climate talks in Turkey later in 2026.
Lower costs
Big Tech companies are under pressure to ramp up clean energy and carbon-removal investments to counter emissions from AI-driven data centres. Google is an investor in Terradot, after taking an equity stake in 2024.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has said removal is needed to help hit the world’s climate goals, although critics argue it can allow companies to continue polluting now.
The companies said the model could eventually be expanded across Brazil’s 1.5 million hectares of rice fields and replicated in other rice-growing regions such as India and Vietnam.
Terradot plans to launch pilots across multiple countries in 2026, with commercial scale-up slated for 2028.
Google and Terradot did not disclose the price of the credits, but a publicly disclosed 2024 deal for 90,000 tonnes of carbon removal from Terradot implied a price of roughly US$300 (S$380) a tonne – some way above the US$100 a tonne threshold many developers are targeting to stimulate broader demand.
CEO James Kanoff said the new project would be cheaper than previous deals and, while not yet at US$100 per tonne, represented “a big step toward that”.
Terradot said as verification can add more than US$100 per tonne to enhanced rock-weathering costs, allowing carbon removal to accumulate for longer before third-party verification would help reduce that in the new project. REUTERS

2026-09-16

A massive search operation is under way in and around a Suffolk village for a missing three-year-old boy with autism, supported by hundreds of volunteers.
Suffolk police have said the hunt for Noah Woods remains a missing persons investigation with no indication anything sinister has happened.
Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and partially deaf, went missing after a visit to a play area in the village of Brantham on Tuesday afternoon when he became separated from a relative. Police have said Noah will not respond to his name if called.
In an update on Wednesday, Supt Tom Pearse from Suffolk police said: “This is being treated as a missing person investigation at this stage and there is nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place although we keep an open mind as to the circumstances.”
The force released new CCTV stills and footage of the little boy in the play area in Merriam Close just before he vanished.
It is thought that he ran down an alleyway beside the playground towards a nearby new-build housing estate.
The surrounding area includes woods and a pond and is near the River Stour and a railway.
Noah is white with curly ginger hair and was wearing a white T-shirt featuring the TV character Bluey, shorts, and black Vans trainers with a white stripe.
On Wednesday, volunteers could be seen in hi-vis jackets helping to search the area, with efforts being coordinated from the village hall and a leisure centre.
They are part of a massive search operation led by police, fire, coastguard and search and rescue teams, with sniffer dogs being used and a helicopter flying overhead.
As well as the ground search, officers are looking at CCTV and other available video footage, going door to door and carrying out aerial and thermal imaging searches.
Noah’s father posted on social media asking volunteers to widen their search beyond the village where possible.
He wrote: “I cannot go another night knowing he’s out there alone, please don’t give up on him guys. He is out there somewhere and I appreciate every single one of you.”
In the update from police on Wednesday, Pearse urged volunteers to report to the coordination centre and to avoid the railway and open water, which need specialist searching.
He said: “It has now been around 24 hours since Noah was reported as missing to us and we are doing everything we can to find him.
“We are extremely grateful for the support shown by the public. If you are helping please report into the coordination centre to ensure the search continues to be done in a systematic and coordinated fashion.
“This will ensure we can carefully plan and take account of people supporting the search.
“We politely ask people to avoid open waters and railways – these are areas that require specialist and professional expertise. We also ask that personal drones are not used as these can interfere with specialist search equipment.
“There may also be times when officers may need to restrict access to certain areas or move away from search locations.
“Please do not be offended if this happens; it is necessary to allow us to carry out our inquiries and search activity as effectively as possible.”
Advice from Brantham parish council to volunteers included: “You are looking for a frightened three-year-old. Think about slight movements in your peripheral [vision], high and low, tiny small spaces use all your senses whilst searching.”
They have been told not to grab or approach Noah if they find him, but instead to call police on 999 immediately and give their exact location using the What3Words app.
Anyone with private CCTV or doorbell cameras in the village, or who was driving through the area with a dashcam is asked to review the footage from 3pm on Tuesday afternoon onwards for any possible sightings of Noah.

‘If you serve the IDF, you're not allowed to come’: Locals push back against influx of Israeli tourists in Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:32:16 UTC
22:32:16 KST

It was a routine evening in mid-August when Samir Shafiq, the owner of a popular gym in Bali, heard an argument break out.
Three foreign tourists were arguing with one of his Indonesian staff members. As the exchange grew more heated, Shafiq heard what he described as foul language.
He approached the men and asked where they were from. They said they were Israeli. He then asked whether they had served in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). One initially denied it, while another acknowledged serving as part of Israel's military service.
Shafiq told them to leave.
"Are you serving in the IDF? ... You guys are not even allowed to be in this country. And be grateful, because I'm not involving the police," Shafiq is heard saying in footage of the confrontation that later went viral.
"You are being rude to my staff, and you're not allowed to be here," he recalled telling them.
Indonesia has no formal diplomatic relations with Israel and has long supported Palestinian statehood. Israeli nationals are subject to Indonesia’s “calling visa” regime, which requires them to obtain a visa before travelling. Dual nationals may in some circumstances travel using another nationality’s passport, but entry requirements depend on the passport and nationality declared to authorities.
Shafiq's interaction with the tourists hs, however, left him with the impression that the men felt "almost untouchable."
The confrontation reflects growing unease in some Asian tourist destinations over Israeli soldiers and veterans arriving after military service, particularly amid Israel's war in Gaza.
Payments received after discharge are also commonly used by young Israelis to fund long trips abroad, making post-military travel a well-established rite of passage. The journey is commonly called Tiul Gadol, meaning “big trip” in Hebrew.
But from Bali to the Philippine surf island of Siargao and India, residents and activists told Anadolu they are increasingly struggling with the presence of visitors who served in a military accused of committing atrocities.
On the small surfing island of Siargao in the Philippines, advocate Rich Tuason said unease among some residents has been growing.
“There is growing sense of restlessness, helplessness and frustration amongst the locals,” Tuason told Anadolu.
But expressing those concerns publicly can itself be difficult, she said.
“We can't too openly express these sentiments because of the fear that they'll be labeled antisemitism,” Tuason said.
For Tuason, the concern is not simply the number of Israeli visitors arriving on the island, but who some of them are and what Siargao is equipped to handle.
Tuason said locals had noticed an increase in visitors linked to the Israeli military, while advocates had identified Hebrew-language websites promoting destinations including the Philippines, Thailand and Bali as retreats for Israeli soldiers after their service.
The island was built around tourism rather than mental health care, she said.
"This is where they try to address their PTSD ... There are no certified psychologists or psychiatrists here in Siargao," she said.
Her concerns extend beyond the island's limited mental health infrastructure.
"They aren't 100% abusive. But when they are abusive, they are very abusive," she said of Israeli visitors, stressing that her concerns did not apply to all of them.
Tuason cited hostile reactions toward residents who expressed support for Palestine, as well as reported incidents involving trespassing, property damage and rented motorcycles that were abandoned or not returned.
“People do try to report them, but it's hard to file cases because the suspects just fly out,” she said.
She also said parts of the island's tourism industry were increasingly catering specifically to Israeli visitors, including events she said excluded Filipinos unless they were working as crew, service workers or venue staff.
She pointed out that such businesses also compete with local providers and suppliers. Tuason also said some Israeli visitors and residents were seeking to establish community structures on the island, including a Chabad Jewish community center.
While small movements opposing its establishment have emerged, Tuason said public protests are generally not well received by the local government.
From Himalayan destinations such as Dharamkot, Kasol, Parvati Valley and Manali to Pushkar, Goa and Hampi in southern India, a network of destinations has become popular with young Israeli backpackers.
The route is informally known as the “Hummus Trail,” a term used by Israeli travelers.
Around 80,000 Israelis visit India annually, according to official tourism figures.
Eitan Gilboa, an Israeli soldier, was vacationing in India’s Himachal Pradesh in early June 2026 when the Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) filed a complaint with Indian authorities seeking his arrest. 
 
The Brussels-based group said that Gilboa had participated in the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza and had recorded and posted some of his activities on social media.
 
Prashant Pundir, a Mumbai-based political activist, told Anadolu that the route is increasingly attracting Israelis.
“A lot of these genocidal maniacs or war criminals develop PTSD and other psychological difficulties after their military service and they look for ways to heal or decompress,” he said.
Pundir said wellness retreats, Ayurveda centers, yoga and meditation had become attractive options for some Israeli travelers.
Over time, he said, an ecosystem catering specifically to Israeli travelers has developed along the route, including cafes, Hebrew-speaking spaces, WhatsApp groups, hotels and Chabad houses, prompting complaints from some residents.
“We've also heard about extremely loud therapy sessions, banging plates and loud music disturbing neighborhoods,” he said.
The unease has also surfaced in Thailand, one of the most popular destinations for Israeli travelers in Asia.
Hundreds of people demonstrated outside the Israeli Embassy in Bangkok recently, calling on foreign visitors to respect the country's laws and culture amid growing public discontent over the behavior of some Israeli tourists.
Organizers accused Israeli tourists of breaking domestic laws, creating public disturbances and showing disrespect for local traditions and cultures.
Specific incidents have also drawn high-level attention.
This month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul ordered the deportation of an Israeli man convicted of threatening a zoo owner on the resort island of Koh Samui after the zoo displayed a Palestinian flag, making him the first foreigner ordered out of Thailand under new rules governing deportation.
The backlash also comes as Israeli arrivals continue to rise.
More than 277,000 Israelis visited Thailand in the first eight months of 2026, up about 7% from the same period a year earlier, according to Thailand's Ministry of Tourism and Sports.
As scrutiny of Israeli travelers has spread across parts of Asia, some of those speaking out have faced repercussions of their own.
In Bali, Shafiq said his confrontation at the gym also brought repercussions.
"They try to frame me as an anti-Semite," he said.
He also began receiving messages and hearing accounts about Israeli-owned businesses and communities across the island.
For Shafiq, however, the issue was not religion or nationality, but military service.
“I don't care if you're Jewish, you're Muslim, you're Hindu, you're atheist,” he said. “But if you serve the IDF, and we all know and have seen these past few years what they did and what they are still doing, yeah, you're not allowed to come. You can call me a racist or whatever, I'm okay with it.”

UN Weighs Moving Ukraine Aid Supplies Underground After Russia Hit 10 Warehouses
The United Nations is considering moving humanitarian supplies into underground bunkers in Ukraine after Russian strikes hit 10 of its warehouses in 2026, destroying millions of dollars’ worth of aid.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on September 15, UN Humanitarian Coordinator in Ukraine Matthias Schmale said the organization is examining underground storage as one way to reduce the exposure of humanitarian supplies to Russian air attacks. The UN is also delaying purchases until closer to the time when the goods are needed.
One of the World Health Organization’s main warehouses containing medical supplies was struck earlier in September, while other attacks destroyed hygiene kits and school supplies intended for children, Schmale told Reuters.
“These deliberate attacks on warehousing capacities (…) is a new trend of the last few months,” Schmale said.
The additional security measures and replacement of destroyed supplies are also increasing the cost of humanitarian operations in Ukraine. Schmale said those expenses had not been included in the UN’s $2.3 billion humanitarian aid budget for 2026.
“This feels increasingly like the front line is moving into the air,” he told Reuters. “That means extra cost also to the taxpayers, who at the end of the day pay for the goods that the U.N. and other humanitarians bring in.”
Reuters reported that the UN is also investing in additional equipment to protect its personnel, including armored vehicles and drone-detection systems. The organization is separately considering requests from Ukrainian authorities for mobile shelters designed to protect civilians from drones in public areas, including near bus stops.
Previously, on August 23, a Russian drone attack struck a Ukrainian Red Cross warehouse in Kherson, destroying or damaging humanitarian supplies worth about $626,000. The facility stored medical supplies, blankets, hygiene kits, and equipment intended to help communities prepare for winter and respond to Russian attacks.

Suspects in Overasselt raid held in custody for another 90 days
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A court has ordered 14 people who were arrested in the aftermath of a shooting in a village near Arnhem to be kept in custody for another 90 days while inquiries continue.
Police arrested 35 people after a group of armed men descended on Overasselt in the early hours of September 1 and opened fire on a farmhouse, killing a 51-year-old guard and seriously injuring two police officers.
The suspects, who had various nationalities including French, Belgian and Algerian, were caught hiding in fields or as they tried to flee by car or train.
Military police later recovered weapons that had been abandoned at the scene, including one location near a primary school.
More suspects are due to appear in court on Wednesday and Thursday, when a judge will be asked to extend their detention. The group is accused of murder or attempted murder of the guard and attempted murder of the police officers.
It is suspected the attack was part of a feud over cocaine dealing linked with the man living in the farmhouse, Jan G., who has been targeted in the past.
Local mayor Joerie Minses has ordered G. to stay out of the village for the next three months.

The Soprano: A magical evening of opera with acclaimed Greek singer Christina Poulitsi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:30:50 UTC
22:30:50 KST

For many years, Christina Poulitsi has turned heads in the world of opera, stunning audiences with her incredible performances, but a chance to perform at The Chios Festival was also a unique chance for the soprano to pay tribute to the legendary Greek singer Maria Callas.
Christina Poulitsi, the internationally acclaimed Greek soprano, who has appeared at iconic opera houses around the world, was a special guest performer at this year's The Chios Festival, organised by the North Aegean Region.
Together with distinguished pianist Dimitris Giakas she gave a concert at the impressive Castelli mansion in Kampos at Chios. The opera evening revolved around famous arias once sung by Maria Callas as well as the documentary by the Greek National Opera"Mary, Marianna, Maria: The unknown Greek years of Callas". (source in Greek)
Maria Callas and me
A native of Chios herself, Christina Poulitsihas a deep affection for her island and its people. This year marked her third appearance at the event. She studied in Germany, where she also took her first professional steps.
When Euronews met Poulitsi she was keen to talk about paying tribute to the legendary American-born Greek opera singer Maria Callas and her own journey in opera:"First of all, as Greeks we are extremely proud that Maria Callas, a giant of classical music and opera, is Greek. I believe she inspires all of us through her performances, not only musically but also through the energy she brings to her arias."
"Unfortunately I never had the chance to see her live, but even through her recordings you can grasp how unique she was. Whenever I sing arias, and especially Italian bel canto, I always go back to her and draw inspiration from her interpretations. I see her as a pillar, a light that opens up a distinct and different path for each of us."
Poulitsi has performed on all the major opera stages, winning the love and adulation of audiences around the world and, along the way, has won several prestigious awards.
"My international career started in Germany, because I studied there and took my first steps there. I have sung in almost all of Germany's major opera houses, and then went on to perform across Europe, America, Asia and Oceania. It is a great joy to discover different worlds, to work with conductors and theatres with whom you are compatible and with whom you can make music at the highest level."
"I was fortunate to have Zubin Mehta as my mentor, a legend in the world of opera. He was the one who wrote a letter of recommendation for me and essentially launched my career. He wanted to keep track of my progress while I was still a student and, when he felt I had reached the right level, he offered me our first collaboration, as Gilda in Florence with him. One thing led to another after that. We gave a great many concerts together. I was invited several times to Israel, to Tel Aviv, and it was there that I met Gianandrea Noseda."
"I have a great love for Germany, because it is the country where I first made a name for myself and began my career. But of course I also have a profound love for Greece. It is my country. I really enjoy singing here. I have a very special relationship with the Greek audience and I love coming back again and again. Today, thanks to this concert, I feel deeply moved to be singing in my home place, because I come from Chios."
What is it that attracts her to venues that are not conventionally associated with opera? How does she feel about singing on smaller stages?
"This is the third year I have sung at The Chios Festival, organised by the North Aegean Region. They are doing a really excellent job. It is a week packed with lectures, documentaries, performances and events that cover a huge range of fields such as medicine, history, art, you name it. I really enjoy singing in spaces that are not strictly linked to the usual concert and recital halls. I love performing in nature. Of course the conditions are very demanding, no question, but the energy is always different."
"These places win you over and give you a completely new sensation. Here we are in a Genoese medieval tower in Kampos, Chios, where all the traditional features are preserved: the orchards, the architecture, the unique building style, the waterwheel well. Here in this magnificent garden, with Chios' fragrant mandarins and lemons, the feeling is unique. It gives you inspiration to carry on into the future."
A mother of two young children, the Greek soprano is trying to strike a balance between family life and the demands of the international career she has built over the years. At the moment she is trying to spend more time in Greece with her children and to avoid large-scale opera productions. Her schedule for the new season is packed:
"Right after Chios we start rehearsals for a new Greek opera to be staged in Athens, called 'Theodora, Empress of Byzantium'. It is the new work by Theodoros Stathis, directed by Panos Angelopoulos. The emblematic figure from Byzantine history will come to life on the stage of the Municipal Music Theatre Olympia 'Maria Callas' on 30 September and 1 October.
"After that I have a recital in Athens again, at Parnassos Hall. Then we go with Plácido Domingo to Malaysia. In December I will appear at the Athens Concert Hall and give two solo recitals at the Athens Conservatoire. Then there is another recital with Plácido Domingo. This is followed by a recital with the American tenor John Osborn in Thessaloniki. I am really looking forward to it, because we have worked together before and we have great chemistry. And I finish the season with a recital in Switzerland."
This year marked the fifth edition of The Chios Festival, which ran for ten days. The festival's rich programme once again left a strong mark on the island. It included performances, concerts, screenings, talks, exhibitions, side events and tribute evenings. Leading figures from science, culture, the arts, history and shipping attended the event, which is held under the auspices of the UNESCO Hellenic National Commission and the American-Hellenic Chamber of Commerce.
The festival's artistic director, Dimitra Moutzouri, tells Euronews: "We have managed to create a multi-faceted festival. I think the word 'festival' does not quite do it justice. It is a blend of conference, artistic events and exhibitions. What we are trying to do is to showcase the cultural identity of Chios, to promote artists from the island and, at the same time and above all, to bring leading figures to Chios."
"We want to make the island a cultural focal point for Greece every September. And we believe that, to some extent, we have achieved this. It is a festival that evolves step by step, year after year. We do not set specific targets; we simply try to improve every year. We will continue in the same way in the years to come, always aiming for what is best for Chios and its people."

How Kazakhstan is reshaping its trade beyond commodities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:30:34 UTC
22:30:34 KST

Kazakhstan is turning its reliance on imported processed goods into an opportunity for investors to build local enterprises, substitute imports and expand the country’s export basket.
The Central Asian nation accounts for around 2% of global oil supply and is also a major supplier of natural uranium and chromium. It is now seeking to diversify its exports beyond raw commodities.
The government sees part of the solution in attracting investors to tap into rising domestic consumption, with projects aimed at substituting imports and expanding the country’s export potential.
According to QazTrade, Kazakhstan recorded a trade surplus of over €7.5 billion, with trade turnover reaching nearly €62 billion.
China remained Kazakhstan's largest trading partner in the first half of the year, followed by Russia and Italy. Turkey, France, Uzbekistan, the Netherlands, Germany, the United States and South Korea completed the top ten.
Imports accounted for nearly 44% of total trade turnover in the first half of the year, rising 5.4% year on year.
Imports reached €27 billion, driven by demand for natural gas, power-generation equipment, railway locomotives, gold, enriched uranium, petroleum products and machinery.
According to the country’s trade agency, the industries best positioned for import substitution include machinery, pharmaceuticals, advanced processing of agricultural products and construction.
“Localising production and implementing investment projects in Kazakhstan can help meet domestic demand while also serving growing demand in neighbouring Central Asia and Eurasian Economic Union,” said QazTrade Deputy General Director Nurlan Kulbatyrov.
He noted that Kazakhstan’s economy grew 4.1% in the first half of the year, with manufacturing among the main drivers of growth.
The biggest shifts driving trade
One of the biggest shifts is taking place in the commodity export base. Oil exports fell by 3.3%, gas plunged by 60.4%, and petroleum products dropped by 51.7%. Together, the decline points to weaker momentum in parts of the commodity sector that has traditionally generated much of Kazakhstan’s trade surplus.
Another shift is geographical. Exports to Turkey rose by 94%, to France by more than 45%, and to Uzbekistan by nearly 40%, while exports to Italy, Kazakhstan’s largest buyer after China, fell by roughly 15%.
Italy accounts for more than 17% of Kazakhstan’s total exports, but barely features among the main destinations for processed goods, suggesting that its demand remains heavily concentrated on oil.
While trade with some major partners remains heavily reliant on commodities, diversification is taking place in newer, less prominent destinations such as Turkey, the UK, where exports grew 2.5 times, and Singapore, where they rose 2.9 times.
Move towards processed exports
Crude oil remained Kazakhstan’s largest export, accounting for 46.5% of the total, followed by copper and copper products, uranium, ferroalloys and wheat.
Although energy and metals continue to dominate Kazakhstan’s export basket, non-resource exports are gradually gaining ground.
Exports of processed goods grew nearly 18% year on year in the first half of 2026. However, Kazakhstan continues to rely heavily on imports of finished products, creating opportunities to expand domestic production.
Animal feed shipments surged nearly 80% to €378 million, while sunflower oil exports rose almost 57% to €460 million.
The rise of Kazakhstan’s oilseed sector
Kazakhstan has the largest agricultural land area in Central Asia and natural and climatic conditions well suited to growing oilseed crops.
It is already a major global supplier of sunflower oil and among the EU’s top three suppliers of sunflower meal.
The country now aims to increase exports of fats and oils to €1.3 billion by 2028, around 60% above current levels.
The National Oilseed Processors Association attributes the sector’s rapid growth to government support, a strong raw-material base, Kazakhstan’s geographical position and the development of export logistics.
“We’re also seeing accelerated diversification towards oilseed crops. For example, sunflower has seen the largest increase in planted area, growing 2.3 times over the past five years”, said Chairman Yadykar Ibragimov.
The potential goes further, with sunflower cultivation capable of expanding to more than four million hectares across the country.
Attracting investment for import-substitution
Over the past four years, Kazakhstan has signed 62 investment agreements worth around €32 billion. These can provide up to 25 years of legislative stability for projects worth around €52 million.
In 2025, Kazakhstan signed a further 173 investment contracts worth around €2.6 billion. Qualifying projects may benefit from tax incentives, exemptions from import customs duties on equipment and components, and in-kind state grants.
Foreign investment also increased. In 2025, gross foreign direct investment inflows amounted to nearly €18 billion, up 14.4% year on year.
With trade ties to some major partners still heavily reliant on commodities, Kazakhstan is looking to attract foreign investment into import substitution and domestic production, reducing its reliance on imported goods while broadening its export base.

How Israel’s backer Robert Kraft derailed Ed Sheeran's tour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:30:16 UTC
22:30:16 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israel's billionaire backer Robert Kraft derailed Ed Sheeran’s tour
Billionaire New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft has come under renewed scrutiny after confirming that he pressured Ed Sheeran over rapper Macklemore’s participation in his US tour following the artist’s outspoken support for Palestine.
Kraft owns Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, one of the venues where Macklemore was due to perform as an opening act for Sheeran’s tour.
Macklemore said Sheeran told him that Kraft had intervened to stop him performing at the stadium and had pushed other venue owners to take similar action.
Kraft confirmed that he had intervened, arguing that allowing Macklemore to perform at his stadium would cross a line because of what he described as the rapper’s “broader history of anti-Semitic rhetoric and imagery”.
Macklemore was subsequently removed from the remaining US dates of Sheeran’s tour, turning a dispute over one performer into a wider debate over Palestine, political expression and the influence of wealthy pro-Israel figures over major cultural spaces.
So who is Robert Kraft, what role did he play in Macklemore’s removal, and why has the episode drawn such intense scrutiny?
Who is Robert Kraft?
Robert Kraft is a Jewish-American billionaire, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, and one of the most prominent American supporters of Israel.
Forbes estimates his wealth at more than $13 billion. He has donated millions of dollars to Jewish and Israeli causes, including more than $20 million to the “Stand Up to Jewish Hate” campaign.
Kraft’s support for Israel has also brought him close to the country’s political establishment. He received the $1 million Genesis Prize in 2019 for his contributions to the Jewish community and humanity.
At the award ceremony, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said: “Israel does not have a more loyal friend than Robert Kraft.”
Kraft has long been outspoken about his connection to Israel, saying in 2019: “After my family, there is nothing I’m more passionate about than the State of Israel and my Jewish identity.”
Kraft has also used his influence in American sport and celebrity circles to promote ties with Israel, including taking prominent American football figures such as Tom Brady to visit the country.
What happened to Macklemore?
The row began after Macklemore appeared as an opening act at one of Sheeran’s US shows at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium earlier this month.
During his set, the rapper delivered an outspoken message of support for Palestinians, saying: “I say free Palestine. I say free Lebanon. Free Cuba to the Congo to Sudan to Iran.”
He also performed Hind’s Hall, his song dedicated to Hind Rajab, the five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces after becoming stranded inside a car in Gaza.
Macklemore also directly addressed Jewish members of the audience, saying: “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid and opposition to genocide are in no way criticism of you. This is a message of peace and love, and of treating all human beings with dignity and equality.”
He later defended his comments, saying that “wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial”.
His appearance quickly attracted backlash from pro-Israel groups, including the Israeli-American Council, which launched a petition calling for him to be removed from Sheeran’s tour.
What did Robert Kraft do?
Macklemore subsequently said Sheeran told him that Kraft had personally intervened.
In an Instagram post, Macklemore wrote: “Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium.”
He also said that Kraft had approached other stadium owners and that they collectively warned Sheeran that they would not host his shows if Macklemore remained on the tour.
Kraft did not publicly address that wider claim.
He did, however, confirm that he had pressured Sheeran over Macklemore’s appearance at Gillette Stadium.
Kraft defended his intervention by saying: “This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf.”
He argued that such advocacy should not come at the "expense" of the Jewish community or “obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.
The result was that Macklemore was dropped from the remaining US dates of Sheeran’s tour.
The distinction over who formally made the final decision, however, has done little to diminish scrutiny of Kraft’s role.
As the owner of one of the venues involved, Kraft used his position to pressure an artist’s participation after Macklemore had publicly backed Palestinian rights.
Why does Kraft’s role matter?
The controversy has put a spotlight on the power that wealthy pro-Israel donors and political advocates can exert beyond traditional political arenas.
Kraft is not simply an individual supporter of Israel. He is a billionaire who owns a major US sports venue and has extensive influence in American sporting, political and cultural circles.
His intervention over Macklemore has therefore raised questions about what happens when an artist uses a major commercial platform to speak about Israel and Palestine.
The latest episode also forms part of a broader pattern in which outspoken support for Palestinian rights can face institutional and commercial consequences, particularly in the US.
Kraft has previously taken action over pro-Palestinian activism. In 2024, amid student protests and encampments calling for an end to Israel’s war in Gaza and for universities to divest from companies linked to Israel, Kraft suspended his financial support for Columbia University.
At the time, he said he was “no longer confident that Columbia can protect its students and staff”.
The move reflected Kraft’s broader willingness to use his financial and institutional influence in response to activism surrounding Israel.
How did artists respond?
Four supporting acts on Sheeran’s tour, including Aaron Rowe, Beoga, Lukas Graham and Finneas, as well as members of the main band, announced their departure from the tour following Macklemore’s removal.
Their decision added another layer to the fallout, showing that attempts to pressure artists over their stance on Palestine can also provoke resistance from within the music industry.
The episode has therefore exposed both the power wealthy figures can wield over major cultural platforms and the limits of that influence when other artists choose to stand with those being pushed out.
It also revealed how attempts to silence artists over Palestine can end up drawing more attention to the very issues they are speaking about.

Dilara Hamit
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
A Paris court has awarded Kim Kardashian a symbolic €1 in damages for a 2016 armed robbery in which she was restrained at gunpoint and robbed of jewelry worth millions of euros.
Her friend and stylist Simone Harouche, who was present at the residence when the robbery occurred, was also awarded €1.
“Today’s decision is not about the compensation, but about accountability and recognition,” they said in a statement provided to People magazine.
They thanked the French justice system and those who supported them during the case, adding that they hoped to continue recovering from the trauma.
The robbery took place in October 2016 while Kardashian was staying at the Hotel de Pourtales during Paris Fashion Week.
A group of men, some posing as police officers, entered the building during the early hours of the morning. Kardashian was held at gunpoint, bound with plastic ties and tape and placed in a bathroom while the assailants searched the residence.
The group escaped with jewelry worth millions of euros, including an engagement ring her then-husband, rapper Kanye West, gave her. Most of the stolen jewelry was never recovered.
French authorities arrested 17 suspects during the investigation, and 10 people eventually stood trial in Paris in 2025.
Kardashian traveled to the French capital to testify, telling the court that she had feared she would be sexually assaulted and killed during the robbery.
Seven men and one woman were convicted in May 2025 of offenses connected to the heist. Those convicted included Aomar Ait Khedache, identified by investigators as the organizer of the robbery.
The defendants became known in the French media as “les papys braqueurs,” or the “grandpa robbers,” because several were in their 60s and 70s when the case reached trial.
The civil judgment on Tuesday came nearly a decade after the robbery and determined the damages to be paid to Kardashian and others affected by the crime.

Syzran and Saratov Oil Refineries Halt Operations After Drone Attacks, Sources Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:28:12 UTC
22:28:12 KST

Two Rosneft-owned oil refineries in the cities of Syzran and Saratov have suspended processing following Ukrainian drone attacks over the past week, three industry sources told Reuters on Wednesday.
The sources said the Syzran plant paused operations on Tuesday, while the Saratov refinery halted work last Friday. Both facilities have repeatedly come under attack since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
At the Syzran refinery, sources said the main CDU-6 crude distillation unit was damaged in a drone strike. The unit, which accounts for 71% of the plant's processing capacity, could take at least a month to repair, they added.
The refinery's second crude distillation unit, accounting for the other 29% of production capacity, was already undergoing maintenance after an attack in July.
Sources said the Saratov refinery has been shut down for several weeks following earlier strikes and was on the verge of restarting operations when it was attacked late last week.
Both refineries have a combined processing capacity of 290,000 barrels of oil per day.
Ukraine has been carrying out a far-reaching drone strike campaign against Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure since the spring, saying its goal is to raise the costs of the war for the Kremlin.
The near-nightly attacks have led to nationwide fuel shortages since June, prompting authorities to introduce rationing measures in some parts of Russia and across annexed Crimea.
U.S. President Donald Trump has recently blamed Ukraine's strikes for the surging cost of diesel across the globe and called on both Moscow and Kyiv to halt their attacks on energy infrastructure. However, neither side of the conflict has indicated that it's ready to agree to Trump's ceasefire request.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Iran: Activists sound alarm as regime seizes Baha'i assets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:28:00 UTC
22:28:00 KST

Iran: Activists sound alarm as regime seizes Baha'i assets
September 16, 2026
As Washington attempts to intensify economic pressure on Iran, ordinary Iranians face mounting financial distress.
Rights groups say Iranian authorities are increasingly using asset seizures against religious minorities, dissidents and government critics, adding a new layer of economic pressure for people already struggling with soaring living costs.
Members of Iran's Baha'i religious minority seem to be bearing the brunt of the crackdown.
The faith, which originated in 19th-century Persia — now Iran — is not officially recognized by the Islamic Republic. Unlike Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, Baha'is are not protected under Article 13 of Iran's constitution, leaving them vulnerable to longstanding discrimination and persecution.
Baha'is portrayed as 'spies' for Israel
The US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRANA) reported "a wave of arrests, searches of homes and businesses, and seizures of property belonging to Baha'i citizens" at the end of August.
Amnesty International said persecution of the Baha'i community has intensified since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, citing what it described as "a coordinated state campaign of incitement to hostility, violence, discrimination and disinformation falsely accusing Baha'is as spies and collaborators for Israel."
"Under current conditions, all people in Iran are facing economic hardship and extremely difficult living conditions, barely putting food on the table for their families," says Padideh Sabeti, spokesperson for the International Baha'i Community.
However, Baha'is suffer even more from the country's economic situation, "as the government's discriminatory practices deprive them of the ability to earn a living," she added.
Sabeti adds that the judiciary uses poverty as leverage, demanding exorbitant bail "which is sometimes equivalent to a hundred years' wages for an average citizen."
Regime goes after prominent critics
The apparatus of repression does not only target religious minorities. The government has announced judiciary orders identifying and seizing assets belonging to over 400 individuals living abroad who authorities described as "supporters of the enemy," including actors, athletes, and overseas journalists.
Domestically, Sadegh Saedinia, manager of the "Saedinia" chain of cafes, received a 12-year prison sentence, a two-year operating ban, and total asset confiscation for posting content related to anti-government protests in Qom, a conservative city considered sacred to Shiites.
The growing number of confiscations has led some observers to ask whether property seizures are also aimed at filling state coffers at a time of economic strain.
The economics of confiscation
Arezoo Karimi, a London-based economic analyst, says the financial impact is likely to be limited. The resources gained through seizures are "very, very insignificant" compared with Iran's massive budget deficit, she said.
According to Karimi, confiscated properties are often auctioned off below market value to individuals with political connections.
Sajjad Khodakarami, a Paris-based journalist, says targeting diaspora dissidents sends a clear psychological warning.
"This tool — which the Islamic Republic previously tested on a segment of society — is now being deployed on a broader scale against its opponents," Khodakarami said.
"Today, this instrument of repression targets not only parts of the Baha'i community, but also various strata of society, including journalists, social and human rights activists, and artists who oppose the ruling political establishment," he added.
"When the Islamic Republic targets the assets of hundreds of people, it sends them a message: Even when you are beyond our physical reach, we will continue to apply pressure on you from all sides."
Toys and wedding rings seized by law enforcement
International human rights monitors reported security forces taking gold, electronics, work tools, wedding rings, and children's toys during recent home raids.
Khodakarami views the confiscation of everyday household items as a dark indicator of the regime's trajectory.
"When government agents stoop so low as to confiscate a couple's wedding rings or a child's toys, it is a sign of barbarism," said Khodakarami. "Moreover, this behavior is not merely a message to the Baha'i community, but a broader warning to all dissidents."
Khodakarami argues that the government is placing a growing share of the economic burden on ordinary citizens rather than on powerful state institutions.
"As the regime's resources shrink, it tightens the screw on the people's livelihoods," Khodakarami said.
Can Iran avoid hyperinflation?
According to Karimi, the government is relying on money printing and subsidy rollbacks to compensate for declining foreign currency revenues. The analyst warns that current fiscal policies risk pushing the country into galloping inflation.
"On one hand, banks are creating money, while on the other, production is effectively paralyzed," said Karimi.
"If we continue down this path at the current pace, I foresee a day when hyperinflation hits Iran — a day when people pay one fare to commute to work in the morning, but have to pay up to double that for the ride back home, just like what we witnessed in Venezuela and Zimbabwe."
While seizing personal assets may serve as a tool of intimidation and generate limited funds for the security apparatus, analysts say it cannot fix Iran's underlying economic problems and is unlikely to ease the financial pressures facing ordinary Iranians.

All of Europe Is Now Threatened by Russia’s Actions

Minister Pollard highlighting the importance of collaboration between government, industry and private finance, to strengthen the capabilities of the British Army and boost economic growth.
Good afternoon. It’s nice not doing a speech in a suit, I have to say, and actually be able to get out there and get some mud going on, which is, I think, one of the great benefits of this event here. So good afternoon.

Now, that model and that funding is vital if we’re going to deliver the Recce Strike model that has been set out so clearly by CGS. That’s built around better targeting, better battlefield surveillance and more lethal long range fire, an increase in lethality of our British forces, to give us a generational upgrade in the abilities of the British Army. That’s not only about long range fire, but if you took long range fire as the example of the upgrades over the next four years, we’re investing £190 million in short range ballistic missiles, £400 million in inexpensive one-way attack drones and weapons, and £220 million in Project Nyx to build an advanced armed autonomous drones to fly alongside our Apache helicopters.
That’s about improving the lethality and delivering against CGS’s 20:40:40 strategy, which has been baked into the Defence Investment Plan. Now, that will be collectively a higher resolution picture of the battlefield and increase the effectiveness and speed of our targeting.

Now enabling our forward land force to fuse existing capabilities such as armoured vehicles with drones and other new capabilities, is vital to deliver that new type of deterrence that we need in the 21st century.

Getting more bang for our buck literally in increasing lethality, but certainly value for money as well, and delivering more for our armed forces.

And in a more dangerous and unpredictable world, they will give the soldiers of our British Army a clearer picture of the battlefield and greater lethality on it.
Now, the government’s guiding mantra are backing UK firms pays us back four times over: in military strength, in industrial strength, in economic growth and in public support for defence. It takes us closer to achieving our objectives of doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027, tripling it by 2030 and growing it tenfold by 2035. That’s not just the government’s story. That’s your story as well. And across the British Army, procurement, and industry, it’s one that if we tell, well, we’ll deliver not only added effect but greater support for defence spending.
Now, for my part, this Autumn I’ll be working hard to stimulate more sources of investment in defence. The Defence Finance and Investment Strategy will be published just after the budget this year. It will talk to how we crowd in private capital, into core defence and into our supply chain, how we use that private capital, both from venture, sovereign and other forms to support our R&D, support our bringing products to market, grow and stabilize SMEs, especially in the Valley of Death, as they go up through the TRL levels for their products.
And it will help deliver via the new Defence Investment Unit that we’ve established in the MOD, something that will get more of that private capital to where it matters. Now for small businesses, growing businesses, start-ups, and the success of the Defence Tech Unicorn Fund, where the MOD has invested a small amount of money helping grow businesses, we have now more defence tech unicorns in Britain than anywhere else across Europe. This is a success story we need to talk about and that will help us build towards the Defence Investment Summit, which will take place in early December, where will be an opportunity for financial institutions and our partners to announce their own investments in defence, both in core defence, the investable opportunities that the MOD is providing for commercial partners to invest in the systems that we use and the products that we use, but also to support our defence supply chain again.
And to each of you in industry, I want to challenge you ahead of that, to tell the story about why defence is a great place to work, why it is a great place to invest, and in particular, why establishing a defence business or growing a defence business in Britain is right, not just to access that growing defence budget here, to provide a market to export to our friends as well.
I saw that firsthand at the recent Guildhall event hosted by the Lady Mayoress of the City of London, seeing the work of the Defence Office for Small Business Growth, bringing together small defence companies with investors to be able to marry opportunity and capital to grow and provide more opportunities. But as the world grows darker, it is incumbent on all of us to tell the story, to build the case, to bring forward technology faster, to get rid of stupid rules, to help us reform procurement quicker so we can speed through the contracting process to deliver capabilities. And if we do that, we can not only attract new investment into defence, but we can show our people, our allies and the defence sector that this is an area of our economy worthy of investment, worthy of attention and worthy of good careers that keep us safe, protect our freedoms and support our way of life.
We have a lot of work to be doing, but I’m really excited to see so much of that work that you are all doing here on showing the vehicles and platforms that we have outside. Let’s keep going. Thank you.

OPINION - No rush for peace: Why a broad peace in Ukraine remains elusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:25:48 UTC
22:25:48 KST

Maksym Skrypchenko
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
- Maksym Skrypchenko is the president of the Transatlantic Dialogue Center, a Ukrainian think tank.
Recent trips to Moscow and Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, preceded by a visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, marked a new attempt by Washington to jumpstart negotiations on ending the Russia-Ukraine war. However, the intensity of diplomatic contacts currently far outweighs their tangible results. The reason lies not so much in the lack of an acceptable peace formula as in the fundamentally different expectations the parties hold concerning the war's continuation: Ukraine seeks ways to stop the destruction, while Russia hopes that, in the coming months, Kyiv will no longer be able to keep resisting.
This divergence can’t be explained by shifts on the battlefield map alone, as there have been almost none. Russian pressure at the front has not secured the kind of victory that would allow Moscow to dictate terms. At the same time, Ukraine lacks the advantage needed to rapidly liberate occupied territories. To call this balance a stalemate would be to underestimate how the nature of the war itself is evolving. What matters most is the ability to destroy the opposing side's economic foundation.
Targeting the economy
Ukrainian strikes on the Russian oil industry are a good example. They are intended to raise the cost of the war to the point where Moscow sees a practical benefit in mutually limiting attacks. Kyiv is open to a wide range of agreements, from protecting Black Sea shipping and grain infrastructure to halting strikes on energy facilities or even a complete mutual cessation of long-range strikes, as this would allow for de-escalation without waiting for the resolution of all political disputes.
The problem is that Moscow has so far been unwilling to discuss such arrangements; instead, it links any meaningful move toward a truce to Ukraine’s prior withdrawal from the remaining parts of Donbas under its control. By insisting on the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from the rest of Donbas, which Kyiv believes it will be able to defend at least for a few years, the Kremlin is demanding what Kyiv considers impossible.
Russia’s reluctance to agree to limits on strikes stems from the conviction that time is on Moscow’s side. In private discussions with American counterparts, the Russian side points to Ukraine’s budgetary difficulties and the uncertainty surrounding future European funding. Upcoming elections in Europe are also presented as an additional sign of weakened support for Ukraine in the future. The Kremlin operates on the assumption that while losses in its own oil sector are manageable, the combination of winter-induced destruction and financial constraints will ultimately force Kyiv to give up.
Ukraine is bracing for attacks not only on its power grid but also on its gas infrastructure, preparing for a massive humanitarian crisis. Under these circumstances, the supply of air defense systems and reliable funding not only help Kyiv defend itself but also undermine Moscow’s confidence that Ukrainian resistance will eventually collapse.
Stalled negotiations
Meanwhile, visits by American negotiators have not brought a breakthrough, and Moscow has linked its willingness to take further steps in the talks to the conclusion of the September parliamentary elections. Both Kyiv and Washington understand that the Russians will likely find new grounds for delay thereafter, allowing them to continue the military campaign into the spring.
The American attempts to offer economic incentives in exchange for de-escalation have not yet resolved the fundamental contradiction. Moscow may well be interested in economic benefits without losing its desire to continue the war.
In the absence of conditions for a broad agreement, the upcoming meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his US counterpart Donald Trump during the UN General Assembly could offer the next opportunity to test the prospects for a limited truce. Draft resolutions calling for an end to strikes on grain infrastructure in the Black Sea are already circulating at the UN. Such an agreement would have significance far beyond Ukraine, mitigating risks to the global food supply and allowing the UN to demonstrate its practical utility after years of criticism regarding its ineffectiveness.
For Trump, a Black Sea truce could also serve as a diplomatic achievement ahead of the midterm congressional elections, particularly as the protracted war with Iran continues to consume American resources. For these reasons, he might be interested in spearheading this process and leveraging American influence to ensure the agreement is upheld. Skepticism over UN mechanisms further reinforces Ukraine’s desire for Washington to assume direct political responsibility for the truce's observance. Ukraine’s readiness for a mutual truce leaves sufficient room for an agreement. To capitalize on this, Washington and Europe must use sanctions, incentives, or both to convince the Kremlin that another winter will not deliver the victory it has so far been unable to achieve on the battlefield.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

Iran blocks ‘Bibi’s Kitchen’ Instagram over ‘cutlet’ joke
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:24:51 UTC
22:24:51 KST

Iranian authorities blocked the Instagram account of a Tehran restaurant after it posted a play on words that was interpreted as a political jab at the Islamic Republic.
The restaurant, called “Bibi’s Kitchen,” posted an Instagram story reading, “Nothing beats Bibi’s cutlet,” accompanied by Iranian pop star Moein’s song “Bibi Gol.” Shortly after the post went viral, the account was blocked by judicial order for what authorities described as “publishing criminal content.”
On the surface, the post appeared to be promoting a dish on the restaurant’s menu. But in Iran’s political vocabulary, both words carry a double meaning. “Bibi” is an old-fashioned Persian term for grandmother. But it is also the well-known nickname of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and has appeared in anti-government memes and posts expressing support for Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic.
The term “cutlet,” meanwhile, became a political taunt after Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani was killed in a U.S. drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020, mocking the condition of his body after the attack.
Since then, opponents of the Islamic Republic have used the word to refer mockingly to senior regime figures killed in military strikes. The combination of “Bibi” and “cutlet” was therefore interpreted as a reference to Netanyahu and senior Iranian officials killed by Israel, although the restaurant itself did not explicitly make such a political statement.
Iranian authorities have acted against similar uses of the word before. In January 2023, prominent chef Navab Ebrahimi was arrested after posting a cutlet recipe around the anniversary of Soleimani’s killing. His restaurant was shut and his Instagram account was taken offline. Contemporary reports said social media users believed the cutlet post was connected to his arrest, although authorities did not publicly establish that as the reason.
In January 2024, doctor and university professor Mohammad Shoja was detained in the northeastern city of Bojnourd after posting a photograph of a cutlet on the night senior IRGC commander Razi Mousavi was killed.
In June 2024, the Iranian judiciary opened a case against playwright and theater director Hossein Pakdel for allegedly “disrupting the psychological security of society” after he wrote on Instagram that politics turns “stupid men into special diet cutlets.”
Sensitivity surrounding references to Israel has intensified amid the current conflict. Iranian authorities said in March that more than 1,000 people had been arrested on accusations including sharing anti-government material online or cooperating with Israel and the United States. The judiciary has also warned that some forms of assistance to hostile states can carry the death penalty.

IN BRIEF: What is known about incident with Russian warship, Danish Air Force helicopter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:23:11 UTC
22:23:11 KST

MOSCOW, September 16. /TASS/. On September 14, the Russian Navy Baltic Fleet’s corvette Soobrazitelny fired two red signal flares toward a Danish Air Force helicopter to prevent an incident, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has compiled the main information available so far.
Statement by Russia’s Defense Ministry
- On September 14 at 2:22 p.m. [Moscow time] (11:22 a.m. GMT), the Baltic Fleet’s Soobrazitelny corvette was conducting operations in neutral waters in the southwestern part of the Baltic Sea when it detected an aerial target, which it identified as a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
- The helicopter was heading toward the Russian warship and did not respond to calls on the international communication channel, the ministry stated.
- The Defense Ministry explained that the corvette commander decided to fire two red signal flares as a precautionary measure. After this, the helicopter left the area where the Russian warship was located.
- Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov awarded the Medal ‘For Military Distinction’ to the commander of the Soobrazitelny corvette for his skillful and decisive actions in preventing a provocation by the Danish Air Force helicopter, the ministry reported.
Russian ambassador summoned to Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs
- On September 15, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen announced that the Russian ambassador had been summoned to the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, allegedly due to the incident involving the Danish helicopter.
- The Danish Ministry of Defense protested about the Russian ship firing flares in international waters toward the Danish Air Force helicopter.
Comment by Russian Ambassador to Denmark
- Attempts by the Danish authorities to explain the provocative actions of the Danish Air Force helicopter toward the Russian ship as "routine practice" raise serious concerns about the possible consequences of such recklessness, Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin said, commenting on the incident.
- He noted that the Russian side will carefully examine all the circumstances of the incident.
- The statement emphasized that this is not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have performed dangerous maneuvers near Russian military ships navigating on the high seas and outside Denmark’s territorial waters.

The Letby inquiry report makes one thing crystal clear: too much NHS management is scandalously poor | Tom Dolphin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:21:10 UTC
22:21:10 KST

The publication of the Thirlwall inquiry report is above all a moment to remember the babies who died or were harmed at the Countess of Chester hospital and the families whose grief was compounded by years of delay, institutional denial and defensiveness. The least we owe those families is a determination to now make the right changes – not the comfortable ones, not the partial ones, but the ones that will stop further avoidable deaths and injury.
Lady Justice Thirlwall’s report lays bare a total failure of NHS management. When doctors dared to raise concerns, they were rebuked and threatened with referral to the General Medical Council (GMC), which could have ended their career. The report describes a kind of “toxic negativity” all too familiar in the health service: a desperate culture of cover-up and denial that prizes saving face over saving lives.
Whistleblowers deserve respect, not ridicule or rejection. It takes courage to speak out against those in power, and the BMA has supported many such courageous doctors. They include Dr Susan Gilby, who at the very same Countess of Chester hospital refused to stay quiet about the failures she saw around her. She was punished with a shocking campaign of repression from management that resulted in her being awarded £1.4m in damages earlier this year. If it wasn’t clear before, Thirlwall has thrown into stark relief the plight of whistleblowers, and most importantly the patients whose lives and health are at risk.
But the real legacy of the inquiry may go even deeper, to the heart of how we think about regulation in the NHS. It is well known that doctors and nurses serve under our professional regulators, the GMC and the Nursing and Midwifery Council. We can be investigated, sanctioned, suspended or struck off if our conduct falls below expected standards. That is as it should be. Regulation protects patients, gives the public confidence and makes clear that authority in healthcare must always come with accountability.
What few know is that non-medical managers – those in charge of a hospital’s essential systems, such as its staffing, buildings, equipment and finances – do not face that accountability. Indeed, non-medical managers are the only safety-critical group in the NHS that does not have a regulator. It seems utterly backwards that some of the most powerful people in the health service face so little oversight, and it is not hard to draw a line between that and the abuses of power that led to the situation at the Countess of Chester and all the tragedy that followed. I am very glad, therefore, to see that Thirlwall has addressed this head-on, making the clear recommendation that it should be possible to strike off these managers just like any other NHS professional.
She has also recommended that the UK government seriously consider creating a statutory regulator for non-medical managers, which the BMA believes is long overdue. Their regulation shouldn’t be crammed in with that of the dozen or so other professions – physiotherapists, dieticians, radiographers to name a few – supervised by the already overloaded Health and Care Professions Council. They need and deserve an expert, dedicated statutory regulator that can give a clear, enforceable set of standards.
The BMA doesn’t just want non-medical managers to fear negative consequences for bad behaviour; we want them to have high standards so more of them can aspire to excellence. The culture of the NHS should be one where we welcome staff and patients raising concerns about failings, with adequate resources for fixing problems, so well-regulated managers can actually improve things rather than shooting the messenger.
That day still looks dangerously far off, though. Despite a Labour manifesto commitment, the inquiry sees these regulatory changes taking until 2032. In the meantime, we do not know how many more examples of poor or dangerous practice will be suppressed and ignored by managers who remain beyond the reach of accountability.
This must not be a commitment left to fall by the wayside in the aftermath of a general election. Work by government to create a statutory regulator must begin now, and by the end of this parliament, the families of those affected should have confidence that any institutional cover-ups will be tackled. For our patients and colleagues – and ultimately in the interests of managers, too – doctors are going to push for these changes to be implemented faster. Accountability matters.
- 
  Dr Tom Dolphin is a consultant anaesthetist in London, and chair of council at the BMA
