Egypt uncovers ancient fortress offering glimpse into military, daily life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
20:51:34 CST
21:51:34 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- An Egyptian archaeological mission has uncovered important structures and artifacts at the Tell Abqain archaeological site in the northwestern Beheira province, shedding light on military and daily life in ancient Egyptian fortresses, the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said Wednesday.
Excavations uncovered a large mudbrick residential complex with a planned street network linked to the fortress's southern entrance, the ministry said in a statement. It contained grain silos, pottery ovens, and storage rooms, including large jars with charred wheat grains.
Residential rooms were also found near three previously discovered stone wells bearing the titles of King Ramses II, the statement read.
A notable find was the complete burial of a young male horse, likely used for military training or pulling war chariots, it said. Alabaster and limestone pieces were also found, believed to have formed part of a chariot harness, providing further evidence of the site's military role.
The discoveries highlight the strategic importance of Tell Abqain, one of a series of military fortresses built along the western edge of the Nile Delta during the New Kingdom (1550-1069 BC) to protect Egypt from attacks by Libyan tribes, it added. ■

Israel's illegal E1 settlement push unacceptable: EU Commission chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:51:31 UTC
21:51:31 KST

The European Commission president has condemned Israel's decision to advance the illegal E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank, telling European lawmakers the move is unacceptable and that a divided Europe is failing to influence events on the ground.
"The Israeli government's decision to advance the illegal E1 settlement project is unacceptable," Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday in an address to the European Parliament, referring to the planned illegal settlement east of occupied East Jerusalem.
The E1 plan, long frozen under international pressure, would extend illegal settlement construction across the corridor linking the northern and southern West Bank, a step Palestinian officials and rights groups say would make a contiguous Palestinian state impossible.
Von der Leyen said the suffering in Gaza and the violence in the occupied West Bank had deeply affected Europeans, and recalled that she had previously urged the bloc to take measures in response to developments in the region. Member states, she said, had been unable to assemble the majorities needed for a unified response.
"When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events," she said.
She added that Europe supports what she called Israel's right to "self-defence", while stressing that Palestinians hold an equal right to live in safety and dignity.
"It is Europe's role to keep the flame of the two-state solution alive," she said.
Israel has built more than 250 illegal settlements across the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem since 1967, housing hundreds of thousands of illegal settlers. All are considered unlawful under international law, a position reaffirmed by the International Court of Justice.
New security architecture
The bulk of von der Leyen's address focused on European security, where she called for the creation of a new "European Security Council" and an EU-wide emergency protocol obliging all member states to convene when a security incident is triggered.
She said Europe's security institutions and decision-making mechanisms had not kept pace with a shifting threat environment, pointing to the continuing war in Ukraine and a rise in alleged Russian hybrid attacks against European countries.
The bloc needs "its own counter-hybrid playbook", she said, calling for agreement on how to respond to incidents that fall below the threshold of armed aggression but still threaten national security.
"I believe it is time for Europe's own Article 4, an emergency security protocol," she said, invoking the NATO charter clause under which allies meet when any member believes its security is at risk.
Any member state could trigger a meeting of all EU countries to coordinate a response, she said, adding that the mechanism would complement rather than replace NATO cooperation.
She said she would bring forward proposals for the European Security Council, a format that would also include Canada, Ukraine, the UK and Norway.
Borders and enlargement
Turning to migration, von der Leyen referred to Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, where thousands of people crossed the border from late July, saying that while such episodes differ in nature, they share common elements.
She accused traffickers and smugglers of exploiting vulnerable people and said European adversaries were also involved in exploiting such movements. The Commission has proposed sanctions targeting those networks, she said.
Europe needs the means to protect its external borders, she added, particularly when mass movements are "engineered and weaponised".
Von der Leyen announced plans for a new European emergency response instrument, to be activated only under a strictly defined set of criteria, allowing time-limited flexibility in standard procedures in such circumstances.
She also said respect for the bloc's values remains "non-negotiable", citing a recent incident in Serbia.
"I was horrified by the pictures from (Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko) Mladic's funeral in Belgrade last week. He committed the most atrocious crimes against humanity," she said.
"Glorifying war criminals simply has no place in the European Union," she added.

Lazzari and Mohamedi: When two artists search for the same silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:49:59 UTC
21:49:59 KST

Installation view In-Rhythm, Bice Lazzari and Nasreen Mohamedi at KNMA Saket
Picture two works hanging side by side. For a moment, forget the labels. The lines are so deftly controlled, the spaces so carefully constructed, that it is easy to imagine they came from the same hand. But the artists are separated by continents, generations and circumstances. They never met, never knew of each other, and as far as records show, never encountered each other's work. But now they share a gallery in Delhi, in a conversation neither artist could have seen coming.'In Rhythm: Bice Lazzari and Nasreen Mohamedi', presented by KNMA in partnership with the Italian Embassy Cultural Centre and the Archivio Bice Lazzari, places the Italian painter Lazzari, known for her minimalist abstraction, in dialogue with the Indian artist Mohamedi, whose work carries a similar stunning subtlety. The exhibition delivers a compelling lesson in brevity, in the discipline of discarding the unnecessary.Lazzari (1900–1981) and Mohamedi (1937–1990) came from different artistic worlds, but both carved out singular places in the history of modern art. Lazzari, regarded as one of the founding figures of Italian postwar abstraction, moved from painting, murals and applied design to the spare, linear language of her late acrylics, created against monochrome grounds.
Her work has since been the subject of major retrospectives in Washington, London and Rome, and is often discussed alongside that of artists such as Agnes Martin. Mohamedi occupies a comparably important place in Indian modernism. Trained in London and Paris before returning to India, she taught for years at the Faculty of Fine Arts in Baroda, developing a radical minimalism and an almost poetic engagement with the grid that had few precedents in Indian art. But the exhibition does not argue that one artist influenced the other; instead, it examines the resonance between two independent paths toward abstraction.
BICE LAZZARI Courtesy_ Archivo
The show is curated by Andrea Anastasio, director of the Italian Cultural Institute in New Delhi, and Roobina Karode, artistic director and chief curator at KNMA. Anastasio was drawn to the idea of pairing the two artists after encountering Mohamedi's work at a KNMA retrospective in 2012-13.Rather than proceeding chronologically, the show opens with each artist's late, most reduced work. "We decided to start with the end of their lives, when they achieved the essence of their practice," Anastasio says. "For both of them, lines, rhythm, space have a very important role to play. They are in a continuous dialogue," he says. Lazzari’s early work was far removed from the spare lines and grids of her later practice. The exhibition traces her beginnings through objects, textiles and paintings shaped by Futurism and domestic materials. Mohamedi’s own trajectory was different. Her early work encompassed colour, collage, watercolour and figuration. Gradually, colour receded as line, geometry, space and interval took over.The word "subtracting" recurs throughout Anastasio's account of both artists. "Towards the end of their lives, in subtracting and subtracting, they come across very interesting... not similarities, but reverberations of each other's work," he says.The physical circumstances of their later years add another layer to the show. In her later years, Mohamedi developed a neurological disorder (Huntington's disease) that caused motor challenges, including tremors in her hands. She then adapted her technique, using precision drafting tools to continue working. Lazzari's own departure from oil paints and tactile mixed-media (like sand and glue) was a direct reaction to physical illness caused by chronic exposure to toxic paint solvents, leading to respiratory and eye issues that forced a complete overhaul of her materials, allowing her canvases more "light, space, rigour, structure, synthesis and a little poetry".Mohamedi's works ask for a different kind of attention. A room devoted to them in the exhibition is conceived almost as a meditation space. Spare lines from her poems unfurl across the walls, asking viewers to stare hard, to think, to find the maximum in the minimum, all of it forming a continuity, like the immense sea. She rarely signed or dated her work and the result is an abstraction that does not ask to be decoded. "The beauty of abstraction is that the artist tries to evoke, in the most subtle way, something that is seen first inwardly, more than outwardly," says Anastasio. That inwardness shapes the exhibition's treatment of space too. The curators build an intimate, almost domestic environment in one section before opening it out toward a larger sense of landscape and horizon.
Nasreen Mohamedi , Photo by _Jyoti Bhatt, Courtesy_ Heirs of Nasreen Mohamedi
There is, finally, a parallel in how the two women came to be recognised. Lazzari was known within artistic circles during her lifetime but did not achieve mainstream recognition. The Guggenheim Foundation had acquired one of her works as early as the 1930s, but wider acknowledgement came much later.
Mohamedi's posthumous recognition followed a similarly delayed arc.The exhibition is, in the end, more than a comparison of two artists who happened to use lines. It asks what happens when two women, working independently and without any direct exchange, arrive at a shared insistence on restraint.'In Rhythm' will be on view at the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, Delhi, till 22 Dec.
Sneha Bhura is an Assistant Editor with The Times of India. She loves exploring stories at the intersection of culture and technology. She is also a published poet and podcaster. Her debut poetry collection 'Velvet Grapes' was released in 2021.

Likud seeks to block initiative to fly Israelis home to vote in election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:48:57 UTC
21:48:57 KST

The Likud party petitioned Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee, on Wednesday, demanding that initiatives aimed at helping Israelis abroad fly home for the election be blocked.
The petition was filed against America-Israel Democracy Coalition, which operates a flight initiative, and the Israeli Camp nonprofit, as well as against the Democrats party. Likud claims there is evidence linking the Democrats' goal of "undermining public support for Likud" with the activities of the other organizations.
According to Likud's petition, filed by attorney Ilan Bombach, AID Coalition's activities constitute election bribery and violate Israel's Political Parties Financing Law. Likud argues that the Fly & Vote initiative is intended to help Israelis abroad for political purposes and that AID Coalition is affiliated with the fringes of Israel's left-wing camp – a claim the organization denies.
The petition argues that even if participants pay for their own flights, they receive other benefits through what Likud says are prohibited means, including group purchasing power, exclusive or early access to flights, coordination services, accommodation and transportation, and assistance with documents.
Likud said it is not seeking to prevent Israelis from voting or to discourage citizens from participating in the election, but rather "to distinguish between general civic activity and organized, funded and targeted election activity."
The party accused the initiative of exerting "unfair influence on participation in the election" and warned that it could "seriously undermine the integrity of the election and the equality and fairness of the electoral process."
AID Coalition said in response that Likud is seeking to prevent Israelis from voting.
"We have received Likud's petition, which seeks to deny those who boarded planes to fight on October 7, who pay taxes and remain involved in the life of their homeland, the right and obligation to take part in determining the future of the State of Israel," the organization said. "We will study the petition and respond accordingly."
Earlier this month, responding to a warning letter Likud sent ahead of the petition, AID Coalition said it operates "completely independently of any party framework" and provides bureaucratic assistance to Israelis seeking to return to the country, rather than financial assistance.
Attorney Omri Segev, who signed the organization's response, also said the project is open to every Israeli citizen abroad, including those intending to vote for Likud.
The organization said its Fly & Vote initiative provides bureaucratic assistance to Israelis seeking to return to vote, including checking their voting eligibility and helping with passport renewals and other documents. It also offers logistical assistance with flight routes, arrival dates and group travel arrangements.

Four years after Mahsa Amini's death, rights groups warn Tehran's crackdown persists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:47:25 UTC
21:47:25 KST

Human rights groups said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus, as Kurdish businesses shuttered across her home region and the UN Special Rapporteur said four years of state violence had failed to extinguish the resistance.
Four years after the death of Mahsa Amini in Iranian police custody, Kurdish businesses across her home region staged a general strike on Wednesday while international human rights organisations warned that those responsible for crushing the 2022 protests remain in power and continue to use the same methods.
Shopkeepers and businesses in Saqqez, Sanandaj, Mahabad, Marivan, Baneh and Bokan shut their doors following a call by Kurdish political coalitions. Video circulating on social media showed empty bazaars across the region.
Amnesty International, in a report marking the fourth anniversary, said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (Malta/EPP) said on X that the Parliament would continue to support young Iranians facing execution or imprisonment, singling out the case of twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, sentenced by Tehran's Revolutionary Court after recent protests.
The European Parliament "will keep their light shining until it breaks through the darkness.", Metsola wrote on X.
UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Iran Mai Sato said that four years of brutal state violence — including lethal force deployed during nationwide protests in late 2025 and early 2026 — have failed to extinguish the resistance.
"Four years on, the resistance Jina’s death gave rise to has not been extinguished," Sato said in a statement on X.
"The women and girls who took to the streets in her name still insist on the right to decide what they wear, where they work and how they live... Those rights will not stay deniable forever."
Sato also noted that despite the Law on Protecting the Family through the Promotion of the Culture of Chastity and Hijab being formally suspended since December 2024, cafes, restaurants and shops have continued to be closed for hijab violations, with arrests reported in some cases.
What happened to Mahsa Amini?
Amini, 22, was detained by Tehran's morality police on 13 September 2022 over compulsory hijab rules and died three days later after being brutally beaten in custody.
The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran concluded she had been subjected to physical violence in custody and that Iranian authorities were responsible for her death. Iranian officials rejected the findings and denied she had been physically assaulted.
Protests spread nationwide in the days after her death. While compulsory hijab and women's rights were central, the movement drew together demands for political freedoms, minority rights, economic justice and changes to the political system.
The UN fact-finding mission documented up to 551 deaths across 26 provinces, including at least 49 women and 68 children, and said some violations — including killings, torture, rape and sexual violence — reached the threshold of crimes against humanity.
Tehran acknowledged detaining more than 22,000 people, according to Amnesty International, which also documented enforced disappearances, unfair trials and death sentences.
Tehran pivots to hi-tech
Compulsory hijab remains law, the political structure is intact, and many participants in the protests are in prison, in exile or under sentence.
The regime has shifted enforcement away from morality-police patrols toward cameras, facial recognition, drones and digital tools. Iran's police announced in 2023 that public cameras would be used to identify women not wearing hijab.
The UN fact-finding mission's 2025 report cited facial recognition being used to monitor students' dress at the entrance to Amirkabir University in Tehran.
A 2025 study published in the journal Iranian Studies at the University of Cambridge described the movement as producing a "cultural revolution" alongside a political one, arguing it weakened the state's ideological hold over public and cultural life.
For instance, images of morality police vans detaining women on the streets were among the most potent symbols of the 2022 protests, prompting Tehran to avoid public confrontation methods.
The growing presence of women without headscarves in public spaces and the central place women's rights and freedoms take in political debate show that the situation has not reverted to where it stood before September 2022 — a direct result of the movement's actions.

GFEAI 2026: science minister warns AI potential to become an invisible dictatorship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:40:51 UTC
21:40:51 KST

GFEAI 2026: science minister warns AI potential to become an invisible dictatorship
TEHRAN – Science, Research and Technology Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf has warned that the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in data analysis could pave the way for a shift from data control to human control, potentially giving rise to what he described as “an invisible dictatorship.”
Simaei-Sarraf made the remarks while addressing the 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (GFEAI 2026), held in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from September 14 to 17, IRNA reported.
 
 Leading an Iranian delegation to the forum, the minister stressed the need to give serious consideration to the ethical implications of emerging technologies.
“Technology is not neutral, and artificial intelligence does not operate fairly on its own. Sometimes, algorithms destroy more than they build, and platforms become sources of harm rather than development,” he said.
Enhanced transparency and oversight of governments and those in power are essential. However, when the surveillance is directed at ordinary citizens, tracking their behavior, relationships, and intentions, it can turn into an invisible dictatorship, he added.
Referring to the ethical responsibility of AI platforms and developers, the science minister said, “Today, data is being used in ways that violate human rights and even lead to the death of children, thereby raising a significant question: do AI platforms accept the responsibility for how their technologies are used?”
Numerous chatbots refuse to answer questions about suicide—and rightly so—yet AI can be employed to identify and precisely target human beings with missiles, as the elementary school in Minab was targeted by US missiles, killing 168 students while they were studying.
According to Simaei-Sarraf, inequality is another fundamental challenge of the AI era. Unequal knowledge and capabilities have always created disparities. AI can widen the gap more than any other technology. Hence, the ethical framework should not be merely limited to preventing harm, but to ensuring equal access.
Developing countries should have the opportunity to develop their own AI systems tailored to their languages and cultures, and international organizations are ethically responsible to help these nations realize this goal. Technology must serve humanity, and AI should enhance human freedom, not limit it, he further noted.
In response to a question about the country’s most important measure to strengthen Iran’s capacity in responsible AI, Simaei-Sarraf said if this question was raised before June 2025, he would have definitely said targeted and sustainable investment in water and energy sectors, followed by strengthening collaborations within Iran’s AI ecosystem.
Regarding the shift in regional priorities, the science minister went on to say that “today, I think the removal of coercive measures and the establishment of peace in the region are the top priorities for Iran as well as the whole region. These sanctions are unethical, and establishing security and peace is a moral imperative.”
The Global Forum serves as a key platform to advance the implementation of the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence across all Member States of UNESCO. It supports the exchange of knowledge and experiences across regions in the development of AI policies, regulatory frameworks, and institutional capacities, to foster inclusive and sustainable social and economic development while safeguarding human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Launched in 2022, the Global Forum was previously hosted by the Czech Republic, Slovenia, and Thailand, with co-funding support from the European Union since 2024.
The 2026 edition of Global Forum aims to create an engaging environment with high-level ethical reflection, bridging discussions on governance with technological innovation. The science minister is scheduled to attend specialized meetings, panel discussions, and hold meetings with representatives of other countries.
Co-hosted by UNESCO and Saudi Arabia, represented by the Saudi Data and AI Authority and the International Centre for AI Research and Ethics, the event has brought together global leaders, policymakers, experts, and stakeholders to strengthen dialogue and promote practical and sustainable approaches to the ethics and governance of AI.

The signatories included leaders who have been mentioned as possible Merz successors, such as North Rhine-Westphalia’s Hendrik Wüst. Markus Söder, the Bavarian premier and an ambitious conservative populist, has also said he was backing Merz.
It remains to be seen how long the demonstration of solidarity with Merz will hold, with much depending on the outcome of the weekend elections. Polls indicate voters are very likely to punish the CDU again in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on the Baltic coast, amid widespread dissatisfaction with Merz’s federal coalition government formed with the Social Democrats.
Merz, who is also the CDU’s chair, will convene a meeting of its leadership on Sunday evening to coordinate a response as the results come in, in what senior party members called a pre-emptive “show of unity” behind the chancellor.
The anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin AfD’s resounding win in Saxony-Anhalt sent a shockwave through Europe’s largest economy and beyond, although the party fell just short of the absolute majority required to govern alone in the state.
It is seeking enough support from other parties’ lawmakers in the state parliament to make its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, the first far-right regional leader in Germany since the Nazi period.
Merz took office in May 2025 promising to cut the surging AfD back down to size by reviving the moribund economy and addressing fears around “irregular” migration.
Instead, the AfD is now topping the national polls with clear momentum behind it. The party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel, has targeted the CDU for “destruction” and pledged last week in parliament that Merz’s party would “never win another election again”.
During the same debate in the Bundestag, a wan and defensive Merz lashed out at Weidel and the AfD’s lawmakers, accusing them of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with their calls for “remigration”, a legally dubious programme of mass deportations. Critics said he failed to outline a clear vision for the remainder of his term.
Weidel, whose party drew congratulations from Donald Trump and Elon Musk for its Saxony-Anhalt victory, on Wednesday taunted the state leaders backing Merz.
“The CDU is making it clear that it is committed to ‘business as usual’ rather than the positive changes that citizens need,” she posted on Musk’s social media platform X. “The only way to achieve those changes is with the AfD!”
The month’s developments have triggered a sense of helplessness and fear among the mainstream democratic parties, with even the opposition Green party calling on the CDU to right the ship before it is too late.
“Get your shit together,” said the Greens co-leader Felix Banaszak in Berlin, appealing to Merz and the CDU to end speculation that he called destabilising.
Banaszak said that while he was no fan of the centre-right-led government, he warned that calls for a Kanzlertausch, a swap of the chancellor from Merz in favour of another Christian Democrat, could trigger new elections in which the AfD could come out on top.
“We live in such dramatic times that this country just can’t afford that right now,” he said.
The next general election is due in 2029.

Heleriin Paeoja: How teachers really spend their working hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

Heleriin Paeoja: How teachers really spend their working hours
The Ministry of Education plans a study to determine teachers' tasks and the time required for them, with a planned cost of €70,000. Teacher Heleriin Paeoja wrote down how her working time was spent over the course of one week.
The Ministry of Education is organizing a study to identify teachers' work tasks and the time they require, and to develop recommendations for keeping teachers' workload within the legally mandated working hours. The study is planned to cost €70,000.
I looked up a completely ordinary September week from my diary from my first year at a new school. I wrote down what I did on those days and how much time it took.
Here is my teacher working‑time study. Completely free.
Monday
I arrive at school at 8:30 to print worksheets, start up the computer and smartboard, and move the tables and chairs so students can sit in groups of four.
Class begins at 9. We start with review, because I still do not know what the students know and what they do not. It is my first year at this school.
I quickly realize that the students have forgotten quite a lot or have not fully mastered some topics from last year. Already during the lesson I am mentally reorganizing the lessons for the next few days. I also notice that the students are very closed off and do not want to talk much. In a language class, that is a serious problem. I need to figure out what activities and tasks will get them talking more.
I'm grabbing lunch with a coworker during our break. She tells me how difficult things are for her right now and that she is even thinking about leaving the school. I try to help her as much as I can. I share my materials and presentations, give advice on how to handle certain students, and try to reassure her that things get a bit easier with time. At the same time, I know exactly what she means. For first-time teachers, the heavy workload can quickly become overwhelming, driving the workweek up to 60 hours.
During the break some students come to me. They want to talk about last week's work and get more detailed feedback.
Classes end at 14:40. I stay at school to fill in Stuudium. For each group, I must write in detail what we did in class, what we learned, and what vocabulary we covered. I add worksheets and links, homework, and check absences and tardiness.
This is not documentation for its own sake. It makes the learning process traceable, the information can be used by a new teacher if needed, and absent students can study independently at home.
At 15:30 I shut down the computer. I have been at work for seven hours and have not even started preparing the next day's lessons.
I go home and collapse on the couch. I've used up all my words for today. I feel like I have nothing left to give. But at home I have a two‑year‑old who also wants my attention. I cook. I take the child outside.
Around 20:00 I open the computer again. Tuesday will be especially tough, with classes back‑to‑back from 9 to 16. Of course I have materials and ideas from previous years, but a new school means new textbooks and new students. Since today's lessons showed that students do not understand even basic phrases needed in a language class like "Please repeat" or "What does that mean?", I create a worksheet for them.
I think about how to get students to talk about themselves and help me get to know them better. I come up with an assignment: each student creates an "instruction manual" about themselves. I look at my slides. They are so boring and plain white. I want something nicer and more Spanish‑themed. I search online for slide templates. I finally find one. Then I notice that the pictures in the 10th‑grade presentation are wrong. They do not match the new textbook. I look for new ones. I cannot get everything perfect, but it is 22:15 and I cannot do any more.
Today's working time: about 9 hours and 15 minutes.
Tuesday
A brutal day. I arrive at school at 8:15 to review a few things in the presentations and print worksheets. I teach straight through until 16:00. I cannot really rest during breaks, because I try to quickly fill in Stuudium and enter all the necessary information.
When the last class ends, I am honestly completely exhausted. A squeezed‑out lemon. I have spent the entire day explaining, talking, listening, and answering questions. At 16:10 I sit in the teachers' room and stare at the wall. I cannot move. I cannot even go home. My brain feels like it has shut down. My head hurts terribly and I take Ibumetin.
By that point I have already worked a little over eight hours, but I still have not started preparing the next day's lessons or dealing with other ongoing tasks. I finally go home. It is 17:00.
I do household chores and at 19:00 I open the computer again. I check Stuudium and then remember that in October I need to hold parent-teacher conferences. I need to arrange suitable times with the parents of 17 students. I am not going to write to each parent individually. I come up with a system: I create available times in a calendar and each parent can choose what suits them. I start creating the calendar but do not finish.
Next, tomorrow's lessons. I want to do something interesting. Maybe a video or a song? But which one? Does it use vocabulary relevant to the lesson? Is the language level appropriate? Is the content suitable for a school class? I ask ChatGPT. I get a bunch of options. I start reviewing them. One does not fit the level, another does not fit the content. Time passes. I give up on finding a video and start reviewing my older materials to find something I can use tomorrow. At 21:30 I shut down the computer. I cannot do anything more.
Today's working time: over 10 hours.
Wednesday
Today my first class starts only at 10:20. I arrive at school at 9:30 to print materials and review the lesson presentations once more. Classes end at 16:00. Then another half hour of Stuudium. Meanwhile, I get an email looking for teachers willing to monitor weekly school-wide make-up tests. Oh dear. I cannot take that on right now. I will not do any more work at home today. I have no classes on Thursday or Friday and I want at least one work‑free evening.
Today's working time: 7 hours.
Thursday
A day without classes. Sounds almost like a "day off." It is not. From 9 to 12 there are two meetings. After the meetings I go to a café to work. First I need to finish the registration calendar for parent-teacher conferences. It takes much more time than I expected.
I need to check when I am available, when students do not have classes, and at the same time I do not want to schedule all parent-teacher conferences in the evenings after the workday. I manage to place most of the times on Thursdays and Fridays. I do not have contact lessons on those days. Then I start grading assignments. I add individual feedback for each student in Stuudium.
In between, a student writes asking whether I would be willing to supervise their research project. Fine. But what exactly does that mean in a new school? What are the requirements? What do I need to do as a supervisor? I add another item to my mental list: look it up later. When I check the time again, it is 14:30. That is enough for today.
Today's working time: about 5.5 hours.
Friday
A day without classes. Today I do not even have to go to school. But Stuudium still needs subject information, grading guidelines, course descriptions, and objectives entered. I have to deal with that. In September, when teaching a new group for the first time, it is quite difficult to predict where we will end up by the end of the school year and how quickly the group will start learning. I still try to put together an initial plan.
At the same time, I discuss next week's lessons with a colleague during a work call. We exchange ideas, I send her some of my earlier materials, and we try to get everything aligned so that we teach on the same basis and the groups reach roughly the same point. We also discuss a meeting with the Spanish Embassy. They have written to the school and want to collaborate with us.
Then I respond to parents. One parent's registration link for the parent-teacher conference does not work. Another registered a time but realized it does not actually fit. A third wants to have the conversation online and needs a separate link.
Then absent students write, saying they have not been able to give their presentations. When could they make them up? I check the calendar. Probably during breaks. Then I write to students who have not added their parents to Stuudium, because a minor must have at least one parent's contact listed. And without noticing, four hours have passed.
Today's working time: 4 hours.
Saturday
In the evening I still open the computer. I have two students whose Spanish level is noticeably higher than the rest of the group. Regular assignments are too easy for them and they need differentiated instruction. Fortunately, we talked at school about what is difficult for them and what they want to practice more. Based on that, I look for separate materials for them.
I remember that one set of quizzes is still ungraded. I think I will finish them today so I have less work tomorrow. I grade the assignments and write feedback for each student in Stuudium.
Today's working time: 3.5 hours.
Sunday
I start preparing next week's lessons, but then remember that in spring there will be a language trip to Barcelona. For that, I need a parent questionnaire through which a child can be registered for the trip and the necessary information entered. I create the questionnaire. At the same time, I am again talking with a colleague about Monday's lessons. We go through the activities and conclude that some of them need to be rethought.
I look for materials. Games. Videos. I review my old materials. I adapt. I change. I plan. At one point I check the time. Five hours have passed again.
Today's working time: 5 hours.
Week
Adding everything together, I worked at least 44 hours and 15 minutes this week. Besides, I was on a 0.9 schedule this school year... If a teacher's full-time load is 35 hours a week, a 0.9 load should be 31.5 hours. I put in 13 hours of overtime this week. Who's compensating me for that?
But for me, the total number of hours is not even the most interesting part of this diary. What is more interesting is looking at what those hours were spent on.
This one week included teaching lessons, preparing lessons, creating learning materials, adapting existing materials, printing, preparing the classroom, determining students' prior knowledge, differentiating instruction, grading assignments, giving individual feedback, documenting lessons, marking absences and tardiness, creating course descriptions and grading guidelines, organizing development conversations, communicating with parents and students, supporting a colleague, joint lesson planning, meetings, familiarizing myself with supervising a research project, discussing international cooperation, and planning a language trip.
Some of these tasks are very visible. A teacher stands in front of the class and teaches. A large part, however, is not.
No one sees the computer open on Sunday evening. The half hour spent searching for a suitable video that ends with not finding one. The break when a student wants feedback on their work. The lunch break when you support a colleague. The message to a parent. The new worksheet you make because you realized in the morning's lesson that students are missing something. The two stronger students who need separate materials because otherwise they have nothing to learn in class.
These are small things. Individually, most of them do not take very much time. But teaching consists largely of hundreds of such small things. And that leads me to an interesting line of thought.
The state has described teachers' tasks quite thoroughly in professional standards, qualification requirements, legal acts, and other documents. We know that a teacher must plan instruction, teach, assess, give feedback, take learners' differences into account, collaborate, communicate with parents, support students, develop themselves, and contribute to the school's development.
When is a teacher supposed to do all of this? If a teacher is at school seven to eight hours a day, when does she prepare the next day's lessons? If a day without classes fills up with meetings, grading, documentation, and organizing development conversations, is it really a day without classes or simply a day when the teacher is not standing in front of the class?
If two students need differentiated instruction, does the teacher skip finding suitable materials because her working hours are already full?
If a student wants feedback on their work during a break, does the teacher say, come tomorrow, because this is my rest time?
If a colleague says at lunch that she cannot cope anymore and is thinking about leaving teaching, does the teacher reply, let's talk another time, because this is my lunch break?
If a student asks for supervision for their research project, does the teacher say, "Sorry, my working hours are already full"?
One of the goals of the study commissioned by the Ministry of Education and Research is to find ways to fit teachers' tasks within the legally mandated working hours.
I cannot wait for that answer.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Like people in other G20 countries,
Italians want their economies transformed to address inequality
and the climate crisis, but do not trust their leaders to bring
about the necessary change, according to a new survey by Ipsos
on behalf of the Earth4All initiative.
                                    
                                       
				The report said 73% of Italians agree there is too much economic
inequality in their country, a level that is even higher than
the average of 70% for the 17 countries the survey was conducted
in, and up from 61% in 2024.
                                    
                                       
				It said 61% of people here agree with the assertion that the
economic system is rigged to benefit the rich and powerful, and
68% agree that the economic system needs major changes.
                                    
                                       
				Yet while the mandate for change is overwhelming, the trust in
governments to deliver it has deteriorated.
                                    
                                       
				Only 22% of people in Italy believe their government will make
decisions that benefit the majority of people 20 or 30 years
from now, significantly below the global average of 31%, with
40% disagreeing.
                                    
                                       
				That collapse in trust runs through the wider social fabric.
                                    
                                       
				Overall, 66% of the Italian public agreed that the country is
more divided than it was 10 years ago, which is in line with the
global average of 67%. Only 8% disagreed.
                                    
                                       
				Earth4All, which is working to accelerate the systemic changes
needed for an equitable future on a finite planet, says the
study shows it is time for a new kind of social contract, which
takes the scale of change people are asking for seriously and
offers it through fair and democratic means.
                                    
                                       
				"Just 22% of Italians trust their government to act in the best
interests of the majority of people over the long term," Owen
Gaffney, the Earth4All co-chair and one of the report's authors,
told ANSA.
                                    
                                       
				"The Italian result is substantially below the G20 average of
31% - which is already very low.
                                    
                                       
				"It is clear that greater trust is needed to adequately deal
with long-term challenges like climate change.
                                    
                                       
				"We need to re-invent democracies to rebuild trust".

Russia’s Defense Ministry said Wednesday that Defense Minister Andrei Belousov awarded a ship captain for his “skillful and decisive actions” after firing signal flares at a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea earlier this week.
The captain, who was not identified by name, received Russia’s medal “For Courage” following an incident during which his ship, the Baltic Fleet corvette Soobrazitelny, “prevented a provocation by a Danish helicopter” in international waters by launching two signal flares at the aircraft.
In a statement, Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that the Danish helicopter failed to respond to the Soobrazitelny’s radio calls when it was detected in the southwestern Baltic Sea on Monday. The helicopter left the vicinity of the Russian ship after the flares were fired, it added.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus accused the crew of the Soobrazitelny of making no attempt to contact the helicopter, which he said narrowly avoided the flare signals that were launched in its direction.
Bruus said the helicopter was following its usual route to photograph the corvette as part of a routine operation that it has done several times before.
Russia has “increased their willingness to take risks in terms of how far they are prepared to go,” Bruus said in comments to Reuters.
Russia’s Ambassador to Copenhagen Vladimir Barbin, who was summoned over the incident, in turn accused Danish military aircraft of “dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships,” creating the risk of collision. Barbin claimed Denmark has rejected Moscow’s proposals to sign a maritime and airspace agreement that could help prevent future incidents.
Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen blamed Russia for seeking to “sow fear and discord” over Monday’s close encounter, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it part of “a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe.”
The Danish straits are the main sea route in and out of the Baltic Sea for commercial and military shipping. They are also a major artery for global oil shipments, including from Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of oil tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.
Reuters contributed reporting.

French former minister on trial over alleged Renault-Nissan lobbying
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

French former minister on trial over alleged Renault-Nissan lobbying
- Published
French former minister Rachida Dati has gone on trial in Paris for corruption, accused of taking money from Renault-Nissan in return for political influence.
Dati, 61, who was justice minister under former President Nicolas Sarkozy and culture minister under Emmanuel Macron, is known to have been paid €900,000 (£770,000) by the car giant between 2009 and 2013.
According to a contract signed in 2009, shortly after she ceased being a minister under Sarkozy and was elected as a member of the European Parliament, the payment was for legal services performed for the company.
But magistrates argue the contract was used to disguise payments for lobbying work. Dati denies the allegations.
Magistrates believe Renault-Nissan's former CEO Carlos Ghosn recruited Dati to lobby on the company's behalf in the European Parliament, and to facilitate contacts with Sarkozy who was head of state until 2012.
Ghosn, 72, is also standing trial and denies any wrongdoing. He will be absent from court, having been a fugitive in Lebanon since 2019.
Dati's lawyers will contest the charges, which if substantiated carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in jail, a large fine, and a five-year ban on holding public office.
This could mean her being forced to surrender the mayorship of the wealthy 7th district of Paris, which she has held since 2008.
Dati returned to national politics in 2024 as culture minister but resigned in February to launch a bid to be mayor of the city of Paris.
She was beaten by the Socialist Emmanuel Grégoire after a campaign in which her forthcoming trial was used as an argument against her.
Anti-corruption groups acting as civil plaintiffs in the trial say stricter legal limits need to be established on political lobbying in France.
"The affair illustrates the risks of public decision-making being captured by private interests," said Patrick Lefas of Transparency International France.

Malaysian embassy in Tehran marks 69th National Day and Malaysia Day 2026 with diaspora
TEHRAN— The Embassy of Malaysia in Tehran hosted a celebration at its premises on Wednesday, September 16, to mark the 69th National Day and Malaysia Day 2026 with the Malaysian diaspora in Iran.
The gathering brought together members of the Malaysian community in Iran to celebrate Malaysia’s national milestones and the strong bonds shared with Malaysians abroad.
The event featured an address by Dato’ Wan Aznainizam Yusri, Chargé d’Affaires of the Embassy of Malaysia in Tehran.
Following is the text of his speech:
My respected and dear fellow Malaysians, Honourable guests, colleagues at the Embassy, and distinguished guests.
Assalamualaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakatuh,
Good day, and Salam Malaysia MADANI.
First and foremost, let us express our gratitude to Allah SWT, for by His grace and permission, we are able to gather here in Tehran, thousands of miles away from our homeland, to commemorate a historic occasion for our country, the 69th National Day and Malaysia Day 2026.
Although we are far away from home, our patriotic spirit and love for our homeland have never faded. Your presence here at the Embassy of Malaysia today is strong testimony that the spirit of independence and the Malaysian identity remain alive and strong, wherever we may be.
Distinguished guests,
Living abroad, amid the cool winds of Tehran, longing for home sometimes touches the heart. We miss the aroma of nasi lemak in the morning, the lively sound of our local dialects, and the peace and tranquillity of Malaysia. Yet, behind that sense of longing lies another feeling that continues to inspire us — the pride of being Malaysian.
Today, I stand before you not only with pride as the Head of Malaysia’s Diplomatic Mission in Iran, but also with a deep sense of gratitude at seeing the unity among us. For the Malaysian diaspora in Iran, Merdeka and Malaysia Day carry a very special meaning. All of you are the “Face of Malaysia” here.
On this occasion, I wish to express my highest appreciation and deepest gratitude to the entire Malaysian diaspora in Iran — our professionals, expatriates, homemakers and students. You are our “Little Ambassadors”, carrying Malaysian courtesy, our strong work ethic and our cultural harmony onto the international stage. Thank you for continuing to uphold the good name of our country, looking after one another’s welfare, and serving as a strong bridge of friendship between Malaysia and Iran. The resilience of our community here is a true reflection of the spirit of “Kesejahteraan Dinikmati” — Prosperity Enjoyed by All.
My respected and dear fellow Malaysians,
The theme of this year’s celebration, “Malaysia MADANI: Kesejahteraan Dinikmati”, carries a profound message. It reflects the Government’s commitment to ensuring that the country’s prosperity and the benefits of development do not remain merely figures on paper, but are genuinely felt and translated into better lives for every segment of society including all of you, the Malaysian diaspora abroad.
As we reflect on our history, let us also look back at our larger home, Malaysia. Throughout 2026, under the stewardship of the MADANI Government, our country has built a highly sustainable and encouraging economic landscape. Despite strong global economic headwinds, the Malaysia MADANI journey continues steadily, supported by tangible structural reforms:
• Our Economy is Growing Strongly: In the second quarter of 2026, Malaysia recorded Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of 6.0%. This remarkable expansion attracted the attention of global economic analysts and was driven by the strength of the domestic and export sectors.
• World-Class Competitiveness: Through strategic investment in artificial intelligence and semiconductor technologies, Malaysia’s global competitiveness rose to 15th place in the world in 2026. We are no longer merely followers, but are becoming trendsetters in global technology.
• Inflation Brought Under Control: The Government successfully maintained inflation at around 1.8% to 1.9%, helping to safeguard the people’s basic needs and keep the cost of living stable.
• Moving Towards Developed-Nation Status: The latest World Bank report confirms that, with the momentum achieved in 2026, Malaysia now stands on the threshold of being recognised as a developed nation.
These statistics are not merely dry figures on paper. They tell the story of the hard work, sacrifices and determination of the Malaysian people to see our country rise with strength and confidence.
Dear Malaysians in Iran,
What do Merdeka and Malaysia Day mean to all of us who are living abroad? Here in Tehran, the meaning of independence goes beyond simply flying the Jalur Gemilang or singing Negaraku.
As members of the Malaysian diaspora, all of you are Malaysia’s “Little Ambassadors”. Every action, your professionalism, work ethic and personal conduct here in Iran reflect the image, dignity and values of an independent nation called Malaysia. For the diaspora, independence means having the ability to stand on equal footing with the international community, contribute your expertise, and at the same time never forget your roots and national identity.
Malaysia Day, meanwhile, reminds us of the importance of unity in diversity. Although we come from different backgrounds, ethnic groups, religions and political
views, when we are abroad, we share one common identity — we are Malaysians. Therefore, let us make the Malaysian diaspora community in Iran one large family that supports one another, remains united, and continues to protect the good name of our homeland.
On behalf of myself and my colleagues at the Embassy of Malaysia in Tehran, we will remain committed to strengthening bilateral relations between Malaysia and the Islamic Republic of Iran, particularly by exploring new post-pandemic opportunities in trade, culture and education. We will also remain committed to providing the best possible consular services, particularly to all Malaysians residing throughout Iran.
Distinguished guests,
As we enjoy the Malaysian dishes that will be served shortly, let us loosen our samping, put on a smile, and strengthen the bonds of friendship and fellowship among us. Let this Embassy be your second home — a place where the Malaysian part of your heart can find comfort from the longing for home.
In closing, I wish to record my highest appreciation to the entire organising committee and everyone who has contributed to the success of today’s event. To all Malaysians in Iran, I wish you a Happy 69th National Day and a Happy Malaysia Day 2026!
May Allah SWT continue to protect Malaysia in peace, bless our diaspora in Iran with good health, and fill our hearts with enduring love and affection.
Wabillahi Taufiq Wal Hidayah, Wassalamualaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakatuh.
Merdeka! Merdeka! Merdeka!
Please enjoy the occasion, and thank you.

Israel's right wing seeks to ban Palestinian parties, candidates from Knesset elections
Israel's far right is seeking to prevent Arab political parties and candidates from standing in next month's Knesset elections, reviving a long-running battle over the political participation of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Disqualification motions have been filed against Ra'am, the Joint List and Balad, as well as individual candidates including MK Ofer Cassif and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh.
The challenges come ahead of Israel's 27 October election and will be heard by the Central Elections Committee later this month.
The official election records show that motions were filed against Ra'am by Likud, Otzma Yehudit and the Choosing Life–Forum of Bereaved Families group.
Likud has also targeted the Joint List and Cassif, while Otzma Yehudit has filed motions against Abu Shehadeh and Balad has been targeted by Orot HaShachar.
The latest moves have once again raised questions over the limits of political participation in a state that defines itself as both Jewish and "democratic".
Under Israel's election law, parties and candidates can be barred from standing if their positions or actions are considered to reject Israel's status as a Jewish and democratic state, promote racism or support armed action against Israel.
Adalah, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, argued that these grounds are broad enough to have been used against Palestinian political positions in previous elections.
In several prominent cases, the Central Elections Committee approved bans that were later overturned by the Supreme Court. In 2003, for example, the court overturned the disqualification of Balad and MK Azmi Bishara.
In 2022, the Central Elections Committee again voted to disqualify Balad, but the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the decision and allowed the party to run.
Adalah, which has represented Arab parties and candidates in disqualification proceedings for more than two decades, says the repeated attempts to exclude them expose a fundamental contradiction in Israel's claims to democratic political participation.
The organisation is representing the Joint List, Ra'am, Balad, Cassif and Abu Shehadeh in the current proceedings.
In a statement shared with The New Arab, Adalah warned that "Once again, Israel’s right wing is using the disqualification process to attempt to silence and delegitimise the political representatives of Palestinian citizens of Israel".
"In more than two decades representing Palestinian political parties and individual candidates, Adalah has seen such accusations proven baseless and rejected by the Supreme Court time and again, and these attempts are equally baseless," it said.
"However, given the crackdown on the rights to freedom of expression, assembly and association of Palestinian citizens of Israel particularly since October 2023, the current conservative orientation of the Israeli Supreme Court, and rampant public incitement against Palestinians, Adalah has grave concerns about the current round of disqualification motions and their potential outcomes."
The Central Elections Committee is expected to hold hearings on the motions on 23 and 24 September.
The committee's decisions can be appealed to Israel's Supreme Court, with the deadline for appeals set for 29 September and the court expected to rule by 4 October.

US House Advances Major Russia Sanctions Bill Targetting Oil Fleet and Child Abductions
The US House advanced a Russia sanctions bill on September 15, clearing a procedural rule vote that teed up final consideration of the measure rather than deciding its passage.
This was reported by The Hill on September 15.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The rule cleared 214-211 after two Democrats, Representatives Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, broke precedent to advance it. It marked their second such break in two weeks, following an identical crossover on a rule vote earlier this month, the outlet noted. Rule votes are typically treated as a test of party loyalty, which made the Democratic support unusual.
The tally opened the way for debate and a final vote on the legislation, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. Passing the rule did not enact the bill; it only advanced it toward final consideration on the House floor.
The rule vote handed a victory to the bill's backers, including Representative Michael McCaul of Texas, who overcame resistance from within his own party and from Democrats. Ahead of the vote, the opposition had left some predicting the measure was "dead again" after nearly a year and a half of negotiations, according to The Hill
.
At a House Rules Committee hearing on Monday, McCaul framed the vote as a message to the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, over US support for Ukraine. He also cast it as a warning to Chinese leader Xi Jinping against aggression toward Taiwan.
"This is a moral issue that requires moral courage," McCaul declared. "When we look back on this moment, I want us to be able to say that we did everything possible to end this war."
The legislation would grant President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs on countries that purchase Russian energy and would extend existing sanctions on Iran, The Hill reported.
According to Eugene Goncharov, policy director of the American Coalition for Ukraine, the measure also expands sanctions on Russian military figures and foreign suppliers. It bans new US investment in Russia, targets Moscow's shadow fleet of oil tankers, and tightens export restrictions. The bill further carries sanctions authority against those responsible for the abduction of Ukrainian children, he added.
The vote took place during the "Ukraine Action Summit," a weeklong lobbying push that drew more than 600 constituents from 50 states and Puerto Rico, the outlet reported. "The Sanctioning Russia Act is the number one priority for Ukraine advocacy right now," Goncharov stated.
Democratic opponents, while supportive of Ukraine, argued that the bill hands Trump tariff powers the Supreme Court has already curtailed, according to The Hill. Representatives Don Beyer of Virginia, Gregory Meeks of New York, and Richard Neal of Massachusetts warned in a joint statement that the measure would do "more harm than good."
"This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable," they wrote.
Not all critics of the tariff powers wanted the bill defeated. Michael McFaul, a former US ambassador to Russia, argued on the social platform X that its passage carried more weight as a signal than the risks of failure. "If it fails, Putin will cheer & Ukrainians will be disappointed," he wrote.
A final House vote remained pending after the rule cleared. Goncharov predicted the measure would ultimately reach Trump's desk for signature. "This is the bill that is likely to pass and be signed into law, and when that happens, it will make this war harder and more expensive for Russia to keep fighting," he explained.
The rule vote marked the latest milestone in a months-long endeavor to advance the sanctions package through Congress. In late July, the Senate cleared its own procedural hurdle in an 86-12 vote, opening debate on the bill and setting up a final vote, weeks after Graham's death.
The legislation, which he drafted, would authorize tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian oil and gas, and it advanced as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Capitol Hill.

Venezuela’s People Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:37:02 UTC
21:37:02 KST

Venezuela’s People Problem
A state that spent decades alienating its professional class has lost the capacity to govern.
Days after two deadly earthquakes struck northern Venezuela on June 24, killing at least 6,000 people and injuring tens of thousands more, the Venezuelan Seismological Research Foundation, known as Funvisis, made an unusual public plea: Could whoever had taken one of its GPS sensors please give it back?
For 13 years, the high-precision instrument had been bolted to a rocky outcrop in the hills of western Venezuela, quietly tracking the millimeter-scale movements of the Boconó fault, which was the likely source of the first of the two quakes. When Funvisis technicians went to recover the readings the sensor had stored, they found that the machine had gone missing. More than two months after the earthquakes, the organization still does not know who carried it off.
The absent sensor is but one gauge of a state that has lost the capacity to govern. Venezuela once operated 250 to 300 seismic-monitoring stations; today, no more than five still function. Many of the engineers, physicians, nurses, firefighters, and rescue workers a country depends on when disaster strikes have long since left Venezuela—part of a generation-long exodus of skilled professionals from state institutions.
President Trump has said that the oil-rich country will be run “properly” and “professionally,” but the earthquakes exposed Venezuela’s deficits. The highest expectations and fondest hopes—whether of Wall Street, Houston, or Caracas—will not conjure up the people needed to rebuild a country that has thoroughly hollowed out its professional classes.
In just 20 years, Venezuela went from Latin America’s wealthiest nation to one of its poorest thanks to the mismanagement, corruption, and poor governance that began under the populist president Hugo Chávez, who served from 1999 to 2013, and continued under his successor, Nicolás Maduro. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez, who took over Venezuela after the United States captured Maduro in January, inherited a state that cannot marshall the technical expertise to rebuild what the quakes destroyed or to reconstruct an economy that collapsed long before the ground did.
Rebuilding is a matter not merely of money and political will but of human capital. Bureaucrats, planners, regulators, and inspectors turn plans into functioning grids, ports, and clinics. Their absence may be the biggest obstacle facing American policy makers overseeing Venezuela’s reconstruction.
Venezuela is not the first country to suffer brain drain to the point of institutional collapse. Afghanistan has reportedly struggled to stand up its health-care sector and civil service ever since many of its professionals fled the return of the Taliban in 2021. Haiti has been losing doctors, judges, and engineers for decades. But Venezuela’s case is one of particularly deliberate self-destruction, in a country where oil wealth helped produce a sizable middle class.
Hostility toward the professional class was a hallmark of Chávez’s particular brand of socialism from the beginning. Adherents saw professional skills, when they were not explicitly placed in service of the revolution, as advancing the interests of capitalism and imperialism, the Venezuelan political scientist Guillermo T. Aveledo told me. In 2003, Guillermo García Ponce, a director at a pro-Chávez newspaper, went so far as to describe technocrats at state-owned companies as a “fifth column” to be “wiped out.”
“For Chavismo, privilege always comes cloaked in a PowerPoint presentation,” the journalist Francisco Toro wrote in 2007. By dismissing expertise and deliberation as ideologically suspect, Toro added, “Chavismo is left to rely on the will of the leader alone.”
The state’s public utilities were among the first institutions to confront the PowerPoint problem. Chávez replaced their professional managers with loyalists who were more compliant than competent, people who used to work in these companies told me. Jacqueline Faría, a Chavista engineer who took over the state-owned Caracas water company Hidrocapital in 1999, invested millions of dollars in a failed program to clean the Guaire River. Now she leads Rodríguez’s reconstruction efforts.
In addition to Hidrocapital, the Chávez government proceeded to dismantle the corporate-style leadership of the Caracas metro and Venezuela’s largest electricity company, Edelca, and to place these companies under the control of military officers. It eventually did the same with Funvisis. In 2009, Chávez took direct control of the country’s airports and seaports.
Water and power shortages, sometimes nationwide, became commonplace as mismanagement, corruption, and doctrinaire regulations gummed the works of nearly all of Venezuela’s public infrastructure. Consider Edelca’s two dam projects. The company began building the Caruachi dam in 1997, under Chávez’s predecessor, but finished it only after nine long years. It began building the Tocoma dam in 2007 and still has not finished it, despite almost $10 billion in investment. A Brazilian contractor involved in the work later admitted to paying Venezuelan officials and middlemen as much as $98 million in bribes from 2005 to 2016 to secure contracts. A U.S.-Argentine company will now take over the project.
Perhaps no sector was more gravely affected by Chávez’s assault on professionalism than the oil industry. And no industry is more crucial to U.S. plans for Venezuela’s recovery—or more central to Washington’s interest in the country in the first place.
Before Chávez, Venezuela’s oil company, known by its Spanish acronym PDVSA, was owned by the state but autonomously governed as a commercial entity. It set the gold standard for such an arrangement, expanding into international markets and fully acquiring Citgo, a major Houston-based refinery, in 1991. Much of the Venezuelan state ran on clientelism, but the oil company was meritocratic. Its research arm, the Venezuelan Institute of Oil Technology, or INTEVEP, employed about 170 full-time Ph.D. researchers and held roughly 1,200 American patents in the period before 2003, according to Francisco Monaldi, an energy expert.
That was the year Chávez began meddling in PDVSA’s affairs. He fired its board on live television and appointed a military officer to run the company. PDVSA’s workers went on strike in protest. Chávez fired more than 18,000 of them—dismissing, in one stroke, 60 to 80 percent of all provisioning, planning, maintenance, and exploration staff.
The finance team was laid off almost entirely; state cronies took over an office that accounted for nearly all of Venezuela’s foreign-exchange earnings. INTEVEP’s scientists were replaced, Pánfilo Masciangioli, a researcher and manager at the institute from 1982 to 2010, told me, “with people who did not even know how important it was to publish a paper.” The institute’s patents fell to about 100 during the decade that followed.
“The company’s gray matter was lost,” Monaldi told me. In its place came party loyalists and military men, who filled PDVSA’s vacancies and directed its revenues into Chávez’s populist schemes. Former employees scattered abroad. The number of Venezuelans in Alberta—the epicenter of Canada’s oil industry—rose from 465 in 2001 to 3,860 in 2011, and in Colombia, former PDVSA oil experts helped nearly double national oil production by 2011. Meanwhile, across the border, clientelism swelled PDVSA’s payroll from 28,841 in 2003 to 177,770 in 2014.
The effect fully manifested a decade later: Global oil prices fell, and Venezuela’s ruined oil industry collapsed, its output falling from about 3 million barrels a day before Chavez’s PDVSA purge to an average of 512,000 a day in 2020.
Employees of Venezuela’s state institutions came under continual pressure. In 2004, more than 2 million Venezuelans signed a referendum to recall Chávez. A lawmaker close to the president drew up what would become known as the “Tascón List” to identify and fire the petitioners from state institutions and companies. Hundreds lost their jobs. At the National Library, “a clique decided who was leaving and who was staying,” Mario Di Giacomo, an information specialist there for nearly 20 years, told me. “Dissent was not acceptable.” Loyalists replaced the professionals, and the library’s collections descended into neglect. Millions of archival records are decaying, Di Giacomo said.
The Tascón List was but one way of identifying people for firing. At the Venezuelan Institute for Scientific Investigation, the country’s premier scientific-research center, the physicist Claudio Mendoza made a public comment mocking Venezuela’s nuclear ambitions in 2006 (he noted that the country would achieve little so long as it rejected scientific expertise). He was dismissed four days later. The Chavista zoologist Ángel Viloria took over the institute and systematically purged its scientists from 2006 to 2011.
“You were either fired or forced to retire,” Mendoza told me. Venezuela slid from Latin America’s fifth-largest producer of scientific papers in the early 2000s to its 11th by 2022. By 2016, researchers who had emigrated accounted for roughly 33 percent of the country’s scientific publications; at least 68 percent of these scholars held doctoral degrees.
Trump has promised that American investors will spend $100 billion to rebuild Venezuela’s “rotting” energy infrastructure, but he hasn’t said who will do the work. The simple truth is that Venezuela has rid itself of the technocrats who could deliver the recovery Washington has promised. Few will return to the bureaucracy that ejected them. Some have emigrated for good; among those who remain, many distrust the authoritarian government or do not wish to be associated with it.
The United States is currently overseeing talks between the Rodríguez government and the democratic opposition about the country’s recovery and reconciliation. It could use that platform to push for basing appointments to public institutions on relevant expertise rather than political loyalty and, in doing so, help restore confidence among the country’s professionals.
Among the hollowed-out agencies that should be high on the list for rebuilding is Funvisis—not only for reasons of public safety but also because the geophysical data that Venezuela no longer collects are the raw material of modern oil exploration. Companies use seismic surveys to image a reservoir before they spend a dollar drilling into it, and Venezuela’s archives are dated, its instruments are scarce, and the geophysicists who once operated both are now working in Calgary or Houston or Bogotá. A state that cannot say whether the fault lines beneath it are moving is poorly placed to tell an investor what lies within the Orinoco Basin.
Washington can disburse the oil money and lift the sanctions; it cannot staff the ministries. Only Venezuelans can do that. Ultimately, the country’s recovery will be measured less in barrels lifted or dollars banked than in how many of those professionals will go back to work for the state.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Su-24 at Saky, Threatening Crimea-Based Aviation Operations
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Su-24 combat aircraft at the Saky airfield in temporarily occupied Crimea on September 15 and overnight into September 16, the country's General Staff reported.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced the operation on its official Telegram channel on September 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the statement, Ukrainian defense units struck “a number of important military targets of the Russian aggressor” during the attacks.
Beyond the Saky strike, the General Staff listed additional targets hit across temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories:
- A storage, preparation, and launch site for Russian strike drones near the city of Donetsk;
- drone control points in Staromlynivka and Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, and in Pokrovske in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- an ammunition depot in Dovzhansk in the Luhansk region;
- fuel and lubricant storage bases in Rovenky in the Luhansk region and Berdiansk in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- "Grenadier" technical reconnaissance posts in Suvorove and Rysove in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The Su-24 is a Soviet-designed supersonic tactical strike aircraft built for all-weather, low-altitude attack missions and recognizable by its variable-sweep wings and side-by-side cockpit.
The upgraded Su-24M variant carries guided missiles, bombs, and rockets across multiple hardpoints and remains a mainstay of Russian tactical aviation. Damage to such an aircraft further thins the pool of strike planes Moscow operates from temporarily occupied Crimea.
The upgraded Su-24M variant remains in Russian service and can carry guided missiles, bombs, and rockets across multiple hardpoints.
The General Staff said operations against Russian military targets would continue.
“Work on key military targets of the enemy continues,” the statement said.
The Saky airfield has repeatedly featured in Ukraine's campaign against Russian military aviation in temporarily occupied Crimea.
On August 22, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Su-24M aircraft and four pieces of airfield equipment there, alongside strikes on drone-control relay stations in Russia's Bryansk region.

American actress Angelina Jolie visited Ukraine, meeting teachers, coaches, families, and local organizations working to support children and communities amid continued Russian attacks on civilians and infrastructure, the actress and humanitarian said in a statement on September 16 .
Jolie said her visit came as Ukrainian children returned to school while communities continued to face frequent aerial attacks. In Kharkiv, located near the Russian border and regularly targeted by Russian strikes, she visited educational spaces created underground to protect children.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Kharkiv sits close to the Russian border and is hit almost daily, so classrooms have been built inside metro stations. Other schools are fully underground, where young children learn to read three stories deep,” Jolie said.
During her time in Kharkiv, Jolie met young athletes from Caramel Studio, led by Tetyana Yermashkevych. The children continue training in an underground facility in Northern Saltivka, one of the areas of the city that has suffered extensive damage during Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Jolie also visited the Aza Nizi Maza art studio, founded by Ukrainian artist Mykola Kolomiets, where children are given space to create art. The studio relocated underground in 2022 to provide protection from Russian attacks.
The visit later took Jolie to the Carpathian Mountains, where she met families participating in Gen.Camp Family, a program run by Gen.Ukrainian that helps Ukrainian men returning from years in Russian captivity reconnect with their loved ones.
Jolie said she spoke with women who had raised their children alone while campaigning for the release of their husbands, some of whom had spent four years waiting for them to return. Her son Knox, who accompanied her during the visit, led a Muay Thai class for children participating in the program.
Jolie also paid tribute to the family of Oleksii Yukov, founder of the Platsdarm search group. Yukov dedicated much of his life to recovering, identifying, and returning the bodies of fallen soldiers from both sides of the war to their families. He was killed while carrying out this work on the frontline in August.

He said the government would conduct a legal study on criminalising bid-rigging in major building maintenance works and submit a proposal to the Legislative Council this year.
The government would also introduce “pre-qualified lists” of consultants and contractors to help owners select professionals for renovation works.
