US set to approve 60,000 heavy bombs for Israel: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:09:45 UTC
21:09:45 KST

US set to approve 60,000 heavy bombs for Israel: What that means
The US taxpayer-funded package of 2,000-pound bombs comes amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and its occupation of southern Lebanon.
United States President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing to sell 60,000 highly destructive, 2,000-pound (907kg) bombs to Israel in a multibillion-dollar package which will be funded by American taxpayers.
US media has reported that the Trump administration has approved the sale, which features some of the most destructive munitions in Western arsenals, and has informally notified Congress.
This is one of the biggest US munition packages to Israel and comes after nearly three years of genocidal war on Gaza, ongoing pogroms by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank and a mighty assault on southern Lebanon – which together have killed tens of thousands and displaced millions in the region.
It also comes as the US’s own munitions stockpile has been depleted due to its war on Iran, with the crisis worsened by Russia’s war on Ukraine.
So, what bombs are the US sending to Israel, and what can Israel do with them?
What weapons are the US planning to sell to Israel?
The Trump administration has not officially confirmed this sale yet. A senior administration official told AFP news agency that “all foreign arms sales are moving through the appropriate process”, but refused to comment on pending transactions.
Meanwhile, a State Department spokesperson told AFP that “as a matter of policy, the Department does not confirm or comment on proposed arms sales until they have been formally notified to Congress”.
However, Washington is reported to be on track to deliver a munitions package to Israel that is believed to include 60,000 warheads, including 20,000 MK-84s, 20,000 BLU-117s and 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator.
The sale is worth $2.8bn, the majority of which will be paid for by the US’s Foreign Military Financing scheme, wherein Washington pays Israel from its own taxpayers’ funds to buy American-made weapons and military equipment.
The three types of bomb are:
- MK-84: The largest among the Mark 80 series of bombs, this unguided, 2,000-pound (907kg) general-purpose bomb is designed primarily for maximum blast and fragmentation against buildings and moderately protected targets. It can destroy buildings and kill or injure people hundreds of metres from the bomb site.
- BLU-117: A 2,000-pound (907kg) general-purpose bomb which looks very similar to the MK-84 but has a different explosive filler and can also be fitted with precision-guidance kits. It also has a thermal protective coating, designed for safer storage, particularly by the US Navy.
- I-2000 Penetrator: Also referred to as a “bunker buster”, this roughly 2,000-pound-class, hard-target penetrator is designed to punch through hardened structures before detonating; its casing is substantially thicker and harder than an MK-84.
In 2024, then-President Joe Biden’s administration paused the delivery of some 2,000-pound-class bombs to Israel amid growing international criticism by rights groups about the disproportionate number of civilians being killed in attacks.
Trump ended the pause when he returned to the presidency the following year – and bypassed a usual congressional review process to approve a nearly $3bn arms sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of these powerful bombs. In January this year, Washington approved a further package of arms sales to Israel worth $6.67bn.
When has Israel used 2,000-pound US bombs before?
Israel had been using 2,000-pound-class bombs, especially in the occupied Palestinian territory and in Lebanon, for at least four decades prior to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered Israel’s war on Gaza.
In 1981, Israel used this bomb during the Osirak bombing, known as Operation Opera, in an air strike which destroyed an unfinished Iraqi nuclear reactor near Baghdad. The next year, Israel dropped these bombs in Lebanon and Syria, accounting for a high civilian toll during attacks.
According to the Project on Defense Alternatives (PDA), which conducts defence policy research and analysis, a 2,000-pound blast will severely damage, injure or kill everything or anyone within 35 metres (115 feet).
Averaged across different types of surfaces, a 2000-pound bomb will carve out a crater 50 feet (15 metres) across and 16 feet (5 metres) deep.
Since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, preliminary research suggests that Israel has used these powerful and destructive bombs more frequently.
For instance, on October 31, 2023, Israel dropped a 2,000-pound bomb on the Jabalia refugee camp in a densely populated area of Gaza City, leaving a giant crater amid bombed-out buildings, and killing dozens of civilians. The UN human rights office said the Israeli air attack could amount to a war crime.
The International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in November 2024. Washington has ridiculed the court’s jurisdiction.
How lethal are these bombs?
According to an Al Jazeera investigation, The Rest of the Story, civil defence teams in Gaza have documented 2,842 Palestinians who witnesses say in effect “evaporated” in the blast of bombs since the war began in October 2023, leaving behind no remains other than blood spray or small fragments of flesh.
Experts and witnesses have attributed this phenomenon to Israel’s systematic use of internationally prohibited thermal and thermobaric weapons, often referred to as vacuum or aerosol bombs, capable of generating temperatures exceeding 3,500 degrees Celsius (6,332 degrees Fahrenheit).
The investigation detailed how specific chemical compositions in Israeli munitions turn human bodies into ash in seconds – and identified specific US-manufactured munitions used in Gaza that are linked to these disappearances, including MK-84 and BLU series bunker busters.
Vasily Fatigarov, a Russian military expert, explained that these weapons do not just kill; they obliterate matter. Unlike conventional explosives, these weapons disperse a cloud of fuel that ignites to create an enormous fireball and a vacuum effect.
“To prolong the burning time, powders of aluminium, magnesium and titanium are added to the chemical mixture,” Fatigarov said. “This raises the temperature of the explosion to between 2,500 and 3,000 degrees Celsius [4,532F to 5,432F].”
How significant are 60,000 bombs?
Very. Together, 60,000 2,000-pound-class bombs weigh 54,400 tonnes.
That is about the weight of the entire steel skeleton of New York’s Empire State Building. Or seven times the weight of the iron structure of the Eiffel Tower.
Its mass also far exceeds the most infamous single conventional air raid of the 20th century. The March 1945 Tokyo firebombing, which killed more than 80,000 people in one night, used roughly 1,600 tonnes of bombs.
On a broader scale, 54,400 tonnes is nearly the total weight of bombs dropped on Berlin throughout World War II, and also roughly one-third of all bombs that fell on Japan’s home islands.
Isn’t the US running short on munition stockpiles?
Yes, a Pentagon watchdog report released on Monday confirmed earlier media reports that the war on Iran is burning through Washington’s munitions – especially the costly Patriot surface-to-air missile defence system – and creating “bottlenecks” in supply chains.
“To mitigate these constraints,” the report said, the Pentagon is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency.”
President Trump wrote on Truth Social that the US is “producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond.”
What reactions have there been to this weapons sale?
News of the sale has been condemned by figures on both sides of the political spectrum in the US.
“By any definition, what the Netanyahu government has done in Gaza is genocide,” conservative commentator Tucker Carlson, who has been highly critical of the US support for Israel’s war on Palestine, wrote on X.
“The 40,000 new bombs the Trump administration is sending will be used to do the same in Lebanon, and likely in other countries in the region. If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do.”
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat, said he would work to block the sale, and accused the Trump administration of “sending bombs paid for by American taxpayers to a government led by a wanted war criminal”.
Former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, who was affiliated with the Republican Party when in the House of Representatives, wrote: “We did not vote for this. America does not support this. Our tax dollars and weapons have been used to kill tens of thousands of innocent people.”
The US-Israel war on Iran, which started in late February with the assassination of then Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, is widely unpopular in the US, with President Trump’s approval ratings dipping.
A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48 percent of voters and 66 percent of Democrats believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 percent and 20 percent when the question was first asked in 2017.

Colonel cleared of not properly handling allegations of soldier who killed herself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:07:51 UTC
21:07:51 KST

A senior army officer has been cleared by a court martial of failing to deal properly with allegations made by a teenage soldier who went on to kill herself.
Col Samantha Shepherd had been accused of “conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline” over the case of 19-year-old Gunner Jaysley Beck, who took her own life in December 2021.
But on Wednesday, Assistant Judge Advocate Gen Edward Legard told the court the crown had concluded there was insufficient evidence upon which Shepherd could be safely convicted.
The board, which consisted of an RAF air commodore, a navy captain and an army colonel, formally returned a not guilty verdict and Shepherd left the court.
Shepherd was on trial at the military court centre at Catterick Garrison, in North Yorkshire, alongside Maj James Hook.
Opening the case on Tuesday, the prosecution alleged that both senior officers “let down” Beck when she told them about an incident which had happened on an adventure training exercise on Thorney Island, in Chichester Harbour, in July 2021.
The court martial board was told Beck had informed both officers about behaviour towards her by a warrant officer, Michael Webber, at a social event during the exercise.
Cdr Paul Patterson, for the crown, had claimed the young soldier “told each of them enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted”.
The trial of Hook continues. On Wednesday, the board heard a summary of an interview he gave to military police.
Hook said that Beck told him Webber had “made a pass at her” and it was possible she also said he tried to kiss her. He said he asked her if Webber had forced himself on her, or if she felt threatened by him. She had replied: “No.”
Hook said he knew Beck was not enjoying the adventure exercise. He said: “She had complained about being there … it caused me to question the veracity of the allegation. I didn’t say I disbelieved her but that was definitely going through my mind. She was saying all she wanted was to return to Larkhill [barracks]. I had at the back of my mind this might be a spurious thing to get away from the training package.”
Hook said Beck told him she didn’t want “anything bad” to happen to Webber. He replied that if he was investigated and found guilty almost certainly something would happen to Webber. He added: “That was not to discourage Gunner Beck. That was to make her aware of the consequences.”
Hook added: “I thought everything I did was empowering and supporting her in making the right decision.” He said he had reported what Beck had said to others, including her immediate boss, and added: “Thereafter the matter was taken away from me.”
The trial continues.

Iran plans to launch three satellites by year-end

The Iranian Communications and Information Technology Minister Sattar Hashemi also said on Wednesday that the development of the space industry was one of the government’s key priorities, highlighting the simultaneous launch of three Iranian satellites in cooperation with Russia as a major achievement.
He said the three satellites — Paya, Zafar and Kowsar — were developed with the participation of different sectors, including the government, universities and the private sector.
Hashemi also said Iran was advancing several launch infrastructure projects, although some facilities had been damaged during the recent war.
He said the first phase of the Chabahar Space Center had reached 98% completion, up from around 40%, and would provide a strategic location for placing communications and remote-sensing satellites into orbit.
The minister also announced plans to place the Nahid-2 satellite into orbit. He said the satellite was developed for the first time in the Ku band, with a woman executive playing a leading role in its development, and would be used for telecommunications purposes.
Hashemi said the Shahid Soleimani constellation consists of 24 satellites — 18 primary satellites and six reserves. Iran plans to place three of them into orbit simultaneously this year, with launches of the remaining satellites planned for subsequent years.

====================================================================================================

EU opens door to Canada as first ‘associate member’ amid growing US trade rift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:06:30 UTC
21:06:30 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday that she wants Canada to become the European Union’s first “associate member,” proposing an unprecedented new relationship as Ottawa seeks closer economic and security ties with Europe amid tensions with the United States.
The status does not currently exist under EU treaties, meaning its exact rights, obligations and legal structure would still have to be worked out. Von der Leyen made the proposal during her annual State of the European Union address before the European Parliament in Strasbourg, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney sitting in the chamber.
The proposal comes as Canada reassesses its traditionally close relationship with the United States following a breakdown in trade negotiations, new U.S. tariffs and President Donald Trump’s repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney has been seeking to reduce Canada’s heavy dependence on trade with the United States and deepen ties with Europe and other partners.
Von der Leyen’s announcement also marks a significant departure from the EU’s traditional reluctance to create flexible categories of membership.
EU members reacted cautiously earlier this year when Germany floated a similar form of “associate membership” for Ukraine as a possible intermediate step toward eventual full membership.
“Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system,” von der Leyen said.
“We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defense, on raw materials and on supply chains,” she said. “But above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy.”
“We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us,” she added. “That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”
Carney, who was invited to Strasbourg by von der Leyen, received a standing ovation from lawmakers after she addressed him directly during the speech. He was the first foreign head of government to attend the annual State of the European Union address and is scheduled to address the European Parliament himself on Thursday.
“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told him.
Von der Leyen said the EU and Canada should move beyond their existing free-trade relationship toward what she called an “Alliance for the Future,” creating a shared space for economic prosperity and security.
She listed advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security as areas for expanded cooperation.
The Arctic, where Canada and several European countries have major strategic interests, would become a “flagship joint project,” she said. Von der Leyen also proposed involving Canada in a future European Security Council alongside other close partners.
Canada has already moved closer to the bloc in defense. It became the first non-European country to join the EU’s 150 billion-euro SAFE defense loan program, while the two sides have long been linked economically through the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, known as CETA.
What would ‘associate membership’ mean?
For now, the answer is unclear. “Associate member” is not a legal category contained in the EU’s treaties, and von der Leyen did not spell out whether Canada would gain access to EU institutions, parts of the single market or other benefits normally reserved for member states.
When a similar concept was discussed this year in connection with Ukraine, one version envisioned allowing Kyiv to attend certain EU summits and ministerial meetings and gain access to some EU programs without receiving full voting rights. The idea received a cool response in Ukraine, which is pursuing full membership.
Von der Leyen stressed that the proposed partnership with Canada was “not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” an apparent effort to frame the initiative as cooperation rather than a move against Washington.
The broader geopolitical context, however, is difficult to ignore. Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed last month, deepening a dispute that has included tariffs and retaliatory measures. Trump’s repeated references to Canada as a potential 51st state have further strained what was long one of the world’s closest bilateral relationships.
Earlier this week, Carney said Canada was seeking a “unique alliance” with the EU rather than full membership. His government has increasingly emphasized diversifying trade and building closer security and economic ties with Europe.
Reports ahead of Carney’s Strasbourg visit said Canadian and European officials had been exploring ways to connect Canada more closely to Europe’s market in strategic sectors including energy, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and defense. Discussions have also included the possibility of making it easier for Canadians to live and work in Europe, though no final arrangement has been agreed.
The proposal comes after months in which Carney has sought alternatives to Canada’s overwhelming economic dependence on its southern neighbor. Around 70% of Canadian trade remains tied to the United States, making any substantial shift toward Europe a long-term project rather than an immediate replacement for the U.S. relationship.
The EU and Canada already have a substantial economic relationship. Their CETA free-trade agreement eliminated most tariffs between them, and the two sides say trade in goods and services has risen sharply since the agreement began provisional application.
What “associate membership” would ultimately add remains to be negotiated. Unlike full EU membership, the proposal currently has no defined legal framework, no agreed voting rights and no established mechanism for participation in the bloc’s institutions.
For now, von der Leyen’s announcement signals political intent rather than an accession process: an effort to create a deeper form of partnership between the EU and Canada at a time when both are seeking greater room to maneuver in a more fractured international system.

25 Belarusian political prisoners arrive in Lithuania after US-brokered release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:06:00 UTC
21:06:00 KST

Twenty-five political prisoners released from Belarus with US mediation arrived in Lithuania on Wednesday, Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said.
None of those released are Lithuanian citizens, the ministry said.
Lithuanian authorities assisted with border-crossing procedures and are ensuring the prisoners’ safe travel from the border to their accommodation, the ministry said. Some of those released did not have identity documents. Medical personnel were also on standby to provide assistance if needed.
Among those released are independent Belarusian journalists and other public figures, including Liudmila Chekina, the former general director of independent news outlet Tut.by; Pavel Belavus, founder of Art Siadziba and Symbal.by, a store selling national symbols and souvenirs; journalist and media executive Andrei Aliaksandrav; political scientist Tatsiana Kuzina; and Dzmitry Navazhylau, director of the BelaPAN news agency.
The release was agreed during a visit to Belarus by John Coale, US President Donald Trump’s special envoy to Belarus, according to Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya’s adviser Dzianis Kuchynski.
As part of the agreement, Washington will lift sanctions on Belarusian paint manufacturer Lakokraska and forestry conglomerate Bellesbumprom.
Hundreds of people remain imprisoned in Belarus after authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko, who has been in power since 1994, suppressed mass protests following his disputed re-election in 2020.
Washington has renewed dialogue with Minsk and eased some sanctions since Trump returned to the White House. Dozens of political prisoners have been released following Coale’s visits to Belarus.
Viasna, an independent Belarusian human rights organisation that monitors arrests in the country, says 912 people are currently recognised as political prisoners. They include protesters and other civilians, journalists, trade union representatives and people linked to the political opposition.
Human rights defenders and activists have warned that while the authorities have released some prisoners, others continue to be arrested and jailed.
Before traveling to Belarus this week, Coale visited Lithuania and met with Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys.
Coale last visited Minsk in March, when Belarus released 250 political prisoners. After that visit, the US envoy urged Lithuania to restore the transit of Belarusian fertilisers and called for a deputy-minister-level meeting between Lithuania and Belarus.

What von der Leyen’s words reveal about the mood in the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:05:45 UTC
21:05:45 KST

Ursula von der Leyen’s big speech covered a wide range of topics, from closer ties with Canada to climate change, from trade with China to artificial intelligence.
POLITICO analysed the past decade’s worth of State of the Union speeches to look at what words were used and reused, showing how the focus has changed since Jean-Claude Juncker, von der Leyen’s predecessor as Commission chief, gave his address in 2015.
That year, the key topics included the Greek debt crisis and an upsurge in refugee arrivals. By the time von der Leyen gave her first State of the Union speech, the Green Deal and the post-Covid Next Generation EU recovery program were firmly on the agenda.
Russia and Ukraine had, of course, become key themes in the 2022 speech, months after Moscow’s full-scale invasion — and they have remained so since. Now, with von der Leyen well into her second term, there’s an additional focus on energy, climate, security and defense.
There were no State of the Union speeches in 2019 and 2024, as EU elections were held in both of those years.

Poland reiterates Ukraine support after Russia drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:04:00 UTC
21:04:00 KST

Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
September 16, 2026
Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland.
After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat.
"Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday.
"Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war.
Poland prepares response
Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details.
"Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening.
On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe.
"There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security.
Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train
Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time.
Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack.
Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train.
"Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do."
"The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said.
Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster.
Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland
Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest.
But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion.
In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up."
Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment."
"In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added.
Polish media sound alarm
The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm.
"Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line."
"These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote.
Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door."
"The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski.
Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat.
"We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further."
This article was originally published in German.

RoboCup IranOpen competition 2026 underway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:03:31 UTC
21:03:31 KST

RoboCup IranOpen competition 2026 underway
TEHRAN – Tehran is playing host to the 20th edition of the RoboCup IranOpen competition, which started on Wednesday and will wrap up on Friday.
Over 400 teams, comprising some 2,000 participants, are competing in 30 specialized leagues, including Rescue Maze, Rescue Line, Design and Construction, Student 2D Soccer, Student Flying Robots, Student Soccer Player, Rescue Simulation, and Soccer Simulation leagues, IRNA reported.
Self-driving car, Rescue Virtual Robot, and Rescue Agent Simulation, creativity, and innovation leagues are among other parts of the competition.
RoboCup is an international initiative covering the areas of artificial intelligence and robotics, with the ultimate goal of developing a team of humanoid robots that is able to defeat the official human World Soccer Champion team by 2050.
The initiative is a platform for testing technologies such as real-time decision-making, multi-agent collaboration, sensor data processing, and navigation in complex environments.
The event was first launched in 1997 and was inspired by the victory of a computer chess player against the then world chess champion, Gary Kasparov.
RoboCup (Originally called the Robot World Cup Initiative) is an international research and education initiative. It is an attempt to foster AI and intelligent robotics research by providing a standard problem where a wide range of technologies can be integrated and examined, as well as being used for integrated project-oriented education.
Recent achievements
Thirteen Iranian students under the age of 12 showcased their scientific, technical capabilities, and creativity, ranking second and third in different leagues of the RobotChallenge 2026 which was held in Beijing, China.

Russia says there is still time to stop an arms race in space after US orbital weapons admission

Russia says there is still time to stop an arms race in space after US orbital weapons admission
MOSCOW – Russia believes there is still time to prevent an arms race in space by drawing up a legally-binding international treaty to outlaw the deployment of offensive weapons there and called on the United States and other nations to set aside their scepticism about the idea, Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on Sept 16.
Ryabkov was commenting after the US acknowledged this week that the Pentagon is operating weapons in Earth's orbit, a landmark moment in the militarisation of space.
US Space Force chief Douglas Schiess said that enlisted members of his military branch “operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the Joint Force against space-enabled attacks”.
Speaking at a news briefing in Moscow, Ryabkov said the United States had not notified Russia – one of the world's top three space powers – about its new weapons capability, but said the US statement had not come as a surprise.
“This is nothing new to us; we are monitoring all of this, recording it all, and drawing the appropriate conclusions,” he said, noting that Moscow had long spoken of the need for a treaty that would rule out the use of force in space or the threat of force against objects in space.
“The Americans and other Westerners, in particular the British, have for many years used inflammatory excuses to cover up their unwillingness to move in this direction; they seek out spurious arguments to avoid doing so and attempt to turn the tables by accusing us of activities which, in their view, are destabilising in nature,” said Ryabkov.
“But we believe that it is not yet too late to create an environment that would preclude an arms race with escalating risks of open conflict in outer space.” REUTERS

Hong Kong aims to raise zero-carbon energy share of fuel mix to 30% by 2030

Hong Kong aims to raise zero-carbon energy share of fuel mix to 30% by 2030
Target is one of four binding environmental protection targets revealed in city’s first five-year plan
Hong Kong has pledged to boost the share of zero-carbon energy in its electricity generation fuel mix to 30 per cent by 2030, up from the current 28 per cent – one of four binding environmental protection targets set out in the city’s first five-year plan on Wednesday.
The binding goal aligns with existing climate protection strategies that target a zero-carbon energy share of between 60 and 70 per cent by 2035, as part of the city’s broader push towards carbon neutrality by 2050.
“With these efforts, we strive to strengthen energy security, lower energy generation costs and stabilise electricity tariffs to minimise the impacts of the war in the Middle East, which has driven up liquefied natural gas prices,” a government source said.
Natural gas currently accounts for most of Hong Kong’s electricity generation, making up more than 50 per cent of the fuel mix as of June this year, followed by coal at under 20 per cent, and nuclear and renewable energy at around 28 per cent.

The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of legal immunity to face charges in his homeland of denying Nazi crimes, an offence that carries a potential prison sentence of up to three years.

Russia must present a list of energy facilities it wants protected if Moscow is serious about negotiating a reciprocal halt to infrastructure attacks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday, Sept. 16.
According to an excerpt from Zelensky’s interview with CBS News, Ukraine is prepared to accept an energy ceasefire but insists that the agreement must cover all forms of attacks and treat both sides’ critical energy interests equally.

“If they say, ‘We are not attacking these facilities,’ then they must put on the table a list of their facilities – those they do not want us to attack,” Zelensky said.
He added that limited de-escalation measures remain possible even during wartime if the parties demonstrate genuine political will to end the conflict.
Kyiv defines energy differently from Moscow
Zelensky said US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility of halting attacks on oil refineries and other energy facilities during their recent visit to Ukraine.
“I told them that we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but it is necessary to understand what this means for Ukraine,” Zelensky said.
“For Putin, energy means selling oil and gas. For us, energy means electricity and gas for our people,” he added.
Zelensky said Ukraine would interpret an energy ceasefire as a complete end to Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure using any type of weapon.

US President Donald Trump announced an energy truce before either Russia or Ukraine had publicly confirmed a formal agreement or monitoring mechanism.
Oil exports central to Russia’s war budget
Zelensky said restrictions on Russia’s ability to transport and sell oil impose significant losses on the Kremlin warfighting budget, estimating the annual impact at more than 100 billion and saying the figure could reach 150 billion this year. He did not specify the currency in the published excerpt.

Zelensky said reciprocal steps could serve as evidence of “goodwill or political will to end the war,” but emphasized that any pause must be clearly defined and apply equally to both sides.

The ‘Ossoff angle’: media-savvy senator borrows from Obama as 2028 chatter builds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:20 UTC
21:00:20 KST

Delivering a speech in Atlanta last month, Jon Ossoff accused Donald Trump of corruption, incompetence and fecklessness, and peppered his remarks with substantive observations of dates and times and places. But the comment that ricocheted across the internet – a clip of just a few seconds – was an almost-throwaway reference about how the US president wants to “travel with Natalie” onboard Air Force One.
The crowd cheered the US senator, who is running for re-election in battleground Georgia and is increasingly seen as a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028. But his target audience that day – and this year – spanned far beyond the concert hall.
After his remark went viral, stories about Trump’s young, exceptionally devoted, presidential aide Natalie Harp rippled through social and established media. Often enough, they were accompanied by an image of Ossoff, his sharp jawline captured from below as he looks into the middle distance.
This photographic framing has increasingly been referred to as the “Ossoff angle”, perhaps in a disservice to myriad politicians from John F Kennedy to Barack Obama who also employed the technique, snapped at a low angle from a camera pit over the past century.
While the approach is not new, it has helped the senator for Georgia to reach the social media feeds of users far beyond his state.
Kathleen Hall Jamieson, professor of communication at Penn’s Annenberg School, likened Ossoff to Kennedy. The first millennial senator has mastered the medium of the moment, she suggested, much as Kennedy was the first president who really understood television.
“How do you communicate that this is a new generation of leadership?,” Jamieson asked. “And how do you do that rhetorically? Because you can’t just stand up and say, ‘This is a new generation of leadership.’
“You have to have people draw that conclusion about you. And part of the way you do that is you master the media of the time, and you demonstrate that in the process you have leadership capacity and that you have the capacity to deal with the old order.”
At 33 years, 11 months and four days, Ossoff was the youngest US senator sworn into the 117th Congress. At 39 today, and ever so slightly gray at the temple, he remains the youngest in a chamber with an average age of 65.
The value of good lighting, a good background and a good angle in a social media post is not lost on a film-maker, as Ossoff was before turning to public office. The former documentarian has a knack for winning the algorithm with plain language, surfacing absurdities in an era of absurdities.
While Trump is also a master of social media, the effect is different. His audience is generationally different.
Trump, who regularly attaches infantile nicknames to his political enemies as a political marketing gimmick, calls Ossoff “Pee-wee Herman”, a tepid sobriquet which hasn’t yet landed.
More recently, the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican-aligned Super Pac, began running ads about Ossoff’s haircare and makeup regime using AI-generated videos of Ossoff in a salon chair. (Ossoff has spent about $1,200 on hair and makeup this election cycle – a drop in the bucket, given a fundraising haul of $81m up to June, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) disclosures.)
Georgia elected Ossoff in a nail-biting runoff in January 2021 with control of the Senate on the line, amid the turmoil of Trump’s election dispute. His election, alongside fellow Georgia Democrat Raphael Warnock, secured the Senate majority for Democrats. Rioters stormed the US Capitol the next day.
Since taking office, Ossoff has built a high profile as an opponent of Washington corruption, maladministration and the so-called Epstein class. He grilled CIA director John Ratcliffe after Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, published a report that senior officials had shared sensitive information about future military strikes on Signal with him. He pressed Russ Vought, Trump’s budget director, after massive cuts to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He questioned former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard on her presence at an FBI raid that seized 2020 ballots in Fulton county.
His questioning of such Trump administration officials have proven as likely to reach wide social media audiences as anything he says on the campaign trail.
Clips circulated of Ossoff repeatedly pressing intelligence director nominee Jay Clayton during a July 2026 hearing to say plainly whether the 2020 election was legitimate. Ossoff’s questions left Clayton sitting in silence at the hearing table, refusing to speak. “Your answers lack credibility,” Ossoff declared. “Your testimony lacks credibility. You’re being evasive and you’re not being candid or forthright. And everybody across the country is going to watch this and know that.”
But outside of the spotlight, Ossoff has held hearings on child welfare and federal prison abuses both in Washington DC and across the state of Georgia. These relatively quiet issues tend to draw little media attention and less financial interest from funders, though they are a vital element of government oversight.
“It is clear that Jon Ossoff believes what he is saying, and people – they get it,” said Charlie Bailey, chairman of Georgia’s Democratic party. “And so it not only matches up with their experience and their their anger and their frustration, they know he’s telling the truth. They know he’s saying what he believes, and that’s why he’s saying it, because he thinks it’s the right thing to do.”

Africa is bigger than we’ve been led to believe – what next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:19 UTC
21:00:19 KST

This month, the UN passed a resolution, brought to the assembly by Togo, to phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe and replace it with another that shows the real scale of territories. That’s right – when it comes to size, the map of the world we have all grown up with is not accurate. The main loser of land on the Mercator map is Africa, and the new “Equal Earth” map reflects its true proportions. I spoke to our west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule about his extensive reporting on the map changes, and why people feel so strongly about it.
Seeing the new map transposed over the old might make you feel oddly disoriented. Logically, there is absolutely no immediate tangible impact on one’s life that comes out of knowing that the entire top part of the northern hemisphere is so much smaller than you were led to believe. And yet, there is still something agitating about it, like you’ve been the subject of a lifelong trick, or at least a breach of trust.
The vast geographical inaccuracies of the old map include the shortening of Africa, and the relative expansion of North America and Eurasia. The new projection shows Africa as taking up almost double the ratio of total land area shown on the map. It all feeds into a sense that there is something domineering about it, portraying some countries as not just political and economic powers, but geographical ones as well, and therefore natural hegemons. It is an emotional response more than anything, but a testament to how much our perceptions of the physical world are linked to our estimations of stature.
No, the world map has not gone ‘woke’
The Guardian’s west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule is struck by how, despite its disproportionality, there was still opposition to retiring the 16th-century map. The US was the only country that vetoed the UN resolution, and six other nations abstained. The US dismissed the effort as “superfluous”, but Eromo sees this as a euphemism for “ideological” or “woke”. “I don’t see why it feels so strongly,” he told me. “This is a scientific discussion. It’s not an imposition.”
There is nothing binding about the resolution, and yet, there is something revealing about the world’s superpower opposing it. It suggests that the US would like to preserve that connection between size and status, even when appearances are deceiving. US president Donald Trump’s interest in Greenland was reportedly influenced by its inflated size on the old map, an acquisition that would swell US territory in the political imagination. Greenland is “massive” said Trump – but in actuality, it’s a fraction of its size as shown in the Mercator projection. The old map depicts it as roughly the same size as Africa, despite it being 14 times smaller. Could huge geopolitical tensions, and confrontation with Europe, could have possibly been avoided by simply showing Trump an accurate map?
Do maps really matter?
“It does matter. Make no mistake,” said Eromo. In his view, the significance is in the momentum such a resolution triggers. “There’s two proverbs we have in pidgin,” Eromo said: “every dance begins with a clap” and “it’s grains of rice that fill up a pot”. In other words, this might feel like a small change, but the boost of one successful campaign could pave the way to what Eromo describes as a “multipolar world order”. He points out that this resolution comes on the heels of a separate landmark one – the UN vote to recognise the transatlantic slave trade as a crime and call for reparations, an effort also led by an African country.
There is a growing traction around a particular kind of advocacy: one that uses the procedures of high-profile international institutions to challenge dominant western understandings of history and reality. These interventions in how we make sense of the world may be symbolic – but they are meaningful, and they are gaining ground.
Moving towards a shared reality?
It is staggering that the Mercator map has pretty much remained the unchanged standard for over four centuries. In questioning what was once assumed to be fact, the resolution has not only addressed issues of accuracy. It has also, somehow, punctured the vast and abstract unrealities established throughout history by the west. The theft of resources and people is only one part of what was stolen from many regions of the world during colonisation. Countries were then stolen from, again, in terms of landmass on maps, and also the subordinating cultural and political associations that followed. There is something intangible and deeply political about the map’s significance – which is symbolic and threatening.
Eromo said that this sort of change makes people nervous because it ties in to all the ways in which legacies of literally carving out the continent and enslaving its populations still resonate. Hanging over the resolution are questions of precedent, of the floodgates being opened – the sort of building pressure that has resulted in calls to decolonise curriculums, for example. If the map that hangs in classrooms all around the world is changed, people may ask: “What else are my children going to be taught now?” Eromo said that there is something diminishing about learning that behemoths such as the US, China and Russia “can all fit into Africa with some space to spare.”
There are broader anxieties at stake – about what constitutes our shared reality, one that is increasingly fractured by social media and AI. These make tussles about maps a matter of holding on to the little that we can establish as concrete and true, in the face of vast political and digital forces that are warping our perceptions of the world. Eromo cites a statement that stood out for him, issued by Africa No Filter, an advocacy group that has been a part of the map justice campaign: “If we got something as basic as Africa’s size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning?”

Microplastics in soil pose global threat by acting like ‘Trojan horse’ to deliver toxins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:19 UTC
21:00:19 KST

Microplastics act like a “Trojan horse” delivering pollutants, pesticides and bacteria through the soil, a five-year multinational research project has found.
The EU-funded project, which has so far resulted in 22 peer-reviewed studies, found microplastics in the soil of all 227 agricultural fields it tested across 11 European countries. The researchers said this poses a global threat, with healthy soils essential for life on Earth.
In many cases, this contamination reflected current farming practices as well as historical land use, demonstrating that plastic pollution can persist for many years.
The researchers also found that microplastics could interact with other agricultural stressors such as pesticides and veterinary drugs.
One study in Switzerland found that fields with the highest levels of tyre-wear particles also had the highest levels of other toxic chemicals and metals.
Microplastics can create new microbial habitats on their surfaces. Known as the plastisphere, these surfaces form a hotspot for interactions between plastics, microbes and agrochemicals, the researchers found.
An increase of antibiotic-resistant genes was found within plastispheres when compared with controls. Pesticides appeared to amplify this effect further.
Edoardo Puglisi, a partner of the project and professor of microbiology at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart in Piacenza, Italy, said the smaller the microplastics were, the more they tended to adsorb pollutants, microbes and DNA, leading to a “Trojan horse effect that can potentially increase the diffusion of pathogens and antibiotic-resistance genes”.
This Trojan horse effect can have an impact on earthworms and soil organisms by disrupting critical processes such as nutrient cycles, one study found.
Earthworms play a vital role in shaping the composition of the soil microbiome as well as the ecological functions of soils.
The EU-funded Minagris research project, in collaboration with the Countryside and Community Research Institute at the University of Gloucestershire, also found microplastics could affect plant growth and function. One study found that higher concentrations of microplastics reduced leaf area, chlorophyll content, photosynthetic efficiency and plant biomass in lettuce.
When drought conditions were added, these effects became even more pronounced, with plants performing less well than under either stress alone.
Environmental assessments often consider pollutants individually, but the findings show pollutants can behave differently when they occur together. The researchers say policy needs to recognise that plastic contamination is part of a wider picture of soil degradation and pollution.
In an effort to reduce plastic pollution, there has been an increase in the use of biodegradable plastics. However, the project found biodegradable plastics were not automatically safer and could still degrade into microplastics, potentially causing ecological damage.
“Once these plastics fragment into the ground, they’re practically impossible to remove, acting as vectors for agrochemicals and altering critical soil ecosystems,” said Dr Esperanza Huerta Lwanga, a research associate in soil physics at Wageningen University in the Netherlands.
“To protect long-term food production and soil health, policy must catch up. We urgently need standardised plastic monitoring, full manufacturer transparency, and risk assessments that evaluate through different species how microplastics interact with co-pollutants.”

How to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:18 UTC
21:00:18 KST

Olive brine is a simple byproduct that has so much flavour, and it elevates a classic salade nicoise dressing while keeping things colourful, elegant and relatively simple.
Salade nicoise with olive-brine vinaigrette
Though this one-bowl wonder began life as a simple tomato and anchovy salad with olive oil, it has become more elaborate over time, and the addition of cooked green beans, eggs and even tuna all make sense to me. What’s worth preserving, though, is its Mediterranean simplicity, and the olive-brine dressing adds a lot of flavour without needing loads of extra ingredients.
In the spirit of simplicity, this vinaigrette keeps to just three wonderfully flavourful ingredients: olive brine for salt and depth of flavour, red-wine vinegar for acidity and olive oil for substance and piquancy. It won’t hold a stable emulsion in the way a mustard dressing does, so give it another good shake just before it goes on the salad. I buy whole olives with the pits in and pit them myself. They, and the brine, taste so much better that way.
Serves 4
For the vinaigrette 
2 tbsp brine from a jar of olives
  1 tbsp red-wine vinegar 
  6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  Black pepper, to taste
For the salad
6 eggs
  200g green beans, topped
200g cocktail tomatoes, or cherry tomatoes
1 red pepper, stalk, seeds and pith removed, flesh sliced into rings
½ medium cucumber, skin on and seeds in, cut into large chunks
4 spring onions, cut into 1cm lengths (white and green parts)
1 small jar black olives
  Anchovy fillets, (optional) to taste; I used a whole standard 50g tin
1 small handful basil leaves, to finish
Put the olive brine, vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil in a jar, and add a grind of black pepper to taste. Screw on the lid and shake until the mixture emulsifies. It won’t stay emulsified for long, so shake again just before you’re ready to eat. The dressing will now keep in the fridge for up to a week.
Put the eggs in a pan of cold water and bring to a boil. Once boiling, add the green beans, bring back to a boil and cook for four minutes. Drain, then put the eggs and beans in a bowl of iced or cold water. Once cooled, drain again and put the beans to one side (they can be left whole or cut into pieces). Peel and halve the eggs.
Cut the tomatoes in half, then arrange all the vegetables on a platter. Scatter over the stoned olives and drained anchovy fillets to taste, then finish with the halved eggs, some torn basil leaves and the freshly shaken dressing. Eat straight away.

Army to replace Watchkeeper with Ukraine-proven drone
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:00:05 BST
21:00:05 KST

The Army is to bring the Tekever AR5 into service under a contract worth up to £400 million, replacing the Watchkeeper system in use since 2014, alongside a separate £16 million deal delivering more than a thousand small drones, the Ministry of Defence stated.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, announced both at Defence Vehicle Dynamics, the biennial land warfare exhibition, on Wednesday.
The AR5 is a long-endurance surveillance aircraft able to carry up to 50kg of cameras and sensors. The deal begins with an initial order of six, rising to up to 24 by 2029, with the aircraft to be built at a new Tekever factory in Swindon. The type has already been used by Ukraine against Russia.
Mr Pollard said: “Our soldiers deserve the best technology, and that’s what we’re delivering. From small drones giving troops eyes on the enemy, to the AR5 offering commanders better intelligence over the battlefield, we’re transforming the Army’s ability to see, understand and act first.
“This is defence procurement that backs British industry, creates skilled jobs and keeps our Armed Forces ahead of our adversaries.”
According to the department, the Tekever contract will support more than 1,000 highly skilled jobs by 2030 across the company’s British sites, which include Bristol, Swindon, Lydd, London, Southampton, Edinburgh and West Wales Airport.
Karl Brew, Managing Director of Tekever UK, said: “We are proud to be delivering the AR5 to the British Army at this critical moment for national security. This investment allows us to grow our UK operations, create hundreds of skilled jobs and bring cutting-edge surveillance technology, proven on the battlefield in Ukraine, into service with British forces.”
The smaller aircraft come from three British small and medium-sized companies, with deliveries nearing completion. Evolve Dynamics of Hampshire is supplying 245 FOXE-NATO drones weighing less than 250g and fitted with infrared cameras for use at night. Marlborough Communications Limited of Surrey is providing 670 Skydio X10 INTL aircraft, which the department says can be ready to fly in under a minute and reach 45mph. A partnership between Brigantes Consulting of Exeter and Harmattan AI is delivering 110 SONORA drones, designed to help train soldiers before they use similar systems on operations.
That deal has created more than 30 new roles so far, with 18 already filled in Hampshire, Surrey and Exeter, including several veterans. The small drone contract was delivered by the National Armaments Director Group and forms part of Project Rapstone, the Army’s programme to bring new technology to soldiers faster, with the stated goal of doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027 and moving new equipment from industry to the front line within 24 months.
Watchkeeper, the system the AR5 replaces, entered service in 2014 after a development programme that ran considerably over time and cost, and was withdrawn from service earlier this year. The Strategic Defence Review identified its replacement as part of a wider shift towards uncrewed systems, and the Defence Investment Plan commits new investment in the Army’s long-range surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities including the next generation of uncrewed aerial systems.

Belarus to release 25 more prisoners as US eases sanctions

Accusations against Lukashenko
Human rights organization Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the government still holds more than 900 political prisoners. The detainees have been accused of extremism, conspiracy to seize power, incitement of hatred, or insulting the president.
During Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the existence of political prisoners and rejected Viasna's claims.
The two companies to be removed from the US sanctions list are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of industrial paints and coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned company that oversees the forestry, pulp, and paper sectors. These sanctions have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also announced the release of tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets currently held in US banks.

Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max Review: For Camera Fiends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Stellar performance and cooling. Great battery life. Excellent and fun cameras with a customizable camera app. Bright, responsive screens with a smaller Dynamic Island.
TIRED
Pricier than ever. No base model (yet). Living in the iPhone Duo's shadow.
There is no iPhone 18 this year. If you were hoping to upgrade your smartphone right now, Apple is only offering the new iPhone 18 Pro models (and a very expensive folding iPhone coming next month). Don't let that be a reason to spend extra money on a phone you might not need.
Apple hasn't confirmed the next base-model yet, but the iPhone 18 is expected in spring 2027 alongside a mid-tier iPhone 18e. If you've historically been more than satisfied with the base iPhone model, you should absolutely wait to upgrade. Don't let the hype machine sway you.
That said, if you're a Pro connoisseur, the iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199) and its bigger sibling, the 18 Pro Max ($1,299), are very good phones, despite the $100 price hike over last year’s Pro models. No, you don't need to upgrade if you're coming from an iPhone 17 Pro, 16 Pro, or even a 15 Pro—hold onto your devices for longer!—but Apple's flagships deliver where it matters, even if they feel eclipsed by the spectacle of the foldable iPhone Duo.
Minor Refresh
Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro models have significant upgrades, but let's be a little more measured here.
Battery life has been stellar on the Pro models over the last few years, and that remains true here. The Pro Max is the more notable of the two because it packs a denser battery. With average use (around 5 hours of screen-on time), I hovered around 50 percent by the end of the day, and easily made it through day two on a single charge. I spent a little less time with the smaller Pro, but so far it has also comfortably gotten me through a day with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Safe to say, most people will very much enjoy the battery life, but the update doesn't feel drastic.
Next, there's the processor: the A20 Pro chip. I hardly run into problems with Apple's flagship silicon, and that hasn't changed. The phones run every app fluidly, and my benchmark tests show a surprisingly sizable leap over the A19 Pro in the 17 series.
It runs Control—a AAA game from 2019 ported to iOS earlier this year—decently well. However, aggressive upscaling makes the graphics look grainy, and character movements can feel a little sluggish. (I maxed out the graphics settings.) It's certainly not perfect, but I still can't believe I'm playing such a demanding title on an iPhone.
More impressive is Apple's thermal management on these phones. The company has expanded the vapor chamber's surface area by three times—the phone's cooling technology that helps spread heat around—meaning the entire phone felt toasty after close to an hour of gameplay in Control, with no uncomfortable localized hot spots. This larger vapor chamber also lets you game longer before phone’s thermal throttling kicks in and slows everything down.
The iPhone 18 Pro models come with iOS 27 out of the box, which features the all-new Siri AI. Yes, Siri AI is infinitely more capable than any version of Siri that Apple has offered before. It still doesn't quite have the spark or versatility of other AI assistants, but you might be fine with that. If you throw Siri AI a question, there's a good chance it can actually give you a satisfactory answer now. Remember that Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features aren't exclusive to the latest models, though you do need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to access them.
The Dynamic Island, the pill-shaped bar housing the selfie camera and Face ID sensors, is noticeably smaller this year. To take full advantage of it, you can now view three live activities—like a DoorDash order status or your Uber ETA—simultaneously inside the Island, up from two. I was navigating in Apple Maps, chatting on a phone call, and had a DoorDash order en route to my home, and it spaced out all of these activities neatly.
Speaking of the iPhone 18 Pro design, I do like the new burgundy color, though I miss brighter, more playful options like last year's Cosmic Orange. But the real headline feature is almost invisible—embedded into the main camera on the back of the iPhone.
Aperture Priority
Apple is debuting a variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro models. This is by no means the first time we've seen a smartphone with a variable aperture—Samsung and Huawei both launched phones with the capability years ago. While Samsung abandoned the tech, Huawei and Xiaomi still ship it on their flagships.
What is a variable aperture? Simply put, the aperture is the physical opening that lets light reach the camera sensor. A wider aperture lets in more light and has a lower “f-stop” number, while a narrower aperture restricts light. Most smartphones rely on fixed apertures—the iPhone 17 Pro's main camera, for example, is locked at f/1.78. A variable aperture gives the lens mechanical blades that physically expand or contract in a circular shape, adjusting how much light hits the sensor. Apple gives you four f-stops to select from: f/1.48, f/1.78, f/2.8, and f/4.
Open the aperture to f/1.48 on the iPhone 18 Pro and more light floods in, delivering cleaner low-light shots and faster Night Mode captures. This also creates a real optical bokeh—the soft blurred background effect phone makers have spent years simulating with computational Portrait modes. Step it down to f/4, this blur recedes, keeping more of the scene and background in crisp focus. All of this can be very confusing for people unfamiliar with these camera terms, which is why Apple defaults the aperture to “Auto.”
I love it. I shoot manual on my mirrorless camera, so I immediately took to the new customization features in the Camera app to show Shutter Speed and Lens Aperture as easy-to-access settings. Shooting at f/1.48 delivers a nice bokeh effect—especially in low light—so I stopped using Apple's Portrait mode altogether. (Some parts of the image may look less sharp than on an iPhone 17 Pro because the plane of focus is narrower.) Apple will point out that Portrait mode is still useful, as you can always add more bokeh post-capture.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
iPhone 18 Pro Max, main camera with a one-second shutter speed.
Move to f/4 for group shots when you want everyone in the frame to be in focus. (Or if you want a very fun starburst effect with light sources!) As you change between the four aperture settings, you can see the blades moving on the main camera—it's very cool. In auto mode, the camera largely sticks to f/1.78, or f/1.48 in low light. It chooses the other two apertures for specific, usually brighter, scenes.
I have also enjoyed the ability to adjust the camera’s shutter speed. Yes, you can already do this with a third-party camera app, but now it's baked in! With a one-second shutter, you can capture some fun shutter drag to accentuate motion in a photo. However, you'll definitely need to buy a neutral density filter for super-bright scenes to balance exposure. It's fun to play around with.
I compared several of the 18 Pro’s photos with shots from Google's Pixel 11 Pro, and I do have to note that the iPhone tends to over-brighten scenes that should be very dark. So much so that it can misrepresent the dark mood you might be chasing. The Pixel tended to preserve more of those shadows, though it delivered more lifted blacks that made the image appear more matte. The iPhone can also struggle with backlit scenes, more so than the Pixel.
Apple has added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles, and this is a fun element to sink your teeth into and explore. Phone makers have realized that ultra-clean, sharp, “perfect” shots are perhaps not what most people want, and these stylings—like the new Camera Looks on Pixel phones—offer a new degree of “authenticity.”
The iPhone 18 Pro's camera system is fun without feeling overwhelming. You can pick and choose what degree of control you want, tweak Photographic Styles to your tastes, and add more depth after the fact, whether it's for videos or photos. Who knew people liked having more control? There aren't any sweeping improvements to the camera lenses or sensors, but this is a system that shutterbugs will love to experiment with, and that's what the Pro iPhone is all about.
Julian Chokkattu is Senior Editor, Gear at WIRED, overseeing personal technology, gadgets, and gizmos. He has been reviewing consumer products for a decade, specializing in mobile—from smartphones, tablets, and smartwatches to smart glasses and virtual reality. This is his sixth year at WIRED. Men estimate higher rates of sexual objectification than women report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Men and women have different perceptions of how often young women experience sexual objectification, with men sometimes estimating higher frequencies than women themselves report. The study, published in Sex Roles, highlights a disconnect in how different behaviors are perceived and measured. The findings challenge the assumption that men underestimate the everyday harassment women face.
Sexual objectification involves treating a person primarily as a body or a collection of body parts rather than a whole human being. This experience is common for many young women and is linked to negative psychological outcomes like depression, body shame, and a reduced sense of personal safety. In professional and public spaces, these experiences range from unwanted explicit sexual advances to everyday instances of inappropriate body evaluation. Researchers wanted to know if men and women had a shared understanding of how frequently these events happen in daily life.
Olivia A. Foster-Gimbel of Rutgers University and Renee Engeln of Northwestern University conducted the study. The researchers initially predicted that men would estimate lower rates of sexual objectification than women actually experienced. They reasoned that men might lack personal experience with being targeted or might be motivated to downplay the issue to maintain a positive view of their own gender group. Additionally, members of a dominant group often struggle to recognize the disadvantages faced by others.
On the other hand, the researchers recognized that the cultural impact of the #MeToo movement might have successfully educated men about the pervasive nature of these experiences. With so many public discussions about sexual harassment and assault in recent years, men might be highly aware of the issues women navigate on a regular basis. To test these competing ideas, the researchers designed a series of three investigations.
The researchers recruited 110 participants between the ages of 18 and 30 for their first study. Women were asked to report how often they personally experienced various objectifying behaviors on a scale ranging from “never” to “almost always.” Men were asked to estimate how often the average young woman had these same experiences using the identical scale. The behaviors were grouped into two categories: overt actions like catcalling or unwanted touching, and covert actions like staring or evaluating a woman’s physical appearance.
The results contradicted the researchers’ initial expectations. Men estimated that the average woman experienced both overt and covert sexual objectification more frequently than the women reported experiencing it themselves. There were no meaningful differences in how men and women perceived the emotional impact of these events. Both groups agreed on how bad these experiences made women feel, suggesting men understood the negative emotional toll of the behavior.
To explore whether men and women were simply interpreting the verbal rating scale differently, the researchers conducted a second study with 199 university students. Participants again provided ratings from “never” to “almost always,” but this time they also provided a specific numerical estimate, such as a set number of times per year. This allowed the researchers to see if words like “frequently” meant the same thing to both groups. Both men and women also read a short vignette about a fictional woman who was catcalled on her way home from work, and then estimated how often this type of event happened to women like the character in the story.
Once again, men estimated that the average woman experienced higher rates of objectification than the women reported for themselves. This pattern held true for both the verbal scale and the numerical count, showing it was not just a misunderstanding of the scale’s wording. When rating the fictional woman in the story, the pattern reversed. Women estimated that the character experienced this overt harassment more often than men did. This suggested that women might report lower rates of objectification for themselves than they do for other women, a phenomenon sometimes referred to as the denial of personal discrimination.
For the third study, the researchers recruited 165 university students and asked both men and women to estimate frequencies for the “average woman” aged 18 to 30. This approach allowed the researchers to compare expectations directly without the complication of women rating their own personal experiences. Participants evaluated both overt and covert behaviors using the verbal scale and the numerical count. They also provided written explanations for why men and women might differ in their estimates.
When imagining the average woman, the results depended heavily on the type of behavior in question. For overt behaviors like catcalling, women selected higher verbal frequency categories than men did, but their actual numerical estimates were roughly the same. Both groups estimated that overt objectification happened about 30 times a year. For covert behaviors like leering, the verbal scale ratings were similar between the genders, but men estimated a much higher numerical count, guessing that covert objectification happened 365 times a year compared to the estimate of 267 times provided by women.
The written responses revealed several potential reasons for these discrepancies. Nearly half of the participants suggested that men’s higher estimates might stem from their awareness of how often they or other men perpetrate these behaviors. Others noted that women might not always notice covert actions like being stared at from behind. Some respondents also proposed that men might deliberately guess higher numbers to avoid seeming ignorant or insensitive in a cultural climate that encourages believing women.
The researchers note a few limitations to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study only included participants who identified as either men or women. This leaves out the experiences and perceptions of transgender and nonbinary individuals, who also face high rates of sexual objectification. A general reader might assume these findings apply to all age groups, but the research focused exclusively on perceptions of women between the ages of 18 and 30.
Future research could explore how estimates of sexual objectification change when considering older women or women of different racial backgrounds. Different communities experience and interpret objectification in varying ways, which could alter the numerical estimates and perceptions of frequency. Additionally, the data were collected in the years immediately following the peak of the #MeToo movement. Social attitudes continue to shift, and subsequent surveys will be needed to see if these patterns hold up over time. Ultimately, focusing workplace and social interventions on the negative mental health impacts of objectification might be more effective than debating exactly how often it occurs.
The study, “A Mile in Her Heels: Do Men and Women Agree on How Often Women Are Sexually Objectified?,” was authored by Olivia A. Foster-Gimbel and Renee Engeln.

According to the Operational Command’s spokesperson, Lt Col Jacek Goryszewski, the most likely explanation is that the drone drifted from international waters to Poland's territorial waters.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Sunday that “the coming weeks and months will be a period of very intense Russian activity,” adding that “the escalation of the Russian Federation's actions is becoming a fact, and examples of this are getting closer and closer to our border.”

Pope Leo says Middle East conflicts strain Jewish-Christian relations
VATICAN CITY, Sept 16 - Pope Leo said on Wednesday that recent conflicts in the Middle East had tested relations between Jews and Christians, adding that differing views of the ongoing violence had strained dialogue but not broken it.
In a new decree to mark the Catholic Church's last 60 years of efforts at inter-religious dialogue, the pope also reiterated the Church's condemnations of both antisemitism and Islamophobia.
"The conflicts that have erupted in the Middle East in recent years have ... left their mark on Jewish-Christian dialogue," said the decree, developed by three top Vatican offices and approved by Leo.
"Many channels of communication have been strained," it said. "Nevertheless, the pillars of dialogue among believers, built over 60 years of common effort, have remained firm. Upon these foundations, it is both possible and necessary to continue building."
The decree, issued to mark the anniversary of a 1965 Church document widely credited with improving centuries of acrimony between Jews and Christians, did not mention any specific Middle East conflicts.
Leo, the first U.S.-born pope, has previously criticised the Iran war, drawing the ire of President Donald Trump on social media.
Wednesday's decree described fighting antisemitism as a "shared struggle" for Jews and Christians. It also said attitudes of Islamophobia "fail to distinguish" between cases of extremist violence and the everyday lives of the world's Muslims. REUTERS
