Auditor general: Defense scandals pose no security threat to Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:58:00 UTC
20:58:00 KST

Auditor general: Defense scandals pose no security threat to Estonia
Auditor General Janar Holm told ERR that the scandals that have emerged in the defense sector in recent months do not pose a security threat to Estonia. He said openly discussing problems instead makes the country stronger.
"I know many countries where it is not possible to talk about such things. This only makes us stronger," Holm said in response to a question about whether scandals in the defense sector pose a security threat to Estonia.
At the same time, Holm said the situation in the defense sector is concerning because several of the problems are systemic. He added that the more money that flows into the sector, the greater the confusion becomes.
The National Audit Office found problems with both the acceptance of goods and the awarding of contracts in 64 contracts handled by the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK). "Wherever we looked, there was some kind of problem," Holm said. In his view, a conventional inventory is not sufficient for accounting for Estonian Defense Forces stocks and a more digital system is needed.
EDF needs accounting rules
Holm said the Estonian Defense Forces, like all other government agencies in Estonia, must begin complying with accounting rules. He said this is important, on the one hand, for the Defense Forces itself, so that it has a quick and up-to-date overview of its assets and where they are located. On the other hand, the public must be able to see whether the money allocated to the defense sector has reached its intended destination.
However, because of problems with the accounting records, a situation arose this year in which the National Audit Office went to audit the annual report and the Defense Forces and Ministry of Defense said they had €1.2 billion worth of stocks. The National Audit Office cannot confirm whether the stocks are actually worth €1.2 billion because of the problems with the accounting records. "It seems to us that the figure should be somewhat higher," Holm said.
When there is confusion, it creates fertile ground for someone with bad intentions to take something for themselves at the state's expense. Efforts are now underway to determine what assets should be there in the first place in order to establish what is missing. Holm said there is also confusion surrounding the artillery shell deal, with the information lacking a clear audit trail.
Difficult to place blame without information
When information is lacking, it is also difficult to determine who is responsible. Holm said the parties are shifting the blame back and forth. "From the National Audit Office's perspective, what matters here is something that is often regarded as bureaucracy — namely, documentation," he said.
The National Audit Office has also told the Estonian Center for Defense Investments that the information does not provide a clear audit trail.
"We are now arguing over this and classified information is also creating a great deal of confusion, but presumably there will be clarity at some point," Holm said. He said primary responsibility always lies with the agency that enters into a transaction. In this case, the main responsibility lies with the head of the Estonian Center for Defense Investments, who signed the contract.

Not Mumbai, not Delhi: This North Indian city tops India in domestic expenditure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:57:31 UTC
20:57:31 KST

As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually.
Chandigarh has emerged as India's highest-spending city on a per-household basis, according to The Many Urban Indias, a report by People’s Research on India’s Consumer Economy (PRICE) and Tata Sons. An average household in the city spends nearly Rs 19 lakh a year, putting Chandigarh ahead of India's biggest metropolitan centres on this measure. The study examines how households across India’s 100 leading cities earn, spend, save and borrow.
Chandigarh has the highest average household spending in India
The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.
Chandigarh is identified as the city with the highest average household consumption in the report. As per the study, an average household in Chandigarh spends nearly Rs 19 lakh annually. The distinction is about average spending per household, not the total amount spent across the entire city. This matters because larger cities have many more households and can generate a much bigger overall consumer market even when their average household spending is lower.The report identifies Chandigarh as a Frontier city, a category comprising the smaller urban centres among India's top 100 cities by population.
It places the city among the country's highest-spending urban centres, alongside Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala. The report also highlights Chandigarh's household financial position, noting that it has high levels of savings and low levels of debt.
Chandigarh and Bengaluru have the highest average household income
Chandigarh’s spending figures become more interesting when viewed alongside household income. According to the study, Bengaluru and Chandigarh have the highest average household income in India, at Rs 28 lakh per year. India's six largest metropolitan centres- Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata and Hyderabad are grouped together as the Big Six in the study. They have more than 10 million people each and account for a substantial share of the country's urban economic activity.
Delhi NCR is a major part of the report’s consumption story. The study says that Delhi NCR has a total consumption market worth $126 billion. This is nearly as much as Mumbai and Bengaluru combined. The report attributes this to two factors: Delhi NCR has around 7.5 million households, compared with 4.6 million in Mumbai. Its average annual household consumption is nearly Rs 15 lakh. This gives Delhi NCR a large overall consumption market, even though Chandigarh leads on average household spending.
Delhi NCR’s transportation spending alone is bigger than some cities
One of the report’s more striking findings concerns transportation. Delhi NCR households spend more than $33 billion annually on transportation, according to the study. That amount is larger than the total consumption market of Pune or Ahmedabad. The report also estimates that Delhi NCR’s annual dairy consumption is around $10 billion.
Mumbai: More high-income households, but not the highest average spending
Mumbai remains one of India’s major consumption centres, but the report places it behind Chandigarh on average household spending. The study says that Amritsar, Ahmedabad and Jabalpur have higher average household spending than Mumbai. At the same time, Mumbai leads the 100-city group in the share of high-income households.
The report defines high-income households as those earning more than Rs 36 lakh annually at 2025-26 prices. Their share across the 100 cities has increased to 12%, from 3% a decade earlier.
Bengaluru: Highest average income, but Chandigarh leads consumption
Bengaluru is another important comparison in the report. The city shares the highest average household income position with Chandigarh, at Rs 28 lakh per year. However, the report says that Chandigarh and Thiruvananthapuram have the highest average household consumption in India. It also identifies Surat as a city where average household consumption is higher than Bengaluru’s. This means Bengaluru’s high average income does not automatically translate into the highest average household spending.The report groups the cities into four categories:
Big Six: Cities with populations above 10 million.
Boomtowns: Cities with populations between 2.5 million and 10 million.
Breakout cities: Cities with populations between 1.5 million and 2.5 million.
Frontier cities: Cities with populations between 0.5 million and 1.5 million.
Chandigarh falls in the Frontier category, while Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are part of the Big Six.

67 killed in gold mine collapse in Sudan’s West Kordofan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:57:18 UTC
20:57:18 KST

Ikrame Kouachi
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
At least 67 people were killed after the Al-Zara gold mine collapsed in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, with search operations continuing for survivors, the Sudan Doctors Network said Wednesday.
“More than 67 people were killed” when the mine collapsed near Al-Nuhud in West Kordofan, which is under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the independent medical network said in a statement.
It said search operations were still underway for survivors or people trapped under the rubble, warning that the death toll could rise due to the mine’s lack of basic safety and protection measures for workers.
The network condemned “the negligence that had put miners’ lives at risk,” saying that mining in areas controlled by the RSF, without safety requirements or adequate protection and rescue equipment, “turns work into a direct risk to civilians’ lives.”
It called for search-and-rescue operations to continue and for the provision of the medical and logistical resources needed to deal with the disaster.
The Sudan Doctors Network also urged authorities controlling the area to “assume responsibility for protecting civilians and mining workers and to halt unregulated mining activities to prevent similar accidents.”
Artisanal mining employs more than 2 million people across Sudan under harsh conditions and accounts for about 80% of the country’s total gold production.
The Sudanese government does not prohibit artisanal mining but has sought to regulate the sector, which provides livelihoods for large numbers of Sudanese despite its risks.
Gold is a major source of foreign currency for Sudan after the country lost three-quarters of its oil revenues following South Sudan’s independence in July 2011, along with about 80% of its foreign-exchange resources.
Sudan has been gripped by war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Returning after unauthorized absence does not mean automatic reinstatement in service - Ministry of Defence
Kyiv • UNN
After a service member returns from unauthorized absence, they may continue their service only through the established procedure. Until the order is issued, duties, payments, and benefits are not restored.
Returning after unauthorized abandonment of a military unit does not mean automatic continuation of military service. This was reported by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The ministry noted that, pursuant to Part Two of Article 24 of the Law of Ukraine "On Military Duty and Military Service," service members whose military service has been suspended:
-  are dismissed from their positions; 
-  are considered not to be performing (not carrying out)
the duties of military service; 
-  are not included in the personnel strength of the Armed Forces of Ukraine or
other military formations. 
After returning to the unit, service must be resumed in accordance with the procedure established by law. Only after the relevant order is issued may the service member be assigned duties, and their monetary support, benefits, and social guarantees be reinstated
To remind you
Earlier, the Ministry of Defense stated that Ukrainian service members who committed unauthorized abandonment of their unit while abroad may use a simplified procedure for returning to service.
Service members who committed unauthorized abandonment of their unit, including abroad, through June 12, 2026, inclusive, may use the simplified program for returning to the military.
UNN also reported that a new status has appeared in the "Army+" mobile application for service members returning after unauthorized abandonment of their unit.

Scotland imposes mandatory environmental assessments on new datacentres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:55:33 UTC
20:55:33 KST

Large-scale datacentres will face mandatory environmental assessments before they can go ahead, the Scottish government has announced, amid growing public concern about the impact of the AI boom.
Ahead of a vote on a moratorium on new hyperscale datacentres in Holyrood on Wednesday, the Scottish government has tightened rules for new projects by requiring any above 50MW to submit environmental impact assessments, but stopped short of agreeing to an outright halt.
Scotland has seen a boom in planning applications for large datacentres as global investment in AI infrastructure has exploded. Datacentres are critical for storing and processing data used by AI. One scheme in Auchtertool, Fife, has been billed as the second-largest in the world, and is among more than 20 large datacentres proposed so far.
Campaigners have raised concerns about water usage and carbon emissions from large datacentres, and questioned whether Scotland has the capacity to cope with the resulting explosion in energy demand.
The Scottish Greens have submitted a motion for Wednesday calling for a moratorium on new projects “until a national strategy and updated planning guidance are produced, which takes into account the cumulative impacts on energy demand and the environment”.
This month, hundreds from community groups protested outside Holyrood against the construction of large datacentres for AI until clear planning rules and the definition of a “green” datacentre had been formalised.
On Thursday, AI leaders will gather at Dumfries House, Ayrshire, for a summit with King Charles on the future of the technology, amid warnings that the speed of its development threatens the survival of humanity.
In a statement, the public finance minister Hannah Mary Goodlad said the Scottish government recognised that evidence on the environmental impact was still developing,
“We must balance the economic and employment interests in developing datacentres with national energy, climate and community wealth-building ambitions, which are vital to our future prosperity, as well as the potential impact on local communities,” she said.
“Ensuring that an environmental impact assessment is always part of the application process will create a level playing field for developers, and will ensure potentially significant environmental effects are considered from the outset.”
Kat Jones, the director of the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, who has spearheaded demands for a datacentre moratorium in Scotland, said requiring environmental impact assessments was a “no-brainer”, but that questions remained about the impact of the datacentre buildout on Scotland’s infrastructure.
“This is extremely good news and something that we have been asking for since the start of our campaign, but without a moratorium, the other essential work can’t be done. A pause on planning decisions is absolutely essential,” she said.
“Just the first four applications under consideration at the moment would use as much energy as is generated by Torness nuclear power station, which is due to close in 2030. A modest pause will give time for the government to put in place the necessary planning guidance, assess how much datacentre capacity Scotland actually needs and where any should go, and assess and manage the impacts on the grid and the climate.”

STRASBOURG, France, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed opening the door for Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union (EU), as she unveiled plans for closer security cooperation, tighter migration controls and stricter bans on children's social media use.
In her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, von der Leyen said the EU and Canada would seek to upgrade their ties from the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) to an "Alliance for the Future," covering manufacturing, technology, defense, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals and artificial intelligence (AI).

Von der Leyen also proposed what she called "Europe's own Article 4," modelled on NATO's consultation mechanism, under which EU member states will convene when one country faces a serious security incident below the threshold of armed aggression.
She further proposed creating a European Security Council involving EU leaders and partners including Canada, Norway, Ukraine and Britain.
The State of the Union address sets out the Commission president's priorities for the EU for the coming year and is the centerpiece of the European Parliament's four-day plenary session, which opened Monday. ■

In the latest such effort, the United States will lift its sanctions on Belarusian paint manufacturer Lakokraska and forestry sector group Bellesbumprom, Coale told the state news agency BelTA.
The United States and the European Union hit Lukashenko and his government with major sanctions in the wake of the 2020 presidential election, in which Lukashenko, in power since 1994, claimed victory.
Further restrictions were imposed in 2022 after Minsk allowed Moscow to use Belarusian territory as a launchpad for its invasion of Ukraine.
“We will continue to improve US-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future,” he wrote on X, having earlier told BelTA that “additional sanctions relief” would continue to be granted in exchange.
Coale later told Reuters in an interview that he expects to return to Belarus in about one month's time, possibly to announce the release of many more prisoners.
"I hope hundreds (are released). I don't know. That's my hope," Coale was quoted as saying.
"I'm confident that we'll get a lot more out."
Following the latest round of diplomacy, exiled Belarusian opposition leader Svyatlana Tsikhanouskaya wrote on X that she was “happy for every person who has finally found themselves free today” and “for their families and loved ones who have been waiting for this day.”
“Every person released is a victory. So today’s release is another humanitarian result,” she said, adding, however, that “it is far from the end of this process,” with hundreds of other prisoners remaining behind bars in Belarus.
According to earlier estimates by the Viasna rights group, which monitors arrests and is banned in Belarus, the country was still holding more than 900 political prisoners, even as Washington negotiated the release of hundreds of detainees beginning in 2025.
While Belarusian opposition figures have largely welcomed US efforts to secure the release of prisoners, experts say Lukashenko is using the issue to “legitimize” his rule internationally and is arresting more people to replace those freed, an assertion denied by the Belarusian leader during his talks with Coale in Minsk.
“For Lukashenko, the most important thing is...strengthening his political agency,” Vadim Mozheiko, director of the Krakow-based Kosciuszko Institute, told Current Time on September 16, adding that this “is especially important given his lack of domestic legitimacy.”
Separately, Mozheiko pointed out that a “significant proportion of those released were forcibly deported from Belarus,” a move he described as “yet another form of repression.”
A September 15 report by the UN experts said that "Belarusian authorities are using the country’s criminal justice system as an instrument of repression, systematically targeting and persecuting individuals deemed to oppose the government."
"Plainclothes officers routinely detain individuals they label as critical of the Government without warrants, subject them to beatings and stress positions, deny access to lawyers, and force them to record humiliating 'repentance' videos under duress and threats against their families," it added.
After Coale released a picture of the people freed on September 16, RFE/RL’s Belarus Service identified several prominent figures among them who had been arrested amid Belarus’s crackdown on anti-government protests and in the years that followed.
Among them was Lyudmila Chekina, the director-general of Belarus’s popular news portal Tut.by, which was shut down amid pressure from the country’s authorities in 2021.
She was sentenced to 12 years in prison on various charges, including “harming the national security of the Republic of Belarus.”
Paval Belavus, a noted art manager and founder of a popular shop selling Belarusian national symbols, was also released. He had previously been sentenced to 13 years in prison on high treason and other charges.

US court dismisses 4chan’s case against Britain’s media regulator
- A US court dismissed 4chan and Kiwi Farms' lawsuit against Britain's media regulator Ofcom, citing lack of jurisdiction and advising them to defend themselves in UK courts.
- The dispute arose over Ofcom enforcing the UK's Online Safety Act, aiming to protect children and vulnerable users from illegal online content, with fines imposed on 4chan.
- Ofcom received full UK government support, and the court acknowledged its right to regulate, rejecting the forums' claims that enforcement violated their US constitutional rights.
AI generated
US internet forums 4chan and Kiwi Farms’ lawsuit against Britain’s media regulator Ofcom has been dismissed by a court in Washington, DC, which said it did not have jurisdiction to rule on the matter.
The owners of the forums clashed with Ofcom over its enforcement of Britain’s Online Safety Act, legislation which has caused broader tension between US tech companies and Britain.
Critics of the law, which is designed to protect children and vulnerable users from illegal content online, have said it threatens free speech. The British government has “fully backed” Ofcom in taking action.
4chan, an irreverent site that hosts content including pornography and conspiracy theories, and Kiwi Farms had said “threatening communications” they had received from the British regulator interfered with their constitutional rights and operations.
Ofcom had accused both of failing to respond to its statutory information requests.
Ofcom sent 4chan a “provisional notice of contravention” on Aug 12, 2025, that threatened to impose a fine of £20,000 (S$34,200) as well as daily fines of £100 for up to 60 days. 4chan brought its suit later that month.
The regulator imposed the fine – the first under the new regime – in October.
The US court ruling, dated Sept 15, said the plaintiffs could defend themselves in British courts. It added that if Ofcom obtained a judgment, that would most likely have to be enforced in the United States, because the companies had no presence or operations abroad.
At that point they could take their case to US courts, the judgment said.
“Put simply, plaintiffs’ suit fails because they seek to use American courts as a sword against Ofcom rather than as a shield to protect themselves,” District Judge Rudolph Contreras said.
An Ofcom spokesperson said: “A US Court has acknowledged that we are within our rights as a UK regulator to investigate breaches of the UK’s online safety laws, and has dismissed claims by 4chan and Kiwi Farms who have sought to stop us doing our job of creating a safer life online for people in the UK.” REUTERS

STRASBOURG, France, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed opening the door for Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union (EU), as she unveiled plans for closer security cooperation, tighter migration controls and stricter bans on children's social media use.
In her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, von der Leyen said the EU and Canada would seek to upgrade their ties from the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) to an "Alliance for the Future," covering manufacturing, technology, defense, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals and artificial intelligence (AI).
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," she told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who attended the address.
"We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics," she said, adding that she wants to bring the relationship with Canada to "the highest level possible."
Von der Leyen also proposed what she called "Europe's own Article 4," modelled on NATO's consultation mechanism, under which EU member states will convene when one country faces a serious security incident below the threshold of armed aggression.
She further proposed creating a European Security Council involving EU leaders and partners including Canada, Norway, Ukraine and Britain.
On migration, von der Leyen cited this summer's crisis in Ceuta, Spain's North African enclave, and said the Commission will propose a European Emergency Response Framework allowing limited flexibility in standard procedures under strictly defined emergency conditions.
She also pledged to strengthen Frontex, accelerate returns, improve early-warning systems and deepen cooperation with third countries. "It is we, Europeans, who decide who comes to our Union and under what circumstances," she said.
Von der Leyen said the Commission will propose an EU Kids Act on Thursday that will prohibit social media use for children under 13 and personal accounts for those under 15. Children aged 13 to 15 will only be allowed limited accounts supervised by parents, while platforms will face mandatory safe-design requirements for users aged 15 to 18.
Von der Leyen also addressed critical raw materials, climate resilience, AI, energy security and the bloc's future enlargement.
The State of the Union address sets out the Commission president's priorities for the EU for the coming year and is the centerpiece of the European Parliament's four-day plenary session, which opened Monday. ■

A gold mine collapse killed at least 67 people in a remote area in Sudan, a medical group and survivors said Wednesday.
The tragedy happened in al-Zara gold mine in the town of Nuhud in West Kordofan province. The area is under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which has been at war with the country’s military for over three years.

US President Donald Trump claimed Moscow and Kyiv have agreed not to target each other’s energy infrastructure, but no deal has been confirmed, and strikes have continued.
Kyiv is ready for an energy ceasefire with Moscow, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, adding that Russia has yet to make the same commitment.
In an interview with CBS, Zelenskyy said US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility during their recent visit to Kyiv. He said Ukraine agreed, on condition that Russia also stops all attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure**.**
“We never attack first. Our tactic is to respond where we can because Putin doesn’t respect and won’t even think of negotiating with weaklings,” Zelenskyy said.
“When Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were here, they proposed thinking about refineries and other energy. I told them we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but you need to know what that means for Ukraine.”
Zelenskyy stressed that an energy ceasefire would have to cover different types of infrastructure: Russian oil and gas facilities targeted by Kyiv, and the electricity and gas infrastructure Moscow has repeatedly struck in Ukraine**.**
“For Putin, energy is selling oil and gas. For us, energy is having electricity and gas supplies for our people,” Zelenskyy said.
“My message was, if the Russians are ready for an energy ceasefire, it means no strikes of any kind with any type of weapon on energy.”
But Moscow is yet to change its tactic. Right after Donald Trump announced the energy truce, the Kremlin-affiliated outlets presented it as a one-way measure, claiming Kyiv will stop its long-range strikes. There was no word regarding Moscow not attacking Ukraine.
The Kremlin has described the proposal as a “very good idea,” but has also linked the wider energy issue to safe commercial shipping, particularly for oil tankers, and the lifting of sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries and other oil infrastructure, saying that energy revenues help finance Moscow’s ongoing all-out war.
Russia meanwhile has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s electricity and gas infrastructure, leaving the country and millions of Ukrainians particularly vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of war.

China Focus: Sci-tech innovation propels China's services trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:54:31 CST
20:54:31 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Zhang Qianchao, a solo exporter armed with just two computers, attracted large crowds at the Alibaba booth during this year's China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), which wrapped up on Sunday in Beijing.
Zhang, whose employees are eight artificial intelligence agents that vet clients, design products and chase orders around the clock, once sold more than 3,000 baseball caps to buyers in Europe, North America and Africa in just two months.
"A client thought I had been in foreign trade for 10 years," said Zhang. When a Middle East customer sent a customized request, the AI "designer" returned three mock-ups within minutes, and a deal worth thousands of U.S. dollars was sealed on the spot. Behind his cap exports is a suite of AI-powered services, handling everything from market research and product design to order management.
Zhang's story indicates that technology-intensive services are becoming a driver of China's services trade. In the first seven months of 2026, China's services exports rose 17.1 percent year on year, and knowledge-intensive services made up more than half.
TOKEN AS COMMODITY
More than 10 million small and medium-sized enterprises worldwide now run their businesses on Accio Work, an agent platform built by Alibaba's international branch. Its user count has grown more than 30-fold in a single year.
"We want every entrepreneur, regardless of team size, to access an intelligent workforce that operates with the scale of a major corporation," said Kuo Zhang, president of Alibaba.com, the company's international website.
China's telecom companies are also supplying the same workforce. China's three major telecom operators showcased their self-developed AI agents in an exhibition hall. Leading the display was China Mobile's MobileClaw, a desktop AI office agent launched for public trials in March with 25 million free tokens. MobileClaw can write code, prepare reports and manage e-mail accounts for its users.
All this work is metered in tokens, units used by large language models to process information and determine pricing. At the fair, China Telecom displayed tiered token packages at its booth, available for purchase as easily as a mobile data plan. Meanwhile, China Mobile International showcased a compute trading platform that allows clients to access models across borders and settle payments by token.
China Mobile says its digital services abroad already serve more than 15,000 enterprise clients, from a port in Peru and factory operations in Thailand to a tax system in Australia.
Various regions across China are also experimenting with token-based trade. In late August, an AI company in the port city of Xiamen completed what the city described as its first commercial "token export": its home-grown model delivered scripts, translations and voice-overs to a livestream-commerce client in Ethiopia, with the first trade totaling 2.7 billion tokens. At the fair, Guangxi-based firm Runjian presented a "token factory" that supplies computing power on demand to Southeast Asian clients.
Tokens are increasingly integrated into finance. At the fair's financial hall, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China launched an eight-product compute-finance suite, from settlement and computing loans to equity services, while insurer PICC rolled out insurance for the compute-power industry.
SHIFT IN SERVICES
The token trade represents just one frontier in a broader transformation, from exporting hardware to exporting services. BeiDou, China's satellite navigation system, has made a similar shift. Unveiled at the fair, its new overseas platform exports a long-lasting service which delivers continuous positioning and timing feeds from Chinese satellites. The service can be accessed inside client countries and is compatible with the world's major navigation constellations.
"In the past, our partners exported devices to many countries, while operations and services lagged behind," said Xu Junjie, a senior expert with the platform's developer. "Moving from equipment exports to service exports will carry the whole industrial chain abroad."
Weather services show the same shift at a larger scale. MAZU, an early-warning system named after China's guardian goddess of the sea and developed for the United Nations' Early Warnings for All initiative, integrates Fengyun satellite observations, numerical weather prediction and AI models. It can be delivered via the cloud or locally deployed. Custom versions now run in seven countries, from Pakistan and Sri Lanka to Djibouti, and its cloud products serve weather services in more than 40 countries.
China Unicom's digital operations have already reached abroad. It has deployed a goods-to-person system in an e-commerce park in the United Arab Emirates and a 5G-powered sorting line in the Czech Republic that handles over 1,000 parcels an hour at 99 percent accuracy.
SELLING INTO CHINA
While Chinese players take their services abroad, foreign companies are also selling their smart services into this market. Honeywell Technologies made its CIFTIS debut with Forge, an industrial AI platform that turns operating data from factories, buildings and data centers into real-time guidance on maintenance, energy use and operations.
Serving more than 25,000 customers at 288,000 sites worldwide, the Honeywell platform opened a Chinese version hosted only on Chinese cloud services in July. "Debuting at CIFTIS carries special meaning for us," said Yu Feng, president of Honeywell China, pinpointing the growing demand for industrial software and whole-lifecycle services.
Schneider Electric came with a concrete version of the same pitch: AI-assisted services for power distribution, critical power and industrial automation that promise to catch failures before they happen. "With AI and digital technologies, we are moving from after-the-fact repairs to proactive prediction and preventive maintenance," said Xu Shaofeng, senior vice president of its services business in China.
China's annual trade in services has exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars. "Services consumption and services trade have become a vital pillar supporting economic growth, smoothing circulation and boosting competitiveness," said Li Jun, who heads international services trade research at an academy under the Ministry of Commerce. "China is moving from a big trader in services to a strong one." ■

Tsahkna on Commission President’s State of the Union address: Estonia supports building a geopolitically stronger Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:54:30 UTC
20:54:30 KST

“Europe must be able to stand up for its interests, preserve and increase its prosperity, and ensure its security. Achieving these objectives requires greater competitiveness, reduced dangerous dependencies, increased investment in defence and closer cooperation with like-minded partners. All of these issues were also addressed in today’s State of the Union address,” Tsahkna said.
“Security and defence were identified in the address as priority areas for the European Union, which is entirely appropriate given the current security environment and the threat posed by Russia. These areas require both sustained political attention and funding from the EU, also on the Eastern Flank,” Tsahkna said. “The Commission President put forward several new ideas on security, which can be assessed in greater detail once they are presented to the member states in a more concrete form.”
According to the Foreign Minister, NATO remains the cornerstone of European security, and all EU activities in the field of security and defence must be aligned with NATO’s objectives.
The Foreign Minister welcomed the idea expressed in the address that ensuring European security requires looking beyond the European Union and developing ever closer cooperation with other NATO Allies and like-minded countries.
“Von der Leyen’s proposal to discuss creating a form of associate membership of the European Union for Canada is a highly ambitious idea, demonstrating that Europe understands the need to strengthen its relations with partners in different ways in the interests of its security and economic success,” Tsahkna said.
According to Tsahkna, it was also welcome that von der Leyen highlighted Europe’s strengths.
“Europe often lacks confidence, even though we actually have much to be proud of and much that we can use to make our continent an even stronger actor on the world stage. We have a large single market, world-class industry, substantial savings and a powerful currency. We must recognise these strengths and make full use of them,” Tsahkna said.
According to the Foreign Minister, Europe’s geopolitical strength is inextricably linked to how Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine ends.
“The Commission President rightly noted in her address that Ukraine is currently fighting for both its own freedom and ours,” Tsahkna said. “Nevertheless, I would have expected concrete proposals on how to ensure that Ukraine has, above all, the financial resources it needs to get through a difficult winter.”
“During my recent visit to Ukraine, the need for financial support was the message I heard most clearly. I would therefore have expected the address to include a proposal to use Russia’s frozen assets to cover Ukraine’s critical financing needs,” Tsahkna said.
According to the Foreign Minister, there should also have been a stronger message about what kind of Europe we want to see once Russia’s aggression has ended and how Europe’s long-term security will then be ensured.
“Europe must work towards achieving a just and lasting peace while at the same time developing the post-war order. I am convinced that ensuring Europe’s long-term security requires us to move decisively forward with European Union enlargement so that there are no grey areas between the EU and Russia,” Tsahkna said. He added that the Commission President’s messages on enlargement could have been even stronger.
“While the positive and fundamental impact of EU membership on acceding countries is often discussed, we should more frequently remind ourselves that EU enlargement also benefits the current member states. It creates a larger single market, thereby improving the economic prospects of member states, and makes the EU an even stronger global actor.”
According to Tsahkna, the Commission President was also right to emphasise that Europe must reduce dangerous dependencies.
“We have done this with Russian fossil fuels, and we must move forward just as decisively when it comes to critical raw materials, energy, technology and other strategic supply chains. This is both an economic and a security issue,” Tsahkna said. He added that the proposal put forward in the address to establish a European critical raw materials corporation, which would help Europe jointly procure critical raw materials and build up reserves, was worth considering.
“No European country can act alone when it comes to critical raw materials. We need cooperation to reduce dependencies, secure supplies of critical raw materials for our industries and increase Europe’s own processing capacity,” Tsahkna said, adding that Estonia has an important role to play in this area through the NEO plant in Narva.
“A strong Europe is built through investment in defence capabilities, continued support for Ukraine, a stronger defence industry, a competitive economy and a willingness to take responsibility for its own security,” Tsahkna said. “Estonia supports this ambition and expects us to move swiftly from words to action.”

EyesOnSci | Chinese Gravity-1 rocket launches new satellites from sea
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
19:54:29 CST
20:54:29 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- China launched nine satellites into preset orbits on Wednesday from waters off the coast of Shanghai in east China.
The Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center carried out the launch mission. The satellites, a new group of Qianfan Constellation satellites and an EUHT technology test satellite, lifted off at 6 a.m. (Beijing Time) atop a Gravity-1 Y3 carrier rocket. The mission was declared a complete success.
The mission set new records for China's single sea launch in terms of payload weight and orbital altitude, with a net payload weight of over three tonnes and an insertion altitude of about 800 kilometers, verifying the sea launch model's adaptability to medium- and large-sized satellite payload missions, according to the Chinese commercial aerospace company OrienSpace, the developer of the rocket.
The Gravity-1 rocket has carried out four sea launches so far, all of which were successful. Today's mission marked Gravity-1's first launch for the networking of a large low-Earth-orbit satellite internet constellation.
According to OrienSpace, the satellites aboard the rocket were manufactured in Shanghai and launched from waters near Shanghai. Such land-sea coordination helps improve the overall efficiency of both commercial space manufacturing and launch operations.

As companies prepare their 2027 business plans, expectations remain cautious. In hryvnia terms, 53% anticipate revenue growth next year, while 29% expect revenues to decline and 18% foresee no change from 2026. In US dollar terms, however, sentiment is less optimistic: 41% expect revenues to fall, 36% predict growth, and 23% expect them to remain stable.

The findings, drawn from the European Business Association’s (EBA) annual survey of member-company CEOs, capture a corporate sector that has learned to operate in a wartime environment with no clear end in sight. That being said, 38% expect output or sales volumes to decline in 2027, 35% predict growth, and 27% anticipate no change.
Despite the caution, some companies are still planning to expand. About 3% of respondents intend to launch new large-scale investment projects in 2027, with an average expected price tag of around $5 million.
“Business today operates under increasing pressure from enemy strikes,” the EBA quoted its executive director, Anna Derevyanko, as saying in a press release.

KHARTOUM, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- At least 63 people were killed in a gold mine collapse in Sudan's West Kordofan State, according to survivors and eyewitnesses on Wednesday.
A survivor told Xinhua by phone that the accident occurred Tuesday at the Al-Zaraa mine in the Al-Riqiq area in West Kordofan.
He said parts of the mine, which consists of about 10 shafts, suddenly collapsed, and estimated that more than 300 people could be trapped inside.
Another survivor told Xinhua that local rescue teams had recovered 63 bodies from the collapsed mine on Wednesday.
"Search operations are still underway for missing people trapped under the rubble," he said. "Search and rescue efforts are facing great difficulties due to the depth of the shafts and the lack of specialized equipment."
Meanwhile, according to an eyewitness at the mine, the collapse affected several adjacent shafts, burying dozens of miners.
Difficulties in reaching the bottoms of the shafts and a lack of appropriate machinery had hampered efforts to recover the victims, the eyewitness said.
Artisanal mining is a major source of income for many Sudanese and produces about 80 percent of the country's gold. The sector operates at more than 800 sites across northern and western Sudan, employing over 1.5 million miners.
Gold is one of Sudan's major sources of foreign currency. According to official statistics, Sudan produced 70 tons of gold in 2025. Accidents are frequent at mining sites due to inadequate safety measures and deteriorating infrastructure. ■

20 dead, dozens missing after war-damaged building falls in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:54:13 UTC
20:54:13 KST

Breadcrumb
20 Palestinians dead and dozens missing after war-damaged building collapses in Gaza
At least 20 Palestinians, including at least 5 children, were killed and more than dozens injured after a war-damaged residential building collapsed in Gaza City at dawn on Wednesday, with around 100 people still missing or feared trapped beneath the rubble, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health, Civil Defence and eyewitnesses.
The six-storey Al-Saada Building collapsed at around 2:15 a.m. on Al-Sina'a Street, southwest of Gaza City, while residents were asleep, according to local eyewitnesses.
The building had been damaged during Israel's war on Gaza and was sheltering families whose homes had been destroyed or damaged.
The collapse also struck tents belonging to displaced Palestinians that had been erected near the building.
In a press statement, Gaza's Ministry of Health said 20 bodies had been recovered and more than 25 people injured as rescue teams continued searching for survivors and those missing beneath the debris.
The ministry said the latest collapse brings to 50 the number of Palestinians killed in the collapse of war-damaged buildings across Gaza since Israel's war began on October 2023.
Gaza Civil Defence said around 100 people were inside or around the building when it collapsed. Its teams, working with the Gaza Municipality, the Egyptian Committee and the International Committee of the Red Cross, rescued 16 people and recovered 20 bodies, while others remained beneath the rubble.
A man emerged from the rubble, but his family did not
Khaled al-Okka, a father of six, was among those who were rescued and taken to hospital, but his family remains trapped beneath the collapsed building.
From his hospital bed, he has been following reports from the rescue site, waiting anxiously for news of his relatives.
"The collapse happened suddenly as residents slept, leaving us with virtually no time to escape," he recalled the incident to The New Arab.
He found himself trapped beneath the rubble before rescue workers eventually reached him and pulled him out.
"My thoughts have been focused on my children and other family members who remained inside the building," he said.
"My greatest fear now is for my children and my family," he added. "I was pulled out, but they are still under the rubble. I do not know what happened to them or whether they were able to reach a safe part of the building before it collapsed."
He said residents had no warning that the building was about to give way.
"Everything happened in a moment. People were sleeping, and suddenly the building came down on them," he explained.
Al-Okka said he remains unaware of where exactly his relatives may be trapped, leaving him dependent on the rescue teams searching through the wreckage.
Cries for help beneath the rubble
At the site, relatives gathered as Civil Defence teams worked through layers of concrete and twisted metal in an attempt to reach those still missing.
Khader Akila, a resident in the area, told TNA that residents heard cries for help coming from beneath the debris after the collapse.
He said one child remained trapped for more than an hour while Civil Defence workers tried to reach him.
"People could hear voices under the rubble, but reaching them was extremely difficult," Akila added, describing the rescue effort as a race against time.
He said rescuers lacked the equipment needed to lift the massive concrete slabs, forcing them to work with whatever limited tools were available.
Another local resident, Ismail Hana, told TNA that the collapse showed the dangers facing Palestinians who continue to live in buildings damaged during the war.
"There is no safe place in Gaza," he said. "Even sleep is no longer safe."
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for Gaza Civil Defence, told TNA around 100 people, including women, children and elderly residents, were inside the building and surrounding area when it collapsed.
He said displaced families were also living in tents nearby, adding that "the building had been damaged during the war and developed structural cracks before collapsing on its residents."
He explained that Civil Defence teams were continuing to search for survivors and recover bodies but were facing major difficulties because of the lack of heavy machinery.
"We urgently need excavators, bulldozers and heavy equipment to remove the rubble and reach those who may still be alive underneath," Basal said.
He accused Israel of preventing the entry of such equipment into Gaza, saying the shortage was not only hampering the current rescue operation but also leaving Civil Defence teams ill-equipped to respond to other building collapses.
2,000 buildings at risk of collapse
Basal warned that around 2,000 damaged residential buildings across Gaza remain at risk of collapse while still being inhabited, raising concerns as winter approaches and already-weakened structures face further deterioration.
He said the collapse of the al-Saada Building could be followed by further incidents if damaged structures remain occupied without proper engineering assessments and urgent repairs or demolition of sections deemed dangerous.
The warning comes as thousands of Palestinian families remain without safe alternative housing after Israel's war caused extensive destruction to homes and infrastructure. Many displaced families have been forced to shelter in damaged buildings or tents erected beside them.
Civil Defence has repeatedly called for heavy machinery to enter Gaza to clear rubble, rescue people trapped beneath collapsed structures and deal with buildings at risk of falling.
Basal said that the provision of heavy rescue and rubble-clearing equipment was included among the humanitarian provisions of the ceasefire agreement, which took effect in October 2025.
He accused Israel of failing to implement the provisions concerning the entry of such machinery into Gaza.
He called on the states that guaranteed the agreement to intervene and facilitate the entry of excavators, bulldozers, and other rescue equipment, warning that continued shortages could increase casualties if further-damaged buildings collapse.

Mainland says Taiwan's DPP shifts blame for halt of cross-Strait dialogue

2026-09-16
19:54:08 CST
20:54:08 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Cross-Strait institutional dialogue was suspended because Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities rejected its political foundation, which is the one-China principle, a mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Previous cross-Strait consultations had been conducted on the basis of the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, said Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, in response to the DPP's claims that the mainland had unilaterally halted institutionalized consultations and restricted travel and exchanges.
The DPP, since coming to power in 2016, has adopted a secessionist line and refused to recognize the 1992 Consensus, which "unilaterally undermined" the basis for cross-Strait dialogue, leading to the suspension of institutionalized talks and communication mechanisms, she noted.
Furthermore, the DPP authorities have restricted cross-Strait travel and cooperation in various fields, she said, adding that such measures had impacted the interests of people and businesses in Taiwan.
"The DPP is accustomed to distorting facts, shifting the blame and turning accusations back on others," she said.
The Taiwan question stems from a full-blown civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the remnants of the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation, though the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
The two sides had established institutionalized communication channels and reached agreements on a range of issues before the DPP took office in 2016. The mainland has repeatedly called for resumption of cross-Strait dialogue on the basis of the 1992 Consensus.
Regarding the mainland's new regulations governing entry and exit, which took effect on Sept. 15, Zhu said these regulations would provide a clearer legal framework for travel between the mainland and Taiwan.
Repeated warnings from the DPP authorities about the new regulations were only aimed at deterring Taiwan residents from visiting the mainland, to prevent them from seeing through the DPP's disinformation attempts, she said.
About 2.85 million visits to the mainland by Taiwan residents were recorded in the first half of 2026, up 24.9 percent year on year.
"The steady flow of Taiwan people traveling between the two sides is the clearest demonstration of how absurd the DPP authorities' efforts to restrict and obstruct cross-Strait exchanges are," she said. ■

Estonian government agrees on preliminary allocation of next period EU support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:54:00 UTC
20:54:00 KST

Estonian government agrees on preliminary allocation of next period EU support
Estonia plans to use EU funding to upgrade police aviation, strengthen border security and expand shelter capacity as part of efforts to improve the country's internal security and crisis preparedness.
The Cabinet has approved the basic framework for Estonia's national plan for the European Union's 2028-2034 budget period, including an initial proposal for allocating funding. The national plan is the central strategic document that will guide Estonia's use of funding from the EU's long-term budget.
The national plan is based on five priority pillars: the economy and competitiveness, security and resilience, rural development, agriculture and fisheries, education and social cohesion and good governance. The most important reforms and investments for the next period will be grouped under these pillars, helping Estonia achieve its long-term development goals, the government's press service said.
Under the national plan's initial allocation proposal, more than half of the funding would go toward boosting economic competitiveness and strengthening security and crisis preparedness, accounting for 33 percent and 19 percent of funding, respectively. Another 38 percent would go toward rural development objectives, including the Common Agricultural Policy, fisheries and the food sector. Education and social cohesion would receive 10 percent, while approximately 1 percent would go toward good governance.
Under the European Commission's proposal, Estonia would receive approximately €6.5 billion in the next budget period. The initial allocation through 2031 covers €5.5 billion in investment needs. The final amount of funding is still subject to change during negotiations and will depend on an agreement on the European Union's 2028-2034 long-term budget.
The final package of EU funding for the next budget period and Estonia's national plan will be completed after an agreement is reached on the EU's long-term budget and negotiations between the European Commission and Estonia on the national plan's content and funding have concluded. This is expected in fall 2027.
For example, €260 million proposed by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications is intended primarily for strategic industrial investments and research and development, with the aim of establishing new production capacity, expanding factories and supporting the production of higher-value-added goods.
To modernize production, the ministry has also proposed allocating at least another €45 million to the digitalization and automation of businesses and the adoption of artificial intelligence solutions. Funding would also support stronger cybersecurity and reduced bureaucracy, helping businesses cut costs and operate more efficiently.
The proposals also emphasize the importance of ensuring that economic growth is not concentrated solely in and around Tallinn and Tartu. A total of €108 million is planned to support regional businesses and the growth of small and medium-sized enterprises outside the country's major centers. Among other things, the funding would be used to develop industrial and business areas with the aim of creating well-paying jobs across Estonia.
Helicopter procurement planned
In the field of internal security, the government plans to purchase multipurpose helicopters and a surveillance aircraft, strengthen border security, combat serious crime, manage migration and create more shelter capacity, the Ministry of the Interior said.
Police aviation capabilities need to be upgraded to ensure that Estonia can continue to provide round-the-clock border surveillance, rescue people at sea, transport patients from the islands and respond to major emergencies. The upgraded aviation capability must also make it possible to respond to several incidents simultaneously and maintain readiness when some aircraft are undergoing maintenance, being used for training or already deployed on other missions.
EU funding will also be used to strengthen surveillance of Estonia's external border. Various procedures will be digitalized to improve migration management, while digital travel documents and visas will also be introduced.
EU funding will also be used to create more shelter capacity in apartment buildings and healthcare, social services, education and cultural institutions. Public warning systems and crisis communications will also be improved to ensure people quickly receive up-to-date information and act accordingly.

German peace groups vow to mobilize civil society against Israeli arms production at Volkswagen plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:53:32 UTC
20:53:32 KST

- Peace campaigners warn project could pave way for broader Israeli defense industry involvement in Germany, Europe
German peace groups have vowed to mobilize against plans to produce defense systems at Volkswagen’s Osnabrueck plant in cooperation with Israeli company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
“We see an opportunity to channel resistance into civil society against arms production in the city. Our project and main focus is to mobilize civil society for it,” Marie Dominique Guyard, a spokeswoman for the Osnabruck Peace Initiative, told Anadolu.
“We want to put more pressure on the political parties and city officials. Our strategy is to initiate a political discussion on the topic of arms production in the city,” she added.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative has been at the forefront of protests in recent months, urging Volkswagen to abandon plans for defense production at the site.
The group has received support from Germany’s opposition Left Party, which has called Volkswagen’s planned cooperation with Israel’s state-owned Rafael “unacceptable,” citing the Israeli government’s conduct in Gaza.
Rafael, meanwhile, has been expanding its European footprint as governments across the continent boost defense spending and procurement.
Under the controversial plan, Volkswagen has agreed to sell its Osnabrueck plant to private equity firm Aurelius and the state of Lower Saxony, with the site set to be developed into a center for defense production.
Systems and components for air defense are expected to be manufactured at the plant for Germany and other European countries.
Volkswagen decided two years ago to phase out vehicle production at the Osnabrueck site by summer 2027.
‘Direct German subsidy for Israeli arms’
Peace activists and some opposition politicians have repeatedly criticized the plan, arguing that the plant should remain focused on civilian production.
Volkswagen has been grappling in recent years with sluggish demand, persistently high production costs in Germany, the impact of trade tensions with the US and fierce competition from Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers.
Speaking on behalf of her organization, Guyard condemned the planned cooperation with Rafael, saying it amounts to “almost a direct (German) subsidy” for an Israeli arms company.
“Furthermore, this amounts to an almost direct subsidy for an Israeli arms manufacturer, which we find particularly inappropriate and politically misguided, given Israel’s current wars in Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and also in Iran. Therefore, we continue to condemn this planned joint venture,“ she said.
“This is, in effect, direct support for the State of Israel’s war policy, and we believe that is wrong,” she added.
Guyard’s criticism was echoed by prominent German peace activist Juergen Graesslin.
“For Osnabrueck, as a self-proclaimed ‘City of Peace,’ this would be a dramatic reversal,” Graesslin said in an interview with the daily taz newspaper.
“For many decades, the city has taken pride in this label, and now it apparently has no problem degenerating into a war-supporting ‘City of War’,” he added.
Graesslin argued that civilian vehicle production was being replaced by cooperation with an Israeli arms manufacturer “which is heavily involved in … activities that constitute the most serious human rights violations, including in Gaza and the West Bank.”
“That is morally extremely troubling,” he said.
Civil society resistance takes shape
Meanwhile, civic resistance to defense production at the Osnabrueck plant is slowly gaining momentum, according to Guyard.
Resistance would mean “forging a broad alliance that already exists. The problem is that so-called left-wing parties like the SPD and the Greens fully support arms production. That’s a major problem,” she said.
“There are already coalition partners in the city who oppose arms production. Unfortunately, the labor unions are not among them, nor is the mayor of Osnabrueck,” Guyard added.
Among the groups involved in the local campaign is the newly created Zukunftswerk Osnabrueck network, an open coalition of individuals, political groups and initiatives.
On its website, the network emphasizes a “clear anti-militarist stance,” while calling for a future based on solidarity, democracy and environmental sustainability for the plant, Osnabrueck and beyond.
Concerns over wider German-Israeli defense cooperation
Guyard also warned that the Rafael project could become a gateway for broader Israeli defense industry involvement in Germany and elsewhere in Europe.
“I think that if the project is successful – and this is no secret, as Rafael’s director himself has said – he sees the project as a stepping stone toward closer cooperation in Germany and Europe.”
Asked whether she was concerned about this development, she replied, “Yes, of course.”
Guyard said the rapid expansion of Germany’s defense industry, backed by rising public spending, was creating opportunities that Israeli weapons manufacturers were seeking to tap.
“Arms production is booming and is also fueled by government debt, and Israeli arms manufacturers want a share of this windfall – and that concerns us.”

Former Kosovo President Thaçi sentenced to 25 years in prison for war crimes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:53:08 EEST
20:53:08 KST

Former Kosovo President Thaçi sentenced to 25 years in prison for war crimes
Kyiv • UNN
The Hague court found Hashim Thaçi guilty of killings, torture and unlawful detention of people during the war in Kosovo. He may appeal the verdict.
On Wednesday, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague found former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi guilty of war crimes, including killings, torture and unlawful detention of people. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Thaçi, 58, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes committed as commander-in-chief of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), which consisted mostly of ethnic Albanians, during the violent separation of the region from Serbia in the 1990s.
The court said Thaçi was guilty of the killing of 96 political opponents and people considered to be collaborators with Serbian security forces, carried out by Kosovo Liberation Army forces during the conflict.
He was also found guilty of the arbitrary unlawful detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of 49 people. The court added that none of the victims was actively participating in hostilities at the time the crimes were committed.
The court said that Thaçi actively participated in and encouraged the crimes as part of a joint criminal enterprise based on a common plan.
The plan was as simple as it was destructive. In particular, it provided for: the creation of detention facilities in all areas controlled by the KLA; the identification of people considered opponents of the KLA; their arrest and detention and, when necessary, their killing
According to him, the victims were held in inhumane conditions, beaten, kept in tiny cells and not provided with sufficient food or medical care.
Thaçi, who stood silently while the judge read out the verdict and sentence, denied all the charges.
He may appeal the verdict.
Supporters gathered in Pristina and The Hague
The verdict was closely followed in Kosovo and Serbia, where the legacy of the 1998–1999 conflict and Kosovo’s declaration of independence in 2008 remain sources of tension between ethnic Kosovo Albanians and Serbs.
Thaçi remains a respected figure for many Kosovo Albanians, while the tribunal itself is extremely unpopular in Kosovo.
Brief clashes occurred in The Hague between several hundred Thaçi supporters and police when demonstrators tried to march to the court from the place where they had been listening to an audio broadcast of the verdict announcement.
In Pristina, the capital of Kosovo, several hundred people marched through the city after the verdict was announced, while dozens of police officers from riot-control units were deployed throughout the city.
"This verdict is shameful. From today, there will be no peace in Kosovo," said Raif Pllana, a former KLA fighter who came to support Thaçi in central Pristina.
Police said that, in case the protests turned violent, a joint action plan had been prepared with foreign peacekeeping forces. The United States urged its citizens to avoid areas where large crowds were gathering.
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama criticized the verdict, posting on social media an image of a map of Europe wrapped in barbed wire and writing one word: "Incredible."
Prosecutors sought 45 years in prison
Prosecutors sought 45 years in prison for Thaçi and three other former senior KLA commanders.
However, the three-judge panel dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity. The judges said prosecutors had failed to prove that these crimes were part of widespread or systematic attacks against the civilian population as a whole.
Thaçi’s lawyers argued that the charges were unfounded and effectively represented an attempt to rewrite history.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, based in The Hague, were established in 2015 under international pressure to hear cases against former KLA fighters accused of war crimes and crimes committed after the war.
On Wednesday, the judges said that the trial had taken place against a backdrop of serious witness intimidation. They also referred to witnesses who had withdrawn their previous testimony, lied to the court or changed their earlier statements.

The Commission chief is resisting calls on the EU to impose consequences on Serbia, which remains a candidate country for membership of the bloc alongside other Western Balkan states.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday that she was "horrified by the images" of covincted war criminal Ratko Mladić's funeral in Belgrade earlier this month, but stopped short of announcing any punitive measures against Serbia.
"The glorification of war criminals simply has no place in the European Union," von der Leyen said during her annual State of the European Union speech. She refrained from directly criticising Serbia despite calls for firmer action from the bloc.
Mladić, known as the "Butcher of Bosnia", died in August while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the Bosnian War in the 1990s.
His body was flown to Belgrade on a state plane, greeted by an honour guard by the Serbian military and various security forces, and commemorated by the public broadcaster and the Serbian Orthodox Church. His coffin was wrapped in a Serbian flag.
Officials in Belgrade had previously denied that he would be given a funeral with state honours.
The images prompted outrage across Europe, with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković criticising the EU's muted response.
The Commission helmed by von der Leyen had been pushing to advance Serbia's bid to become an EU member by unlocking Cluster 3 talks on economic growth.
But EU capitals blocked the move, citing persistent concerns over democratic backsliding – even after the Venice Commission said Belgrade had implemented most of its recommendations on judicial reforms.
Diplomats have told Euronews that the funeral given to Mladić has effectively put Serbia's accession push on hold, with one saying that "anyone even considering opening Cluster 3 will think twice".
Henrik Dahl, a Danish lawmaker for the European People's Party (EPP), told Euronews on Tuesday that "Serbia has put themselves in the back of the waiting line (to join the EU) because they gave a state funeral to a war criminal".
Several EU lawmakers have also questioned the affiliation of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party to the EPP, the centre-right political family to which von der Leyen belongs.
The EU's enlargement chief, Marta Kos, postponed her planned visit to Belgrade in response to the funeral, prompting speculation that von der Leyen could announce similar repercussions.
The Commission chief is widely expected to tour Western Balkan candidate countries including Serbia this autumn, but the executive has refrained from confirming whether the programme for the visit is yet confirmed.

No word from Riyadh on oil delivery cancellations as scale of disruption remains unclear
Unknown

2026-09-16
11:50:52 UTC
20:50:52 KST

The pipeline shutdown has put pressure on Saudi oil supplies to Europe as further conflict in the region threatens shipping routes. Riyadh has yet to comment on reports that some refiners face delays until November.
Saudi Arabia has remained silent on reports that it has cancelled or delayed crude oil shipments to European refiners following last week's drone strikes on its East-West pipeline, as the scale of the disruption to European deliveries remains unclear.
Energy pricing agency Argus reported on Tuesday that at least three European refiners had cargoes scheduled for late September cancelled or postponed, in some cases until November, citing unnamed market sources.
Saudi Arabia’s state-controlled oil company Aramco told Euronews it "declined to comment" on this and other similar reports in a brief email on Wednesday afternoon.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry announced a precautionary shutdown last Friday after drone attacks on the pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions the previous day.
Saudi and Iraqi authorities said the drones came from Iraq. The ministry said technical teams were checking the pipeline, but did not say when pumping would restart.
The pipeline carries crude from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
From Yanbu, tankers heading to Europe sail north towards the Suez Canal. Egypt’s SUMED pipeline provides another route for crude to reach the Mediterranean from the Red Sea.
Oil stored at export terminals can keep cargoes moving during a shutdown. How long those stocks last depends on the amount available and how quickly pipeline deliveries resume.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Tuesday that the pipeline interruption would be “measured in days”.
Bab el-Mandeb in Houthi crosshairs
The Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday that it had intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca the previous evening. The Houthis denied targeting the city.
Last week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea after seizing the port of Mokha and nearby islands from Yemen's Saudi-supported internationally recognised government.
Bab el-Mandeb lies south of Yanbu, on the direct route to Asia. Europe-bound tankers sailing north from Yanbu do not pass through it, but the strait is a key passage for trade between Europe and Asia.
Qatar warned on Tuesday that losing access to Bab el-Mandeb would worsen the disruption already affecting shipping through Hormuz.
Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of media and communication at Qatar’s foreign ministry, told a briefing in Doha that this would be “catastrophic for the entire world," calling for international efforts to keep the waterway open.
Meanwhile, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi discussed the security of regional shipping routes in Cairo on Tuesday.
El-Sisi said Saudi and Gulf security formed part of Egypt's national security, expressing support for Saudi measures to protect the kingdom and calling for a political settlement in Yemen.

Russian authorities order destruction of vaccine batch linked to mass dog deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:50:40 UTC
20:50:40 KST

Russian authorities order destruction of vaccine batch linked to mass dog deaths
Rosselkhoznadzor, Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance, has ordered the recall and destruction of batch No. 20 of the “Multikan-8” vaccine, which has been linked to dog deaths. The agency sent the order in a letter (.pdf) to the vaccine’s manufacturer, the company “Vetbiokhim,” and published the document on its website.
The letter directs “Vetbiokhim” to recall and destroy batch No. 20 itself, then report back to Rosselkhoznadzor.
Why Rosselkhoznadzor ordered the destruction of only one batch of “Multikan” remains unclear. “Vetbiokhim” had already recalled four batches of the vaccine amid earlier reports of mass dog deaths following vaccination.
Dog deaths after vaccination with "Multikan"
Dog owners began speaking out in large numbers in mid-August about pets that died after being vaccinated with “Multikan-8,” saying at least 300 animals died across several Russian regions. Those affected asked lawmakers in the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, to look into what happened.
No official figures on the number of dogs that died exist, and it’s unclear whether such statistics were ever compiled. Rosselkhoznadzor’s regional office and the prosecutor’s office in the Yaroslavl region, where the first reports of dog deaths surfaced, launched an inspection of “Vetbiokhim,” though no results have been announced.
Some of those affected (1, 2, 3) have linked the deaths to contamination of the “Multikan-8” vaccine with the virus that causes Aujeszky’s disease (pseudorabies), whose symptoms resemble those seen in the dogs that died. Unofficial testing of vaccine samples allegedly also detected the virus, according to those affected, but laboratories soon began refusing to run the tests, citing “pressure from above.”
“Vetbiokhim” claimed its own tests had found no contamination of the vaccine with the Aujeszky’s disease virus.
On September 10, Meduza reported that “Vetbiokhim” had drawn up settlement agreements with those affected. The company did not acknowledge any link between the dog deaths and the vaccine but offered to compensate the owners of animals that died. The agreements, however, required owners to waive any claims against “Vetbiokhim” and to stop discussing what happened to their animals in the media, on social media, or in messaging apps without the company’s consent.
“Multikan-8” is a vaccine that protects dogs against canine distemper, adenovirus infections, parvovirus and coronavirus enteritis, leptospirosis, and rabies.
Imported veterinary drugs, including rabies vaccines, largely vanished from the Russian market after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the Western sanctions that followed, leaving veterinary clinics to rely mostly on Russian-made products.

Belgium unveils new AI strategy to strengthen national control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:50:03 UTC
20:50:03 KST

Melike Pala
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Belgium has adopted a new national strategy on artificial intelligence aimed at strengthening the country's capabilities, skills, and policy tools while ensuring greater control over the technology, the government said Wednesday.
Digitalization Minister Vanessa Matz said the strategy seeks to ensure that AI creates value for Belgium while allowing the country to "keep control" of its development and use, French-language broadcaster RTBF reported on Wednesday.
Matz noted that 42% of Belgians are already using generative AI, while 34.5% of Belgian companies have adopted AI technologies, placing Belgium among European countries experiencing rapid uptake of the technology.
The new strategy updates Belgium's first National Convergence Plan, adopted in 2022, taking into account changes in the technological and geopolitical environment.
It aims to build on existing investments in research and innovation, public services, infrastructure, and access to European capabilities, while concentrating resources on priority areas and accelerating the transition from AI experimentation to deployment.
It will now be discussed with Belgium's federated entities to determine how it will be implemented.
Among the measures envisaged is a reform of the Strategic Committee on AI to include representatives of the federated entities and strengthen monitoring of priority projects.
The strategy also calls for greater focus on sectors where Belgium has particular strengths, improved access to data for priority AI projects, and the introduction of a "sovereignty grid" for public procurement involving cloud and AI technologies.
