Finland aims to launch direct-to-phone emergency alert system by end of year
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
14:49:07 EEST
20:49:07 KST

Finland aims to roll out a new emergency alert system before the end of this year, according to a spokesperson from the digital and population services data agency.
The system will use cell broadcast technology to send alerts directly to mobile phones without users needing to download a separate app.
Finland's government submitted a proposal to parliament at the end of last month requesting legislative changes to the Act on Emergency Warnings, which would allow for the introduction of a public warning system based on cell broadcast technology.
"A cell broadcast service would enable the transmission of rapid, prompt and geographically targeted emergency warnings to devices across all mobile networks within the affected area," a statement from the interior ministry explained.
The new system will complement the country's current emergency warning system, which will also remain in place. Currently, emergency warnings are issued through the 112 Suomi app, radio broadcasts, teletext page 112 and, when necessary, on television.
Interior Minister Mari Rantanen (Finns) said in June that building the system was a "priority" for the government, and that funding had been allocated to the project to ensure its swift construction and rollout.
The need for such a system has been heightened by an increase in the number of warhead-carrying drones that have strayed into Finnish airspace. An incident in May saw authorities order people in Uusimaa, the country's most populous region, to move indoors and stay there due to concerns a drone had entered Finnish territory.
Finnish authorities previously estimated that the system would be ready by October this year at the earliest, or by the end of 2027 at the latest.

Congo's Ebola epidemic might have gone unnoticed for months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:49:00 UTC
20:49:00 KST

Congo's Ebola epidemic may have gone unnoticed for months
September 16, 2026
The Democratic Republic of Congo officially declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo variant on May 15. However, the first infections likely occurred much earlier.
Just how far back the start of the epidemic actually goes is still a matter of debate. But one thing is certain: Congolese authorities did not respond in the best possible way, with several international organizations highlighting delays in the initial response.
Congo is no stranger to crisis response. The country experiences Ebola outbreaks on a regular basis, and has in the past been praised for its expertise in combating the disease.
Early warnings came from WHO, Africa CDC
A good starting point for tracing the origins of the outbreak is the timeline provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) in collaboration with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
According to their data, the first known case, identified retrospectively, was a health worker from Mongbwalu in northeastern Ituri Province. The person, sources said, developed symptoms characteristic of Ebola around April 24 or 25.
They died at a medical center in Bunia, the capital of Ituri. To date, 80% of all cases have been reported in the province.
It wasn't until May 5 that the WHO said it had been informed of "an unknown illness with high mortality reported in Mongbwalu Health Zone." The global health body then issued its first warning.
Congo's delayed response questioned as Ebola spread
Ten days later, on May 15, the Congolese government announced the Ebola outbreak.
Tests conducted by the National Institute for Biomedical Research in Kinshasa had confirmed the presence of the rare Bundibugyo type of Ebola.
Three days later, the Africa CDC raised concerns about the speed of Congo's response.
About three weeks had passed between the onset of the first symptoms in the suspected index case and the laboratory confirmation — even though the fatality was a health worker.
"This significant delay [...] highlights a critically low initial index of clinical suspicion among local healthcare providers, which facilitated wider geographic spread prior to the initiation of containment efforts," the Africa CDC concluded.
According to reports gathered by DW, residents of Mongbwalu had already reported suspicious deaths as early as the end of April.
"Several deaths were reported following high fevers, and the victims often showed traces of blood around various body orifices," said Dieudonne Lossa Dekhana, the provincial coordinator for civil society in Ituri.
Red Cross reported 'widespread' public fear 'since March 30'
There were other indications that Ebola was already circulating long before the emergence of this first confirmed case.
A May 16 report by the Red Cross of the Democratic Republic of the Congo stated: "Since March 30, 2026, there has been widespread fear among the population of the Mongbwalu Health Zone following a series of deaths."
Here, too, the symptoms matched those of Ebola: high fever, chest pain, severe exhaustion, persistent cough, nosebleeds, vomiting, loss of consciousness, a comatose state and ultimately death.
The Red Cross report said the trigger was believed to have been the body of a Mongbwalu resident "who died and was placed in a coffin purchased in Bunia, which was then replaced by another in Mongbwalu."
US researchers: February outbreak is plausible
The funeral that brought various people into direct contact with the body and the contaminated coffin is believed to have been the cause of a rising number of infections and deaths that were subsequently observed in Mongbwalu and Bunia.
But from the data available, it is not possible to confirm without doubt that these deaths were related to the Bundibugyo virus. However, they show that an unusual health phenomenon had already been observed more than six weeks before the outbreak was officially declared on May 15.
In addition, investigations since May 15 have come to support the thesis that Ebola might have been circulating even earlier than that.
In a study published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on June 11, a team of researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reconstructed the early course of the epidemic.
An initial transmission from an animal to a human, or spillover, between mid- and late February is "plausible," the researchers concluded. A late-April spillover, on the other hand, would be difficult to reconcile with the scale the epidemic had already reached at the time of the study.
WHO: Genome sequencing suggests February outbreak
On August 10, Mohamed Janabi, the WHO Regional Director for Africa, said genome sequencing analyses suggested the outbreak likely began "as early as February 2026."
Several early infections were mistakenly attributed to diseases that were far more common in the region, particularly malaria and typhus, he said.
In an August interview, Janabi told DW that there was a significant gap in case reporting. "The Ebola situation is catastrophic... In three months, we only had access to one-third of the patients," he said.
Could 'pig Ebola' shed some light on the matter?
Jules Villa, a researcher in the anthropology and ecology of disease emergence at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, points to a phenomenon observed in the connection with previous Ebola epidemics.
Villa'sstudy does not encompass the 2026 outbreak, but takes stock of local reports collected during earlier Ebola outbreaks in northeastern Congo.
Villa shows that livestock farmers, veterinarians and residents had reported unusually high animal mortality even before the outbreak of at least two Ebola epidemics in humans.
In 2017, several witnesses reported on what they called "pig Ebola" — a high mortality among pigs, which was ultimately attributed to swine fever.
According to Villa's research, monitoring livestock in the general population could provide the first useful warning signs long before an outbreak is confirmed by a laboratory.
This article was originally written in French.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:48:37 UTC
20:48:37 KST

About 70 percent of electricity generators at hospitals in Gaza have gone out of service due to shortages of fuel, oil, and spare parts amid the ongoing Israeli blockade, the health ministry has said.
Zaher Al-Wahidi, director of the ministry’s Health Information Centre, said during a press conference at al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Wednesday that shortages of fuel and oil threatened to bring critical and life-saving hospital departments to a halt at any moment.
Wahidi rejected Israeli claims that it was facilitating the entry of medical aid and logistical supplies into Gaza, emphasising that there are attempts to “improve the image” of the situation and conceal a campaign of “ethnic cleansing” in the enclave.
He said the supplies allowed into Gaza “represent only a very small amount” and do not meet even the minimum operational needs of health facilities, leaving them “struggling between life and death.”
“The health system in Gaza is being driven toward a systematic and mass execution, going beyond a humanitarian catastrophe to a fully fledged health genocide,” he said.
‘Immediate and urgent action’
Wahidi said the fuel crisis also led public transport companies and buses to announce a complete or near-total halt in operations on Wednesday, preventing hundreds of medical workers from reaching their workplaces and further isolating health facilities and hampering their ability to respond to emergencies.
“Health facilities have turned into isolated structures slowly dying amid the continued comprehensive blockade and the prevention of essential necessities of life from entering,” he said.
He said the situation coincides with an “unprecedented shortage” of medicines and medical supplies, the disruption of diagnostic equipment and the closure of treatment routes abroad for patients and wounded people on waiting lists.
Wahidi urged the international community, the UN Security Council, the World Health Organization, and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs to take “immediate and urgent action” to allow the entry of essential medical and operational supplies.
Since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, nearly 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 wounded, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Mortgage demand from homebuyers drops 19% from a year ago, as interest rates surge abruptly higher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:47:11 UTC
20:47:11 KST

Fast-rising interest rates are taking their toll on mortgage demand, as both potential homebuyers and current homeowners head to the sidelines. Total mortgage application volume dropped 4.1% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. Last week's results include a separate adjustment for the Labor Day holiday.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 6.97% from 6.85% percent, with points rising to 0.72 from 0.67, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. That is a weekly average run by the MBA, but by last Thursday, rates had moved over 7%, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily.
"Ongoing market concerns over spiking energy prices, persistently high inflation, and future monetary policy pushed bond yields and mortgage rates higher last week," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA.
Applications to refinance a home loan, which are most sensitive to weekly rate changes, dropped 9% for the week and were 65% lower than the same week one year ago. Last year at this time, the interest rate on the 30-year fixed was 58 basis points, or more than half a percentage point, lower.
"The current level of rates eliminated much of the benefit to refinance for many borrowers, resulting in declines in conventional, FHA, and VA refinance applications," Kan added.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home dropped 1% for the week and were 19% lower than the same week one year ago. Potential buyers are still contending with high home prices. While the supply of homes for sale has been gaining in much of the country, much of that supply is on the higher end of the market.
Mortgage rates continued to move higher to start this week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.22% on Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily, just ahead of the next meeting of the Federal Reserve on Wednesday. Rates are now almost a full percentage point higher than they were a year ago.
"Over the past 6 [business] days, the average is up 0.33%, which is is the most abrupt jump since October 2024," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "At least some of the recent volatility is due to the implications of recent economic data and oil price implications on Fed policy."

London Jews warn of security crisis after antisemitic arson attacks

20:46:53 KST

Jewish security leaders praised London Fire Brigade (LFB) for its response to the spate of antisemitic arson attacks across the city this year, while warning that the attacks exposed a broader security crisis facing British Jews.
On Tuesday, the London Assembly Fire Committee met to discuss LFB’s response to the antisemitic arson attacks that occurred between March and May, including the burning of Hatzola ambulances.
Present were CEO of Community Security Trust (CST) Mark Gardner, Hatzola NW London responder Yanky David, London Fire Commissioner Jonathan Smith, and two LFB commissioners.
Gardner spoke of how the “randomness” of the attacks had originally confused the police, who sought advice from CST on what connected the different synagogues and Jewish sites.
“The only thing that connects them is that they’re Jewish or, as was said by the group, the so-called group responsible for the attacks, that they’re Zionist. That’s the only thing,” he said.
Concern about attacks becoming normalized
In part because of the breadth of targets – from Jewish businesses to ambulances to reform synagogues – “it felt to the entire Jewish community that everybody was at risk of attack,” Gardner told the Assembly.
He also expressed concern that, after the attacks became less frequent and then paused entirely, “the awareness of police, of fire brigade, of the assembly members, of government, etc., that they basically relax about the situation.”
Nevertheless, praised the LFB for its “terrific” response to the attacks, and described the efforts as “vitally important.”
Just last weekend, LFB carried out an emergency response demonstration at Finchley Fire Station to show the Committee and Jewish leaders how it would respond to a future terrorist attack.
LFB borough commander Rob Davis said this run-through was important given the changing face of attacks, and stressed that firefighters should be able to enter potential incidents “knowing from start to finish what the protocols and steps look like.”
Visitors were shown the LFB’s marauding terrorist attack response capability, which was introduced following the Manchester Arena attack in 2017, and were also shown measures that could be put in place at Jewish community buildings to help them prepare.
David cited this in Tuesday’s assembly, and said “the amount of resources that the London Fire Brigade had brought forward to that event to make it as realistic as possible and to prepare us, God forbid, for an eventuality that may happen was phenomenal. And we felt the support, and we felt as an organization that we had partners.”
David recalled being one of the first people to attend the burning ambulances when it was initially a small fire.
“The fire brigade who attended, they literally dove straight in and started tackling it, and they were phenomenal. We had to evacuate elderly residents from the neighboring apartment blocks, and we just worked alongside each other on that night phenomenally.”
Nevertheless, David acknowledged that the incidents were “traumatic” for the community and it lost four of its frontline ambulances.
“For an ambulance to be attacked, it’s almost as if someone is ripping out the defibrillators from every public building in London,” David said.
Gardner said that the existing Jewish security measures would be regarded as quite extreme to anyone outside the community, but within the Jewish community, “there’s a horrible normality around them.”
“We can’t keep building bigger walls. It just can’t continue like that,” he said, adding that it will continue to get worse until Jews either leave or the underlying reasons for the hatred are addressed.”
'I've never quite seen operational pressure like it'
Jonathan Smith, London Fire Commissioner, said listening to the praise from Gardner and David for the London Fire Brigade “is something I’m incredibly proud of.”
“When what can at times appear to be the rest of the world is against a particular community, I think our role as the London Fire Brigade as the emergency service to step into that space and provide that level of reassurance is incredibly important,” he said.
Smith, however, spoke of the operational pressure the organization has been under this year.
“And in 27 years as a firefighter and officer, I’ve never quite seen operational pressure like it.”
Smith said the London Fire Brigade will need direct funding from central government to support its national security role.
That aside, Smith said in terms of the actual response to the attacks that we saw at the start of the year, “I couldn’t be prouder of what the London Fire Brigade has done.”

Gaza, grief & memory: Amira El-Zein's At the Hour of the Eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:45:39 UTC
20:45:39 KST

Breadcrumb
At the Hour of the Eclipse: Amira El-Zein's poetry of Gaza, loss and displacement
The hour of the eclipse is the hour of death, when darkness prevails, and the light goes out. In Gaza, it is a time of relentless strikes on homes, children burned alive, and lives shattered by grief and devastation.
This darkness lies at the heart of Amira El-Zein’s collection, where the eclipse becomes a symbol of displacement, rage, loss, and death.
At the Hour of the Eclipse is a poetry collection dedicated to the children of Gaza. It consists of ten long poems that give voice to the experience of those caught in this darkness, portraying a people marked by loss, grief, and uncertainty.
In Is the River a Spirit’s Tongue?, El-Zein writes:
"At the hour of the eclipse,
You came, death!
You are the obedient servant
who carries the gods’ commands
each time they raise their eyebrows.
You are the one who
erased pages from our book.
You are the thief who grabs
our children while asleep."
Amira El-Zein renders this suffering through verses that speak directly to the reader, evoking a profound sense of grief and anguish.
She captures the agony of Palestinians as "the forgotten ones," who rush toward death while fleeing "the emperor’s sword," portraying a people with nowhere left to go.
A dark night of displacement
El-Zein captures the suddenness of leaving home and fleeing from Israeli soldiers who have taken their houses and destroyed their olive trees.
Through her words, readers can sense the pain and terror of those forced into displacement, as well as the uncertainty and longing that come with leaving behind everything they know. In The Ancient Rain, We Drift, she writes:
"Are we walking?
Are we still?
Did we leave?
Are we packing?
And the children,
are they awake and ready?"
These questions reflect the confusion of a people forced to leave and escape death without knowing what awaits them.
Meanwhile, memory becomes a way of holding on to what has been lost: the homeland. In Is Echo the Memory Keeper? El-Zein presents memory through the remnants of a lost past:
"Is it our memory,
that smoke we see from afar,
rising above
the ancient chimneys?"
Throughout the poem, the displaced are portrayed as vulnerable and powerless, left at the mercy of forces beyond their control. They have become uncertain figures moving through a world in which even their homes have disappeared.
"Are we bottles
that wobble
on an unsteady table?
Are we shadows
leaping to the other side,
passing through doors
that have lost their houses?"
Displacement is never the choice of a people; it is the fear of death that forces them to leave behind their homes and memories.
For those who survive, that loss becomes a source of rage, grief, and a longing for what has been taken from them.
The rage of the people
"Language, if you depart,
we will express our thoughts
in elliptical forms,
that will cause the eclipse
of the sun."
In Dust, Amira El-Zein emphasises the power of language as a form of resistance.
Even when people are silenced, broken, and desperate, their words can still carry their pain and anger.
The reference to the "eclipse of the sun" suggests a world covered in darkness, where words give the oppressed a voice to challenge those who have caused their unbearable suffering.
The rage of those displaced becomes more direct and brutal in A Passage to Eternity:
"They slaughtered
the cattle
in the market.
They burned the elders
in their beds.
They recited
the verses of evil
day and night.
They trampled
the fresh corpses
with their boots."
These verses depict the rage of a people forced from their homes and confronted with death. The brutal images of slaughter, burning, and corpses convey the violence and agony of those who have lived through hell on earth.
The terror of death
The book portrays death as a monstrous presence haunting children at night, recalling the killing of children in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have hit schools and refugee camps, turning shelters into scenes of complete destruction.
In A Passage to Eternity, El-Zein addresses death directly, questioning its role in the loss of innocent children:
"Why did they throw the keys into the river?
Why did they trap the shadows of dusk?
Why did they paint the sun
with your paleness,
O Death?"
El-Zein also explores the idea of nothingness and uncertainty into which refugees are pushed, with the sea becoming an image of both terror and emptiness.
It reflects their feeling of being lost, with no clear destination or sense of safety. The refugees struggle to understand the violence surrounding them.
"Throats scream with the rage of the sea.
Is it dismay?
Is it the rattle of death?
Is it folly?
Is it betrayal?"
Amira El-Zein gives language to displacement, rage, and death, preserving the voices and memories of the people of Gaza.
Her verses speak a painful truth that is difficult to ignore. She depicts the tragic fate of millions of displaced people, forced to endure the constant threat of death.
At the Hour of the Eclipse is a poetry collection that reaches the heart, carrying the grief of a people through ten powerful poems.
Yet within this darkness, El-Zein’s poetry keeps their voices alive, refusing to let their memories and history be erased.
Joyce Bou Charaa is a Lebanese freelance writer and book editor, with a keen interest in writing about literature, culture, and history

British lawmakers demand probe into cost of Trump NHS deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:44:54 UTC
20:44:54 KST

LONDON — British lawmakers called on the U.K.’s spending watchdog to investigate how much the U.K.-U.S. drug pricing deal will cost taxpayers.
Six U.K. parliamentary committee chairs sent a letter to the National Audit Office Wednesday arguing there is “significant public interest in understanding its implications for public expenditure,” after the U.K. government refused to release details of the costs of the deal agreed with the Trump administration.
“Given the potentially significant financial implications of this agreement … we would like to formally request that the National Audit Office undertake a rapid investigation into the costs of the arrangement and assess whether it represents value for money for the taxpayer,” the lawmakers wrote.
Advertisement
The deal — agreed in December last year — saw the U.K. commit to spending more on new medicines in exchange for three years of zero tariffs from the U.S. on pharmaceutical products.
The U.K. government agreed to double its pharma spending to 0.6% of GDP by 2035. It laid secondary legislation to update the rules used by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, allowing the body to raise its cost-effectiveness threshold — the point at which it considers a medicine to provide sufficient value for money — by 25%.
“Without a comprehensive impact assessment covering future years, parliament and the public are unable to fully understand the long-term implications of the agreement for NHS budgets and wider public expenditure,” the lawmakers wrote.
The U.K. government has so far refused to publish how much the deal will ultimately cost Britain's National Health Service. Instead, it has estimated the agreement will cost approximately £1 billion over the current spending review period.
Sally Gainsbury, senior policy analyst at independent health think tank Nuffield Trust, was previously refused access to the government's impact assessment of the deal. The Information Commissioner’s Office said the Department of Health and Social Care argued that releasing it would “prejudice ongoing policy development, international relations and commercial interests.”
Gainsbury launched an appeal to the Information Tribunal on Aug. 17 over the government’s decision to withhold the assessment. The case is due to be heard between December and February.
Advertisement
Gainsbury said in comments that the trade deal will have "a huge negative impact on the NHS’s ability to improve the health of the population as it will divert resources away from much more cost-effective forms of care and towards much more expensive and often less certain treatments.”
She added: “The government has said the deal is necessary to support economic growth, but it has not been prepared to reveal the details of its assessment on that. We shouldn’t have to go to court to get transparency on something so significant and impactful on our nation’s health services, but that is where we find ourselves. This call, from no fewer than six parliamentary committee chairs, really underlines the strength of public interest in transparency and we hope the government is listening.”
Signatories to the letter include Health and Social Committee Chair Layla Moran; Science, Innovation and Technology Committee Chair Chi Onwurah; Business and Trade Committee Chair Liam Byrne; Northern Ireland Affairs Committee Chair Tonia Antoniazzi; Scottish Affairs Committee Chair Patricia Ferguson; and Welsh Affairs Committee Chair Ruth Jones.

Ukraine’s SBS Drones Hit 6,280 Russian Troops in 15 Days, Outpacing August Figures
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces reported more than 6,000 confirmed strikes on Russian personnel during the first half of September, surpassing the figure recorded over the same period in August, commander Major Robert “Madyar” Brovdi said on September 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Brovdi, Unmanned Systems Forces units killed or incapacitated 6,280 Russian troops during the first 15 days of September, compared with 4,998 over the corresponding period in August.
Brovdi said the largest share of the reported strikes on Russian personnel was recorded in the Dobropillia, Huliaipole, and Pokrovsk sectors. Ukrainian drone units reported 1,806 such strikes in the Dobropillia sector, 1,927 in the Huliaipole sector, and 617 near Pokrovsk.
If the current pace of Russian troop deployments continues and weather conditions remain favorable for drone operations, Brovdi said the monthly figure could reach around 12,500 by the end of September. By comparison, the Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 11,010 confirmed strikes on Russian personnel throughout August.
Brovdi also said Ukrainian drone units expect operations to intensify between October and December, citing anticipated Russian efforts to deploy additional personnel.
“We expect an intensification in October–December 2026 due to the enemy’s intention to deploy an additional 300,000 personnel, which would be exactly twice the previous monthly reinforcement levels,” Brovdi said.
His assessment comes as Russia continues to sustain substantial personnel losses in Ukraine. According to Ukraine’s General Staff, Russian forces recorded 301,030 personnel killed or wounded between the beginning of 2026 and September 15.
To illustrate the scale of the reported losses, the General Staff said the figure is equivalent to the personnel strength of nearly 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an average of roughly 2,000 troops per brigade.
The heaviest losses were recorded during the summer, when 124,170 Russian troops were reported killed or wounded between June and August. The monthly toll stood at 39,290 in June, increased to 42,860 in July, and reached 42,020 in August.
The losses continued into September, with another 20,360 Russian personnel reported killed or wounded between the beginning of the month and September 15, according to the General Staff.
As Russian battlefield losses continue to mount, Moscow is seeking to expand its military ranks. Russia could mobilize as many as 600,000 additional personnel by the end of 2027 to replenish losses and sustain manpower levels for ongoing offensive operations in Ukraine.

Air pollution exposure linked to higher risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:42:58 UTC
20:42:58 KST

Short- and long-term exposure to air pollution may contribute to a higher risk of suicidal thoughts and death by suicide, according to a new analysis.
Exposure to polluted air may increase the risk of suicidal ideation and death by suicide both in the short and long term, highlighting the influence of environmental factors on people’s health.
A new analysis, published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health, found evidence that short-term exposure to small particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), as well as long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and PM2.5, increases the risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation.
Researchers analysed more than 40 studies examining different types of air, noise, light and water pollution, and their relationship with death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal thoughts.
Over 720,000 people die by suicide globally every year. In the European Union, more than 48,000 people died as a result of intentional self-harm in 2023, according to the latest Eurostat data.
“While there is no one single cause for suicide, reasons have been described as multifaceted and include several individual and biological factors in addition to wider cultural and social factors,” the authors wrote.
These findings contribute to a broader understanding of the role environmental exposures play in suicide risk, the authors noted. Yet, the environmental risks remain not fully understood, they noted.
How does the environment influence health?
The analysis points to possible mechanisms connecting air pollution and suicide. For example, air and water pollution have been linked to neurological effects, including chronic inflammation and neurotoxicity, which can harm brain function and influence mood and stress resilience.
Traffic and other sources of environmental noise and light pollution have also been linked to higher stress levels via circadian rhythm disruption.
“The main contribution of the study is not to demonstrate that pollution is a causal factor in suicidal behaviour, but rather to remind us that psychological suffering always occurs within a particular context,” said Susana Al-Halabí, a psychology professor at the University of Oviedo in Spain, who did not participate in the study.
She added that pollutants can also be a maker of more vulnerable social environments, such as neighbourhoods with poorer living conditions, lower environmental quality, more everyday stress or higher levels of inequality.
According to the authors, further research should investigate the cumulative effect of these environmental exposures to better understand their role in shaping suicide risk.
“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they wrote.
If you are contemplating suicide and need to talk, please reach out to Befrienders Worldwide, an international organisation with helplines in 32 countries. Visit befrienders.org to find the telephone number for your location.

Kosovo's former president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes

Kosovo's former president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
- Published
The former president of Kosovo, Hashim Thaci, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison after being found guilty of war crimes.
A hearing at The Hague on Wednesday sentenced the 58-year-old for crimes during Kosovo's independence war against Serbia in the 1990s, in which more than 10,000 people died.
He was convicted after a three-year trial of crimes including murder, illegal arrests, torture and cruel treatment. A number of other allegations against him were not proven.
Thaci was a co-founder and commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), a group that fought for independence. He is regarded as a hero in Kosovo.
He was accused of killing nearly 100 people and of committing other atrocities including enforced disappearances.
Thaci was facing trial alongside three former commanders of the KLA who faced similar charges.
The Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) was set up in the early 1990s as a militant group of ethnic Albanians, in what was then a province of Serbia, and during the war is alleged to have carried out attacks on the region's ethnic Serb minority.
Thaci became Kosovo's first prime minister when it declared independence in 2008. He later became president but resigned in 2020 to face the charges in The Hague.
Thousands of people gathered in Kosovo to watch the verdict on large screens as they were handed down.
In the capital, Pristina, photographs and videos showed people in tears as they learned of the verdict.

French President Emmanuel Macron has directed his government to step up efforts to secure fuel supplies and contain prices as rising costs put pressure on service stations, government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said Wednesday.
“About 10% of stations have had difficulty with at least one fuel,” Bregeon said.
She added that about nine in 10 of those stations belong to TotalEnergies.
Bregeon said Macron had called for a “total mobilization” on fuel supplies and price control.
She said TotalEnergies' decision to maintain a price cap on gasoline and diesel had attracted increased demand.
“That creates an influx of consumers, higher volumes sold than usual and a logistics chain that can sometimes come under pressure to restock, particularly after weekends,” Bregeon said.
She said the government had provided the necessary exemptions, including allowing fuel trucks to operate on Sundays and public holidays, and would continue working with the industry.
Bregeon noted that there were no “abnormal difficulties” in domestic logistics chains but that France was stepping up efforts to secure supplies internationally.
“The objective, in the coming days and weeks, is really for the president of the Republic to secure these supplies, secure the volumes,” including through other countries, she said.
She also said the government was working on the possibility of greater flexibility in European regulations, including to “loosen the system a little” for refineries.
Bregeon added that Macron was also holding regular discussions with US and Iranian counterparts and countries in the region to work toward a rapid easing of tensions and the “peaceful reopening” of the Strait of Hormuz.
Fuel prices in France have risen sharply in recent weeks amid disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East, with gasoline and diesel prices reaching record levels.
The rising prices have also prompted protests. About 100 fishermen and their supporters blocked a fuel depot in Frontignan in southern France on Wednesday.

The Armored Sarcophagus Saving Ukrainian Soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:41:08 UTC
20:41:08 KST

The Armored Sarcophagus Saving Ukrainian Soldiers
Unmanned ground vehicles are conducting once-impossible medical evacuations along Ukraine’s front lines.
The inside of an armored sarcophagus smells of gunpowder, gasoline, and gangrene. Remotely operated, unmanned ground vehicles, nicknamed MAULs, are revolutionizing casualty evacuations along the most dangerous sections of the Ukrainian front lines. They bristle with drone-jamming antennae and carry bulletproof black pods for carrying wounded soldiers to safety.
The MAUL goes in when other options have failed. After every rescue, it is cleaned and disinfected. Vitaly, call sign “Ash,” is a medical-evacuation coordinator with the 1st Separate Medical Battalion. (He asked to be identified only by his first name and call sign for security reasons.)
“You scrub and scrub,” he told me, “but the smell—it never goes away.”
I asked Ash what MAUL stands for. “It’s not initials,” he explained. “It’s a Star Wars thing—you know, Darth Maul? We’ve got a few nerds here.” The name is in all caps because the battalion’s stencil kit has only capital letters.
On the battlefield, these new machines have become priority targets for Russia’s drone pilots. They know that, for the morale of the Ukrainian crews coordinating rescues, losing a comrade in vivid detail on the monitors tracking the mission can be devastating. Russian operators wait until the wounded are loaded, then strike.
Aerial drones have created a death zone on the front lines, up to 20 miles wide, where anything caught in the open is likely to be struck. Unmanned ground vehicles began arriving in late 2024, mostly running resupply routes parallel to the front. But a mission in early 2025 proved that they could do more than this—that they were capable of reaching deep into the death zone to remove personnel. That mission began with a Facebook post.
In February 2025, near Kupiansk, Ukraine, a Russian advance trapped three Ukrainian soldiers from the 154th Mechanized Brigade behind enemy lines. All were wounded, two severely. For weeks, unit commanders attempted to pull them out. “We tried everything,” Kseniya Vynohradova, a veteran of the 154th who now leads an online support group for the unit, told me. Every effort failed.
“The brigade dropped supplies by drone,” Vynohradova told me, “but there was no way to get the guys out.” After a month of fending off Russian attacks and surviving on air-dropped rations, the soldiers were ready to give up. Their wounds had turned gangrenous, and their chance of survival was near zero. “I did not know what else to do,” Vynohradova said, “so I turned to Facebook.”
The first person to offer hope was Viktor Dolhopyatov. In a secret facility in central Ukraine, he runs Burevii, one of the country’s most innovative defense-tech companies. Russian bombardments have shattered most of the windows, but this superficial damage, common to thousands of buildings across the region, offers a kind of camouflage. From here, Burevii has transformed the modern battlefield. When Dolhopyatov read Vynohradova’s Facebook post, he answered immediately: “Tell us more, we want to help.”
Burevii’s engineers were developing a ground drone at the time. It would need a few modifications for a mission deep into the death zone—anti-drone netting, software updates, and a trailer attachment to carry three soldiers at once—but it could be ready within days. Olha Garbovskaya had joined the company two weeks prior and threw herself into the mission. “We called our machine Ardal,” she told me, after a son of the Greek god of craftsmen and technology. With engineers still attaching its final pieces, Ardal was rushed to the front.
The rescue began at dusk, with daylight fading but temperatures warm enough to partially mask Ardal’s heat signature. From a command bunker, Burevii’s engineers watched the mission unfold. High-definition screens displayed a ground’s-eye view from the drone. Overhead feeds tracked Ardal’s route to the stranded soldiers, who followed its progress over their radio. Without warning, a massive heat bloom filled the infrared monitors in the bunker. Ardal had struck a mine.
“Our hearts sank,” Garbovskaya said. “The commanders told us we had less than a 1 percent chance of succeeding, and we feared they were right.” Over the radio, the stranded men responded stoically: “We can’t take any more—just finish us off.” They begged to be bombed by Ukrainian drones. The team from Burevii asked them to hold out a little longer.
“Give us 48 hours,” Dolhopyatov said. “We have another machine.”
The second Ardal followed a different path through the minefield, and overhead bomber drones scoured the route to clear suspected mines. Ardal finally reached the men’s trench. They emerged ragged and wounded, but alive. Overhead, Russian drones closed in. From the command bunker, medics offered encouragement over the radio: “Climb in fast—we’re getting you out.”
Ardal carried them to safety, under the watchful eye of Ukrainian aerial drones. In the command bunker, Garbovskaya surveyed the scene. More than 50 people—pilots, medics, electronic warfare crews, engineers—had all assembled to save three men.
For most of history, recovering injured personnel from an active battlefield has not been a military priority. If the wounded could not make their way to safety, they were left until the fighting stopped. Serious injuries almost always ended in death, and the ratio of wounded to killed was about 3 to 1.
During the First World War, evacuating wounded soldiers became its own professionalized combat discipline. Many injuries were still fatal, but the ratio of wounded to killed began to improve. By the time of the Vietnam War, the widespread adoption of helicopters and the doctrine of the “golden hour”—the narrow window in which medical intervention is most likely to save a life—drove the survival ratio to 5 wounded for every soldier killed.
During America’s wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, rapid evacuation and advanced medical interventions brought survivability to historic highs. For every American soldier killed in those wars, approximately 10 survived their injuries. But in Ukraine, the death zone has made rapid evacuation all but impossible. Survivability has fallen, with a wounded-to-killed ratio of about 5 to 1.
Units such as the 1st Medical Battalion are trying to change that. The old battlefield math held that in many instances, rescuing a wounded soldier required more resources and risk than could be justified for a single life. But Ukraine has opted for a different way of calculating.
The military has introduced a points system that assigns varying values to different missions, rewarding units with credits that can be traded for new gear and supplies. Under the “ePoints” scheme, a routine resupply run earns two to three points; a casualty evacuation earns upwards of 70. On today’s battlefield, saving a single Ukrainian soldier is worth more than destroying a Russian tank.
Inside the death zone, Ukraine’s trenches are so difficult to reach that medics have had to reimagine the golden hour. Wound treatment must be provided on-site, by fellow soldiers. There simply are not enough medics for every trench.
Andrii Fedoryshyn, call sign “Jared,” is a trainer with the 1st Med. “The best thing we can teach a soldier is combat first aid,” he told me. “It’s more important than knowing how to shoot.”
The numbers bear this out. Less than 1 percent of the injuries seen by the 1st Med are gunshot wounds, and a soldier is far more likely to be called on to aid a buddy than to engage with the enemy. Everyone near the death zone, even journalists, carries a tourniquet. Many soldiers carry two or more, in the event that shrapnel severs multiple arteries. Once immediate care is provided, the waiting begins.
“For a front-line soldier, evacuation can take weeks,” the deputy commander of the 1st Med, who asked to be identified by only his first name, Igor, told me. “We once evac’d a patient who had a tourniquet on for 33 days.” That soldier’s unit tried everything to get him out: six attempts, six failures, and multiple armored vehicles lost in the process. The decision was made to send in a MAUL. “He lost the limb,” Igor said. “But we saved his life.”
As battlefield resources, MAULs are severely limited. Still, they are treated as expendable. Soldiers’ lives matter more. On average, two MAULs are lost for every five lives saved. I asked Ash, the battalion’s evacuation coordinator, if he ever got sentimental about the machines. “They’re tools,” he answered. “We don’t get attached.”
The platoon commander, call sign “Devi,” interrupted. “Except for this one,” he said, pulling up a video on his phone. It showed a MAUL that had lasted 10 missions, surviving drones and mines and saving the lives of 11 soldiers. After it was finally destroyed, its operators compiled a tribute video and posted it online, endowing the dead MAUL with a small but devoted fan club.
Officially, the logo of the 1st Med is a coiled snake, the ancient Greek symbol for medicine. The MAUL drivers have an unofficial logo of their own: a coffin overlaid with a progress indicator. They call themselves the “Tomb Raiders,” because, as Devi explained, “we bring people back from the dead.” Hence the movie posters plastered around the bunker, featuring Angelina Jolie in her Tomb Raider role. Opposite a wall of monitors, a scantily clad Jolie is covered in stickers featuring the coffin-and-timer logo. Each one represents a life saved. “When we fill the whole poster,” Igor explained, “we’ll auction it off to buy more machines.”
As much as medics value their MAULs, the soldiers I spoke with hated them. “No windows, no ports,” one told me. “I would rather have less protection and see what’s coming at me.” Once sealed in, a patient’s only link to the outside is a single ray of light streaming through the hinge seam and an intercom connected to the medic.
On a range far from the front, I rode inside a new MAUL undergoing testing. The coffin-like pod was stifling, and the bumpy ride nearly shook the bones out of my body. “I understand why soldiers hate it,” I told Devi. He received the feedback like a bad Yelp review. “Fair enough,” he said, “but a soldier able to complain is a soldier who survived.” The overwhelming majority of those rescued by a MAUL live to talk about it.
In the command bunker, a casualty call came in: severe internal bleeding, with developing sepsis. A MAUL set off. Overhead surveillance drones tracked its progress as the bombers scanned the route for potential mines. Ash checked in via radio about the soldier’s condition.
From the overhead feed, we saw the MAUL stop at a tree line. Two Ukrainian soldiers emerged from the foliage. One helped load the other into the sarcophagus, sealed the lid, and disappeared into the woods. Inside the command bunker, a calm professionalism prevailed. No voices were raised, except for Ash’s; he spoke loudly into his headset so that the patient could hear him over the noise of the machine.
Midway through the eight-mile return journey, the electronic-warfare team detected a heavy Russian suicide drone, a Molniya, lurking overhead. The MAUL took cover, let the Molniya pass, then continued to the transfer point where a medical team awaited. As it approached the rendezvous, the Ukrainians spotted another approaching drone. “Three kilometers, closing,” came the call. The patient was quickly lifted into an armored vehicle, which sped off toward the field hospital.
Ash’s job was done. He took off his headset and slumped into a couch. In the dim light, I noticed for the first time that he was wearing Crocs. His T-shirt, a Polish streetwear brand, said Ghosh. I sat next to him, somehow exhausted even though I had done nothing but observe. Through the walls I felt the thump of nearby drone strikes. No one else in the bunker seemed to notice them.
I asked Ash what he did before the war. “Musical theater,” he said. “I was a performer.” I asked about his greatest fear as a combat medic. “Losing one of our guys en route,” he answered. Not seeing the gore of injuries, or wondering whether his bunker would be hit. His heaviest burden was the thought of a disabled MAUL, one of his patients trapped inside, unable to make it home.
“Has this ever happened?” I asked.
“Yes,” he said. “Twice.”
In the Russian military, by contrast, being wounded and abandoned is the norm. At a POW camp in western Ukraine, I spoke with several Russian prisoners of war. “I was wounded in the legs,” one prisoner, who asked that I withhold his name for fear of reprisal, told me. “There was no rescue—my own guys left me to die.”
The first medical attention he received was from the Ukrainian military. Reliable figures for Russia’s wounded-to-killed ratio are difficult to pin down, but conservative estimates place it at about 2 to 1, worse than the survival ratio of Russian soldiers during World War I.
At the foothills of Ukraine’s Carpathian Mountains, far from the front lines, lies a rehab facility for injured soldiers. I met Pavlo there, four months into his recovery from injuries sustained trying to rescue another soldier. He had successfully driven his truck to the pickup point for his wounded comrade when he was struck by a Russian drone. Shrapnel entered his abdomen, tore through his bladder, and broke his pelvis. Someone dragged him into a trench. Pavlo begged to stay there, remembering the wrecked and burning vehicles littering the road he drove in on. Over the radio, the medics insisted, “If you do not leave, you will die for sure.”
At dusk, the unmanned ground vehicle came. Over the next three hours, the teams behind it—medics, ground-drone operators, bomber- and aerial-surveillance-drone pilots, and electronic-warfare crews—performed the intricate choreography needed to carry Pavlo to safety.
From the top of a Carpathian ski resort, under a cloud-dappled sky, Pavlo recounted every detail, from his failed attempt to rescue his fellow soldier to the moment he went into surgery. Every few minutes, we glanced skyward to scan for threats. We were safe, but such habits die hard. Pavlo would soon return to his new wife, and he knew that this would have been impossible without the ground drone and the humans who operated it, all working together to save this one soldier.
“I never met them,” Pavlo said. “A robot carried me, but people saved me. So many, just for me.”
He looked up again. “I don’t even know their names.”

Rescuers excavate rubble to retrieve bodies from a collapsed building in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City on September 16, 2026. (AFP Photo)
At least 20 Palestinians, including five children, were killed on Sept. 16 when a residential building housing displaced people that had been damaged during Israel’s attacks collapsed in western Gaza City, according to Palestinian sources.
Zaher Al-Wahidi, director of the Health Information Center at Gaza’s Health Ministry, said that 20 Palestinians were killed when the Al-Saada building in the city’s Al-Sinaa area collapsed.
Earlier, Gaza’s Health Ministry said in a statement that 16 people were killed and more than 25 others were injured in the collapse.
The ministry said the incident brought the total number of people killed in the collapse of buildings damaged during Israeli attacks to 50.
Palestinian Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said during a news conference at the scene that the building had previously been targeted by Israeli bombardment during the war before collapsing.
Bassal said around 100 people remained trapped under the rubble.
He warned that around 2,000 damaged buildings at risk of collapse remain occupied by residents and displaced Palestinians across the Gaza Strip.
Bassal called on the international community to provide the equipment and machinery needed to enable rescue teams to recover those missing.
Gaza Mayor Yahya al-Sarraj said during the news conference that the building’s collapse “warns of the danger of more damaged residential buildings collapsing.”
He stressed the need to allow mobile homes to enter Gaza before winter to provide alternatives for residents and displaced people.
The collapse came as Israel’s defense minister said on Sept. 16 that it was only a matter of time before the country resumes full-scale war in Gaza and moves to force out its two million Palestinians.
Israel Katz said 70 percent of Gaza had already been emptied of its population in the Israeli offensive.

AI leaders divided over pace of development as safety concerns mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:39:56 UTC
20:39:56 KST

The leaders of Anthropic, Nvidia, and OpenAI offered competing approaches to artificial intelligence at Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention in San Francisco on Tuesday, exposing an industry divide over whether development should be slowed, regulated, or primarily managed by technology companies themselves.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei renewed his call to slow the development of frontier AI, while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued against deceleration and new regulations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged that the public was justified in fearing the technology but maintained that developers could keep safety measures ahead of growing capabilities.
 
Amodei surprised by pace of growth
Amodei said AI’s technological and economic development had moved faster than even Anthropic anticipated.
“It’s been the pace of the progress, not just of the technology but of the economic side of it,” he told Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff during their Dreamforce conversation.
Anthropic had anticipated how capable AI models could become, Amodei said, but had not fully appreciated how rapidly those capabilities would drive the growth of AI companies and become embedded in the wider economy.
He used an automotive analogy to argue that a safety failure at one developer should prompt the entire industry to review its practices.
If a competing carmaker suffered brake failures, responsible manufacturers would examine their own vehicles rather than simply use the incident to attack a rival, he said.
“It’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” Amodei said during a conversation streamed by Salesforce. Companies should instead accept that none of them was likely to have a perfect safety record, he added.
Amodei has proposed embedding independent third-party evaluators inside AI companies, coordinating safety standards among democratic countries, and eventually establishing broader global cooperation.
He said Anthropic had committed to independent evaluations and would begin discussions with the industry on the other steps.
In a recent essay titled “We must pace the frontier,” Amodei argued that AI capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards needed to control them.
The proposal received support from Altman, xAI CEO Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis. It followed warnings from former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who resigned and claimed AI could pose an extinction risk to humanity within the decade.
 
Huang says ‘run as fast as you can’
Huang rejected calls for a general slowdown when he appeared at Dreamforce later Tuesday.
“Run as fast as you can,” he said during a discussion with Benioff.
The Nvidia chief described AI safety as an engineering problem that companies should address through secure testing environments and rigorous product evaluations.
Developers should pause an individual product if they lost confidence in its safety, he said, but governments should not restrain the wider industry.
“We don’t need any new laws. We don’t need new regulations,” Huang said, arguing that rapid innovation and safe products did not represent a “false choice.”
He also rejected fears that AI would eliminate large numbers of jobs, calling the suggestion “completely nonsense.”
Huang argued that companies would become more productive and ambitious as they adopted AI, increasing demand for workers capable of using the technology. He envisioned a future in which every business became an AI company and warned that those that failed to embrace the technology risked being left behind.
Nvidia has a significant commercial interest in rapid AI adoption. Its processors and computing systems are used to train and operate many of the industry’s leading models, while demand for AI infrastructure has driven the company’s profits and valuation sharply higher.
 
Altman says public is ‘right to be afraid’
Altman, speaking later Tuesday, said the speed of AI development had created legitimate public concern.
“I think the world is right to be afraid of this,” he said, adding that it now required less imagination to see how increasingly powerful systems could go wrong.
He described an incident in which OpenAI agents compromised another company’s systems during testing as a “wake-up call” for the industry and called for a new level of rigor in monitoring and cybersecurity.
Altman warned that openly available models capable of causing serious damage may not be far away and urged companies to use their current advantage to prepare for AI-enabled cyberattacks.
Although he previously supported Amodei’s slowdown proposal, Altman said he was disappointed with how parts of the argument had been framed.
He criticized companies that suggested they would behave responsibly only if competitors did the same, saying such messaging increased public fear.
“The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing,” Altman said.
He maintained that OpenAI would slow or stop development if it could no longer keep alignment and safety measures ahead of its models’ capabilities.
Critics, however, say companies competing for investment, customers, and technological leadership cannot be trusted to regulate themselves. US Sen. Bernie Sanders, US President Donald Trump's former adviser Steve Bannon, and Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark are among those calling for stronger oversight.
The debate comes as OpenAI and Anthropic prepare for possible initial public offerings, increasing the financial stakes surrounding any decision to accelerate or restrain frontier AI development.

Residents in an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum, protesting government plans to house more than 1,200 asylum seekers nearby, according to media reports on Wednesday.
Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a nearby Defense Ministry base in Bicester, the BBC reported.

Following the result, council chair Tim McNally said: "This is an example of democracy in operation.
"We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world."
In January, the UK Home Office announced its plan to use the base, known as Site A, located at the former Bicester Garrison site between Piddington and Upper Arncott, to house migrants.

Reacting to the convictions for war crimes of Hashim Thaçi, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi by the Kosovo Specialist Chamber, Esther Major, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe, said:
These verdicts give hope that the victims and relatives of the missing will finally see justice
Esther Major, Amnesty International
“These convictions give hope to thousands of victims of the Kosovo war who have waited for more than two decades to get justice for the horrific crimes committed against them and to know the fate of their loved ones.
“These convictions show that senior officials are not above the law.
“These verdicts give hope that any attempt to obstruct justice, truth and reparation will not be tolerated, and that the victims and relatives of the missing will finally see justice.”
Background
The Trial Panel of the Kosovo Specialist Chamber found the four former officials guilty of the war crimes of arbitrary detention against 385 individuals, cruel treatment against 49 individuals, torture against 303 individuals, and murder against 96 individuals.
The Trial Panel sentenced Hashim Thaçi to 25 years of imprisonment, Kadri Veseli to 18 years, Rexhep Selimi to 13 years and Jakup Krasniqi to 25 years in prison, with credit for time already served.
They were found not guilty of the charges of crimes against humanity.
These verdicts were first instance decisions and could be subject to appeal.

The world comes to New York: What’s at stake at UN General Assembly high-level week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:37:03 UTC
20:37:03 KST

The world comes to New York: What’s at stake at UN General Assembly high-level week
Each September, New York becomes the centre of global diplomacy as presidents, prime ministers, ministers and diplomats from around the world gather at United Nations Headquarters.
At a time of mounting geopolitical tensions and overlapping global crises, leaders will tackle a packed agenda that includes conflicts and international security, climate change, pandemic preparedness, sea-level rise, the fight against racism and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The high-level week of the UN General Assembly’s 81st session unfolds against a backdrop of growing divisions between countries and pressure on the multilateral system. The session will be presided over by newly elected Assembly President Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh under the theme: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.”
The world’s biggest diplomatic gathering
The centrepiece of High-Level Week is the General Debate, which begins on 22 September. Over several days, presidents, prime ministers and senior representatives of all 193 UN Member States will address the General Assembly from its iconic green marble podium.
The speeches provide a global snapshot of national priorities and concerns, with conflicts, economic challenges, humanitarian crises, climate change, development and emerging technologies expected to feature prominently.
Yet much of the diplomacy takes place behind closed doors, where hundreds of bilateral and multilateral meetings offer leaders a rare opportunity to meet allies, partners and rivals in one place.
Can the world still meet the 2030 deadline?
Ahead of the General Debate begins, leaders will gather on 18 September for the annual SDG Moment.
In 2015, countries adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals aimed at tackling challenges ranging from poverty and hunger to education, clean water and access to energy by 2030.
With less than five years remaining, the meeting will focus not only on assessing progress but also on highlighting practical solutions that can be expanded and replicated elsewhere.
Climate action in a warming world
On 23 September, UN Secretary-General António Guterres will convene world leaders for a High-Level Event on Climate Action and the Just Transition.
With global temperatures continuing to rise, discussions will focus on accelerating the shift to renewable energy, expanding climate finance for developing countries and strengthening support for communities already experiencing the impacts of climate change.
The following day, leaders will turn their attention to sea-level rise, one of the most visible consequences of global warming. For many small island developing States and low-lying coastal communities, rising seas are already threatening homes, infrastructure and freshwater supplies.
The meeting aims to strengthen international cooperation and mobilize support for countries most at risk.
Preparing for the next pandemic
On 25 September, Heads of State and Government will revisit the lessons of COVID-19.
The pandemic demonstrated how quickly a local outbreak can become a global emergency and exposed major inequalities in access to vaccines, medicines and other essential resources.
Leaders meeting on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response will discuss how to strengthen health systems, improve readiness, and ensure a more equitable international response to future health crises.
Rights, equality and inclusion
Another major meeting on 23 September will mark the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development, adopted by the General Assembly in 1986. The declaration established that development is about more than economic growth, emphasizing participation, opportunity and equity.
On 28 September, the UN will also commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, one of the principal international frameworks for combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance.
The anniversary provides an opportunity to assess progress and examine why discrimination remains a persistent challenge in many parts of the world.
Keeping nuclear disarmament on the agenda
The series of major meetings concludes on 29 September with a high-level plenary meeting marking the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons.
Nuclear disarmament was among the first issues addressed by the United Nations, yet nearly eight decades later nuclear weapons remain part of the global security landscape. The UN continues to regard their complete elimination as its highest disarmament priority.
‘We the peoples’
This year's High-Level Week takes place at a moment when international cooperation is under strain. From armed conflicts and climate change to widening inequality, countries face a growing number of challenges that no nation can solve alone.
Reflecting on the opening words of the UN Charter, Secretary-General António Guterres recently offered a reminder of the organization's founding purpose:
"Not we the powerful. Not we the victorious. We the peoples – all of us – bound by a single conviction: that we are safer, stronger and more human when we stand together."
Over several days in September, world leaders will have an opportunity to demonstrate how far they are prepared to turn that principle into action.
A changing of the guard
The 81st session will also be the final General Assembly session to begin under António Guterres as Secretary-General. His second and final term ends on 31 December 2026, concluding a decade at the helm of the Organization.
The process of selecting his successor is already under way. The next Secretary-General will take office on 1 January 2027, inheriting an Organization confronting many of the same challenges likely to dominate this year's High-Level Week.

Tax on parcels worth up to EUR 150: Parliament takes first step
That is according to the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine, Ukrinform reports.

The Finance Ministry recalled that the adopted amendments provide for abolishing the VAT exemption for imported goods purchased through marketplaces, which will create a level playing field for Ukrainian and foreign businesses.
The reform is also part of Ukraine's cooperation program with the International Monetary Fund under the EFF program and a condition for the European Union's macro-financial assistance.
The bills provide for:
- introducing special taxation rules for the distance sale of goods through marketplaces when their total invoice value does not exceed EUR 150;
- imposing VAT on the import of goods in international postal and express shipments from EUR 0;
- exempting non-commercial parcels worth up to EUR 45 from VAT, in line with the EU approach.
A list of goods for military personnel will also be introduced that will be exempt from VAT on the import of goods in international postal and express shipments.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada had previously rejected twice bills that would abolish the tax exemption and introduce VAT on international parcels worth up to EUR 150.

Why the world’s great powers are thinking about empire again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:35:29 UTC
20:35:29 KST

Why the world’s great powers are thinking about empire again
An empire is perhaps the most expensive indulgence that even the most powerful nations can afford only for a limited time. Arguments that empires are profitable are largely unconvincing and while they may enrich a narrow section of the elite, and perhaps do so spectacularly, it’s rarely for very long, and for everyone else, empire eventually means costs.
Consider the lives of ordinary people in 19th-century Britain, the colonial veteran portrayed by Rudyard Kipling, or the Russian village during the period of the Soviet Union’s greatest geopolitical power, as depicted by Russia’s remarkable “village prose” writers. Imperial grandeur didn’t necessarily translate into prosperity for those expected to sustain it, and eventually, the costs become impossible to ignore.
The ruling class begins to understand that the people fighting its wars may one day turn their bayonets against those who sent them, and this broadly speaking is what happened in the Soviet Union, although Britain, and to a lesser extent France, managed the retreat from empire more successfully in the second half of the 20th century.
But this leaves the fundamental question of how great powers can guarantee their security without absorbing potentially unstable neighbors into expensive imperial structures?
One of the paradoxes of international relations is that the more resources a state possesses, be they economic or demographic, the less it needs constant confrontation because the powerful can often obtain what they want with kind words rather than a gun.
This helps explain the relatively restrained policies of Russia and China toward many of their neighbors, given both possess vastly greater resources than the smaller states around them. Conversely, the fact that the United States, particularly under Donald Trump, increasingly reaches for the stick rather than the carrot can be interpreted as evidence that its relative capabilities are declining, but Russia will eventually have to confront similar questions.
Trump’s habit of publishing maps in which other countries or territories are colored in the American flag is of course partly political theater, but it also reflects a serious question troubling political elites and thinkers as they ask what we are to do with a world containing such an extraordinary number of sovereign states?
If Americans have begun asking the question, then the problem has acquired a genuinely fundamental character.
After all, it was the United States that emerged in the early 20th century as the principal advocate of dismantling the old European empires and creating more independent states with President Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points speech in January 1918 placing national self-determination near the center of the emerging international order. This was a challenge not merely to America’s enemies, but to its allies.
Britain and France were then the world’s largest colonial empires, so undermining one’s partners while displaying remarkably few qualms about doing so is therefore hardly an invention of the Trump administration, yet openly discussing the annexation of vast territories is something genuinely unusual in modern American foreign-policy rhetoric.
The United States had already acquired its ideal Lebensraum between two oceans, taking territory from a weakening European presence and purchasing Alaska from Russia. After that, Washington showed little interest in further enormous territorial acquisitions and there were practical reasons. Until the middle of the 20th century, other great powers could resist such ambitions, while most desirable territories lay inconveniently across oceans.
America instead developed another method of projecting power, with military bases and its habit of placing them across the world. That is partly a consequence of geography because a country separated by oceans from the principal centers of Eurasian civilization needs forward positions if it wishes to influence events there. Without them, America’s capacity to interfere with adversaries, and occasionally friends, would be considerably reduced.
Whatever its motives, Washington nevertheless spent much of the 20th century presenting itself as an opponent of traditional European imperialism, and curiously, on this question American anti-imperialists found common ground with the Russian Bolsheviks, given the Council of People’s Commissars proclaimed the right of peoples to self-determination immediately after taking power in November 1917.
The borders that eventually emerged from the former Russian Empire were determined largely by the outcome of the Civil War. Where the Bolsheviks prevailed, national republics were incorporated into the Soviet Union, and where they failed, often with Western assistance to their opponents, independent nationalist governments emerged.
The Bolsheviks didn’t think principally in terms of rebuilding the old Russian Empire and Stalin certainly contemplated a more centralized relationship between Russia and the other Soviet peoples, provoking Lenin’s famous criticism of him and Felix Dzerzhinsky as “Great Russian bigots.” But by then the foundations of the old imperial system had already been dismantled.
Nor did the Bolsheviks particularly need traditional empire, because like the Americans who came later, they imagined global influence through the spread of ideas.
Communist victory was supposed to make territorial empire unnecessary because governments sharing communist values would naturally share fundamental interests. Decades later, Western liberalism produced its own version of the same proposition as Francis Fukuyama’s “end of history” thesis and the democratic optimism of the Clinton era rested on a comparable assumption: liberal democracies would have fewer fundamental conflicts because they shared political values.
Neither experiment produced the universal harmony its advocates anticipated.
The modern political map was created largely from the wreckage of Europe’s territorial empires, including Russia’s, and the result is an international system containing an enormous number of sovereign states whose interests cannot easily be reconciled.
For a century, politicians attempted to overcome this problem through ideology, as Communists believed common socialist values could unite states and liberals later placed similar hopes in democracy and international institutions.
That era now appears to be fading and even the European Union is struggling with the limits of political integration despite its members sharing broadly liberal conceptions of the state.
So, the underlying problem therefore returns. How can large, established powers guarantee their security in a fragmented world without reconstructing the empires whose enormous costs eventually destroyed or exhausted them?
There’s no convincing answer yet and perhaps that’s why political leaders have returned to coloring in maps.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

Russia unveils air defence system against Ukrainian long-range drones – photos
Russian defence company Kalashnikov has unveiled for the first time the Zveroboy air defence system, armed with Kraken FPV interceptor drones.
Source: press service for Kalashnikov
Details: Kalashnikov claims that Zveroboy is designed to provide round-the-clock protection of facilities against reconnaissance and strike drones.
Among the targets of the system, Russia specifically lists Ukrainian drones such as Leleka, Liutyi, Bober and Hornet-XR.
"The system consists of an automated workstation at the ground control station, an optical targeting system, three launch containers, a digital repeater, a technical compartment with a distribution panel and switching unit, a compass on a telescopic pole, and a radar system," the company said.
The system's primary means of engagement are high-speed, multirotor Kraken FPV drones with a specialised warhead. Each of the three launch containers holds three interceptors, giving the system a total of nine such drones.
The Kraken drones can be used during the day and at night. The night-time Kraken-N version is additionally equipped with a thermal imaging camera.
Zveroboy is offered in two versions: stationary and mobile. The latter is mounted on the chassis of a mass-produced pickup truck, which is intended to simplify the system's relocation and concealment.
Kalashnikov also claims that Zveroboy can be integrated with existing surveillance and perimeter security systems.
Russia has not disclosed the system's detection and engagement range, the speed of the Kraken interceptor drones, the mass of their warheads or other key specifications.
Background:
- It was previously reported that Russia had developed the Met interceptor drone, designed to counter drones at short ranges.
- In June, Russian holding company Shvabe unveiled a system for guiding interceptor drones towards strike UAVs. The system, whose name has not been disclosed, consists of a ground-based electro-optical station, interceptor drones and an operator workstation.

Merz's fate in the balance as second eastern German state goes to the polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
