Palestinian youth may soon get to vote for the first time. Few believe it actually matters.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip are scheduled to vote on November 28 for the first time in 20 years. For most of the electorate, it will be their first time at the ballot box. And for many of them, it may not matter.
Palestinian factions that have spent two decades in bitter — and at times violent — division are joining forces ahead of the upcoming legislative election, forming the broadest political coalition seen in the occupied territories in years. The Alliance of National Forces (ANF), formed following a series of talks in Cairo, includes Hamas, the two main dissident currents of Fatah led by Muhammad Dahlan and Nasser al-Qudwah, the Gaza-based paramilitary Popular Resistance Committees (PRC), which was never interested in politics, and the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ), a faction that has historically opposed elections in principle. The Palestinian left-wing factions, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) and the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), are still considering whether to join.
Fatah, led by President Mahmoud Abbas, has said it will run independently and rejected the possibility of running on a joint list with Hamas.
In the background, Abbas has amended the elections law to require that any candidate subscribe to the official PLO political program, including all signed agreements with Israel — a condition that civil and legal groups have denounced as undermining political diversity and freedom. But the amended law also raises the number of legislative council seats from 132 to 200 and lowers the age of candidacy to 20 years. The Palestinian Authority (PA) says that these changes are designed to encourage broader participation.
According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, 64 percent of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza are under the age of 30. The majority of the electorate was either not born or too young to vote when the last elections took place in 2006. They are now being asked to choose between factions founded decades ago that are largely led by the same figures and run on programs that have not changed in years, divided along disputes that trace back to the Fatah-Hamas split of 2007 — decades before most of today’s first-time voters were old enough to understand what was at stake.
The energy of 2021
When Abbas announced legislative elections in January 2021, before calling them off a month before the vote, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were briefly swept by a surge of political energy. Thirty-six electoral lists were announced and began campaigning. Of those, only seven represented traditional factions. Five were explicitly youth lists, seen at the time as evidence of a generation hungry for participation and frustrated by the options available to them.
One, named “Karamati” — Arabic for “My Dignity” — included young professionals from both Gaza and the West Bank, and campaigned on democratic participation, opportunities for young people, and care for vulnerable sectors.
Another, the Generation of Democratic Reform, known by its Arabic acronym JAD, included intellectuals, professionals, and activists. JAD launched a virtual shadow parliament as an alternative to the official electoral process, campaigning — among other things — against the legal requirement of a $10,000 deposit as a condition for candidate registration.
The most outspoken and independent list was called Freedom and Dignity, headed by Palestinian activist Nizar Banat, a carpenter with a graduate degree in the Arabic Language and Law, and who had become an online political commentator known for his blunt, often scathing criticism of the PA. His list campaigned on fighting PA corruption, rejecting the Oslo-based order of negotiations with Israel, and opposing politically-conditioned European funding.
Then, in April of that year, Abbas canceled the elections. Nizar Banat criticized the decision and called on donor countries to cut off funding to the PA until it abided by the popular demand to hold legislative elections. A few months later, PA security personnel abducted and killed him, beating him to death while in custody.
Demonstrations broke out across the West Bank in protest over his killing, galvanizing a wave of popular outrage that was met with a swift PA crackdown. The assassination of Banat marked the denouement of political engagement in the Palestinian street, and with it the brief period of political enthusiasm around the legislative elections.
The scar of cancellation
The 2021 call for elections brought to light figures, ideas, and trends that were invisible in the Palestinian political mainstream, a far cry from the level of engagement demonstrated since the 2026 announcement of legislative elections. So far, only party lists have been announced, and the majority of Palestinians remain skeptical.
Much of the current detachment goes back to 2021 — not just to what the elections promised, but to what their cancellation cost.
Zein Abu Daqqa, Senior Fellow at The Institute for Social and Economic Progress, where he researches trends in Palestinian society, told Mondoweiss that “the cancellation of the 2021 elections had a deep and negative impact on how Palestinians think about elections.”
“Psychologically, the cancellation functions as an anchoring event which people remember vividly,” Abu Daqqa, who participated in the JAD initiative in 2021, said. “They also remember that some candidates sacrificed money, jobs, and other livelihoods to stand, only for the elections to be canceled shortly thereafter.” Abu Daqqa described the cancellation as “a real scar on the Palestinian psyche, which anyone considering forming a list now will have to reckon with.”
But Abu Daqqa also points to the compressed timeline. Elections were announced in late August with a vote scheduled on November 28, leaving barely three months for candidates to organize, register, and campaign. “Even in an open political environment, this would be a short window,” he explained, “and we have not had an open political environment or an active political life for many years.”
Haneen Abu Omar, a Palestinian in her early thirties who also participated in the JAD initiative, goes further, stating that many youth who showed enthusiasm in 2021, including herself, “have lost trust in the idea that Palestinian elections would fix things.”
“After a genocide in Gaza, and the ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, we saw a wholesale acceptance by Palestinian leaders from all factions of U.S. conditions, especially to the condition of creating a technocratic committee to run Gaza outside of the Palestinian political institutions, as if accepting the disintegration of Palestine,” she explained. “New elections seem designed to give legitimacy to this new order of things. I personally don’t trust this political system anymore, and I don’t trust that elections can fix it.”
She also points to the shock of the past three years. “Before October 2023, things weren’t rosy, and there were large Israeli raids in the West Bank, and people were arrested for no reason, but today things are on a whole different level,” she said. “Today, Palestinians feel that there is an existential attack on their presence in their country, and if I were a Bedouin who was expelled from his home and was still looking for a place to stay, or a mother from Gaza who is living under a tent and looking for food for her children, I don’t think that democratic participation in Palestinian institutions would be my first priority.”
As for Abu Daqqa, he sees this shift in attitudes reflected in his research. “Priorities have moved toward the economy and stability,” he said, drawing a historical parallel with the aftermath of the Second Intifada, during which stability and security also dominated Palestinian concerns. Yet, when elections were announced in 2005, Palestinians still participated in large numbers, with both presidential candidates, Mustafa Barghouthi and Mahmoud Abbas, campaigning on job opportunities, reconstruction, and fighting corruption, alongside national liberation goals.
“Attitudes toward the present elections are shaped by three perceptions,” Abu Daqqa noted. “Whether the elections will actually take place; whether they will be free and fair; and, following from these, whether they will have any bearing on people’s lives. If all three conditions are satisfied, the same hope and interest recorded in earlier questions on reform, democracy, and governance can be expected to return.”
‘Will it bring back our lost homes?’
In Gaza, the outlook for elections is grimmer still.
Razan Abdel Raheem, 26, is a children’s writer from al-Shati’ refugee camp in eastern Gaza. She has lived all the episodes of Israel’s genocidal war on the Strip, been displaced twice with her family, and lost her home to an Israeli airstrike. She now lives with multiple other families in a relative’s house.
In 2021, at 21, she also considered casting her first-ever vote for an independent youth list. Today, she told Mondweiss that she has no interest in the upcoming elections.
“I find it difficult to believe in anything at all after all that we have gone through,” Razan said. “What will a new legislative council do with the wholesale destruction here in Gaza? Will new elections fix all the injustices that we have been forced to live through since Hamas took over in 2007? Will it give us back the youthful years that we lost to Israel’s bombing campaigns? Will it bring us back our lost homes or our lost friends and family?”
Razan raises the questions that animate Gaza’s post-genocide politics with particular precision. “Will a newly elected council push back the Yellow Line that the occupation keeps moving toward us?” she said, describing Israel’s progressive expansion of the invisible line demarcating the Israeli-controlled part of the Strip. “Will it bring justice for Hind Rajab and the thousands of children like her who were killed? Will it make it possible for the people of Beit Hanoun, Rafah, and Khan Younis to go back to their land? Will it pursue cases to hold the occupying state accountable worldwide? Will it rebuild my parents’ house?”
“If the answer is ‘yes,’ then I will be the first to vote, and even demonstrate and campaign, too,” she said. “But I don’t think it is.”
Razan also points to a quieter demographic shift that she says is draining Gaza of the generation most likely to drive political change. “Most young people in Gaza who had a chance of leaving have left through scholarships or artistic residencies — I’m talking about the intellectual elite of Gaza’s youth who survived the genocide,” she explained. “Most of our friends from Gaza’s small Christian community also left, leaving a void in the city.”
Gaza, Raheem concludes, “is not what it used to be, and new elections are not enough to repair what has been broken.”
According to Abu Daqqa, the dark shadow that the Israeli genocide casts on elections is related to the precise moment Palestinians now experience. “Hope itself rises and falls with political events and with the political horizon,” Abu Daqqa explained. He believes it is “likely temporary, and will lift once people come to believe in a new process or new leadership.”
A generation disengaged
In mid-August, the Palestinian daily newspaper Al-Quds reported findings from the latest youth poll by the Palestinian Center for Polls and Survey Research, which surveyed 1,281 Palestinians aged 18 to 29 across Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.
According to the findings, 72.4 percent of young Palestinians in Gaza aged 18 to 29, alongside 26.7 percent of the same cohort in the West Bank, did not follow the municipal elections held last April.
Up to 45 percent of those surveyed said they weren’t interested in internal Palestinian politics, 15.3 percent said they had lost trust in Palestinian elections, and 13 percent said they found no convincing candidate.
According to the report, 64.1 percent said they often or seriously think about leaving their country.
Yet Abu Daqqa’s research points to another aspect of the Palestinian youth’s outlook on their country’s politics. “When Palestinians are asked how they expect change to come about, they consistently point to elections,” Abu Daqqa said. “When asked about reform, most understand reform to mean elections. What people want is an electoral process through which they can choose their representatives. Elections, in short, remain both credible and a priority.”
The gap between the political energy of 2021 — with its youth lists, independent candidacies, and public debate — and the near-silence of 2026 reflects something beyond disillusionment with any particular party. It reflects a generation that watched elections canceled in 2021, a genocide unfold in 2023 and after, and a political class unable or unwilling to respond to either.
Abu Daqqa believes that the opportunity isn’t entirely lost for the current generation of Palestinian youth. “Each generation must develop the tools, tactics, and strategies through which it builds its own approach to liberation, and I am confident that the current generation will develop its own set of tools, principles, and strategies to do exactly that,” he said. “Innovation, creativity, and determination are everywhere in Palestine.”

Russia continues Ebola response in Uganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:59:48 UTC
19:59:48 KST

Russia continues Ebola response in Uganda
Russia is continuing its work in Uganda following the country’s Ebola outbreak, with specialists remaining on the ground, the head of Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, said on Tuesday.
Speaking at a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Popova said Russian experts were deployed to Uganda shortly after the outbreak began and helped local authorities bring it under control. “Efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak in Uganda are still underway right now,” she said.
The East African state was declared free of Ebola on August 27 after recording no new infections for 42 days. The outbreak, which began in May, caused 20 confirmed cases and two deaths in the country. Fifteen infections were imported from DR Congo, while five occurred among contacts and health workers linked to those cases, the authorities said.
“The test, which we brought there during the very first few days, proved to be highly effective,” Popova noted, adding that, after being further refined on the ground, the test has since passed the first stage of the World Health Organization’s qualification process.
Russia has provided Uganda with broader support in tackling Ebola and other infectious disease threats. Moscow sent epidemiologists to the country in May to assist with the outbreak investigation and supplied diagnostic tests, while a Russian mobile anti-epidemic laboratory was donated to Uganda in 2024. More than 80 Ugandan specialists have also received training at Rospotrebnadzor institutions in pathogen monitoring, laboratory diagnostics, biosafety, and other areas.
Earlier this month, ten specialists from the Ugandan Health Ministry and research institutions began a two-week course in Moscow covering disinfection, pest control, and field surveillance.
While Uganda has brought its outbreak to an end, Ebola infections continue to rise in neighboring DR Congo. The latest government figures show 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths, putting the case fatality rate at 48.4%. A total of 1,726 patients have recovered, while 905 remain in isolation or hospital care.
The outbreak has now spread to 62 health zones across seven provinces, with Ituri the worst affected. Cases have also been recorded in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, and Sud-Ubangi.

Prisma Peremarket files redundancy notice, 67 support jobs lost
Finnish-owned supermarket Prisma's Estonian arm, acquired by Coop this year, has filed a collective redundancy notice affecting 67 support unit employees.
This represents about 10 percent of its workforce, and the company said store staff will not be affected.
The Coop sale has meant existing support roles overlapping with the new owner's structure are redundant, the company said. Affected roles include product category coordinators and the communications manager.
Maren Penu, head of Prisma Peremarket's support units, said employees who received redundancy notices will be paid the compensation required under Estonian law.
"The final number of employees to be laid off will become clear during the process. The notice period depends on the employee's length of service and ranges from one to three months. Store employees will not be affected by the layoffs," Penu said.
Prisma Peremarket AS, formerly part of Finland's SOK Group, has been operating in Estonia since 2000. In September this year, Coop Eesti Keskühistu became the owner of Prisma Peremarket, following the sale announced in spring. The company had 13 stores in Tallinn, Harju County, Tartu, Narva and Rapla, and these are in the process of being reopened as Coop outlets, between now and year-end.

Belarus Frees 25 More Political Prisoners in Return for U.S. Sanctions Relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:58:42 UTC
19:58:42 KST

Belarus has agreed to free 25 prisoners in return for a further easing of U.S. sanctions, an envoy for U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.
The deal was part of lengthy negotiations in which Washington is urging Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko to free hundreds of people, including human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers in exchange for sanctions relief and an easing of his international isolation.
Trump's envoy, John Coale, told reporters in the Belarusian capital Minsk: "We agreed to an interim deal, and as a show of goodwill Belarus will release 25 people and in exchange the United States will lift sanctions on two companies."
The figure of 25 was much lower than the 250 that Coale persuaded Lukashenko to release when he last visited Minsk in March.
Coale said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues to pave the way for another prisoner release and the removal of further sanctions.
"We will continue to improve U.S.-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future. We are not finished!" he posted later on X.
Belarusian human rights group Viasna said a new round of prisoner pardons had started, with relatives of some detainees being told they could pick up their loved ones from prison on Wednesday morning.
Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the former Soviet state still holds more than 900 political prisoners, even after Coale negotiated the release of hundreds since the middle of last year.
Among the most frequent charges against them are "extremist" activity, conspiring to seize power, incitement to hatred or insulting the president.
At Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the people in question were political prisoners and rejected assertions by rights groups and the exiled opposition that he is steadily arresting more people to replace those he releases.
The two companies to be removed from U.S. sanctions are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of paints and industrial coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial concern that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors. Sanctions against them have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also promised Lukashenko on Tuesday to get U.S. banks to hand back tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets.
Coale's efforts since last year have led to the release, among many others, of Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales Bialiatski and leading opposition figures. His diplomacy has earned gratitude from many Belarusians, while also raising concerns.
"We should use every opportunity to save lives. But we should not confuse releases with political change. Repression continues, and Lukashenko continues supporting Russia's war," exiled opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said in comments to Reuters on Tuesday.
"The purpose should be to empty the prisons, not to rehabilitate the dictatorship."

Berlin seeks tougher security measures after Pride attack
BERLIN, Sept 16 - The German government proposed new measures to prevent militant violence, including tougher penalties for knife attacks and propaganda, after a man who pledged allegiance to Islamic State attacked a Pride celebration in Berlin this summer.
Here are more details from Wednesday's proposals by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig:
• The use of electronic-ankle monitors will be expanded, restricting the movement of high-risk suspects.
• Knife attacks will be classified as felonies with a minimum prison sentence of one year.
• Germany's 16 state governments will be granted additional authority to store communications data as part of preventive security measures.
• Hubig also said that authorities aim to clarify when suspended sentences are appropriate. "If the consequences of a potential offense – or even a previous offense – could be tremendous for the public, then this must be explicitly taken into account," she said.
• In July, a 21-year-old man attacked Berlin's Pride celebration, killing one woman and injuring dozens, according to investigators.
• The German citizen, who in May was convicted and sentenced to jail time for preparing an attack, had been freed under supervision. REUTERS

IAI debuts new tactical vehicle for German special forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:57:52 UTC
19:57:52 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) has introduced a new tactical vehicle for Germany’s special forces, marking the first public appearance of the TAHR, a platform built on IAI’s ELTA ZD chassis and produced by Flensburg Technology Systems (FTS).
The first pre-series vehicle was unveiled ahead of schedule at the annual conference of the German Special Forces Command, the Kommando Spezialkräfte (KSK), in Altensteig‑Wart on Tuesday.
The TAHR is based on the Israeli ZD platform developed by IAI ELTA, which has been battle-proven by Israeli special forces. FFTS, a joint venture between IAI’s ELTA division and German defense contractor FFG, developed and manufactures the vehicle in Germany.
Designed as a light, air‑transportable platform, the TAHR incorporates operational modifications requested by the KSK, including an open architecture for integrating weapons and sensors and a layout intended to improve situational awareness. Its compact dimensions also enable two TAHRs to be transported inside CH‑47 Chinook helicopters, with crews able to achieve combat readiness shortly after landing, a core requirement for airborne special operations.
The TAHR will be delivered to the KSK in two variants, a combat configuration and a support model. Both are based on an existing all‑terrain platform already in service. FTS adapted the design to meet the KSK's mission-specific requirements, which rely heavily on rapid deployment and mobility in demanding environments.
“The KSK’s mission is to conduct special forces operations worldwide and under all conditions successfully. To do this, the KSK requires not only high mobility but also a variety of suitable modes of transport depending on the situation, mission, and terrain,” said KSK commander, Brig.-Gen. Andreas Kühne.
“With the TAHR, we are getting an operational and combat vehicle that is air-droppable and ready for deployment in any terrain. Together, we have succeeded in advancing this important armament project for the KSK in such a way that the first pre-series vehicle can be presented within just one year,” he added.
FTS signed a framework agreement in October 2025 with the Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support, the German Army’s procurement authority, to supply up to 200 vehicles.
IAI’s leadership described the rollout as a milestone in the company’s cooperation with Germany.
“IAI views Germany as a strategic partner in developing joint defense capabilities over the long term. Our cooperation spans multiple domains, from air and maritime to land, and is grounded in the combination of technology, expertise, and industrial capabilities on both sides. We are committed to further deepening this cooperation and jointly developing solutions to address the evolving security challenges of the years ahead,” IAI CEO Guy Barlev said.
ELTA CEO Dror Bar noted that delivering the first vehicle ahead of schedule showed the effectiveness of the industrial collaboration and the ability to tailor proven Israeli platforms to German operational needs.
“We are proud to present the first TAHR vehicle ahead of schedule. This achievement reflects the strength of our industrial cooperation with our German partners and our ability to deliver advanced, proven platforms tailored precisely to the customer’s operational needs,” he said.
Europe has increasingly turned to Israeli defense technology over the past decade, especially after Russia invaded Ukraine and the growing demand for rapid, combat‑proven systems.

====================================================================================================

Feature: Bridging two medical worlds: an American doctor's Hainan story
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:57:32 CST
19:57:32 KST

HAIKOU, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- When Dr. Timothy Stephens arrived in south China's Hainan Province in 2013, he didn't expect patients there to bring him mangoes from their gardens, fish their husbands had caught, or mooncakes they had baked at home, to express their gratitude.
"It's very endearing," said the 46-year-old American physician. "They want me to participate in the local culture."
Known in China as Shen Yiyang, Stephens works at the International Clinic of the Haikou People's Hospital in the provincial capital. He left a comfortable practice in Boston to help build Hainan's nascent primary care system.
"I saw the opportunity because China was looking to start developing primary care, and as a family doctor, that's my specialty," he recalled. "I could come and share my experience in the United States and how we do primary care, and also help with developing the training of local doctors."
Speaking four languages, he is the go-to doctor for international patients in Hainan. But it is his bond with local families that defines his practice.
"I could say that I symbolize being a bridge between the United States and China," he said. "By coming here, and by being a part of things here, we have a chance to connect in ways that wouldn't happen if we were in separate countries."
CHINA SPEED AND SCALE
Having lived and worked in Hainan for more than a decade, Stephens still marvels at how efficient the local hospitals are. Patients here can see a doctor, get blood tests, or book a CT scan all within the same day.
"Patients here are easily able to access their doctors," he said. "This really changes the way that we provide care, because in the United States, most of the time we provide care by appointment only."
The doctor also highlights the role of the Boao Lecheng International Medical Tourism Pilot Zone in Hainan in introducing the newest diagnostics and treatments.
A special medical area within the Hainan Free Trade Port, the zone has become a regional hub for international pharmaceutical equipment manufacturers and innovative small and medium-sized pharmaceutical and medical enterprises.
The zone offers patients access to overseas-approved medical devices and pharmaceuticals that are not yet available elsewhere in China. Additionally, it provides Chinese doctors with the opportunities to explore the latest international medical technologies without leaving the country.
In 2025, the zone recorded a total of 865,300 medical tourism visits, a remarkable 109 percent surge from the previous year.
Earlier this year, Stephens helped a lung cancer patient from Hong Kong access a new Chinese targeted therapy. The patient's symptoms stabilized, and the quality of life improved dramatically.
MEDICAL EXCHANGE AND COOPERATION
Stephens believes both China and the United States can learn from each other.
He observed that in terms of medical education, the United States has done a good job with standardized training and credentials. Yet he warned against current pitfalls in the American healthcare system, such as unsustainable cost increases and insurance coverage gaps.
Stephens praised China's universal health coverage efforts, noting that the Chinese government has expanded insurance, free elderly screenings, and chronic disease management.
"One of the great aspects of China's healthcare development is that the government is looking at the needs of the whole population," he said.
Stephens speaks highly of Hainan, which began island-wide special customs operations last year. New policies in the island province now recognize foreign physicians' credentials without local exams, he said, adding that the Haikou hospital he works in recently hired a Sierra Leonean pediatric specialist.
"Medicine is an international field," he said. "When we're able to have international teams of clinicians working together, we can have a much better and more solid framework for understanding how to meet patients' needs."
Looking ahead, the American doctor is expecting greater exchanges and cooperation between the two countries.
"Whereas people often want to emphasize the differences, I think there's so much more that we actually have in common," he said.

Mainland slams Taiwan's DPP for marginalizing traditional Chinese culture in education
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
18:57:10 CST
19:57:10 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) for trying to reshape education along its secessionist line, warning that such actions could leave Taiwan detached from its Chinese cultural heritage.
Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a regular press conference in response to a question about the DPP authorities' long-running efforts to reduce Chinese cultural elements in education and remove classical Chinese texts from school curricula and textbooks.
Zhu said the DPP authorities' secessionist education has had "serious consequences."
Chinese culture constitutes an essential part of the spiritual heritage of Taiwan people and has provided cultural impetus for the island's economic and social development, she said.
When Chinese cultural traditions are severed on the island and classical Chinese works are removed from textbooks, Taiwan students will have fewer opportunities to study Chinese classics and learn about important historical figures and events in school, Zhu said.
"This is not children's fault that they are ignorant about Chinese history and tradition but the fault of the 'Taiwan independence' forces," Zhu said.
With "education reform" starting in the 1990s amid a rising secessionist narrative, the changes to curriculum and textbook guidelines in Taiwan have been highly political, aimed at removing Chinese cultural elements and severing historical ties with the Chinese mainland.
Taiwan adopts a textbook selection system in which the education department issues guidelines on what should be included in textbooks, and schools can then choose from different editions of textbooks that follow the guidelines.
With the implementation of the 2019 guidelines, the number of recommended classical texts for senior high school students has been reduced to 15 from 30 recommended by the previous guidelines. Several landmark works that are important for Chinese identity and values are no longer on the recommended list.
Before the 2019 textbook guidelines, Taiwan's history textbooks generally followed a chronological structure, starting from the birth of Chinese civilization and covering various imperial dynasties before reaching contemporary history. Under the current senior high school curriculum, Chinese history is more often taught as part of a broader East Asian and regional history, with greater emphasis placed on Taiwan's history.
Many educators and parents on the island have repeatedly voiced their concerns about the rising secessionist tendency in education. Some of them have operated an association and a website since 2018 to compile and teach history and Chinese language courses themselves. ■

US to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discrimination
Unknown

2026-09-16
10:56:45 UTC
19:56:45 KST

The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners.
The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies.
Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution.
“The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X.
“The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.”
The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added.
The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activist Leo Brent Bozell III, said on X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.”
South Africa’s foreign ministry said in response that its policies were being misrepresented. “The announcement, once again, aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa’s domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of “minorities” and Afrikaners in general,” the ministry spokesperson Chrispin Phiri said in a statement that was first published in Afrikaans.
Phiri added: “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice … South Africa respects that the United States may hold different views regarding particular measures and their implementation.”
Afrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.
Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute.
These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according to a 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal.
Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted.
Rubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land.
Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chant was played by Trump when he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year.
The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and is therefore not hate speech.

Germany’s special forces get their first new TAHR vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:54:39 UTC
19:54:39 KST

- FTS and Germany's Special Forces Command unveiled the first pre-series TAHR light airborne combat vehicle on Sept. 15, 2026, in Altensteig-Wart.
- A German framework agreement signed in October 2025 covers up to 200 TAHR combat and support vehicles for the KSK.
Flensburg Technology Systems and Germany’s Special Forces Command unveiled the first pre-series TAHR light airborne combat vehicle on Sept. 15, 2026, at the opening of the 10th KSK Defence Symposium in Altensteig-Wart, Germany.
FTS presented the vehicle to Brigadier General Andreas Kühne, commander of the Special Forces Command, known by its German acronym KSK. The Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support, or BAAINBw, signed a framework agreement with FTS in October 2025 covering delivery of up to 200 vehicles. That contract set a new vehicle class for German special operations forces, built in a 3.2-ton range on a platform from Israel Aerospace Industries and its ELTA subsidiary that has already seen combat use elsewhere.
The TAHR comes in two versions, a combat vehicle and a support vehicle, both based on the same all-terrain 4×4 chassis. The combat variant reportedly seats three and can mount a 12.7mm heavy machine gun, an MG6 minigun or a grenade launcher. The support variant carries two crew and no main weapon, built instead to move equipment and supplies. FTS says the vehicle’s open layout gives operators a clear line of sight from inside, while still allowing different weapon systems to be fitted. Two TAHR vehicles fit inside a single CH-47 Chinook, and FTS says troops can reach full combat readiness within a short window after landing and exiting the aircraft.
“The KSK’s mission is to successfully conduct special forces operations worldwide and under all conditions,” said Brigadier General Andreas Kühne, Commander of the Special Forces Command. “To do this, the KSK requires not only high mobility but also a variety of suitable modes of transport depending on the situation, mission, and terrain. With the TAHR, we are getting an operational and combat vehicle that is air-droppable and ready for deployment in any terrain. Together, we have succeeded in advancing this important armament project for the KSK in such a way that the first pre-series vehicle can be presented within just one year.”
“IAI views Germany as a strategic partner in developing joint defense capabilities over the long term,” said Guy Bar Lev, CEO of IAI. “Our cooperation spans multiple domains, from air and maritime to land, and is grounded in the combination of technology, expertise, and industrial capabilities on both sides. We are committed to further deepening this cooperation and jointly developing solutions to address the evolving security challenges of the years ahead.”
“We are proud to be making a direct contribution to the future operational readiness of the Bundeswehr and the KSK by presenting the first pre-series vehicle ahead of schedule,” said Jörg Kamper, Managing Director of FTS. “Achieving this important milestone is only possible if, as in the current EGF project, all parties involved work together in a focused and coordinated manner. We would like to take this opportunity to thank the KSK and the BAAINBw for their excellent and trusting cooperation during the first phase of the project. With today’s presentation, we have laid an important foundation for making this project a lasting success story.”
FTS is a joint venture between FFG Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft and IAI/ELTA Systems, combining FFG’s vehicle and combat engineering work with IAI/ELTA’s robotics, autonomy and electronic warfare technology.
Reports around the October 2025 signing put the framework agreement’s initial order at 40 combat vehicles and 14 support vehicles, worth roughly 30 million euros ($35 million), with deliveries expected by the end of 2028 and further vehicles possible over the seven-year agreement. FTS said today’s unveiling came ahead of that original schedule. The company has said it plans to offer the TAHR to international special operations customers beyond Germany, though no foreign order has been announced.

US Charges Five in Russian Intelligence Network Over Violent Plots in America and Europe
The US Department of Justice has charged five alleged members of a Russian intelligence network accused of recruiting operatives for terrorist attacks in Europe and plotting to assassinate a Russian dissident in the United States, US Attorney General Todd Blanche announced.
According to the US Department of Justice, the five defendants allegedly operated as part of a global network working on behalf of Russian intelligence services since at least 2024. The network specialized in organizing contract killings and acts of terrorism, with its activities targeting Russian dissidents and defectors as well as countries supporting Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“It is our job to stop America’s adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil. And that’s precisely what we are doing thanks to the work of the FBI and our Justice Department prosecutors,” Blanche said.
According to ABC News on September 16, the case, filed in the Southern District of New York, centers in part on an alleged plot to assassinate a prominent Russian dissident whom the defendants believed was in Washington, DC.
US investigators identified 63-year-old former Russian intelligence colonel Yuri Khrameev and his son, 27-year-old FSB officer Kirill Khrameev, as alleged leaders of the network. Investigators said its leadership also included 35-year-old Cuban national Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, who resides in Russia.
Two other defendants, 35-year-old Cuban national Yaidel Delgado Suarez and 22-year-old Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, helped identify and recruit potential operatives in the United States.
“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said.
According to investigators, the network recruited a US resident during the summer of 2026 to conduct surveillance and help arrange the killing of a prominent Russian dissident. The alleged recruiters offered between $1,000 and $1,500 for surveillance and $40,000 for the killing.
The indictment also describes an earlier effort in Lithuania, where the network allegedly recruited a US citizen in 2025 to surveil a person whom the Russian operatives described as spreading damaging information about Russia. Yuri Khrameev later allegedly offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the Russian dissident using either an incendiary device or a knife.
After the individual refused, Khrameyev proposed what he described as simpler assignments involving arson attacks against food warehouses or electrical substations. Investigators said he identified potential targets as countries supporting Ukraine and promised substantial payments.
The alleged network’s activities extended beyond assassination plots. Investigators said Durruthy coordinated preparations for an attack in Prague, Czechia, in June 2024 and another planned attack in Lithuania in September of that year.
“The Russian-led network charged in today’s indictment is brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching, and the charges levied against the defendants should send a clear message: no matter where you are, and no matter who you work for, we will investigate and prosecute you for your crimes,” US Attorney for the Southern District of New York Jay Clayton MacDonald said.
All five defendants remain at large. They have been charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Three of the defendants also face conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire charges, punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
The charges come amid broader efforts by European countries to counter suspected Russian covert operations and hybrid threats. Germany and Ukraine have agreed to strengthen security cooperation in response to such threats, with Ukrainian intelligence and law enforcement specialists set to share their experience in countering drones, sabotage, espionage, and cyberattacks.

Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in 2022 protest crackdown, Amnesty says
Investigation says senior and local officials coordinated the lethal repression of the Woman Life Freedom uprising in 2022
Amnesty International has accused Iranian authorities of committing crimes against humanity during the suppression of the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising and called for 87 officials to face criminal investigation.
In a report released four years after the death in custody of Mahsa Amini triggered nationwide protests, the organization alleges that Iran used coordinated lethal force to silence demonstrators. It documents murder, torture, rape, enforced disappearance, imprisonment and persecution.
Amnesty recorded the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, including 56 children. It said security forces fired rifles, handguns and shotguns loaded with metal pellets into crowds, sometimes pursuing and shooting people as they fled.
The report is based on 270 interviews, more than 2,000 videos and records including court rulings, forensic documents and leaked official orders. Amnesty said the evidence points to a state policy implemented through Iran’s security councils, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps and the national police.
The 87 officials identified include senior commanders, Interior Ministry officials and provincial and county authorities. Amnesty said their inclusion establishes grounds for investigation, not a finding of individual guilt. Iranian authorities did not respond to the organization’s findings before publication.
Kurdish and Baluchi communities suffered a disproportionate share of the violence, accounting for 62% of the deaths documented. Amnesty said this included 106 Baluchi victims and 95 Kurdish victims, concluding that the targeting of both communities amounted to persecution on ethnic and political grounds.
Amnesty called on the UN General Assembly to establish an international justice mechanism for Iran. It also urged national prosecutors to pursue cases under universal jurisdiction and asked states to press the UN Security Council to refer the situation to the International Criminal Court.
The organization said international accountability is necessary because Iran’s judicial system lacks independence from the officials and security institutions implicated in abuses.

New photos reveal extensive damage to US bases from Iranian missile and drone strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:52:56 UTC
19:52:56 KST

New images obtained by CBS News reveal extensive damage to U.S. military aircraft, vehicles and buildings following Iranian missile and drone strikes on American bases across the Middle East.
The photographs were provided to the network by active-duty U.S. service members who asked to remain anonymous. “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” one deployed service member told CBS News. “We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”
The images document damage from Iranian missile and drone attacks at several U.S. positions in the region.
One of the most striking photographs was taken at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. It shows a direct hit on the rear section of a U.S. Air Force Boeing E-3 Sentry, a four-engine airborne warning and control aircraft.
The aircraft’s tail is separated from its charred fuselage. The E-3, distinguished by the large rotating radar dome above its fuselage, is used for airborne surveillance, command and control and monitoring activity across large areas of airspace.
Other photographs from Prince Sultan show heavily damaged buildings and troop living quarters.
Some of the damaged structures stand alongside concrete barriers known as T-walls that appear to have remained intact. Such barriers have long been used to provide protection against threats including mortar fire and explosions, but the images underscore their limitations against aerial attacks involving missiles and drones.
Additional images were taken at Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a major staging area for U.S. Army ground forces in the Middle East.
There, photographs show damage to several armored vehicles as well as military aircraft and other equipment.
The new photographs add a visual dimension to the scale of losses described this week in the first inspector general report to Congress on the U.S. conflict with Iran.
According to the report cited by CBS, equipment losses were valued at as much as $3.7 billion and included nearly 60 aircraft. The report said U.S. Central Command recorded Iranian attacks against American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The figures cover broader equipment losses connected to the conflict and should not be read as a valuation of the damage shown in the newly released photographs alone.
CBS has also reported damage to U.S. aircraft at other bases during the fighting. At Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, for example, sources told the network that an A-10 Thunderbolt lost a wing in an Iranian strike while roughly eight F-15 fighter jets sustained lighter damage and were returned to service.
For the service member who spoke to CBS, however, the newly released photographs point to a broader concern about the vulnerability of U.S. positions in the region.
“These are not ‘squirters’ getting through,” the service member said, referring to terminology previously used for isolated incoming threats that penetrate defenses. “We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed.”

Turkish FM: Attacks against Saudi Arabia unacceptable

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan (AA Photo)
Türkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has denounced intensifying attacks against Saudi Arabia as “unacceptable,” pledging full solidarity and support under the terms of the newly formed Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
“It is unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be hit from both the south and the north, and to be targeted by attackers stationed in Iraq,” Fidan was quoted as saying by the Turkish media on Sept. 16.
Fidan referred to attacks from Yemen-based Houthi groups that target critical energy infrastructure and threaten the use of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the expense of disrupting maritime security.
“The Yemen problem has existed for a long time, taking various shapes and forms. When the situation turns into an activity aimed at containment [of Saudi Arabia] from both the north and the south, destroying critical infrastructure, and harming not only Saudi Arabia but the entire region, it is impossible for anyone to remain indifferent to it,” Fidan stated.
Türkiye is acting in line with the spirit of the Mecca agreement and has already announced its support and solidarity to Saudi Arabia, he added.
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan announced the creation of the defense pact in early August. Under the alliance, an attack against one member is considered an act of aggression against all.
Responding to a question, Fidan noted that technical talks are still underway to establish the pact’s framework and determine how the alliance’s mechanisms will function.
“This is about to be accomplished. Our objective is to enlarge the Mecca Alliance. More concrete steps will be taken,” he stated.
Regional countries should act together
Addressing regional issues, Fidan underscored that continued cooperation among regional nations is indispensable for achieving concrete results, citing the collaborative approach taken on Gaza as a key precedent.
“Now, we are implementing this cooperation model in the Iran-U.S. war as well, and we are institutionalizing it further. In the face of Israel’s destabilizing role in the region, we are engaged in an effort based on cooperation and peaceful diplomacy,” he stated.
Describing Israel as the highest threat to the stability of Syria and the region, Fidan said, “Israel does not particularly like its neighboring countries being strong and stable. It views this as a threat to itself. Due to its definition of this threat, it engages in destabilizing actions toward these countries.”
HH Greece should not arm Aegean islands
Fidan also commented on Greece’s militarization of certain Aegean islands that hold demilitarized status.
“We don’t want Greece to be used as a tool by those who want to destabilize, drag the region into chaos,” Fidan said, indirectly referring to Israel, which signed a multibillion arms deal with Greece.
The minister noted Türkiye aims to pursue good neighborly relations with Greece, emphasizing that both nations must take steps to avoid disrupting regional security.
“Naturally, we have a very serious sensitivity regarding the militarization of certain islands. They know this; we have conveyed it to them. Particularly, the militarization of islands with a demilitarized status constitutes a threat to us,” he added.

FNSS finishes testing first Kaplan APC for Indonesian Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:50:54 UTC
19:50:54 KST

- FNSS and PT Pindad completed pre-delivery acceptance tests in Turkey on the first Kaplan APC built for the Indonesian Army.
- The armored vehicle extends the companies' earlier Kaplan MT (Harimau) tank program, with a second prototype now in production in Indonesia.
The first Kaplan APC, an armored personnel carrier Turkish manufacturer FNSS is building for Indonesia, has completed its pre-delivery acceptance tests in Turkey.
FNSS and Indonesian state defense manufacturer PT Pindad ran the tests under their Kaplan APC Development and Production Agreement, signed in October 2024 to meet an Indonesian Ministry of Defense contract for a 30-ton class tracked personnel carrier. The vehicle will now ship to Indonesia, where FNSS and PT Pindad will run final acceptance tests with the Indonesian Army. A second Kaplan APC is being built in parallel at PT Pindad’s own facilities in Indonesia, part of a technology transfer arrangement between the two companies.
The Kaplan APC extends a partnership that dates back further. FNSS and PT Pindad jointly developed the Kaplan MT, known in Indonesia as the Harimau, a medium tank the companies began delivering to the Indonesian Army starting with an initial batch of 18 vehicles. That program’s technology transfer model was a factor in the Ministry of Defense’s decision to award the follow-on APC work to the same two companies, according to FNSS. Deliveries of the Kaplan APC were previously expected by the end of 2026, and the completed pre-delivery tests keep the program on that general timeline.
The vehicle is built to carry a crew of up to 13, including a driver, commander and gunner, with the remaining seats for dismounted troops who enter and exit through a power-operated rear ramp. It shares automotive components with the Kaplan MT to cut through-life costs, and FNSS says the design also draws on subsystems from its Marine Assault Vehicle, already in service with the Turkish Naval Forces Marine Infantry Brigade.
FNSS describes the Kaplan APC’s protection as including ballistic armor and mine protection systems, along with an automatic fire suppression system, air conditioning and a CBRN filtration system that keeps the crew compartment sealed. Customers can add an active protection system to defend against anti-tank missiles and rocket-propelled grenades if they choose. The vehicle’s electronics are built on an open architecture, which FNSS says makes it easier to add a battlefield management system or a 360-degree situational awareness system with day and night vision.
The Kaplan APC is designed as a modular platform. Depending on customer requirements, it can mount light or medium-caliber weapons such as 30mm or 35mm cannons, or heavier systems including 120mm mortars and anti-tank guided missiles, in either manned or unmanned turrets. FNSS says the same modularity lets the vehicle be configured for mechanized infantry, reconnaissance, command and control, medical evacuation, rescue, combat engineering, and direct or indirect fire support roles.

what do we see when we look at clouds? the MET traces two centuries of skywatching
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:50:36 UTC
19:50:36 KST

A small blue-tinted mirror, on display as part of Chasing Clouds at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, once asked its user to do something novel. Instead of facing a landscape directly, the so-called Claude mirror was held over the shoulder, so that the scenery behind became a miniature reflection. Its slightly convex surface compressed the view while its dark glass deepened the colors. Artists used them, but so did tourists.
Long before the camera arrived, people were already finding ways to transform the world into an image before looking at it.
Now open in New York, the ephemeral exhibition is curated by Stephen C. Pinson and follows more than a century of people looking upward, from plein air painters studying changing skies around 1800 to Alfred Stieglitz pointing his camera almost exclusively at clouds in the 1920s. The subject is familiar enough to disappear into the background.
It becomes an excuse to ask what happens when we really look. ‘Around 1800, you have this convergence of scientific study of the clouds,‘ Pinson explains, ‘and then painters also going out into nature and trying to capture clouds.‘
Johan Christian Dahl, Norwegian, Bergen 1788–1857 Dresden, Cloud Study, 1820s, oil on paper, Thaw Collection, Jointly Owned by The Metropolitan Museum of Art and The Morgan Library & Museum, Gift of Eugene V. Thaw, 2009
the sky becomes an observatory
John Constable made looking into a practice of its own. During the 1820s, he repeatedly visited Hampstead Heath in London to paint cloud studies, returning at different hours and under changing weather. He sometimes wrote the conditions directly onto the work: time of day, wind direction, where he was facing. He called the practice ‘skying.’
Hampstead became something close to a natural observatory, although the images retain all the looseness of paint moving quickly across paper. ‘For him, the sky and the light in the sky was the most important part of the picture,‘ Pinson says during a preview of Chasing Clouds at The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Constable was looking up at the same moment scientists were trying to organize what they saw. In 1802, Luke Howard proposed the cloud classifications still familiar today, including cumulus and cirrus. His ideas traveled well beyond meteorology. Goethe wrote in response to Howard and circulated his work among artist friends, while clouds were appearing throughout Romantic poetry.
‘It was something that people were actually paying attention to and sharing amongst friends and colleagues,‘ He continues. The sky had become a subject to study, name, paint, and contemplate.
John Constable (British,1776–1837), Hampstead Heath with Bathers, ca. 1821–22, oil on canvas, Thaw Collection, jointly owned by The Metropolitan Museum of Art and The Morgan Library & Museum, Gift of Eugene V. Thaw, 2009
when photography struggled to see the sky
Photography seemed to promise an easier answer. A machine could record the world in front of it, bypassing the painter’s hand. The sky quickly exposed the limits of that idea. Early photographic chemistry reacted poorly to blue light, so an exposure that captured the land could wipe out the clouds above it.
In John Beasley Greene’s photographs of Egypt from the 1850s, the problem produces something unexpectedly beautiful. Sea and sky break into mottled fields, almost dissolving into abstraction. ‘It’s exquisite and it looks very modern,’ Pinson says. What now reads as an expressive image emerged partly from a camera struggling to see.
Photographers even began building the sky themselves. Édouard Baldus painted it away on the negative, leaving a blank field overhead. Gustave Le Gray took another approach, joining one negative exposed for the sea with a second made for the clouds. He became so skilled at the technique that he kept a library of skies to use across different pictures. Pinson continues: ‘You might find the same clouds over a different ocean completely.‘
John Beasley Greene (American 1832–1856), The Nile in front of the Theban Hills, 1853–54, salted paper print from paper negative, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Gilman Collection, purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2005
the camera begins constructing the sky
There is something unusually contemporary about the trick. The photographic image carried an expectation of truth almost from the beginning, yet its makers were already cutting the visible world apart and putting it back together. The person standing before the finished picture had little reason to know that the ocean and the sky had ever existed separately.
Elsewhere in the exhibition, photographers paint clouds directly onto negatives while painters begin making images that seem to absorb photography’s strange cropping and tonal effects. The camera changes how people look, and painting changes alongside it.
Roger Fenton’s cloud studies push that exchange somewhere more emotional. He allowed the ground to fall deep into shadow in order to preserve the sky above, producing photographs far removed from the work for which he became best known.
Pinson describes them as ‘more about capturing a feeling or an emotion‘ than recording the scene in front of the lens with complete objectivity. By this point, the show’s early distinction between seeing and interpreting has become increasingly hard to maintain.
Gustave Le Gray, French, 1820–1884, Mediterranean Sea – Sète, 1857, Albumen silver print from glass negatives, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Gilman Collection, purchase, Robert Rosenkranz Gift, 2005
decontextualized clouds become abstractions
Then Stieglitz points his camera upward and removes almost everything else. At Lake George in the 1920s, he began photographing clouds without the familiar cues of horizon or landscape. He initially called the series Music. Eventually these images became part of what he termed his Equivalents. By then photographic technology could capture the sky with ease, so the challenge had changed. The cloud became a vehicle for something the camera could never record directly.
‘He was not trying to capture this sort of objective reality,‘ Pinson says. ‘It was for him a representation of his emotional state at the time that he made the photographs.‘
It’s a fitting place for Chasing Clouds to stop. Across the show, artists and great thinkers invent new ways of seeing the same thing overhead, from a darkened piece of glass to increasingly capable cameras. But each new device complicates the view as much as it sharpens it. By the time Stieglitz removes the ground beneath the cloud, looking has become an act of projection too. The sky is still there but what we see in it depends, as ever, on who is looking.
Alfred Stieglitz (American, 1864–1946), Equivalent, 1933, gelatin silver print, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Alfred Stieglitz Collection, 1949
Jean-Michel Cels (Belgian, 1819–1894), Cloud Study in the Late Afternoon, October 1840, oil on paper, Thaw Collection, jointly owned by The Metropolitan Museum of Art and The Morgan Library & Museum, Gift of Eugene V. Thaw, 2016
Gustave Le Gray (French, 1820–1884), The Great Wave, Sète, 1857, Albumen silver print from glass negatives, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Gift of John Goldsmith Phillips, 1976
John Singer Sargent (American, 1856–1925), Clouds, 1897, watercolor, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Gift of Mrs. Francis Ormond, 1950
Marie-Charles-Isidore Choiselat (French, 1815–1858), Stanislas Ratel (French, 1824–1904), The Pavillon de Flore and the Tuileries Gardens, 1849, Daguerreotype, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Gilman Collection, purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce

Gallery: Exhibition of French photographer Jean‑Louis Courtinat opens in Tallinn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:50:00 UTC
19:50:00 KST

Gallery: Exhibition of French photographer Jean‑Louis Courtinat opens in Tallinn
On 15 September, the Juhan Kuus Documentary Photo Center opened an exhibition by French photographer Jean‑Louis Courtinat titled "It Concerns All of Us," featuring nearly 80 photographs ranging from his social‑documentary work of the 1980s to the present day.
For more than forty years, Courtinat has photographed people who often fall outside society's attention or toward whom we tend to avert our gaze: children undergoing cancer treatment, people nearing the end of life, caregivers and medical workers, people living in homelessness and poverty, abandoned children, prisoners, and refugees.
"This exhibition is not only about those whom society tends not to notice. It is about all of us, because vulnerability is not an exception but part of being human," said curators Kristel Aimee Laur and Toomas Järvet. "All of us have needed someone's gaze, hand, or presence. Courtinat's photos place the question before us as well: do we notice, do we look away, or do we stay? He does not ask us to pity the people in the photographs from above, but invites us to recognize in them something of ourselves and of our shared humanity. In the end, there is no 'them' and 'us' — there is only us."
Jean‑Louis Courtinat received the prestigious Prix Niépce in 1991 and, in 2025, the Visa d'or des Solidarités award for his life's work at the Visa pour l'Image festival. He took part in the major national photography commission "Radioscopie de la France," organized by France's Ministry of Culture and the Bibliothèque nationale de France. His works are held in collections including the Centre Pompidou, the Bibliothèque nationale de France, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie, and the Musée Réattu.
France's Ministry of Culture has selected the exhibition curated by the Documentary Photo Center for the official program marking the 200th anniversary of photography. It is also the only event in Estonia included in the international jubilee program.
The exhibition "It Concerns All of Us" will remain open at the Juhan Kuus Documentary Photo Center until 3 January.

Canada invited to become EU’s first ‘associate member’ as Trump trade war intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:49:12 UTC
19:49:12 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday said the European Union is opening the door for Canada to become the first associate member of the 27-nation bloc.
The announcement marks a significant change in EU policy and signals a major deepening of ties between Brussels and Ottawa.
Speaking in her annual state of the European Union address in Strasbourg, France, the EU chief said the bloc wants to bring the relationship with Canada "to the highest level possible."
"And, dear Mark, I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships so I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union," von der Leyen said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in attendance for the speech and is due to address EU lawmakers on Thursday, had previously said Ottawa was keen to pursue a "unique security and economic alliance" with Europe, but not full membership.
Canada is currently locked in a bitter trade war with the U.S. and has pledged to match President Donald Trump's tariffs dollar for dollar.
Von der Leyen said the EU and Canada "see the world with the same eyes" and pledged to work together on issues such as artificial intelligence, climate change, geopolitics and Arctic security.
The EU and Canada already have a free trade agreement, one that eliminated 99% of all tariff lines when it provisionally came into force in 2017. The pact is known as the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA.
"We will move from CETA to an alliance for the future, to create a common prosperity and economic security space," Von der Leyen said.
The EU has previously been reluctant to entertain the prospect of flexible membership categories, notably when German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pushed for the EU to consider associate membership for Ukraine earlier in the year.
Asked whether von der Leyen's push to embrace Canada as the EU's first associate member was history in the making, Berenberg's chief economist, Holger Schmieding, said, "I think this is a big step, indeed."
"Europe is trying to openly form new partnerships or deepen partnerships with all countries in the world that are sort of like-minded," Schmieding told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.
"It is not necessarily against the U.S., but it is clearly in favor of making us less dependent on the U.S. and less dependent on China, and that deeper partnership with other countries, like-minded democracies, is actually something we see in the economic re-arm," he added.
In early June, Finnish President Alexander Stubb outlined his vision for a much larger European Union, saying the bloc should "think big" to project power on the global stage. As part of this, Stubb said the EU might consider increasing its membership to 40 states and named Canada, the U.K., Turkey, Norway and Iceland as potential candidates to join.
"Wouldn't it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" Stubb said on June 3, referring to Trump's ambitions to annex Canada.
'Middle powers'
At the start of the year, Carney told delegates at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, that so-called middle powers must band together to counter the rise of hard power and build a more cooperative and peaceful world.
"We have a situation where it is totally unpredictable what the United States are doing and we have aggressive industrial policy by China — and therefore, it's so important that we strengthen our ties with democratic countries, and Canada is one example," Bernd Lange, who chairs the European Parliament's trade committee, told CNBC on Wednesday.
Alongside Ottawa, Lange said the EU should push to build stronger economic ties with Brazil, Indonesia Japan and South Korea.
"It's so important that we work together and build a bloc and as Mr. Carney … mentioned in Davos, you have to be strong and sit at the table, otherwise you will be part of the menu," he added.

Germany: Chancellor Merz is fighting for his political survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:49:00 UTC
19:49:00 KST

Germany's Chancellor Merz tries to rally his troops
September 16, 2026
Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers (about 1,100 miles) north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various countries had gathered there for the European Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change.
When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent.
"That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said.
Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
Why is Merz so unpopular?
Another heavy defeat looks likely in the state election coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low 7%. Failure to clear the 5% hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election.
The election earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt was won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, in this central German state.
Before taking office, Merz promised he would cut support for the AfD "in half." Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system?
Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change."
One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy."
When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm.
"You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now," said SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese on the Welt TV channel. "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better."
Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst
But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor.
SU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party.
Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April in North Rhine-Westphalia.
Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag.
However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment.
Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the chancellor."
Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."
The statement was signed by all eight premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Pivotal state elections coming up
So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down.
If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him.
Merz's schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources have confirmed.

Central banks’ gold demand still high, Karahan says

19:48:36 KST

Turkish Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan (AA Photo)
Central banks’ demand for gold remains strong as geopolitical risks reshape reserve management, Turkish Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan said on Sept. 16.
Speaking at the Budapest Financial Summit, he said reserve managers needed to consider access to assets alongside safety, liquidity and returns.
Assets that were liquid under normal conditions might not be readily available during periods of stress.
Karahan said central banks were reassessing gold’s role, but this did not mean the end of the U.S. dollar’s dominance.
The dollar still accounted for a large share of foreign exchange reserves, supported by deep and liquid markets.
He called for diversification and contingency planning, saying the key question was how much of a country’s reserves could be used during a crisis.
Gold had long held an important place in Türkiye’s financial system and household savings, he added.
Karahan also warned that geopolitical rivalry could expose central banks to larger and longer-lasting economic shocks, affecting inflation expectations and decisions on wages and prices.
