Bulgarian student joins elite ETH Zurich programme to study AI safety
Maria Drencheva wins one of just 20 places from a field of 2,500 applicants
Wednesday 16 September 2026 13:07
Wednesday, 16 September 2026, 13:07
Maria Drencheva
PHOTO mon.bg
Font size
Bulgarian student Maria Drencheva has been selected for a prestigious research programme at ETH Zurich, winning one of just 20 places from a field of 2,500 young talents, the Ministry of Education said.
The Student Summer Research Fellowship (SSRF), organised annually by ETH Zurich, attracts some of the world’s top students. For two months, Drencheva worked on a key question in modern AI safety: what happens when an AI agent is given a task but clear limits are placed on the actions it is allowed to take. Her research examines whether an AI agent can take actions that fall outside those limits.
Drencheva is an INSAIT fellow in the EXPLORER programme and a student at Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski. Bulgarian media have dubbed her the “golden girl” of mathematics for her success in numerous Olympiads and international competitions.

India summons Pakistani diplomat after incident in Arabian Sea
India accuses Pakistan of ignoring bilateral agreement after collison between the two countries’ navies.
India has summoned Pakistan’s top diplomat in New Delhi in protest against a collision between the two countries’ navies in the Arabian Sea.
The Indian Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday that a Pakistani naval ship had collided with an Indian warship in international waters the previous day.

The ministry said it had lodged a protest with Pakistan’s charge d’Affaires of the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi.
It accused Pakistan’s navy of “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct” leading to a collision with an Indian Navy unit.
It said the incident violated a 1991 bilateral agreement that requires naval ships and submarines of both countries to keep at least three nautical miles apart in international waters.
The ministry said the charge d’affaires was asked to convey to his government the need for military units to respect the agreements between the two sides “to prevent any repeat of such incidents”.
India’s charge d’affaires in Islamabad was also instructed to lodge a similar protest with Pakistan’s foreign ministry.
There was no immediate comment from Pakistan’s government.
This incident is the first case of direct military tension between the nuclear-armed neighbours since they fought a four-day direct conflict last year.
The two countries have not had ambassadors in each other’s capitals since 2019, when they downgraded diplomatic ties after New Delhi revoked the special status of Indian-administered Kashmir.
India and Pakistan have fought three major wars, two of them over the status of Kashmir, since they gained independence from British rule in 1947.

Şimşek pledges to sustain inflation fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:45:56 UTC
19:45:56 KST

Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek has stated Türkiye will stick to its disinflation program despite slower progress, estimating that the war in Iran left inflation at least seven percentage points higher than it otherwise would have been.
“We will not abandon disinflation during the election period,” Şimşek said in a joint Bloomberg HT-Habertürk interview on Sept. 16.
“We need disinflation for sustainable growth.”
He said the war had raised prices across commodities, extending its impact beyond oil and natural gas.
Without the conflict, inflation would have ended this year at around 20–22 percent, he estimated, acknowledging that disinflation could take longer than initially planned.
Annual inflation stood at 31.51 percent in August. The government’s 2027–2029 Medium-Term Program forecasts a year-end rate of 28.4 percent.
Şimşek said inflation was proving more persistent than models had predicted because rents, education fees and wages remained closely tied to past price increases.
Monetary policy had been more effective in slowing goods inflation, although services were also beginning to respond.
Describing the cost of living as the government’s top priority, he said public-sector pay and pension payments would rise by at least the rate of inflation.
On exchange rate policy, Şimşek said a floating currency remained the preferred system, but conditions did not yet allow greater flexibility.
Strong demand for the lira could cause it to appreciate excessively without intervention, he said, adding that a more flexible regime could be considered once inflation reached single digits.
Turning to public finances, he forecast a budget deficit of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product this year, below the original 3.5 percent target, despite revenue forgone through fuel tax relief.
Şimşek described the budget as the most binding element of the Medium-Term Program because it was largely under government control.
He also cited the exit from exchange rate-protected deposits and stronger reserves as achievements of the program.
He forecast economic growth of 3.3 percent this year, acknowledging that the program had contributed to slower growth but saying external conditions were also weighing on activity.
Net exports were the only component subtracting from growth, he said.
For manufacturers, Şimşek said a working capital support program that began this year with 250 billion Turkish Liras could be expanded.
He also pointed to a separate 750 billion lira investment loan program offering 10-year financing for selected manufacturing investments.
“We are trying to ease the pressure on businesses through selective and targeted policies,” he said, adding that support should not undermine the broader monetary policy stance.
On taxation, Şimşek said the government did not plan to extend its fuel tax relief into 2027, although support for diesel would continue until the end of this year.
The mechanism cushions increases in pump prices by reducing excise duties.
He said next year’s projected increase in tax revenue reflected economic growth, the assumed end of fuel tax relief and efforts to bring undeclared economic activity into the tax system.

Eindhoven start-up Euclyd has raised more than €200 million to develop AI chips, and former ASML boss Peter Wennink has become chairman of the board, the company said on Tuesday.
The company is designing chips for what the industry calls inference, which is when an AI model is being used rather than trained. Most of that work is currently done on US-owned Nvidia processors. Euclyd says its chips will use less power and cost less.
Wennink was chief executive of ASML in Veldhoven from 2013 until 2024. In the statement he said Europe has “world-class capabilities across semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and systems engineering” and that Euclyd could build these into “a globally competitive AI infrastructure platform”.
Kastrup said in the same statement that the money would go on hiring engineers and speeding up development. “AI is becoming a foundation of economic growth, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness,” he said, “but its potential will remain constrained unless we fundamentally change the infrastructure beneath it.”

NATO-backed Kosovo separatist ‘responsible for war crimes’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:42:27 UTC
19:42:27 KST

NATO-backed Kosovo separatist ‘responsible for war crimes’
The former leader of the NATO-backed Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) has been found responsible for war crimes committed by the militant group during its NATO-backed campaign to break away from Serbia in the 1990s.
Hasam Thaci, who served as the first president of the self-proclaimed Republic of Kosovo, has been found guilty of the murder of 96 political opponents and suspected Serbian collaborators, the verdict said. He was also convicted for the unlawful detention and torture of hundreds of people.
The 58-year-old Thaci and three other former KLA leaders tried in The Hague are widely regarded as heroes in Kosovo. Thaci’s defense argued that senior figures in the KLA could not control rank-and-file separatist fighters and thus could not be held responsible for crimes committed under their leadership. Lawyers described the group as lacking a strict military hierarchy during the 1998-99 conflict.
NATO’s bombing campaign targeting Serbia, which Washington and its European allies framed as a humanitarian intervention, ensured KLA’s victory. Belgrade does not recognize Kosovo as an independent state, having rejected the unilateral declaration passed by the breakaway entity’s parliament in 2008.
The US, the UK, France, Germany, and many other Western and European nations, however, officially recognize Kosovo’s independence. Camp Bondsteel, the headquarters of NATO-led Kosovo Force (KFOR), is the largest American military base in the Balkans.
Among the more gruesome claims related to the Kosovo conflict was that the KLA harvested organs from Serbian prisoners and sold them on the black market, which former Chief Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia Carla Del Ponte detailed in her 2008 memoir.
The allegations were further substantiated in a 2010 European Council report, which also implicated former Thaci subordinates in the trafficking of humans, drug and arms, as well as protection rackets and other organized crime. His government allegedly ensured impunity for those “mafia-like” networks, the document said.
The Serbian government accused the West of pursuing selective justice in the wake of the Balkan wars, allegedly focusing on Serbian suspects and overlooking crimes attributed to their opponents.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), where Thaci was tried, was set up in The Hague in 2016, after earlier cases failed in Kosovo due to alleged political interference and witness intimidation.

‘If you’re building Frankenstein, stop’: JD Vance dismisses calls for AI regulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:42:07 UTC
19:42:07 KST

The US vice-president has dismissed calls for global regulation of AI safety risks, telling companies creating the most advanced models: “If you’re building Frankenstein, stop.”
In remarks addressed towards Dario Amodei, the co-founder of Anthropic who has called on Washington DC to coordinate control of AI systems, including with China, JD Vance said: “If you’re gonna create Frankenstein, don’t come to the government and say we need regulation.”
He said tech bosses should instead: “Look inward and accept that if you’re building Frankenstein, No 1, you should stop and No 2, when companies come to you and say: ‘We need the tools to fight back against Frankenstein,’ give them those tools.”
Vance was speaking at an AI summit in Los Angeles after a week of rising global concern at the risks to humanity posed by the prospect of the creation of an artificial superintelligence, a technology that does not yet exist.
Amodei on Saturday warned that the accelerating rate of capabilities meant a swarm of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months.
Although many doubt that claim, it added fuel to the suggestion from Anthropic’s alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, that there was a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within 10 years. He was responding to a researcher, Jacob Coxon, who quit Anthropic with a similar warning.
On Tuesday night, Coxon gave an amended prognosis: “I do think that if we go slower we can take risk to 0%, but this requires radical action.” He also admitted “it is very difficult to convey specific scenarios” in which AI kills all humans and said: “I need to work on communicating this point.”
Vance’s willingness to consider that AI could pose a real risk marked a split from the US president, Donald Trump, who wrote this week: “AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” Trump posted on social media that AI is going to be “the greatest economic development engine in history – bigger than oil, gold, diamonds, or even the internet”.
Vance has said he suspects AI leaders of raising the alarm about safety risks as a “Trojan horse”. Amodei has proposed industry coordination to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” while US and global regulation is implemented. Critics of the companies believe they are encouraging the US government to create tough new rules – shaped in their interests – that could limit wider competition in a tactic known as regulatory capture.
OpenAI, which lost control of hundreds of AI agents during testing this summer which then conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website, said on Monday it was backing bipartisan efforts by lawmakers in Washington to address catastrophic risks from AI and it has been coordinating with Google and Anthropic.
On Wednesday, Reuters reported claims from an independent researcher, Jonas Wiedermann-Möller, that OpenAI’s rogue agents had started probing Hugging Face for weaknesses nearly two months before the attack.
Sam Altman, the Chat GPT-maker’s chief executive, on Tuesday criticised suggestions from other companies that “we will only slow down if, or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible”. Altman said: “There should be no qualifier on that.”
Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and chief executive of Meta, advocated that companies should take unilateral safety action. He said his company had recently delayed the release of its most recent AI model, Muse, “for several months to focus on safety and security”.
“We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” he said. “We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.”
Meta has been forced to pay out billions in legal cases related to harms caused by its social media platforms. Last month it settled a case with US states claiming Facebook and Instagram harmed children by agreeing to pay up to $18bn (£13.3bn).
Zuckerberg stressed: “[AI] labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.”

Ukrainian combat robot maker Ratel sells for up to $224M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:41:55 UTC
19:41:55 KST

- Swarmer agreed to acquire Ukrainian ground robot maker Ratel Robotics in a cash-and-stock deal worth up to $224 million.
- Most of the deal's value depends on Ratel hitting revenue and profit targets through 2028, with closing expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.
Swarmer, an Austin, Texas-based defense technology company, has agreed to buy Ratel Robotics, one of Ukraine’s largest makers of combat ground robots, in a deal that could be worth up to $224 million.
Alexander Kamyshin, a former advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on strategic affairs, first laid out the deal’s structure on X, writing that Swarmer is acquiring 100 percent of Ratel Robotics.
According to Kamyshin, the agreement combines cash and Swarmer stock. At closing, Ratel’s owners receive about $7.2 million in cash plus roughly 1.06 million Swarmer shares. They can earn another $7.2 million in cash if Ratel hits 2026 revenue and profit targets, and up to about 4.42 million additional Swarmer shares tied to performance goals through 2028. Most of the deal’s potential value depends on Ratel’s future results rather than money paid up front. Closing still requires standard legal, regulatory and shareholder approvals, and Swarmer takes full ownership of Ratel once the deal closes.
Swarmer develops AI-powered, vendor-agnostic software that lets a single operator coordinate large numbers of autonomous drones and unmanned systems at once. The company, founded by Ukrainians, says its technology has supported more than 100,000 combat missions in Ukraine since it was first deployed in April 2024. Swarmer went public on the Nasdaq under the ticker SWMR earlier in 2026, and Erik Prince, the founder of Blackwater, chairs the company.
Ratel builds modular unmanned ground vehicles already used on the front line for logistics runs, casualty evacuation, engineering work, reconnaissance and remote mine laying and clearing. Its vehicles also launch drones directly from the ground. The company is developing two aerial drone variants, mobile repair workshops and other equipment meant to support units in the field. Ratel’s ground vehicles accounted for roughly 37 percent of the money Ukraine’s Defense Procurement Agency spent on unmanned ground vehicle contracts between January 1 and April 18, 2026, a period in which the agency spent about $247 million on the category. Ratel has secured $86 million in contracts so far in 2026 and is in talks with several NATO countries through the Build With Ukraine initiative.
Combining the two companies puts Ratel’s ground vehicles together with Swarmer’s coordination software, work both companies describe as building toward a single system where ground and air drones operate with less direct human control. Ratel’s vehicles already double as launch platforms for aerial drones in the field, which is part of what drew Swarmer’s interest.
“My experience serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine gave me a clear understanding of the risks soldiers face every day,” said Taras Ostapchuk, founder and CEO of Ratel Robotics. “That is why we build robotic systems capable of taking on the most dangerous missions. Together with Swarmer, we will combine ground and air capabilities and develop their autonomy so fewer people have to risk their lives.”
Ostapchuk will keep running Ratel Robotics after the deal closes. More than 300 Ratel employees are expected to join Swarmer, which would grow the combined company to nearly 500 people. Ratel’s team will continue developing its existing products, scaling manufacturing and pursuing sales to militaries beyond Ukraine.
The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, pending the approvals both companies still need to secure.

Our task remains unchanged — to support Ukraine as strongly as we can

Putin weaponizing migration to destabilize Europe, Kyiv says

2026-09-16
10:40:46 UTC
19:40:46 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking to drive migration to Europe to destabilize governments and weaken support for Ukraine ahead of key upcoming elections, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sept. 16.
"The Black Sea blockade is part of his plan," Sybiha said, as Russian strikes against ports and vessels in Ukrainian waters are choking off Ukraine's maritime exports, a key source of food for countries across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.
This strategy not only takes a humanitarian toll on families directly dependent on these supplies, but is also intended to drive an influx of migrants toward the European borders, according to Ukraine's chief diplomat.
"Moscow believes its strategy will create tension, sow division, strengthen radical anti-European movements, and ultimately weaken Europe's support for Ukraine," Sybiha commented on X.
read also
The comments come as the anti-immigration, Russian-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secured a historic win in a regional election on Sept. 6, and France's far-right opposition leader Marine Le Pen is a frontrunner for the French presidential run next year.
Next year will also see parliamentary elections in Spain — where the anti-immigration Vox party polls third at around 18% — and in Italy, where right-wing but Ukraine-friendly Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing pressure from the new far-right National Future movement.
A wave of far-right victories could weaken the support for Ukraine across the European bloc, which has become a key backer of Kyiv after U.S. President Donald Trump cut off much of the American support.
"Putin knows that migration is one of the most sensitive and divisive issues in European election campaigns — especially after seeing how effectively Russian-linked networks exploited the recent Ceuta crisis," Sybiha said.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez previously accused Russian and Israeli disinformation networks of fueling tensions over an August rush of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.
Next to the Black Sea blockade, Moscow also continues using its ally, Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko, to smuggle migrants across the EU's northeastern borders, Sybiha added.
While Russia has been striking Ukrainian ports throughout the full-scale war, Kyiv this summer also expanded the list of targets for its drone attacks to Russian ports in the Black and Azov seas, disrupting Russia's own food exports.
The escalation of hostilities in the Black Sea has driven a surge in global food prices, which had already been rising since the start of the U.S.-Iran War in late February.

Belfast yard installs new cranes for support ship build
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:40:38 BST
19:40:38 KST

Harland and Wolff has completed the installation of eleven cranes bought from a County Down supplier for £1.5 million, in preparation for building three Fleet Solid Support ships for the Royal Fleet Auxiliary, Navantia UK stated.
The purchase forms part of a £98.5 million modernisation and recapitalisation of the Belfast yard under its new owner, intended to prepare it for advanced shipbuilding and naval projects.
The last of the eleven, a gantry crane with a twenty metre span known as a semi-Goliath, was commissioned at the end of August. It can lift twenty tonnes, which the company compares to two double-decker buses, and will move steel and other shipbuilding components around the site.
A semi-Goliath runs one leg along a ground rail, making it a halfway version of the two yellow Samson and Goliath cranes that dominate the Belfast skyline and are currently undergoing renovation.
Alongside it, the company has bought six electric overhead travelling cranes and four jib cranes for use in and around the fabrication hall, which has been enlarged with a 5,000 square metre extension. The specification included full radio control, anti-collision technology, digital weigh load indication and magnet enabled preparation within each control panel.
All eleven came from Walter Watson Ltd, a family-owned structural steel and industrial crane business based at Castlewellan in County Down and established in 1967.
Carlos Lopez Carregado, General Manager at Harland and Wolff, said: “Our local-first means that we award contracts to local businesses wherever possible. That means the economic benefits of shipbuilding for the Ministry of Defence flow straight into the community.
“This new crane will play a key role in shipyard operations. It will be a vital piece of equipment as we assemble ship blocks in readiness to build the Fleet Solid Support ship, and many future ships in Belfast. We’re pleased to be working with Walter Watson, a world class local supplier.”
David Barr, Managing Director of Walter Watson Ltd, said: “We’re delighted to have been awarded the contract to manufacture, instal and commission these 11 cranes for Navantia UK’s Harland and Wolff site. In particular, it’s a privilege to have been entrusted to supply and commission this twin hoist Semi Goliath Crane under the shadow of the iconic Samson and Goliath cranes, from which this model takes its name.
“All of these units were manufactured and tested at our County Down based facility in Castlewellan. We used our in-house transport capabilities to deliver them to Harland and Wolff’s site on Belfast Harbour, prior to erecting them with an 80-tonne mobile crane from our own plant fleet.”
According to the company, the purchase is the latest in a series of recent contracts with local suppliers, under an approach to procurement it describes as local-first, intended to ensure investment from the Fleet Solid Support programme delivers economic benefits across the region. The company says it is committed to using British suppliers wherever it is technically and commercially feasible.
The wider recapitalisation of the yard has involved installing a new panel line and plasma cutting equipment, along with digital design tools and improvements to buildings and infrastructure.
Work has begun at Belfast on the three Fleet Solid Support ships, which will carry ammunition, stores and provisions to warships at sea, and Navantia UK says it is ready to take on additional work funded under the £298 billion Defence Investment Plan published in June.

US charges 5 over alleged Kremlin-directed global network targeting Ukraine supporters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:39:00 UTC
19:39:00 KST

The US Department of Justice on Tuesday charged five people with organising attacks and killings around the world, including in the United States and Lithuania, as part of a global network prosecutors say has operated on behalf of Russian intelligence services since at least 2024.
The network most recently sought to recruit people in the United States to surveil and kill Russian dissidents at the direction of the Kremlin, according to an indictment released by the department.
Prosecutors also allege that members of the network recruited and paid others to carry out or attempt terrorist attacks against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries supporting Ukraine.
Three of the defendants are alleged to be senior members of the Russian intelligence network: former Russian intelligence Col. Yuri Khrameyev; his son, Kirill Khrameyev, an officer with Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB; and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a Cuban citizen living in Russia.
Further reading
The other two defendants, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro, are alleged recruiters based in the United States who worked for the Russian spy network.
In one case, prosecutors allege that this summer Delgado Suarez and Castro recruited a person living in the United States to surveil a prominent Russian dissident. The person was initially offered between $1,000 and $1,500 for surveillance, followed by an offer of $40,000 to “eliminate” or make the target “disappear”, according to the indictment.
The Khrameyevs also allegedly tried in 2025 to recruit a US citizen to kill a person in Lithuania whom they accused of “spreading lies about Russia”.
After the US citizen rejected an offer of about $25,000 to carry out the killing, Yuri Khrameyev allegedly proposed what he described as “easier work”, including setting fire to a warehouse or attacking an electrical substation.
Khrameyev said the targets were “all countries helping Ukraine” and offered “serious money for serious work”, according to the indictment.
Durruthy is accused of coordinating attacks in the Czech Republic and Lithuania in 2024.
“These defendants allegedly acted as part of a global murder-for-hire network that reached the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreign nationals to carry out murders at the direction of the Kremlin,” said John Eisenberg, the Justice Department’s assistant attorney general for national security.
The charges include conspiracy to provide material support for terrorism, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Khrameyev, Delgado Suarez and Castro also face charges of conspiracy to commit murder for hire, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years.
US officials said the alleged activities pose a threat to national security.
All five defendants remain at large.
Russia has intensified what Western governments describe as hybrid operations against countries supporting Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. Suspected Russian agents have been accused of espionage, sabotage and attempted assassinations in the United States, Europe and other Western countries.
Lithuania’s State Security Department said the US charges illustrate concerns outlined in its national security threat assessments. Lithuanian intelligence has warned that hostile regimes use unconventional methods to influence public opinion, create a sense of insecurity and pressure societies to make decisions beneficial to those regimes.
The department said the case also demonstrated the importance of close and consistent cooperation among international partners in responding to hostile countries.

Gaza war shines new light on Australia's most secretive spy base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:38:44 UTC
19:38:44 KST

Breadcrumb
'We want our land back and to stop the genocide': Gaza war shines new light on Australia's most secretive spy base
It was in mid-July when hundreds of activists gathered on the road leading up to the secretive military base in the heart of Australia.
They had arrived in the sleepy town of Alice Springs (Mparntwe) from across the country to demand the closure of a facility that has contributed to the historic dispossession of Indigenous Australians and is feared to be enabling the current displacement of Palestinians.
The US-led Pine Gap spy base has long been controversial in Australia. Since its establishment more than five decades ago, the facility has witnessed recurrent protests by activists opposed to the US military's presence and its occupation of land belonging to the Aboriginal Arrernte people.
But its presence has taken on a new significance since October 2023, when Israel began its genocidal assault on the Gaza Strip. Its activities remain shrouded in mystery, but it is believed to have played an important role in aiding the Israeli military in its destruction of the Palestinian enclave.
The three-day convergence, which took place on the 60th anniversary of the signing of the Pine Gap treaty, brought more than 600 pro-Palestine and anti-war activists, academics and politicians together with the Hayes family, the traditional custodians of the sacred land of Kuyunba.
The gathering culminated in hundreds marching to the base, chanting "From Arrernte to Gaza, Globalise the Intifada" and "Always was, always will be, Aboriginal land". At the gates, Arrernte Elder Felicity Hayes handed a letter to the local police chief asking for the land to be returned to its owners.
"We have every right to say we don't want this base here," Aunty Felicity told the inspector, before describing how her grandfather was taken advantage of to hand over the land without his consent.
Also among her requests was compensation for Palestinians in Gaza, where Israel has killed and injured almost a quarter of a million people since it began its assault in October 2023.
"Close the base because what it's doing is destroying other people's countries," she said. "We want our land back and to stop the genocide."
Nathalie Farah, a spokesperson for the convergence, said the protest was the largest at the facility since 1987. Farah, a Syrian-Palestinian activist in the Anti-Militarism Action Network, was among 100 people who had driven for four days from Melbourne to attend the gathering.
"We're very conscious of the fact that we can't stop what's happening in Palestine from Australia, but Australia plays a significant role in the system and if it can be stopped that system won't be as effective," she told The New Arab.
July's convergence was the third major protest to be held on the road to the base since October 2023, and it is unlikely to be the last.
Anti-war groups, trade unions and pro-Palestine activists are planning to hold rallies and events in cities and towns across the country on 20 September to protest the US military alliance, Israel's war on Gaza, and Australia's participation in AUKUS, the security partnership with the US and UK.
"What needs to happen is we need to build a proper anti-war movement here similar to what happened on this continent during the Vietnam war," Farah said.
From Australia to Israel
Australia's strategic position close to the Indo-Pacific has made the country an important location for US overseas military operations. In all, the US military controls 17 facilities in the country and has access to 75 more Australian-owned installations, according to recent research by the Nautilus Institute, an Australian think tank.
Northern Australia is of particular focus to the Pentagon. The US has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into building new military infrastructure in the area since 2024, making it the top overseas location for Air Force and Navy construction spending.
Pine Gap has attracted particular scrutiny because of the lack of oversight afforded to Australia's elected officials and its status as one of the most important American intelligence facilities outside the US.
The base, known officially as the Joint Defence Space Research Facility, is jointly operated by Australia's military and several American spy agencies, but Australian authorities are largely kept in the dark about the US's intelligence activities.
Classified US documents leaked by whistleblower Edward Snowden in 2013 revealed that the US National Security Agency (NSA) uses the facility to collect massive amounts of electronic signals and communication data. Intelligence is often used to identify military targets, including for drone strikes across the Middle East and Afghanistan.
Many suspect that Pine Gap has played a major role in the US's ongoing war on Iran, but the Australian government has remained tight-lipped.
The Snowden leaks also confirmed that Israel routinely receives intelligence from the NSA, with which it has eight intelligence-sharing agreements.
In 2023, investigative news site Declassified Australia published testimony from a former NSA employee who said that the base collects intelligence on Gaza.
"We know that signals intelligence data, captured by Pine Gap-controlled Orion satellites, has been historically made available to Israel," said Professor Richard Tanter, a senior research associate at the Nautilus Institute who is widely regarded as the country's leading expert on the base.
"Unless the Australian direct and indirect military relationship to Israeli activities in the Gaza Strip are closely reviewed by the Inspector General of Intelligence and Security, it is not possible for the Australian government to assure the parliament and the Australian public that Australia is not complicit in acts of genocide," he added.
"The base's intelligence-sharing with the Israeli military has been one of the key ways that Australia has failed to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention," Jorgan Doyle, a spokesperson for the convergence, told The New Arab.
Doyle is an organiser for Mparntwe for Falastin, a local pro-Palestine group set up after 7 October 2023 that has staged fortnightly rallies on the road to the base and held frequent events and vigils in the town.
He described the Australian government's approach to the US military relationship as "don't ask, don't tell", which he says is particularly problematic given expectations that the country will soon host nuclear-capable American bombers.
The Tindal air base, located 1,000 kilometres north of Pine Gap, is being expanded by the US to host up to six B-52 bombers, which are expected to arrive by the end of the year.
Political backing
The campaign has attracted support from the Australian Greens, whose senators have called on the government to rethink its military alliance with Washington. Lawmakers in the left-wing party have been staunch critics of the Israeli military's actions in Gaza and have called for cutting trade ties with Israel and sanctions on ministers in the government.
The Greens, while still a minor party, are currently polling in fourth with around 15-16% of the vote and hold 10 seats in the 72-seat Senate.
"We don't want to be a part of the United States's forever wars," Senator David Shoebridge told The New Arab.
The New South Wales senator attended the convergence and plans to submit the Hayes family's letter for a debate in parliament later this year. Among the family's demands are the closure of the base, the return of the land to its traditional owners, and the payment of compensation to the dispossessed Arrernte people and families in Gaza.
"First Nations owners of the land on which Pine Gap sits have never given consent to the US presence, they don’t want their land contributing to US wars and the killing we can all see in places like Iran, Palestine and Venezuela," Shoebridge said.
"Australians are watching as the US becomes an agent of chaos, causing instability and violence in the world… For the first time since the Iraq war, we have a mass movement of people in Australia taking a clear stance against US war and our government's role in them."
The campaign against Pine Gap comes as polls show falling support for the US among the broader public amid the chaos of the Trump administration.
Successive surveys have shown that, while the military relationship remains popular, Australian voters are increasingly supportive of a more independent foreign policy and are less willing to trust the alliance with the US.
A poll by the Lowy Institute in June found that just 21% of Australians have confidence in the US president. Meanwhile, the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre found that a third of the public believe that the second Trump administration has been very bad for Australia, while almost four in 10 see the US as mostly harmful for Asia.
Doyle, of Mparntwe for Falastin, said the convergence happened at a "really interesting geopolitical moment" amid shifting public opinion.
"We increasingly hear ordinary Australians becoming uneasy about the US alliance and Australia's place in the world," he said.

He said the supplies allowed into Gaza “represent only a very small amount” and do not meet even the minimum operational needs of health facilities, leaving them “struggling between life and death.”
 
“The health system in the Gaza Strip is being driven toward a systematic and mass execution, going beyond a humanitarian catastrophe to a fully fledged health genocide,” he said.
 
Wahidi said the fuel crisis also led public transport companies and buses to announce a complete or near-total halt in operations Wednesday, preventing hundreds of medical workers from reaching their workplaces and further isolating health facilities and hampering their ability to respond to emergencies.
 
“Health facilities have turned into isolated structures slowly dying amid the continued comprehensive blockade and the prevention of essential necessities of life from entering,” he said.
 
He said the situation coincides with an “unprecedented shortage” of medicines and medical supplies, the disruption of diagnostic equipment and the closure of treatment routes abroad for patients and wounded people on waiting lists.
 
Wahidi urged the international community, the UN Security Council, the World Health Organization, and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs to take “immediate and urgent action” to allow the entry of essential medical and operational supplies.
 
Since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023, nearly 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 174,000 injured, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Sunderland gets its Kicks: Nissan to invest £170m to build new hybrid SUV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:38:17 UTC
19:38:17 KST

Nissan has said it will invest £170m to build a new SUV at its factory in Sunderland – but said the move was subject to the UK weakening its electric vehicle sales mandate.
The new hybrid model, the Kicks, is Nissan’s latest attempt to secure the future of the plant, which employs 6,000 people in Tyne and Wear and is Britain’s biggest car factory.
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s head in Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, said the move would not bring new jobs but was part of “securing and maintaining” jobs at the site, which has been running at 50% capacity.
The Kicks will be the fourth Nissan model produced at the Sunderland plant, which already makes the Qashqai, Juke and Leaf. It is already sold in more than 70 markets but has never been built in Europe.
The announcement is a boost to Britain’s automotive sector, which was last week hit by the news that Jaguar Land Rover will cut 4,000 jobs. Carmakers have come under pressure from US tariffs, competition from Chinese rivals and high industrial energy costs in recent years.
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said the investment and new car model was “a huge vote of confidence in the UK’s manufacturing expertise and automotive future”.
However, it also came with an apparent warning from Messina, who said: “Of course we’re going to keep discussing with the UK government because large part of this is subject to the ZEV [Zero Emission Vehicles] mandate amendment.”
The government is consulting on cutting the UK’s electric vehicle sales targets for manufacturers. Under the ZEV mandate, carmakers ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero-emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.
But after heavy lobbying pressure from manufacturers, the government said last month that it was considering cutting that figure to as little as 50% by the end of the decade, which it is consulting on until late October.
When pressed on whether Nissan would still make the investment if the targets were not weakened, Messina said: “We try to assess always if this is more likely than unlikely.”
He added that the company was pushing for a cut to 50% of sales needing to be EVs. “I just want to think that this is done,” he said. “For me, yes, it’s going to happen.”
Nissan is separately in talks to share production with the Chinese carmaker Chery, which is looking to build its own cars in the UK, to bring the site closer to full capacity again.
Messina said he was putting “pressure internally and externally” to complete the deal which was announced in June. “We are ready to go. We are waiting just that Chery finalises volume and lineup.”
Separately, LEVC, the maker of London’s black cabs, said on Wednesday that it will launch its next-generation taxi model next year, built at its factory in Ansty, near Coventry. The Chinese company, owned by Geely, said the new taxi would replace the current all-electric TX range introduced in 2018.
Nissan is also lobbying Brussels over the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules, which would require cars to be built within the bloc to qualify for subsidies and public procurement.
The company has previously said that it could be forced to close Sunderland if the rules go ahead as currently drafted.
Messina said: “You might imagine how much time I’m spending on this to secure that this comes together in order to have Sunderland and the UK part of it.
“There are good indications that this will be achieved. We believe strongly, regardless what will be the outcome, that UK cannot be left anyway outside.”
Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said the investment was “a major boost for Nissan Sunderland, the thousands of highly skilled jobs it supports and the wider local supply chain”.
On Wednesday, McLaren announced it would invest £500m in its UK operations, including a new factory, 1,000 jobs and its first SUV.

Forest and peatland fires raging across Indonesia are threatening to become more than an environmental emergency, with analysts warning that the thickening haze could weigh on economic activity, strain public health and test confidence in the nation’s fledgling carbon market.
Indonesia is no stranger to forest and peat fires, but this year’s super El Nino has helped make it the country’s most intense wildfire season in 11 years. Toxic haze and smoke have also drifted to neighbouring countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines, forcing some employers to impose work-from-home policies while numerous schools have resorted to remote learning.
A health crisis is also in the offing. Data from the Indonesian health ministry last month showed that acute respiratory infection cases topped 15.6 million from January 1 to August 20 this year.
The ministry recorded 400,000 new respiratory infection cases per week at the height of the dry season between the end of July and the beginning of August.

Bank of Japan gears to hike policy rate to highest level in 31 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:36:52 UTC
19:36:52 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Ali Canberk Ozbugutu and Emir Yildirim
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is preparing to raise its policy interest rate, currently at 1%, by 25 basis points to the highest level in 31 years due to rising energy costs fueling inflationary concerns and the yen’s depreciation.
 
The US-Israel-Iran conflict in the Middle East created and continues to fuel significant inflationary pressures, affecting the Japanese economy alongside other major economies worldwide.
Rising inflation and growth expectations exceeding estimates strengthened expectations that the BoJ will adopt a tighter monetary policy.
Risks to energy supplies via the Strait of Hormuz due to geopolitical risks in the Middle East contributed to inflationary pressures in Japan.
Japan’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 1.9% year-on-year in July, marking its fastest pace since December 2025.
The Japanese economy grew 1.4% in the second quarter, above preliminary estimates.
BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda may face some pressure from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s inner circle as her agenda focuses on supporting economic growth.
Sadi Kaymaz, an Asian markets analyst, told Anadolu that the BoJ will likely hike rates for a third time in less than 10 months, while forward-looking messages will be more important than the decision itself on Friday.
Kaymaz stated that BoJ members believe the pace of rate hikes will depend on the data, with inflation taking primary focus, as core inflation accelerated for the second consecutive month by rising to 1.8%.
He noted that Japan’s core inflation could surpass 2.5% in the second half, while nominal wages increased 4.7% on an annual basis.
“The growth variable is not particularly strong, while public spending is the primary driver of growth,” he said. “Private consumption remains stagnant.”
Kaymaz stated that another rate hike by January 2027 may be on the horizon, as many economists expect.
“Relatively rapid rate hikes could attract Japanese capital to the country,” he said.
“I don’t expect Ueda to signal consecutive rate hikes as such a commitment would fuel volatility in the yen and bonds, so I expect Ueda to remain cautious,” he added.

Yle: Senior psychiatrists resign from HUS amid restructuring
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
13:34:35 EEST
19:34:35 KST

Several senior psychiatrists working for Helsinki University Hospital, HUS, have resigned as the organisation prepares changes to the management of psychiatric services in eastern and central Uusimaa, Yle reported on Wednesday.
The resignations will take effect in October, according to an internal HUS notice obtained by Yle. The document says planned changes to the management structure have caused concern among staff.
The resignations concern senior doctors working in HUS psychiatric services in eastern and central Uusimaa. Helsingin Sanomat reported that five senior psychiatrists at Hyvinkää Hospital have resigned, citing information obtained by the newspaper.
HUS Psychiatry Director and Chief Physician Jesper Ekelund did not confirm the number to HS. He acknowledged that losing several senior doctors from a small unit at the same time creates difficulties.
“We have agreed on how operations will continue during the autumn,” Ekelund told the newspaper.
HUS plans to bring psychiatrists from other parts of its organisation to cover the vacancies while recruiting replacements. Ekelund said patients at Hyvinkää Hospital should not see disruption to their treatment.
The departures come as HUS prepares to reorganise its psychiatric services. According to Yle, Ekelund and another senior HUS official discussed the planned management changes with doctors at a meeting in early September.
An internal notice obtained by Yle said participants held “very different views” about the effects of the changes. Several senior doctors working in eastern and central Uusimaa announced at the end of the meeting that they intended to leave HUS.
Ekelund disputed a direct link between the meeting and the resignations. He told Yle that the doctors had considered their decisions before the meeting and described the departures as decisions made by individual employees.
One doctor contacted by Yle confirmed resigning but cited personal reasons. Other doctors approached by the broadcaster did not confirm or deny that they had submitted resignations.
The restructuring is due to take effect at the start of 2027. HUS plans to replace a system that combines geographical, diagnosis-based and other organisational divisions with five service lines based on functions.
Ekelund said the changes concern administration rather than the location of jobs or treatment units. HUS intends clinical patient care to continue under the new structure.
Staff concerns include workloads and the effect that the restructuring and departures will have on the operation of psychiatric units, according to HS.
Ekelund told Yle that HUS would review how services should operate with the staff available.
“If key senior physicians are not working in a unit, its operations are of course under threat,” he said.
Recruitment poses another problem. HUS already has a shortage of psychiatrists before replacing those who have resigned. Ekelund told HS that 47 psychiatrist positions are vacant out of more than 300 posts across HUS.
The shortage extends beyond the hospital group, with specialist psychiatrists in short supply across Finland.
Hyvinkää Hospital serves as a major hospital outside the Helsinki metropolitan area and operates round-the-clock emergency services. HUS said psychiatrists from other units will support services during the autumn while recruitment continues.

IMO urges member states to stop attacking merchant ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:33:19 UTC
19:33:19 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The head of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) urged member states to stop actions endangering merchant ships and seafarers amid rising geopolitical tensions.
 
Addressing the the organization's Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers, Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez warned of the severe impacts of geopolitical tensions on the shipping industry.
 
Dominguez said they were reaching a point where these conflicts were used as a pretext to attack merchant vessels and innocent seafarers.
Since the current conflict in the Middle East began on Feb. 28, the IMO verified 80 attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in the deaths of at least 22 seafarers and injuries to many others.
In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, dozens of fatalities reportedly resulted from attacks on international shipping in recent months.
Attacks in the Red Sea also resumed, with four fatalities confirmed in the latest attack by the Houthis on a merchant vessel on Aug. 11.
Dominguez emphasized that the attacks across these conflicts were not attributable to one single actor, noting that multiple entities were attacking merchant vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
He underlined that addressing the root causes of these geopolitical conflicts was beyond the IMO's remit, but their impact was increasingly evident across global maritime trade and shipping operations.
Dominguez urged delegates to raise these impacts on international shipping with their governments and in the appropriate international fora.
When shipping operations face disruptions, the consequences extend far beyond the maritime sector, affecting economies, supply chains and everyday lives.
He called on members to share these impacts with relevant bodies in their capitals so the UN can address the root causes and find solutions.
The IMO Secretariat stands ready to contribute to workable solutions for the shipping industry that member states can bring forward at the technical and operational level.
The Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers meets in London on Sept. 14-18 to discuss safety issues related to the transport of dangerous goods, bulk cargoes and containers by sea.

Family of Charlie Kirk plans suit against Utah university over alleged security lapses
Sept 16 - The family of conservative U.S. political activist Charlie Kirk plans to sue a Utah university over his fatal shooting there, alleging inadequate security contributed to his death, according to a notice of claim sent by the family's lawyers.
A September 9 letter from the family's law firm notified Utah Valley University and the State of Utah of its intent to seek damages over Kirk's September 10, 2025, killing, according to a copy of the document sent to media.
The notice alleges that Kirk’s organization, Turning Point USA, warned university police about security risks posed by rooftops overlooking the university's amphitheater where he was due to speak. According to the notice, the university police chief responded in a text message to a Turning Point USA staff member: "I got you covered."
The notice says that university police failed to control access to the rooftop from which Kirk was shot.
The Utah attorney general's office and Utah Valley University did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Tyler Robinson, 23, a former electrical apprentice, is accused of shooting Kirk from the roof of the university's student resource center. Utah prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.
Robinson had a boyfriend who was considering gender transition and targeted Kirk for his views against gay marriage and transgender rights, prosecutors allege. Though Kirk spoke "hatefully" about people who were not heterosexual, or gender norm conforming, that does not rise to evidence of motive, defense attorney Richard Novak has said in court.
Robinson has pleaded not guilty . A trial date is expected to be set at an October 23 hearing. REUTERS

EU capitals caught off guard as von der Leyen announces ‘associate membership’ for Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

EU capitals caught off guard as von der Leyen announces ‘associate membership’ for Canada
Further alignment than currently planned would create new issues around steel, cars, genetically modified crops and other substantive issues, diplomats said.
BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's announcement that the EU will explore "associate membership" for Canada came as a surprise to member countries — and left governments concerned about the potential trade-offs.
During her annual State of the Union speech in Strasbourg, von der Leyen floated the upgrading of relations with Ottawa to meet the need to "urgently reimagine our partnerships" and "build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies."
Canada, which is locked in an escalating trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, will begin "opening the door" to become "the first associate member of the EU."
Advertisement
But the message wrong-footed national capitals, which were never asked to sign off on the idea before the speech, said three diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely. Granting membership to the EU is a responsibility of the European Council, and no model for associate membership exists.
"Nobody really knows what it means," said one of the envoys, who has been involved in talks with the Commission about relations with Canada in recent days. "Member states have tried to manage expectations. There are only warm feelings for Ottawa, but we need to know what the details are."
A second diplomat put it more bluntly, predicting that while Canada could be given an equivalent of the EU's Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Areas deal — a market access arrangement offered to Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine — there is little mandate for other economic or political integration. "Member states will not agree on anything else," the diplomat said.
A third diplomat added that any associate membership status would require changes to the EU’s fundamental treaties — which is “impossible” due to a lack of support.
Among the potential issues that would come up if they considered going beyond that, according to the diplomats, are thorny questions around Ottawa's Made in Canada preference, which could fly in the face of single market rules; Canada's steel industry, which rivals Europe's own; taxation on the EU's car exports and its rules limiting imports of European alcohol; and its differing guidance on genetically modified produce.
Ambassadors from across the bloc met with the European Commission and the European Council last week, where they broadly agreed on the idea of closer relations with Canada — including those from right-wing governments usually more cautious of potentially angering Trump.
Responding to the announcement, Irish European Affairs minister Thomas Byrne said that “the expansion of our Union to full members, and maybe associate members, is in our strategic interest.”
But lawmakers in the chamber were less convinced. The Left MEP Manon Aubry asked von der Leyen, "Who gave you a democratic and popular mandate for that?"
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney attended the speech as part of a trip first reported by POLITICO. Amid trade and political threats from Washington, he has called for his country to ax its dependencies on the U.S. and form a club of like-minded, pro-free trade democracies. The visit was designed "to clearly signal the intention and ambition on both sides to upgrade our partnership," a senior EU official said at the time.
Carney will set out his own vision for the future of the relationship on Thursday in a speech in front of the European Parliament.

UK passengers with cancelled trains will now be able to use services on a different operator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:30:31 UTC
19:30:31 KST

Cross-operator ticket acceptance after train cancellations has been expanded to include several new lines.
Seeing your train has been cancelled is infuriating, but even more so when you’re in the UK.
Under the current system, passengers face lengthy waits as many tickets aren’t accepted on similar services being run by different operators.
But that’s all about to change from this Sunday, 20 September, as you will now be able to use your ticket on another participating operator’s train.
The original ticket will be valid for use on trains departing within two hours before or after the cancelled service “using a direct or reasonable alternative route”.
You won’t need to download a new ticket – simply show it to the inspectors on board and it will be accepted.
“When passengers are delayed, they just want to get where they need to be, not worry about whether their ticket will be accepted on another train,” Alex Robertson, chief executive of independent watchdog Transport Focus, said.
“This is a welcome change that we have long called for and should make it easier for people when services are cancelled.
“The key now is making sure passengers get clear information about their options whenever disruption occurs.”
Cross-operator ticket acceptance was already in place across all publicly-owned operators, but from Sunday it will be expanded to also include Avanti West Coast, Chiltern Railways, CrossCountry and Great Western Railway. East Midlands Railway will also join the scheme at a later date.

Mark Gerassimenko: Why Estonia's minimum‑wage purchasing power is the lowest in the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Mark Gerassimenko: Why Estonia's minimum‑wage purchasing power is the lowest in the EU?
The upcoming talks on next year's minimum wage come as Estonia faces the lowest minimum‑wage purchasing power in the European Union and one of the weakest minimum‑to‑average‑wage ratios. A year ago, the government backed away from a tripartite good‑faith agreement meant to address the problem, writes Mark Gerassimenko.
In early August, one of the most‑read articles in the business news sections of both Delfi and Postimees was the report on Estonia's low minimum‑wage purchasing power. Recent Eurostat data showed that Estonia's minimum‑wage purchasing power is the lowest in the European Union, falling just below Latvia's.
As negotiations soon begin between the Confederation of Trade Unions and the Employers' Confederation to reach an agreement on next year's minimum wage, it is worth recalling how Estonia's minimum‑wage purchasing power reached its current state.
Generally low purchasing power
Some readers reacted with disbelief: how is this possible, when Estonia's minimum wage in euros (€946 gross per month) is clearly above Latvia's (€780 per month)? The answer lies in the overview of price levels across EU countries.
Eurostat data show that Estonia's price level is by far the highest in Eastern Europe, ranking 11th among the 27 EU member states. In terms of food and non‑alcoholic beverage prices, Estonia is the sixth most expensive country in the EU.
It is therefore not surprising that actual individual consumption (which also accounts for purchasing‑power differences) is among the lowest in the EU: only Hungary, emerging from Viktor Orbán's 16‑year rule, performs worse, and Latvia's indicator matches Estonia's at 73 percent of the EU average.
Does this mean that minimum‑wage purchasing power is not worth worrying about, because overall consumer purchasing power in Estonia is weak, even though average and median earners receive more euros per month than in many Eastern EU countries? Unfortunately, that is not quite the case.
The minimum wage's ratio to the average wage is also poor
The minimum wage's ratio to both the average and median wage in Estonia is also among the lowest in the EU. While the EU's recommended target is for the minimum wage to equal about 60 percent of the median wage or 50 percent of the average wage, Estonia's figures are roughly 50 and 43 percent, respectively. Estonia and Latvia are the only EU countries where the minimum wage does not reach even half of the median wage.
This metric matters because it is not affected by purchasing‑power differences between countries: it measures how far the minimum wage lags behind the wage level typical in society. In other words, it reflects wage inequality, focusing on the lowest legal end of the wage scale.
The minimum‑wage directive adopted in 2022 states that the minimum wage must be sufficient for a decent life. As recommended benchmarks, it includes the previously mentioned targets: at least 60 percent of the median wage or 50 percent of the average wage. Unfortunately, although these figures were initially intended to be binding for member states, pressure from some countries and members of the European Parliament resulted in them becoming recommendations in the final text.
Before the most recent parliamentary elections, the Social Democrats added raising the minimum wage to the directive's recommended level to their platform. During coalition negotiations, SDE representatives publicly emphasized that without an accelerated minimum‑wage increase, no agreement could be reached on other major issues such as tax changes.
The good‑faith agreement for accelerating minimum‑wage increases
The pressure worked, and accelerated minimum‑wage increases were included in the coalition agreement. Based on that mandate, as well as trade‑union demands and the obligation to implement the directive, representatives of the government, the Confederation of Trade Unions, and the Employers' Confederation reached a good‑faith agreement in May 2023 stating that the minimum wage would gradually rise to 50 percent of the average wage by 2027.
Later, when negotiating the specific minimum‑wage levels for 2024 and 2025, the parties largely followed the good‑faith agreement. As a result, the minimum wage rose by 13.1 percent in January 2024 and by 8 percent in January 2025.
In March 2025, a change occurred that directly harmed minimum‑wage increases and the fulfillment of the good‑faith agreement. The prime minister announced a coalition restructuring, and instead of a three‑party coalition, Reform and Eesti 200 continued as a two‑party coalition.
The consequences appeared quickly. The new coalition agreement did not mention the minimum wage at all, and by late March, Minister of Economic Affairs Erkki Keldo (Reform Party) told trade unions that the government no longer considered the good‑faith agreement binding.
This decision significantly weakened trade unions' position in the 2026 minimum‑wage negotiations. The government abandoned its role as a party to the previous agreement and shifted to the role of indifferent observer.
The result? Agreement on the 2026 minimum‑wage figure was reached only by spring, the increase took effect in April instead of the usual January, and the 6.8‑percent rise was the lowest in five years, barely exceeding last year's inflation (4.8 percent). As a result, improving minimum‑wage purchasing power stalled this year, bringing us back to the starting point of the entire discussion.
To raise the minimum wage or not?
Should the good‑faith agreement to raise the minimum wage to half of the average wage be revived after the next elections? According to the University of Tartu's 2021 study on the socioeconomic impact of the minimum wage, such an increase would improve the well‑being of minimum‑wage earners and reduce both wage poverty and overall poverty indicators. The positive impact would extend not only to wage earners but also to child‑poverty indicators (report p. 92).
Opponents of minimum‑wage increases often claim that they harm employment. According to the University of Tartu study, however, the impact of minimum‑wage increases on the employment probability of minimum‑wage earners was statistically significantly negative in only one year between 2010 and 2019. In several years, the impact on employment probability was statistically significantly positive (pp. 37–38). Modeling 13‑percent and 30‑percent minimum‑wage increases, the authors concluded that employment could fall by 0.2 and 0.6 percent, respectively (pp. 93–94).
A simple but telling fact also suggests that concerns about negative employment effects are exaggerated: Estonia has one of the lowest shares of workers earning near the minimum wage (up to 105 percent of the minimum wage) in the EU, staying within three percent.
Both tax‑authority data and the University of Tartu study confirm this: the number of minimum‑wage earners in Estonia has remained stable at around 20,000 people, and in 2019, about 6,000 of them worked in single‑employee companies (p. 29). These cases likely involve paying oneself a minimum wage through a company and taking the rest of the income as dividends.
Setting aside value judgments about said practice — people may have various reasons for doing it — we must acknowledge that nearly one‑third of minimum‑wage earners are effectively self‑employed, for whom paying themselves the minimum wage is a way to obtain health insurance while legally optimizing their tax burden.
According to the University of Tartu study, such single‑employee minimum‑wage companies are disproportionately concentrated in Harju County, and their most common fields are construction, wholesale, legal services, and accounting. It is unlikely that a minimum‑wage increase would cause these individuals to lose their jobs.
However, a faster minimum‑wage increase is crucial for the remaining two‑thirds of minimum‑wage earners, who currently live in official wage poverty because their monthly net income falls below the relative poverty threshold. Raising the minimum wage is an especially attractive social‑policy measure because, unlike social benefits, it does not require additional state funding; in fact, minimum‑wage increases have a net‑positive impact on the state budget. In the current fiscal situation, that is a weighty argument.
For these reasons, the good‑faith agreement for a faster minimum‑wage increase deserves to be revived, because the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former US national security officials will assess Taiwan’s defense preparedness alongside National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) at the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience International Forum in Taipei on Saturday.

Taiwan will also share its experience of handling information manipulation and natural disasters, per Formosa Television.
Technology’s role in strengthening democracies’ defenses will feature in the opening address by Palmer Luckey, founder of US defense technology company Anduril Industries. At midday, international representatives will review progress on Taiwan’s resilience work since the last forum.
Other participants include Palau National Security Coordinator Jennifer Anson, former Philippine National Security Adviser Hermogenes Esperon Jr., Japanese Senator Takinami Hirofumi, and former Lithuanian Vice Minister of National Defense Tomas Godliauskas.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Sharp has begun accepting orders for AI servers developed with parent Foxconn, Nikkei Asia reported Wednesday.

Sharp will draw on Foxconn’s procurement and production capabilities as memory and other server components face tight supplies. In Japan, it will use its nationwide maintenance network, originally developed to service multifunction printers installed at convenience stores.
Sharp is partnering with Daiwabo Information System and Ryoyo Ryosan as sales agents, while Tomorrow Net will handle operations and maintenance. Sales are expected to be booked starting next fiscal year.
The servers will target AI inference, which involves running trained AI models and is often handled within businesses rather than large data centers. Sharp plans to expand into areas including physical AI, with President Kawamura Tetsuji saying the server business is part of its strategy to bring AI into daily life and work, per Nikkei Asia.
Utoku Koji, head of Sharp’s AI server business division, said component shortages and delivery delays remain challenges in the AI server market. He said Sharp plans to use its close relationship with Foxconn to connect customer needs with supply chain conditions.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Marine Research Academy said Monday that its coastal observatory in Tainan will soon be operational.

Zelenskyy responded to the "win-win" framing in a CBC interview published on 16 September during his visit to Canada, saying the war's human losses made such an outcome impossible from the first day of the full-scale invasion.
The US and Ukraine are framing a possible end to the war differently. Washington has pushed for a negotiated settlement in which both sides could gain something, while Kyiv has rejected territorial concessions and pressed for security guarantees.
The US approach was to "think about things in the context of win-win" and "create opportunities for both sides," Jared Kushner told reporters after visiting Kyiv on 6 September alongside US special envoy Steve Witkoff, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

US charges 5 people over Russia-backed plots
September 16, 2026
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has charged five men with working for Russian intelligence to carry out surveillance and plan targeted killings in the United States and Europe.
"The men were recruited to carry out attacks and assassinations around the world, including the United States," the DOJ said in the indictment.
Yuri Khrameev, 63, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, both Russian nationals; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Angel Eduardo Castro of Venezuela, 22, were charged with conspiracy to commit financial terrorism.
Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire.
All the individuals are still at large.
The DOJ announced the unsealing of charges against the five individuals one day after DW published an investigation looking into one of the members of the murder plot.
The DW investigation identified Romagoza Durruthy as a salsa teacher in Russia who recruited a number of people in 2024 to carry out sabotage across Europe. The agents were mostly from Spanish-speaking countries and had been sent across Europe to commit arson attacks on businesses and military equipment destined for Ukraine. The investigation found that Romagoza Durruthy had been the person who directed them and organized their travels.
What else did the DOJ say?
Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the plans included attempts to assassinate a Russian dissident in Washington, DC.
According to the DOJ, several people were recruited in the US alone to surveil Russian dissidents, in addition to monitoring civilian and military infrastructure in European countries such as Lithuania.
The Justice Department also reported that one recruit was allegedly offered "$40,000 to 'eliminate' or 'disappear' a US resident."
Last year, another recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania. Russia has previously denied carrying out such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States.
The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

BAE gets $818M more to build U.S. Army’s AMPVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:28:50 UTC
19:28:50 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded BAE Systems an $818 million modification for Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle production, bringing the contract's total value to roughly $3.3 billion.
- The AMPV replaces the U.S. Army's Vietnam-era M113 carriers, with work continuing at BAE's York, Pennsylvania plant through May 2030.
The U.S. Army is putting another $818 million into production of the vehicle meant to replace its Vietnam-era M113 troop carriers, part of a contract with BAE Systems that has now grown past $3.3 billion.
The Department of War said the $818 million award is a modification to BAE’s existing contract for the Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle, bringing the deal’s cumulative value to roughly $3.3 billion. The Army funded the work with fiscal 2025 and 2026 weapons and tracked combat vehicle procurement money. Army Contracting Command at Detroit Arsenal, Michigan, is overseeing the contract. BAE will do the work at its plant in York, Pennsylvania, with an estimated completion date of May 31, 2030.
The AMPV is a tracked, armored vehicle built to replace the M113, a personnel carrier that has been in Army service since the 1960s. It shares a common powertrain and suspension with the M2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicle and the M109A7 Paladin self-propelled howitzer, a design choice meant to simplify maintenance for the armored brigades that operate all three. The M113 lacks the armor and mobility of the vehicles it rides alongside, a gap the Army has flagged as a survivability problem for the crews and medics who depend on it.
The Army builds AMPVs in five variants, each aimed at a role the M113 currently fills: general purpose, mortar carrier, medical evacuation, medical treatment and mission command. The full program calls for close to 2,900 vehicles across those variants, including roughly 993 mission command carriers, 790 medical evacuation vehicles, 522 general purpose carriers, 386 mortar carriers and 216 medical treatment vehicles. Together they are meant to replace the M113 across the Army’s armored brigade combat teams, where the older vehicle still makes up roughly 30 percent of the tracked fleet. Army officials have said the worldwide AMPV fleet could eventually reach nearly 3,000 vehicles over the next two decades.
Low-rate production began in January 2019, and the first AMPVs reached troops in March 2023. The Army awarded BAE a full-rate production contract worth up to $1.6 billion in September 2023, followed by a $754 million order in March 2024 covering deliveries through February 2027. The 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team, 3rd Infantry Division, became the first unit to swap its M113s for a full brigade set of AMPVs, receiving more than 130 vehicles.
Part of the Army’s ongoing need for AMPVs traces back to Ukraine. The United States has sent at least 900 M113s to Ukrainian forces since Russia’s 2022 invasion, according to a Department of Defense fact sheet on security assistance, and the Army has been buying additional AMPVs to backfill its own units. Congress set aside $250 million this year for that purpose, and Army officials told Inside Defense that lower per-unit pricing let the service stretch that money to cover 50 vehicles instead of the 38 originally planned.
BAE has also pointed to the AMPV as a possible option for allied militaries still operating older M113 variants, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region, though no foreign sale has been finalized.
The contract’s cumulative value reflects the sum of all orders placed against the underlying agreement since it began rather than a single new purchase, and the Army routinely adds to it as funding becomes available. With an estimated completion date of May 31, 2030, production and deliveries under this modification will continue for several more years.

Guidance: UK Armed Forces Entry Medical Employment Standards
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
11:28:31 BST
19:28:31 KST

UK Armed Forces Entry Medical Employment Standards
The medical standards used to determine whether someone is healthy and medically fit enough to safely begin military service and carry out their duties.
Documents
Details
Medical Employment Standards help ensure that people joining the UK Armed Forces are medically able to meet the demands of military service. Unlike most civilian jobs, military personnel may be required to work in challenging, hazardous, and unpredictable environments, often with limited access to medical care. The standards are designed to protect both the individual and their colleagues by ensuring that existing medical conditions do not place anyone at increased risk during training, operations, or deployment.
The standards set out the minimum medical requirements for entry into the Armed Forces. They apply to both Regular and Reserve service. They provide clear guidance on which medical conditions are compatible with service, and which may prevent entry. The document is organised by body system, making it easier for candidates, healthcare professionals, and recruiting staff to understand how different medical conditions are assessed.
Medical Employment Standards are regularly reviewed to ensure they remain evidence-based, fair, and appropriate for the needs of Defence. As medical knowledge, treatments, and military requirements evolve, the standards are updated to reflect current best practice and operational demands.

US House takes up Russia sanctions bill backed by late senator Graham
