Belarus frees more prisoners after US envoy's visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:17:56 UTC
18:17:56 KST

Trump's envoy wins release of 25 Belarus prisoners as US drops more sanctions
VILNIUS, Sept 16 - Belarus has agreed to free 25 prisoners in return for a further easing of U.S. sanctions, an envoy for President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.
The deal was part of lengthy negotiations, under way since last year, in which Washington is urging Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko to free hundreds of people including human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers in return for sanctions relief.
The process is sensitive because Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has long been shunned by the West for repressing his opponents and supporting Russia's war in Ukraine. European Union sanctions against Belarus remain firmly in place.
"We agreed to an interim deal, and as a show of goodwill Belarus will release 25 people and in exchange the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," Trump's envoy, John Coale, told reporters in the Belarusian capital Minsk.
ENVOY HOPES FOR MORE RELEASES SOON
The figure of 25 releases was much lower than the 250 that Coale negotiated when he last visited Minsk in March.
However, the American said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues to pave the way for more prisoners to go free and further sanctions to be removed.
"We will continue to improve US-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future. We are not finished!" he posted later on X.
Exiled Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said the 25 had been safely brought to neighbouring Lithuania.
Among those released, according to human rights group Viasna, were prominent journalist Andrei Alyaksandrau, who was serving a 14-year term, and his wife Iryna Zlobina, sentenced to nine years.
Authorities also freed Liudmila Chekina, head of the independent news portal TUT.BY, which was shut down in 2021. She had been serving a 12-year term.
A source familiar with the situation told Reuters that, in addition to the 25, a significant number of prisoners were expected to be freed and remain inside Belarus.
Viasna said relatives of some detainees had been told they could collect their loved ones from penal colonies on Wednesday morning.
LUKASHENKO DENIES REPLACING SOME PRISONERS WITH OTHERS
Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the former Soviet state still held more than 900 political prisoners as of the start of this week, even after Coale negotiated the release of hundreds since the middle of last year.
Among the most frequent charges against them are "extremist" activity, conspiring to seize power, incitement to hatred, or insulting the president.
At Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the people in question were political prisoners and rejected assertions by rights groups and the exiled opposition that he is steadily arresting more people to replace those he releases.
The two companies to be removed from U.S. sanctions are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of paints and industrial coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial concern that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors. Sanctions against them had been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also promised Lukashenko on Tuesday to get U.S. banks to hand back tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets.
Coale's efforts since last year have led to the release, among many others, of Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales Bialiatski and leading opposition figures. His diplomacy has earned gratitude from many Belarusians, but human rights groups and opposition politicians say arrests continue and Lukashenko has yet to end repression in the country.
"Today, alongside our joy for those released, we remember those who remain behind bars," Tsikhanouskaya posted on X.
"There are hundreds of them. Behind every number is a person, their family, and their loved ones who continue to wait." REUTERS

Lebanon's Aoun seeks security deal with Israel, peaceful Hezbollah disarmament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:16:06 UTC
18:16:06 KST

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun says Beirut wants to negotiate a security agreement with Israel after its withdrawal from southern Lebanon, while insisting that Hezbollah’s weapons must be brought under state control without triggering a confrontation.
In an exclusive interview with AFP ahead of his visit to France on Wednesday, Aoun said Lebanon had “no choice but negotiations” because war would be too costly for the country.
He said a security agreement with Israel should initially focus on ending the state of hostility and securing the border, potentially paving the way for a future peace agreement.
“We cannot jump directly to a peace agreement,” Aoun said.
Aoun calls for temporary force in south
Aoun also called for the creation of a temporary international force to prevent a security vacuum in southern Lebanon after the UN peacekeeping mission there ends its mandate at the end of the year.
“What matters is that there is no vacuum,” he told AFP.
He said the force could be European, American, Asian, Arab or a combination of countries and would remain in place only until the Lebanese army is capable of deploying throughout the area.
The UN peacekeeping mission, known as UNIFIL, has operated in southern Lebanon since 1978. The UN Security Council voted in 2025 to end its mandate following pressure from the United States.
Aoun is due to attend a meeting in Paris hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron and attended by Jordanian King Abdullah II. The meeting will seek international support for the Lebanese army as it expands its deployment across the country.
Aoun urged the US, European Union and Arab countries to help strengthen Lebanon’s military and state institutions.
Hezbollah disarmament to be peaceful
Aoun reiterated that Lebanon is determined to disarm Hezbollah, an Iran-backed armed group that has long maintained its own military capabilities alongside the Lebanese state.
He described the decision as “neither negotiable nor open to discussion,” but said the government does not want to achieve it through confrontation.
“The objective is not a confrontation,” Aoun said. “We are determined to resolve this issue peacefully.”
He said the process should not come at the cost of “a bloody conflict” or another civil war.
Aoun also said Lebanon’s international partners must share responsibility for strengthening the Lebanese army and state.
“Our Arab and European partners, as well as the United States and our friends, must share with us the responsibility of supporting the army and strengthening the Lebanese state,” he said.

US Charges 5 In Russian Intelligence Sabotage And Assassination Plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:15:32 UTC
18:15:32 KST

Russian intelligence agencies oversaw a series of surveillance and assassination plots targeting dissidents in the United States and Europe, US authorities charged, adding to a growing number of warnings about Russian spy operations in the West.
The allegations, detailed in a new federal indictment, were also the latest warning from Western officials detailing how Russia increasingly uses people not trained as professional spies --- sometimes unwittingly -- to carry out operations.
Among the five people charged in the indictment unveiled late on September 15: a father and son linked to Russia's Federal Security Service: Kirill Khrameyev, identified as a colonel in the agency, known as the FSB; his father, Yury, identified as a retired FSB officer.
Three others -- two Cuban men named Oemis Durruthy and Yaidel Suarez and a Venezuelan man Angel Castro -- were also charged. Durruthy lives in Russia, the US Justice Department said in a statement. The whereabouts of the two others are unclear.
According to the indictment, as recently as this summer, Castro, who had been living in Brooklyn, New York, was hired to surveil a prominent Russian dissident who was living in Washington, D.C.
The Russian dissident is not identified in the court filings.
The person was sent to two addresses and given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance,” authorities said. In exchange, the person was promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the surveillance.
The person then allegedly sent photographs to one of the FSB officers, who then later offered $40,000 to the person to “eliminate” or “disappear” the dissident.
After the person declined the offer, the FSB officers allegedly sought out others in the United States to carry out the murder plot.
In another incident detailed in the indictment, an American man living in Lithuania traveled to Estonia, to the border with Russia on June 25, 2025.
There, he met Khrameyev who allegedly offered to pay the man an unspecified amount to return to Vilnius and take photographs of an address where a “bad guy” who was “telling lies about Russia" lived.
The person was paid $200 for the surveillance. The person was then put in touch with Khrameyev’s father, Yury, who allegedly offered him $25,000 to kill the person because he was "spreading dirt about my country" and "telling the media and the common people that the Russians are the aggressors."
Khrameyev also explained how the killing could take place, including "throwing a bottle of gasoline" or "sticking a knife" in the person," according to the court filing.
After the person declined, Yury Khrameyev allegedly proposed he could set fire to a warehouse or electrical substation for an unspecified amount of money.
Khrameyev allegedly wrote to the man, saying he was offering "serious money for serious work," and he was interested in targeting pro-Ukrainian countries, according to the indictment.
The group was also accused of a plot to set fire to buses in the Czech Republic. Durruthy, US authorities said, enlisted a Colombian man, who allegedly tried to burn public buses in the capital, Prague.
After the man's arrest, the Czech prime minister said the plot was "very likely" organized by Russian authorities.
The FSB had no immediate comment on the charges.
Neither Yury nor Kirill Khrameyev could be reached for comment either.
Photographs posted by Kirill Khrameyev to the Russian social media platform VK show him posing at a St. Petersburg academy graduation ceremony, alongside his father.
The indictment includes extensive quoted material taken from chat messages, as well as photographs, that were exchanged between the Khrameyevs and their contacts.
It does not specify how the material was gathered, but in past years, US authorities have used search warrants to access cloud-based storage services -- for example Apple's iCloud, or Google Drive -- to obtain backed-up files, including things like WhatsApp chat logs.
Other plots have been uncovered by authorities accessing Google Translate files stored online, according to the investigative website The Insider.

Why It Seems Like Great White Sharks Are Overrunning Maine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Lifeguard Greg Wilfert was swimming off the coast of Scarborough, Maine, in August when he was yanked underwater by a force tugging on his rescue buoy. Wilfert, a lifeguard of 55 years, told local news outlet WFSB that he first thought he’d gotten caught on a boat propeller, but the real culprit was a great white shark.
The incident is one in a long line of great white sightings off the coast of Maine this year. It was a busy summer for shark sightings along the rest of the East Coast, but Maine, in particular, seems to have had a great white bonanza. A dozen sightings were reported in a two-day period near Pine Point Beach in southern Maine in August. Beaches were temporarily closed all over the state following multiple sightings throughout July and August. The sharks followed beachgoers through the end of summer: A great white was spotted off Wells Beach over Labor Day weekend, while a fisherman caught another on the holiday about 30 miles down the coast.
The waters off the coast of Maine are some of the world’s fastest-warming, and the Atlantic has seen a series of marine heat waves. The El Niño weather phenomenon is only boosting global heat further. But experts told WIRED that the reason for our recent glut of shark encounters is a lot more complicated than just attributing them to climate change, especially when it comes to great whites. Instead, a successful conservation effort decades ago is likely starting to pay dividends, coupled with more people bringing technology that can spot sharks to the beach.
When Steven Spielberg’s classic movie Jaws came out in 1975, great whites were in trouble. The species had declined in waters off both the east and west coasts of the US thanks to overfishing, bycatch, and trophy hunting. In the 1990s, federal protections were instated for both the sharks and for gray seals, one of their key prey species.
Maine’s state shark monitoring system uses a technology called acoustic telemetry, which outfits the animal with a tag that emits a unique electronic signature. Underwater stations can then pick up on that signal and log the tagged sharks, helping track their movement up and down the coast. Maine’s program is less than a decade old, and “not every shark is tagged,” says Matthew Davis, a shark expert at Maine’s Department of Natural Resources. That makes pinpointing exactly what is going on with this uptick in sightings a little more challenging.
But Davis and Walter Golet, an associate professor at the University of Maine School of Marine Science who collaborates on shark research, both believe that there were more great whites off the coast this summer compared to decades past. They attribute it in part to federal protections working. Great whites males take 26 years to reach adulthood, while females can take up to 33 years. That timeframe aligns with when federal protections were put in place and could help explain why more sharks are showing up off of Maine. Research generally backs this up: Multiple studies have found that protections for both sharks and seals helped to increase populations along the East Coast.
While climate change has driven massive changes in the ocean, including pushing many species northward as waters warm, its direct effect on great white sharks is a little more murky. Some research has suggested that great whites could suffer from very hot ocean temperatures by causing them to overheat and forcing them to slow down or move to colder water to seek food. But James Sulikowski, the director of the Coastal Oregon Marine Experiment Station at Oregon State University, emphasizes that great whites can control their body temperature, which enables them to withstand much larger ranges in ocean temperatures than other shark species.
“They’re not so subject to these huge fluctuations—they’re really good regulators,” he says.
Davis says that the knock-on effects of climate change—like warmer ocean temperatures changing certain prey species’ habitat range—are more likely to impact great whites than the hotter ocean temperatures do. Prey species may “hang around a little bit longer because the water is going to be a little bit warmer,” he says, which could mean great whites spend more time in areas they previously would’ve been in for only a few months.
Another indirect impact of climate change: more people at the beach during hot days. And, since it’s 2026, more and more people bring equipment, from iPhones to hobby drones, that can capture high-quality footage of marine life. All three experts say that the raft of shark sightings in Maine this summer may just be a result of people going outside with better, more technologically advanced eyes on the ocean.
“There are more of them, but they are also easier to see, so you have to untangle that,” says Golet. “I think we’re all sort of a prisoner of our own timeline.”

The US Department of Justice announced charges Tuesday against five alleged agents for Russian intelligence accused of conspiring to carry out attacks and murders around the world, including in the United States.
The group, which has been active since at least 2024, attempted to have a "prominent Russian dissident" believed to be living in the US murdered this summer, the department said in a statement, without naming the target.
Its members allegedly operated as part of "a global assassination network that reached into the United States", Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said.
They attempted to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings on the Kremlin's orders, Eisenberg said.
According to the statement, the three main suspects are Yuri Khrameev, a 63-year-old former colonel in the Russian intelligence services, his son Kirill, 27, and Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a 35-year-old Cuban.
The other two suspects, Yaidel Delgado Suarez of Cuba and Angel Eduardo Castro of Venezuela, were allegedly working as recruiting agents in the US.
All five suspects remain at large.

The Al-Zaraa mine is near El-Nahud in Sudan’s West Kordofan region. The mine began to collapse on Tuesday after tunnels were dug very close together
At least 60 small-scale miners are dead, with many missing, after the collapse of a gold mine in Sudan's West Kordofan region.
The mine reportedly began to collapse on Tuesday after two shafts that had been dug close together began to give way.
Survivors say they do not know how many people remain trapped.
One surviving miner Khair al-Sayyed Jabara told AFP there had been an overnight rescue operation since the collapse, and that fellow miners were having to dig using the same rudimentary tools they use to mine.
"Everyone's working very hard to retrieve the bodies or any survivors, but it's difficult. We need heavy machinery to clear the rock and soil."
Heavy machinery is often not readily available at small-scale mining sites. Sudan’s gold industry has become increasingly important since the civil war began in April 2023, providing a significant source of revenue in an economy devastated by conflict.
The civil war began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. As a result, the country is facing the world’s largest displacement crisis, with nearly 20 million people experiencing crisis-level hunger.

LONDON — The U.K. government plans to update the Online Safety Act to clamp down on so-called “doxxing”— publicly sharing private or personal information about a person online without their consent — following the harassment of volunteers at a charity which helps people at sea, Digital Secretary Lisa Nandy said.

Nandy met with social media platforms on Tuesday to discuss a recent wave of online abuse targeting Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) volunteers and workers after they helped a boat carrying migrants land in Portsmouth.
Advertisement
Nandy said the companies disclosed inconsistent approaches to removing names and addresses of people shared online — and accused Elon Musk’s X of “contempt” for failing to send a representative to the meeting. X did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
More broadly, Nandy said the U.K. government would be “moving at pace to make sure that we keep people safe and we clean up our online space, which has been left to the private sector to police for far too long.”
“Our government intends to be more interventionist in this area,” she said.
In a separate interview on Wednesday, Nandy said the government wanted to see regulator Ofcom enforcing the Online Safety Act “more robustly and more quickly.”
A review of Ofcom’s resources and enforcement powers is ongoing, with the regulator set to soon take on additional responsibilities to enforce a social media ban for under-16s.
“We’ve been more active than any other regulator in the world when it comes to enforcing online safety law,” an Ofcom spokesperson said.
“In the first 18 months of the Online Safety Act coming into force, we've investigated more than 100 platforms, and issued fines totaling more than £7 million against 11 providers,” they added.

Saudi running out of oil export options as routes choked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:12:02 UTC
18:12:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi running out of oil export options as Iran, allies choke routes
Saudi Arabia is running out of options to export its vast oil reserves as attacks force its main pipeline shut while Iran and its allies cement their chokehold on the kingdom's two main maritime routes, analysts say.
The world's top oil exporter last week shut its East-West pipeline, which runs some 1,200 kilometres (700 miles) between its main oil fields in the east and the Yanbu terminal on the Red Sea, after attacks on its oil facilities originating in Iraq, home to pro-Iran armed groups.
The pipeline became essential for Riyadh's oil trade after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, choking its main export route.
But the usefulness of the pipeline's Red Sea outlet has been curtailed by Houthi attacks from Yemen and their weeks-long maritime blockade on vessels serving Saudi ports.
The kingdom is still able to export part of its oil, which is piped to Yanbu and then exported either via the Suez Canal or Egypt's Ain Sokhna, where it is carried by another pipeline to the eastern Mediterranean.
The other option is embarking on a dangerous journey through the Hormuz strait, where Iran has repeatedly attacked commercial shipping.
"The East-West pipeline is a critical energy artery for Saudi Arabia, especially within the current geopolitical context," Robert Mogielnicki of the US-based Arab Gulf States Institute told AFP.
Since the start of the war, Saudi exports via Yanbu increased fivefold to nearly four million barrels per day, according to commodities data firm Kpler.
But in July the Houthis announced a maritime blockade against Saudi Arabia, sending exports through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait spiralling to nearly zero by August, Kpler said.
The attack on the East-West pipeline showed that even infrastructure meant to secure Gulf exports was not a "silver bullet", said Torbjorn Soltvedt, an analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
Back to Hormuz?
Due to the risks, Saudi Arabia is already increasingly using the Suez Canal as well as Egypt's Sumed pipeline from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, which is used because some supertankers cannot pass through Suez at full load.
Transits of Saudi crude through the canal approached 500,000 barrels per day at the end of July, compared with almost none in June, according to Kpler.
By combining the Suez and Sumed pipeline routes, up to 3.4 million barrels of Saudi crude could theoretically bypass Bab al-Mandeb each day, Kpler estimated, but this capacity has never been tested on such a scale.
For crude bound for Asia, Saudi Arabia's main export market, this route would also require sailing up to the Mediterranean and then around Africa, adding weeks on to any journey.
Saudi Arabia has also been shipping some of its oil through the risky Hormuz route, where Iran regularly attacks tankers that do not use its preferred corridor.
Ships transit the waterway with their tracking systems switched off and ship-to-ship transfers still allow crude to be moved out of the Gulf, but daily volumes remain highly volatile and average only about half of their pre-war level, according to Verisk Maplecroft.
Market pressure
The consequences of the squeeze on Saudi exports are already being felt in the markets.
After the announcement of the East-West pipeline's closure, Brent soared to nearly $110 per barrel, while average diesel prices in the US struck a record high of just under $6.27 a gallon on Tuesday, though the Ukraine war is also impacting diesel.
"The global economy will also feel the heat from upward pressure on oil prices resulting from ongoing tensions in and around the region's two choke points and damaged energy infrastructure," said Mogielnicki.
Adding to pressure is Saudi Arabia saying that "its oil production fell last month to its lowest level since 1990," Ipek Ozkardeskaya of Swissquote wrote in a note to clients.
Repairs of the East-West pipeline could be complicated by the conflict, with disruptions to maritime transport delaying equipment imports, according to Verisk Maplecroft.
For Soltvedt, the attacks are reducing oil exports, while the resulting disruptions to trade in turn complicate the repairs that the kingdom needs to increase them.
"The damage to the pipeline and delays to its repair underscore the growing feedback loop from the regional conflict," he said.
For governments in the region, that vicious circle is taking hold as the US-Israeli war on Iran drags on.
"This is not the direction that Gulf officials were hoping for after six months of war," Mogielnicki said.

Israel poses greatest potential threat to Syria's stability: Turkish foreign minister

ANKARA (AA) - Israel currently poses the greatest potential threat to Syria's stability, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this week during a visit to Damascus.
As developments in Syria moves in a positive direction, Israel takes “destabilizing actions,” Fidan told Turkish journalists on Monday during his visit.
"Extremely critical developments are taking place in our region. During this process, we are increasing our contacts with Syria. We wanted to pay a two-day visit here. We have many issues to discuss," he said.
He said the overnight visit was also an indication that life in Syria is beginning to return to normal.
"We had a meeting with President (Ahmad) Sharaa that lasted about two hours. We discussed all issues," said Fidan.
"The threat with the greatest potential to destabilize Syria at the moment is Israel. Thankfully, other issues concerning Syria have been moving in a positive direction for the past two years. They have been removed from the sanctions list, and there are no obstacles to economic investment. Their removal from the terrorism list was also extremely important."
Fidan said that Syria needs time and has significant potential if stability is accompanied by good governance.
"But Israel doesn’t particularly like neighboring countries being strong and stable. It sees this as a threat to itself. Because of how it defines this threat, it engages in destabilizing actions against these countries," he said.
"Syria, however, wants to live in peace in its region. At some point, Israel will either recognize this approach and accept living in peace with its region, or it will continue these aggressive policies and become even more isolated within the international community."
"Netanyahu sees all the countries around Israel as threats. Israel is a country that derives its own strength from the weakness of those countries," Fidan added.
Fidan said the first priority for Syria is for the SDF group to cease being a threat, no longer be a hostile element.
"The elements announced in principle currently contain positive messages. We are closely following how the process proceeds in practice. We expect implementation to be consistent with the messages announced to the public," he said.
Last month Türkiye’s National Defense Ministry welcomed the announced dissolution of the SDF group and its integration into Syrian state institutions, calling it an important development for preserving Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Fidan also said that the progress achieved so far could be taken further.
"We know the existing threats and the path that needs to be followed. There is an ongoing path. We must continue along this path of success. After the regime fell on Dec. 8, I said that everything had only just begun," he said, referring to the end of the Assad regime in December 2024.
"At the point we have reached, positive things are happening both tactically and strategically. Many problems that have shackled us for 40 to 50 years, particularly the issue of terrorism, essentially originated from Syria and Iraq."
Fidan said that after Türkiye’s Justice and Development (AK) Party came to power, Ankara, under the will and vision set out by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, addressed its domestic political and economic issues while rebuilding its strategic and security culture in terms of external developments.
"We established a security paradigm that responds to today's needs. We managed to appropriately resolve our problems originating from neighboring countries. However, our work on this issue is not finished. We will continue to work and make efforts," he added.
Fidan said that the joint efforts of regional countries, particularly on Gaza, have produced important results.
“We have analyzed developments in a highly professional manner through cooperation and solidarity. We also used our cooperation there in Syria. Now we are using this cooperation in the Iran-US war as well, and we are increasingly institutionalizing it.”
"We are making an effort based on cooperation and peaceful diplomacy in the face of Israel's destabilizing role in the region. God willing, the seed we have planted in the region will sprout and grow. If this constructive understanding grows, a larger zone of stability will emerge."
Fidan cautioned, however, that actors seeking instability in the region, particularly Israel, could take other steps.
"They will not remain idle; they will also take action," he said.
"But countries in the region see that stability is possible, that something can be achieved if we work together, and that there is no alternative to working together. Either we work together and solve the problems, or, as in the previous approach, we go to the hegemon or the hegemon's representative here and say: 'Don't touch me, burn wherever you want.’"
"But every place that is set on fire eventually burns you too. Jordan, for example, is affected by everything that happens in Iraq and everything that happens in Syria. There’s no place to hide. So everyone is seeking cooperation in this very intense new period."
Fidan said that Erdogan's efforts to set out a vision, demonstrate leadership, and use his relationships to bring actors together had generated confidence in the process.
"Since this is something that has not been seen before, people frankly trust this process," he said.
Fidan also said that efforts to institutionalize the new Mecca Alliance are continuing, with the three countries that formed the group last month – Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan – holding talks at the technical level.
"We are discussing issues such as what the structure of the headquarters will look like and how many people will serve in each unit. This process is about to be completed. Our aim is to expand the Mecca Alliance. The steps to be taken from now on will be more concrete," he said.
Fidan said that attacks on Saudi Arabia from either the south or the north, including attacks by actors based in Iraq, are unacceptable.
On the long-standing conflict in Yemen, and military moves by the Houthi group there, he said: "The Yemen issue has existed for quite some time and has taken various forms. When the situation turns into an effort to encircle (Saudi Arabia) from the north and south, destroy critical infrastructure, and harm not only Saudi Arabia but the region, it is impossible for anyone to remain indifferent.”
"We are acting in accordance with the spirit of the Mecca Alliance. We have already declared that we stand with the Saudis. We have also conveyed the necessary messages to the other relevant parties. We are acting in solidarity."
Fidan said that Türkiye doesn’t want Greece to become "a plaything of those who want to destabilize the region and drag it into chaos."
"We want to have good neighborly relations. There should be no misunderstandings, particularly over security. Both sides should prevent this," he said.
On Greece’s move to militarize islands in the Aegean near Türkiye, in violation of long-established treaties, Fidan said: "We of course have very serious sensitivities over the militarization of certain islands. They know this; we have conveyed it (to them). The militarization of islands that have demilitarized status is a threat to us."
Fidan also noted that Greece is in the runup to general elections next May, adding that opposition to Türkiye had historically been widespread in Greek politics.
"One of the issues which we are focusing on most closely is Greece's efforts, contrary to its treaty obligations, concerning islands that have been placed under demilitarized status by international treaties and whose status must indisputably be preserved," he said.
"This actually isn’t a new situation. It is an issue that has existed since the 1960s and constitutes an important dimension of the interconnected Aegean disputes. Türkiye has expressed the necessary response since the 1960s. We have issued warnings and objections to Greece through bilateral channels, stated our position when the issue was raised at NATO, and also brought the matter before the United Nations."
Fidan called on Greece, “Türkiye's neighbor and ally,” to fulfill its treaty obligations "in a more mature manner, consistent with the spirit of alliance."

Budget Gap in 2027: How Much Ukraine Is Short Of and Where They Will Look for the Money
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
12:11:30 EEST
18:11:30 KST

Budget Gap in 2027: How Much Ukraine Is Short Of and Where They Will Look for the Money
Kyiv • UNN
The 2027 draft budget envisages a deficit of 15% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of GDP. UAH 4.885 trillion is planned to be allocated to security and defense.
In 2027, Ukraine will need $52.6 billion in international financial support, the state budget deficit is planned at 15% of GDP, and public debt may exceed 110% of GDP. At the same time, as recently as early September, the Ministry of Finance preliminarily estimated the uncovered need for external financing next year at $32.6 billion and called the current budget situation the most difficult since 2022.
UNN examined what was included in the draft State Budget for 2027, why Ukraine’s need for funds is growing, and how dependent the state will be on financing from international partners.
Expenditures are growing twice as fast as revenues
On September 15, the Cabinet of Ministers approved and submitted to the Verkhovna Rada the draft State Budget for 2027. The document was registered in parliament under No. 16000, and lawmakers are currently reviewing it in the relevant committees. This means that the indicators set out in the state budget may still change as the document passes through all the necessary stages in the Verkhovna Rada.
Returning to the figures, the draft budget for next year provides for UAH 5.648 trillion in revenues. This is UAH 452.1 billion, or 8.7%, more than the 2026 plan, taking into account the amendments made to it. Expenditures, meanwhile, are expected to reach UAH 7.272 trillion. They are increasing by UAH 864.9 billion, or 13.5%, all at once. In other words, the expenditure side of the budget is growing significantly faster than revenues.
According to the Ministry of Finance’s calculations, the state budget deficit will amount to approximately 15% of projected GDP. For comparison, the expected figure for 2026 is approximately 12% of GDP. Total deficit financing is planned at approximately UAH 1.67 trillion, with external borrowing expected to play the key role.
At the same time, the ceiling on public debt at the end of 2027 may reach approximately UAH 12.31 trillion, or 110.4% of projected GDP. In terms of the debt structure, about 84% may consist of external liabilities and only 16% of domestic liabilities.
Ukraine needs $52.6 billion from abroad
One of the most telling figures in the draft budget is the need for international financial support. For 2027, the Ministry of Finance estimated it at $52.6 billion. The money is planned to come from the European Union, the G7 countries under the ERA mechanism, the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the United Kingdom, and other partners.
The problem is that the financing need and the funds already guaranteed to Ukraine are not the same thing.
On September 4, Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko stated that Ukraine’s preliminary uncovered need for external financing in 2027 amounted to $32.6 billion. According to him, Ukraine’s basic annual need for external financing remains at approximately $50 billion. Marchenko called the budget situation the most difficult since 2022 and warned that without the necessary assistance from allies, the state might have to cut some non-military expenditures.
After the draft budget was finalized, the estimate of the overall need increased to $52.6 billion.
What the IMF says
The International Monetary Fund’s estimates differ somewhat from the government’s new budget calculations. During the first review of the new EFF program, the IMF estimated Ukraine’s financing gap for 2027 at $43.4 billion under the baseline scenario. At the time, the Fund assumed that about $40.7 billion could come from official creditors and donors, another approximately $1.8 billion directly from the IMF, while about $0.9 billion would result from debt-service relief.
However, these figures should not be mechanically compared with the $52.6 billion envisaged in the new draft budget. The IMF’s calculations were based on information available as of May 2026 and concerned the broader financial balance under the Fund’s program. Since then, Ukraine’s needs, primarily defense-related, have continued to grow.
This is already clearly evident from the current year: according to the parliamentary budget committee, one day of war in 2026 costs Ukraine approximately $190 million, whereas in 2024 the figure was about $140 million.
Ukraine needs nearly UAH 4.9 trillion for the war
The security and defense sector remains the main item in the draft 2027 State Budget. The Cabinet of Ministers proposes allocating UAH 4.885 trillion to it, or 43.8% of projected GDP. This is UAH 517.9 billion more than was included in the 2026 budget after amendments were made.
Of this amount:
-  UAH 1.792 trillion - for wages and related charges; 
-  UAH 2.299 trillion - for weapons and military equipment; 
-  UAH 499.9 billion - for other defense expenditures; 
-  UAH 264.9 billion - as a reserve; 
-  UAH 30 billion - in state guarantees for the purchase of
weapons and military equipment. 
In practice, defense absorbs the bulk of the state's domestic financial resources. Civilian expenditures - social programs, education, healthcare, support for internally displaced persons, reconstruction, and some economic programs - depend to a considerable extent on external funds.
That is why disruptions in international financing for Ukraine point to the critical need to determine which nonmilitary expenditures should be postponed, cut, or provided with additional domestic sources of funding.
The government does not expect an economic breakthrough
The draft budget for 2027 was prepared based on a conservative scenario that assumes the continuation of high security risks. As economic analysts explain, the Cabinet of Ministers used a scenario under which real GDP will grow by only 1.3% in 2027. Inflation is forecast at approximately 8%. At the same time, in the more optimistic scenario presented in June, which envisaged a significant improvement in the security situation, the Cabinet of Ministers expected the economy to grow by 4.5%. These facts indicate that the authorities are no longer preparing the main financial document based on the assumption of a rapid end to the war and a sharp economic recovery.
Why the budget situation is being called the most difficult since 2022
A large deficit in Ukraine's wartime budget is not, in itself, a new phenomenon. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, the state has spent significantly more each year than it has been able to collect domestically, covering the difference through international aid and borrowing. However, several problems are converging simultaneously in 2027.
Military expenditures continue to grow, while the economy, according to the government's forecast, is barely accelerating. The deficit is again rising to 15% of GDP, debt exceeds the annual GDP, and more than $50 billion in external support is needed to fulfill all the commitments included in the budget.
This is compounded by uncertainty over what portion of this money will be guaranteed by partners in advance and when exactly it will arrive.
Therefore, the main risk of the 2027 budget is not that the state will suddenly run out of money on January 1. What is critical is that the ability to execute the entire planned volume of expenditures increasingly depends on decisions by partners, international programs, and Ukraine's fulfillment of the conditions to which individual tranches are tied.
At the same time, draft budget No. 16000 is only beginning to undergo all the necessary procedures in the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. During the first and second readings, its revenues, expenditures, and individual sources of financing may still be revised. The final configuration of 2027 financing will become clear after agreements with key international partners and the parliament's adoption of the final version of the state budget.
We remind you
The other day, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on lawmakers to vote in favor of seven bills to finance the budget deficit and emphasized defense needs.

Ukraine's parliament can fill Zelensky's budget black hole, if it does the reforms, EU letter reminds

The letter, first reported by the Suspilne public broadcaster and seen by the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 16, comes as a series of reforms remains blocked in the parliament, and weeks after President Volodymyr Zelensky identified a $27 billion hole in the 2026 budget.
"Over 20 billion euros in EU financial assistance remains available for disbursement until the end of 2026, subject to the fulfillment of reforms in line with the EU requirements," reads the letter, which was sent by the EU's economy and enlargement commissioners, Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos, respectively.
"The Verkhovna Rada (the Ukrainian parliament)… has a decisive role in turning reform commitments requiring legislative action into tangible results for Ukraine," the letter continues.
The letter also reminds that the reforms are beneficial for Ukraine more broadly: increased income to fund public resources, an improved business climate, more investment, and unlocking further support from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), all of which are among the reasons cited for Kyiv to stick with the reform agenda.
On the same day the letter was sent, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi met with lawmakers to clarify the timetable for future votes.
And on the morning of Sept. 16, the Parliament advanced one of the bills required to unlock funding, on tax exemptions for packages, which had been blocked for months.
So far, the EU and its member states have provided 220 billion euros ($254 billion) of support for Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion, claims the letter.
"Other international partners should also step up their commitments, with the (Verkhovna) Rada playing an important role in mobilizing broader support," the letter reads.
The EU's 90 billion-euro ($104 billion) loan to Ukraine, approved in April 2026, is designed to cover two-thirds of Kyiv's total budgetary needs until the end of 2027.
Other allied countries were expected to contribute the remaining third, though this has not yet happened, and figures both from the EU and Ukraine have begun insisting on this more explicitly in recent weeks.
The letter also mentions that progress on EU integration is held up by the need for the parliament to take "further steps on the protection of persons belonging to national minorities and their education rights."
While not naming any specific countries, the letter does say "member states attach particular importance to resolving this issue" for the accession process to advance.
It is widely understood in Brussels that Hungary is the main country pushing for concrete progress on this topic.
"The Verkhovna Rada has been central to Ukraine's democratic resilience and European choice... we count on the Rada's continued commitment to taking these reforms forward in the long-term interests of Ukraine and its citizens," reads the letter.

A tiny village in the south-East of England has symbolically “voted” to leave the U.K. in protest at the housing of asylum-seekers at a nearby military site.
Residents in Piddington, Oxfordshire, have been angered by a U.K. Home Office plan to accommodate just over 1,200 asylum-seekers at a site owned by the Ministry of Defense.
The non-binding referendum, organized by the local parish council, saw 285 villagers vote to leave, 26 vote to remain, and one spoilt ballot paper. The exercise has no legal authority, but is a show of local opposition on a hot-button issue.
Advertisement
Council Chair Tim McNally told the BBC that the result was “an example of democracy in operation,” and said the villagers had “given a message to the world.”
Government minster Lisa Nandy told Times Radio Wednesday morning that the result indicated “serious frustration” at the Home Office and acknowledged that “we do have to share the load” between poorer and wealthier communities.
But she pointed to a backlog in the asylum system inherited from the previous Conservative government, and pointed out that since 2024 decisions on asylum claims have been sped up, a move that should reduce the need for temporary accommodation while people’s claims are processed.
Nandy added: “[We’ve had] record numbers of removals [of failed asylum-seekers]. And we saw the small boat crossings [of the English Channel] fall this summer for the first time. So we are working very hard to get a grip on the asylum chaos that we inherited.”
Some local residents have expressed concern that their village has become a flashpoint for a wider political battle. Far-right activist Danny Tommo has suggested that followers of his Patriot Platform group could descend on the village to stop asylum-seekers should the government press ahead.
Opposition political parties have been swift to leap on the row over Piddington. Reform UK MPs Suella Braverman and Sara Pochin visited the village prior to the referendum.
Braverman said people in Piddington were “terrified” and that no one “is listening to their voices.”
“For Labour, open borders are a project,” Pochin argued, “They’re a problem for everybody else — and a particularly large problem looming here for the residents of Piddington.”
Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch also seized on locals’ concerns in Piddington, warning last month in the Daily Mail newspaper that the village becoming independent was “only slightly less absurd” than the government forcing it to accept four times its population.
The symbolic independence of Piddington will have little practical impact, but locals have already suggested taking the stunt further by renaming the village or electing new leaders.

‘We need to get it right’: union gusto for Burnham to face make-or-break tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:10:04 UTC
18:10:04 KST

Louise Haigh, the UK first secretary, got a standing ovation from trade union members in Brighton this week, as she acknowledged what she called “the necessity to be bolder in this second chance that we’ve been allowed”.
Haigh was the stand-in at the annual TUC congress for Andy Burnham, absent because of his father’s death.
The headlines from the seaside gathering were dominated by party funding, after Reform announced £72m of donations in a single weekend and Unite called for a cap on donations by individuals in response.
But as they gathered to swap gossip in Brighton’s pubs and hotel bars, senior union figures seemed reinvigorated for the moment by the “Burnham bounce”.
Relations between the new No 10 team and the unions – including those less than popular with Keir Starmer’s regime – have improved significantly; general secretaries speak warmly of recent chats with “Andy”.
Yet there is a clear sense that the real tests are to come – on the implementation of improved workers’ rights; on oil and gas licences, of particular concern to Unite and the GMB; and on John Healey’s crucial autumn budget.
TUC delegates voted through policy statements on a slew of tricky issues in Burnham’s prime ministerial in-tray, from the future relationship with the EU – unions want him to drop Labour’s “red lines” – to Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms.
And senior union figures were keen to point to issues they see as make-or-break.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said she was pleased to see her former schoolmate Jonathan Reynolds back in cabinet as business secretary – but would judge him by results.
In particular, she hopes to see the provisions in the Employment Rights Act on abolishing zero-hours contracts implemented in a way that embraces all workers in the retail and hospitality sectors she represents.
“A lot of people think, job done – but the implementation means everything,” she said. “For this to make a real difference to people’s lives, we need to get it right. We want everybody to have a contract that reflects the hours they work.” The TUC is also gearing up to campaign on the issue in the coming weeks and months.
“We will be getting our message out loud and clear, to Johnny Reynolds in particular,” she said. “It’s about reducing that one-sided flexibility, which employers have got in abundance.”
Thomas also echoed a concern shared by several other senior union figures, about whether Reynolds’s newly expanded Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), would end up lacking focus.
“I would like to see a minister for work. BIST has so much to do, I worry that the labour stuff gets lost,” she warned.
Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, whose members include scientists and engineers – and which is not affiliated to Labour – expresses a similar concern, from a different perspective.
Prospect is campaigning against real-terms cuts to science budgets by the taxpayer-backed UK Research and Innovation agency. Clancy frets that folding science into the department may lead to it being seen primarily through a business lens.
“This is the first test of BIST … and whether this department’s really going to understand science culture,” he said.
The GMB and Unite are waiting anxiously for the government’s ruling on the controversial question of whether to allow drilling in the Jackdaw gas and Rosebank oilfields.
A decision had previously been expected this week, but appears to have been postponed until after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in early October, in which the Green party’s leader in England, Zack Polanski, is standing.
The two unions’ leaders are such ardent champions of continuing to exploit the North Sea’s declining fields, that Unite’s Sharon Graham and the GMB’s Gary Smith raised concerns about the idea that former energy secretary Ed Miliband would be Burnham’s chancellor.
“What that gives us is time,” Graham said of the idea of exploiting Jackdaw and Rosebank. “It gives time for someone to get their backside into gear and realise we have to create an industry over the other side of this, whether it’s green fuel, whether it’s something else. All of that has to be done before you start saying you’re going to choke off what’s going on over here.”
But the apparent delay until after a tricky London byelection underlines the fact that other parts of Labour’s electoral coalition are unlikely to welcome a “yes” to future drilling.
Meanwhile Graham, who was an outspoken critic of Starmer, said she hoped the first Burnham budget would contain what she characterises as “winter fuel in reverse”.
Rachel Reeves’s early decision to severely limit winter fuel payments to pensioners – eventually reversed – came to symbolise the last government’s missteps. “The abhorrence of that: do something as good as that,” Graham said.
Unite’s (costly) suggestion is for the government to unfreeze the income tax thresholds that have seen a growing number of workers dragged into paying the basic or higher rates, and take fresh action on household bills.
Healey has hinted he would like to do more to give the public a “breathing space” in the face of rising energy costs.
But the shaky global backdrop, with oil prices rocketing and febrile markets driving up interest rates on government bonds, means he is likely to be left with little room for manoeuvre against Labour’s fiscal rules.
For Graham, the answer is obvious: tax the wealthy more, and tax the banks. She rejects the idea that bond market turbulence is a reason for caution.
“We cannot keep being told that we cannot do anything because of the markets. Because if that is the case, what is the point of us electing politicians?” she asked delegates in a fiery speech on Monday afternoon. The TUC has also called for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support.
Judging by the mood music emerging from the Treasury of a “focused” budget with big spending decisions kicked into next year, Graham looks set to be disappointed.
And as Farage’s lavishly funded Reform gears up for the next general election, the pervasive anxiety in Brighton this week was the same one that preoccupies even senior figures in the new government. The radical rhetoric of Burnham’s early weeks in power seems to have won him a fresh hearing with voters – but in straitened times, can he match them with action?

Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with ants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:09:50 UTC
18:09:50 KST

A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law.
The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won, Newsis reported.
Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m wonfine for the company.
The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants.
He said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants.
Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, he said.
Both sides have seven days to appeal. The Guardian contacted Evett for comment.
Evett was founded by the Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood, who has appeared on the Netflix cooking competition Culinary Class Wars and is the restaurant’s public face. He was not a defendant and was not charged.
Under South Korean food safety law, the legal duties fall on the person registered as operating the business. Ginny Kim, Lidgerwood’s wife, is registered as the company’s chief executive and was named as a defendant, alongside the company that operates the restaurant.
Only 10 insect species are approved as food ingredients in South Korea, including grasshoppers, mealworms and silkworm pupae.
Businesses wishing to use an unapproved insect must obtain temporary approval from the ministry of food and drug safety, a step the restaurant did not take. Violating the law carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison or a 50m won fine.
The ministry launched its investigation after seeing mentions of the ant dishes in blog posts and social media.
Prosecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post from April 2021, and served three to five of them atop a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink, until January 2025.
They estimated the dessert was served to 12,274 customers, using 49,096 ants, for total revenue of about 120m won.
Lawyers disputed that figure in court, arguing that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.
The restaurant also noted that only a small number of dishes on their 15-course menu included ants, and that restaurants in countries including Denmark, the UK and Australia use ants as an ingredient.
Insect-eating is neither new nor unusual in South Korea. Beondegi, steamed silkworm pupae, has been sold from street carts for decades and remains a nostalgic popular snack for children.

Russian anti-war candidate puts fears aside to mount long-shot bid for parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:08:08 UTC
18:08:08 KST

Meet the anti-war candidate risking plenty to challenge Russia's ruling elite
MOSCOW, Sept 16 - As a digital billboard behind her displays an advert urging Russians to sign up to fight in Ukraine, Polina Lermant tries to hand out flyers to passers-by urging them to "vote for peace" in a parliamentary election starting on Friday.
It's a risky enterprise.
Lermant, 24, a candidate in Moscow for Russia's liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political force inside Russia to oppose the war in Ukraine, said she feared the authorities might accuse her of wrongdoing and jail her, a fate some of her party colleagues have suffered.
"I'm really afraid. My parents and my husband are really worried about me. I am afraid that the repression will start," Lermant told Reuters in an interview as she campaigned.
Lev Shlosberg, a senior party colleague, was jailed for 11 years for comments about the war last month, and Yabloko's deputy leader, Maxim Kruglov, was jailed for seven years on similar charges in June.
Recalling how her great-grandfather was exiled to the Ural Mountains from Moscow in the Soviet era after being convicted of discrediting the Red Army, a charge now levelled against war critics over the modern Russian military, she said fear had returned to society.
"It's really terrifying that 90 years later people in Russia are still afraid that they will be jailed or that something will be done to them," she said, referring to the increasingly narrow space for public dissent.
The Kremlin says wartime censorship and national unity are vital because of what it says are increasingly dangerous efforts by Ukraine's intelligence services and other enemies to stir unrest inside Russia.
OUTCOME NOT IN DOUBT
Lermant is one of around a dozen candidates in Moscow from Yabloko running in the three-day election to the 450-seat lower house of parliament, the State Duma, which has a track record of faithfully approving the Kremlin's initiatives.
Yabloko wants Russia to agree to a ceasefire in Ukraine. The Kremlin has ruled this out, saying it wants an overall deal that meets its own conditions.
The parliamentary election is the first since President Vladimir Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022 and will be used by authorities to gauge the depth of society's war weariness when the economy is under strain — with fuel shortages caused by Ukrainian drone strikes, high interest rates, a labour crunch and Western sanctions.
For the Kremlin, it is also an exercise that it traditionally uses to project stability.
An advert being run on state TV urging people to vote shows Russian military commanders down the ages before cutting to soldiers holding up the national flag after winning a battle in Ukraine with the slogan: "Their voice is the voice of victory. Your vote is the strength of Russia!"
Western political analysts say the Kremlin is likely to tout the election's outcome - which in Russia's tightly controlled system is not in real doubt - as a fresh endorsement of Putin and his actions towards Ukraine.
The governing United Russia party (UR), which backs Putin, is expected to comfortably retain its dominance.
Four other parties in parliament, which all broadly vote in the same way as UR on major issues - the Communists, the nationalist LDPR, Just Russia and the New People party - are expected to win re-election too.
Battered by arrests and jailings, Yabloko, whose participation gives it a platform for its anti-war views, is unlikely to win any national seats.
STONE IN KREMLIN'S SHOE
Once a leading liberal force in post-Soviet Russia, Yabloko holds only a handful of seats in regional parliaments and none in the national parliament although, unlike self-exiled opposition figures, it has for years worked within the system.
Most Yabloko candidates were barred from contesting the election after the Supreme Court ruled on August 10 that they had broken electoral rules, a ruling Lermant said was prompted by official fears that Yabloko would make it into parliament and raise awkward questions about subjects including the war.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news are punishable with long jail terms.
In many regions, filming and posting online the aftermath of Ukrainian drone strikes is also a criminal offence.
Lermant was initially one of 16 Yabloko candidates left in the race in Moscow because they were contesting single-mandate constituencies rather than competing on a party-list basis. More of her fellow candidates have since been disqualified.
Despite her concerns, Lermant said she felt strongly she was doing the right thing.
"It's really important for us to tell people that there is the chance right now to vote for peace, to express their political position, and to say that we choose peace and a free life without fear," she said.
RISING SUPPORT FOR PEACE TALKS
Lermant said she was encouraged by polling showing public support for peace negotiations had risen this year. This, she said, showed people were increasingly open to Yabloko's ideas.
Polling from the Levada Center - which the authorities have designated a foreign agent - put public support for peace talks above 60%.
Lermant also referenced data from a government pollster showing support for Yabloko had been rising before most of its candidates were barred from contesting the election.
Regular pre-election polling by the main government-aligned pollsters no longer includes Yabloko, making it hard to gauge its popularity. The same pollsters have usually put its support in low single digits.
Anton Malyshev, a candidate in another part of Moscow for New People - a liberal-leaning party which says it is focused on the needs of people and entrepreneurs and favours a freer and more efficient state - told Reuters he was heavily focused on local issues.
He spoke of older residents' concerns when bus routes changed and about an idea to raise money for the state budget by letting people officially buy personalised number plates for their cars.
Malyshev said the more parties that enter parliament, the better. He described New People as an authentic political force, pushing back against critics who say it is a vehicle to siphon off votes from young liberal urbanites to make them less likely to consider street protests.
His party's programme avoids offering any opinion on the war in Ukraine beyond saying most Russians want a long-term peace concluded as soon as possible and that the country needs to be well placed to flourish when fighting ends. This broadly aligns with the Kremlin's stance that an all-encompassing settlement on Moscow's terms is the only acceptable outcome.
Asked whether he could outline his party's thoughts on the conflict, Malyshev said it was interested in how best to support veterans and made no reference to what is happening on the battlefield or in global diplomacy.
"We prefer to build a new future and talk about what lies ahead," he said. "Through our initiatives, we are looking to the future." REUTERS

Climber rescued from Swiss cliff by helicopter after venomous snake bite
On Monday, the Rega air rescue service rescued a 35-year-old climber from steep terrain near Balsthal in canton Solothurn after he had been bitten by a venomous snake. The man was given the appropriate antivenom at a hospital in Bern.
The 35-year-old was out in the area near Balsthal with a companion when, whilst lead climbing, a snake bit him on the hand, the press office of the Swiss Air Rescue Service (Rega) reported on Tuesday.
As his hand swelled up rapidly, the two climbers alerted the cantonal emergency medical services on the emergency number 144. The service immediately requested a rescue helicopter from Rega’s national air rescue centre.
As the accident site was in steep and difficult-to-access terrain, Rega stated that, in addition to the helicopter crew from the Basel base, it had organised a rescue specialist from Swiss Alpine Rescue. The specialist was lowered by winch and prepared the injured man for airlift.
The rescue helicopter then flew the man to Inselspital in Bern, where a suitable antivenom was on hand. The decision to take him to this hospital was made following consultation with the Swiss Toxicological Information Centre, it was reported.
The reptile is believed to be an asp viper. This species of venomous snake is native to the Balsthal region in Solothurn.

Ancient iron-smelting site discovered in Hyrcanian forests of northern Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:07:00 UTC
18:07:00 KST

Ancient iron-smelting site discovered in Hyrcanian forests of northern Iran
TEHRAN – Archaeologists have discovered the remains of an ancient metal-smelting site in the forested highlands of Sowme’eh Sara in northern Iran, a find that could shed new light on the history of metallurgy in the western Alborz Mountains.
The remains were identified during field surveys at an elevation of approximately 420 meters above sea level, in an area covered by dense vegetation in the Hyrcanian forests. The site contains furnace clinkers and metallurgical slag spread across an area with an estimated radius of 100 meters.
The site’s location along a ridge near the peaks of the western Alborz Mountains had helped protect the remains from illegal excavations and treasure hunters, according to Majid Kouhi, an archaeologist with the Gilan provincial office of the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
“The initial surface evidence and the type of ores found strongly support the possibility of iron-smelting activities,” Kouhi said.
He added that the discovery could establish a link between historical mining areas, including the Shadadi mines, and Iron Age and early first-millennium BC cemeteries nearby.
According to the archaeologist, the discovery has also raised a new hypothesis about the region’s role in ancient metal production. Given the elaborate and finely crafted metal objects unearthed in nearby areas, the site may have served as a major center for smelting and producing raw materials, or possibly as a hub for supplying metals to workshops that manufactured weapons and equipment for warriors in parts of the Iranian plateau.
Kouhi stressed, however, that this hypothesis requires metallurgical testing of materials from the site and neighboring regions.
The findings point to a potentially important role for the western Alborz and Talesh mountain ranges in the supply chain of metals during different historical periods. Further archaeological investigations could help clarify the scale and nature of these activities.
Kouhi said more detailed surveys, test excavations and extensive scientific archaeological work would be necessary to confirm or reject the hypotheses and establish the area’s actual role in the economy and ancient industry of Iran.
Sowme’eh Sara is located on the southern coast of the Caspian Sea, about 25 kilometers west of Rasht, the capital of Gilan province. The Hyrcanian forests form a lush zone of lowland and mountain forests covering approximately 55,000 square kilometers along the Caspian shores of Iran and Azerbaijan.

Von der Leyen's heatwave plan comes as Europe runs out of time to adapt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:06:32 UTC
18:06:32 KST

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a European Heatwave Plan to anticipate intense heatwaves expected to return next summer. A new Climate Insurance Alliance was also unveiled as the EU struggles to close the financing gap needed to address climate adaptation and mitigation.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a "new European heatwave plan" during her inaugural State of the Union speech on Wednesday, after a dramatic summer that saw thousands of hectares burnt and tonnes of crops lost to raging wildfires.
"We need better early warning systems and better health preparedness. We need urban adaptation and cooling. And we need to support the most vulnerable," von der Leyen told EU lawmakers in Strasbourg.
She described the summer as a “summer of truth”, pointing to hundreds of thousands of hectares burned, crop losses and more than 35,000 excess deaths.
However, the timing is hard to ignore. The EU needs no further warning that extreme heat is becoming a major climate risk—it has just experienced it, with repeated heatwaves sweeping across Europe this summer.
The continent experienced an exceptionally early heatwave in May, with daily average temperatures in parts of western France, England and Wales more than 10°C above normal. June then brought another intense heatwave across much of Europe, while western Europe recorded its second-highest June temperature on record.
By the time the Commission unveils its package, much of the emergency work that a heatwave plan is supposed to prepare Europe for will already have happened — or failed to happen.
Failed strategies?
However, the EU won't start from zero.
Its 2021 Adaptation Strategy already set out the goal of making Europe climate-resilient, while the bloc's Mission on Adaptation is supporting regions and communities in building resilience. But heat has largely remained a national and local responsibility, leaving a patchwork of warning systems, cooling measures, building standards, worker protections and emergency responses.
The new European Heatwave Plan, unveiled by von der Leyen on 16 September, matters less because Brussels is finally recognising heatwaves as a European-wide problem than because of what it actually requires governments to do.
The Commission’s biggest challenge will be deciding whether to establish a coordination framework or step in where national action is proving insufficient.
Cooling is an obvious example. A European survey cited by the Commission's Sustainable Energy Week found that 26% of EU households could not keep their homes comfortably cool in 2023, rising to almost 35% among the lowest-income households.
That turns extreme heat from a climate issue into a broader challenge spanning energy, housing and social policy. Simply telling Europeans to install air conditioning is not much of a solution if millions simply can't afford it.
Urban residents face another challenge. Concrete-dominated cities can remain dangerously hot overnight, while hospitals, schools, care homes and workplaces must be equipped to cope with temperatures that were once considered exceptional.
A serious European heatwave strategy would need to link cooling with building renovation, urban greening, water management, electricity demand and social protection, rather than treating extreme heat as a short-term weather emergency. This would require the Commission to adopt a truly holistic approach.
Ticking bomb
Meanwhile, climate projections point towards more frequent and intense heat, while the EU's climate center, Copernicus, estimates that Europe already recorded about 62,800 heat-related deaths in 2024, following roughly 47,700 in 2023 and 61,700 in 2022.
"More than 35,000 additional deaths during the heatwaves. Care homes and hospitals dangerously overheated. And all of this is a mere preview. These were the hottest summer months ever — but probably the coolest of the years to come," von der Leyen said.
For years, the EU’s climate debate focused largely on how quickly emissions could be cut. Now, the Commission must urgently determine how to adapt to the warming already locked in — a daunting task, as the newly announced plan highlights the gap between Brussels’ climate ambitions and the pace of implementation on the ground.
Facing a financial gap amounting to billions of euros, Von der Leyen also announced the setup of a Climate Insurance Alliance, noting that only around 25% of catastrophe losses in Europe are covered by private insurance.
"This means that, far too often, national budgets become the insurer of last resort. We need to take action to close this gap," the Commission chief said.

Tajikistan looks to a new chapter after 35 years of independence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:06:18 UTC
18:06:18 KST

As Tajikistan celebrates 35 years of independence, the milestone offers an opportunity to reflect on how far the nation has come while looking towards the years ahead.
Thirty-five years into independence, with decades of peace and stability established, Tajikistan turns increasingly outward. The country’s international agenda is now focused on tackling some of the defining challenges of the modern world, from peacebuilding and water security to climate change and digitisation.
In an anniversary address in Dushanbe on 8 September, President Emomali Rahmon highlighted Tajikistan’s ongoing commitment to promoting global peace, referencing the nation’s role in advancing the UN resolution for a “Decade for Strengthening Peace for Future Generations,” from 2027.
Another proposal by Tajikistan saw the United Nations General Assembly adopt a resolution to establish the International Day of Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence, to be observed annually on 31 August.
Taken together, the two initiatives offer a glimpse of how Tajikistan seeks to frame its next 35 years within a global context, looking outwards to address shared challenges of digital transformation and sustainable development for the health and prosperity of future generations.
35 years of independence and peacebuilding
Tajikistan declared independence on 9 September 1991, following the dissolution of the Soviet Union. The early years were marked by civil conflict, with a peace agreement reached in 1997.
President Emomali Rahmon, who has led Tajikistan since the early years of independence, has placed peace, national unity and stability at the centre of the country’s development narrative.
Since gaining independence, the country has rebuilt infrastructure, expanded energy and transport networks, and developed education and social services, while strengthening connections with neighbouring countries and the wider world.
To celebrate the milestone, anniversary events are taking place across Tajikistan, including cultural performances in Bokhtar and a military parade in the capital of Dushanbe. In his address at the National Theatre, President Rahmon spoke about the country’s progress and his vision for Tajiks to be recognised internationally as a forward-looking society.
That ambition is reflected in investments in the skills, digital infrastructure and institutions needed to participate in an increasingly technology-driven global economy.
Water, diplomacy and sustainable growth
Tajikistan’s mountainous landscape offers a huge clue to one of the nation’s defining priorities.
Tajikistan is home to snowfields and glaciers that bring water down from the Pamir and other mountain ranges to feed rivers across the region. It is one of Central Asia’s most important sources of freshwater, with a water security strategy that matters well beyond its borders.
Tajikistan has pushed water security and sustainable management higher on the global agenda, contributing to the establishment of the UN’s Water Action Decade (2018-2028) which has created cross-border projects, promotions and partnerships in efforts to avert a global water crisis.
In line with national energy strategy, Tajikistan seeks to further harness its significant hydropower potential, with large-scale renewable energy projects such as the World Bank-funded Rogun Hydropower Plant playing a central role in its plans to improve domestic energy security and strengthen regional connectivity.
All this spills over into another of Tajikistan’s priorities: technology. In May 2026, Tajikistan and the United Nations convened a ‘Water and AI: A Two-Way Nexus’ forum in Dushanbe, examining how artificial intelligence could support more sustainable water management while considering the water demands of AI itself.
All this illustrates how Tajikistan’s priorities are evolving beyond its own borders, looking to shared technologies and regional cooperation in its strategy to tackle challenges that will shape the coming decades.
Looking beyond 35 years
Tajikistan’s 35th anniversary is both a moment to reflect and to aspire.
The country’s journey since independence has included the difficult work of establishing peace and stability, rebuilding after conflict and developing the foundations of a modern economy.
The next 35 years will bring a different set of challenges – from managing water resources and adapting to climate change to creating economic opportunities while navigating rapid digitisation.
As celebrations take place across the country, Tajikistan is looking towards a future in which it plays a growing role not only in tackling challenges at home, but in bringing them to the international spotlight.
