Kosovo ex-president Thaci faces Hague war crimes verdict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:28:00 UTC
16:28:00 KST

Kosovo ex-president Thaci convicted of war crimes
Published September 16, 2026last updated September 16, 2026
A Kosovo war crimes tribunal on Wednesday found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998-1999 war for independence from Serbia.
Thaci, a former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commander, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention.
He was tried along with three other former KLA guerrilla leaders in The Hague.
What did the tribunal rule?
The tribunal said Thaci was guilty of the murder of of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces at the hands of the KLA during the conflict. He was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people and torturing more than 300 people
The court added Thaci had "actively participated in and encouraged crimes."
Prosecutors alleged KLA forces killed more than 100 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces during and just after the Kosovo war.
This included prisoners held at KLA facilities in Kosovo and Albania, along with politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.
The defense argued that the senior KLA figures could not control or be held responsible for such acts, as the group lacked a strict command structure.
Lawyers had argued there was no direct evidence linking Thaci's command to any of the alleged crimes.
Seen as heroes in Kosovo
The accused are revered as national heroes in Kosovo, and the KLA and Thaci are seen as symbols of the independence movement. Thaci remained a central political figure after the war and was instrumental in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia.
The verdict in The Hague was livestreamed in the Kosovo capital, Pristina, where thousands of Thaci and KLA supporters gathered.
This follows rallies over the weekend that drew tens of thousands calling for the men's acquittal.
Foreign embassies warned of the possibility of unrest after the verdict.
"Our war was just, a war of liberation," Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said ahead of the verdict.
"We believe and hope … that the KLA leaders will return free to their country and to their families," he added.
After being indicted in 2020,Thaci resigned as president and has been detained in The Hague since then.
The Kosovo War left 13,000 people dead, of which some 9,000 ethnic Albanian Kosovars who were subjected to a campaign of ethnic cleansing at the hands of Serbian forces. The conflict ended after NATO intervened in 1999, pushing Serbian forces out.
Serbia still does not officially recognize its former province Kosovo as an independent state.
Tribunal deeply unpopular in Kosovo
Throughout the proceedings, prosecutors tried to distinguish between Kosovo's struggle for independence from Serbia and the alleged crimes committed by the men on trial.
During the verdict, the presiding judge, Charles Smith, emphasized that the trial was "not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army" or its goal of Kosovo independence.
The tribunal responsible for prosecuting the case, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), was set up in 2016 after earlier cases in Kosovo failed due to alleged political interference and witness intimidation.
Although based in The Hague, and staffed by international judges, the KSC was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged KLA war crimes.
Nevertheless, the KSC remains deeply unpopular in Kosovo. Out of 15 people indicted so far by the KSC, three are serving sentences.
"Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice," Thaci told judges in February as the proceedings concluded.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

Ukraine Successfully Tests New Interceptor Against Jet-Powered Russian Drones
Ukraine has successfully conducted testing on another drone interceptor engineered specifically to counter jet-powered attack drones fielded amid Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the trial results following a report from Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi, noting that the new system successfully hit a Shahed drone during tests on September 15, 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Engineers and developers are still fine-tuning specific components of the interceptor’s control system.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized that active development remains underway and additional time will be required before the aerial defense system reaches full operational readiness.
"I am grateful to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine for a thorough approach to operational support. Together with Yevhen Khmara and the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, we defined the following priority goals, the necessary volume of assets for this, and preparation measures. The results of the long-range impact on the Russian oil foundation of the war are significant enough, and this is precisely what adds the necessary potential to diplomacy," Zelenskyy said.
Previously, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry reported that the LITAVR interceptor drone, developed by the Ukrainian company F-Drones, was designed primarily to intercept aerial targets and could reach speeds of up to 350 km/h.
Development began in the fall of 2024, and by the following summer, the drone passed testing, received codification, and entered serial production. Its main feature was an automatic terminal guidance system that tracked targets independently once the operator locked them for engagement.
Equipped with daytime and thermal imaging cameras alongside a navigation system independent of GPS, the drone operated at altitudes of up to 9 kilometers, with one unit recording a flight that extended over 80 kilometers from its launch point.

Because some people who do not understand politics led things to a point where people are dying. They did that through what they did in 2021. Hong Kong launches maiden 5-year plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:25:18 UTC
16:25:18 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Hong Kong Wednesday released its first Five-Year Plan, a move seen as a step toward aligning the semi-autonomous city's development policies with mainland China.
It is the first time since Hong Kong was handed back to China by the UK on July 1, 1997, ending 156 years of British colonial rule, that the city has launched a targeted five-year development plan with binding and anticipatory goals.
After unveiling the plan, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee also delivered an annual policy address to the Legislative Council, stressing the need to implement "One Country, Two Systems" fully and faithfully, RTHK reported.
Mainland China launched its 15th Five-Year Plan this year, which runs through 2030.
“Pursuing development does not mean we can neglect national security. We will continue to improve and enhance these mechanisms for safeguarding national security,” he said.
However, he added that the city administration will “stick to the executive-led governance model, driving and coordinating efforts to maintain social stability and improve people's well-being,” the report said.
In the last year of his current term, which began in 2022, Lee’s administration had launched a two-month public consultation before unveiling the plan Wednesday.
Lee said Hong Kongers will “better understand how the government will turn the long-term blueprint into concrete policy measures in the coming year,” the South China Morning Post reported.
Describing the five-year plan as “forward-looking and strategic,” Lee said it maps out the long-term direction for the city, while the policy address is the annual report on how the government will implement the blueprint, the report said. “The two documents are closely related,” he stressed.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in her weekly press briefing, in response to a Mehr News Agency correspondent's question, that Russia views the U.S. and Israeli aggression against Iran as direct and without prior provocation, and that Moscow's position on Tehran has not changed.

She said this position is not temporary or emotional, but encompasses the full set of facts and factors. She said the only legal method for restricting a country's activities is UN Security Council sanctions. "Has the Security Council sanctioned or authorized what is happening in the Strait of Hormuz? ====================================================================================================

Disinformation follows latest Russia-linked drone incident in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:22:55 UTC
16:22:55 KST

- A suspected Russian drone crossed from Belarus toward Kaliningrad this week, and a second one following the same route was shot down the next night by an Italian NATO Eurofighter.
- Poland's defense ministry and the Prime Minister's Chancellery both corrected a doctored photo that falsely claimed the drone was a Polish design under testing.
A suspected Russian drone crossed from Belarus into Lithuanian airspace this week before continuing into Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave, and a second drone following the same route the next night was shot down by an Italian fighter jet flying NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission.
Retired Polish military pilot Michał Fiszer described the episode in a post this week, saying the route matched one Poland’s defense minister laid out publicly a day earlier. Lithuania and the Italian air unit involved both confirmed the details independently.
Polish radar tracked the first drone as it crossed the border, and wreckage recovered afterward carried a serial number beginning with the Cyrillic letters “ЫЫ,” a marking tied to Russia’s Alabuga drone plant in Tatarstan. The aircraft was a Gerbera, a cheap, plywood-and-foam drone that Ukrainian intelligence describes as a stripped-down relative of the more dangerous Shahed-136. Gerberas are built mainly to overwhelm and confuse air defenses or gather basic reconnaissance, though some carry a small explosive payload. Poland has run into this exact drone type before: in September 2025, close to 20 Gerberas turned up scattered across Polish farmland in a single overnight incursion that Warsaw called a deliberate act of Russian aggression.
An Italian Eurofighter scrambled from Šiauliai Air Base to intercept it but couldn’t reach the aircraft before it slipped into Kaliningrad. Šiauliai hosts a rotating detachment of allied jets flying NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission, which keeps fighters on standby to respond to unidentified aircraft near the Baltic states. The unit on duty was a detachment from Italy’s 36th Fighter Wing, normally stationed at Gioia del Colle in southern Italy. The next night, the Italians were already airborne when a second drone made a similar run from Belarus. This time, they caught it and shot it down.
What followed the intercept was a deliberate disinformation push. Someone took a real photo of a Gerbera drone, one that had actually washed up on a Polish beach, and altered it before pushing it out online. The edited version swapped the drone’s genuine “ЫЫ” marking for a Polish-style “SP-” prefix, framing the aircraft as a secret Polish design under test rather than a Russian drone that had crossed the border. The claim doesn’t hold up: Poland doesn’t register drones with “SP-” codes at all. That prefix belongs to civilian aircraft. Drone operators get a code starting with “POL” instead, and individual drones aren’t registered the way manned aircraft are. The same doctored photo also changed a marking associated with newer Russian drone variants, swapping “5+0” for “540” to strip away anything that looked Russian.
The fake image spread quickly, and several mainstream Polish outlets published it before catching the discrepancy. Poland’s Ministry of National Defense and the Prime Minister’s Chancellery each posted their own corrections, setting the real photo side by side with the doctored one to make the manipulation clear to the public.
A retired Polish general, unnamed in Fiszer’s post but described as holding views sympathetic to Russia, then publicly backed the fake photo, insisting the drone really was a new Polish design in testing. The claim spread rapidly online anyway, resting entirely on a registration format Poland has never used for drones. Neither the Polish government nor NATO has issued a joint statement addressing the general’s remarks.

Video: Why does Finland need women-only taxi services?
Finland
Unknown Publisher

10:21:11 EEST
16:21:11 KST

Women-only taxi services are gaining traction in Finland amid growing concerns over women's safety.
The issue came to prominence once again this week after Yle reported that a taxi driver convicted of raping a passenger was allowed to continue working for almost two years before his licence was revoked.
More than 100 criminal reports over suspected sexual offences by taxi drivers have been filed in Helsinki since the taxi industry was deregulated in 2018.
Two women-only taxi companies now operate in Finland, while Bolt also allows passengers to request a female driver.
Meanwhile, the government is tightening taxi regulations, with all taxis set to receive green registration plates next year.

India, Pakistani naval ships collide in international waters; MEA calls conduct 'unprofessional'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:20:51 UTC
16:20:51 KST

The ministry said the Pakistani Charge d’Affaires was advised to convey to the concerned authorities (file photo)
NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday summoned Pakistan’s top diplomat in New Delhi and lodged a strong protest over the “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct” of Pakistani naval units that led to a collision with an Indian Navy vessel in international waters.“While the incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was in direct contravention of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991,” the MEA said in a statement.The ministry said the Pakistani Charge d’Affaires was advised to convey to the concerned authorities that all military units must exercise due care and comply with relevant agreements between the two countries.“The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents,” it said.The MEA also said India’s Charge d’Affaires in Islamabad had been instructed to lodge a similar protest with Pakistan’s ministry of foreign affairs.
This is not the first time Indian and Pakistani ships have come into close contact in the Arabian Sea.In 2011, a diplomatic row had erupted over the MV Suez episode, then Navy chief Admiral Nirmal Verma said Pakistani warship PNS Babur had come “much closer” than was prudent, damaging a helicopter net on INS Godavari. He said the Indian crew had acted “very professionally” and stressed that “there are clear rules of navigation at sea”.What the 1991 agreement saysThe 1991 India-Pakistan agreement lays down rules for advance notice of major military exercises, manoeuvres and troop movements.Under the agreement, the land, naval and air forces of both countries are to avoid major exercises close to each other. If such exercises are conducted within specified areas, the main force cannot be directed towards the other side and there should be no logistical build-up close to it.
For land forces, exercises involving a division or larger formation are restricted within 5 km of specified areas along the International Border, Line of Control and the area between the Manawar Tawi and Ravi rivers. The agreement also requires advance notice for division-level exercises in designated areas, corps-level exercises within 75 km, and all exercises above corps level regardless of distance.
For naval forces, an exercise involving six or more destroyer- or frigate-sized ships crossing into the other country's EEZ is covered. Air-force exercises at regional command level or above also fall under the agreement.

US House passes third resolution in four months attempting to curb US military presence in Iran

The US House of Representatives passed a resolution on Tuesday designed to severely limit US military action in Iran, directing US President Donald Trump to remove all US Armed Forces from the Islamic Republic "other than those elements of the Armed Forces that may be necessary to defend [US and allies] from imminent attack."
The Democrat-sponsored resolution was originally submitted in April and passed Tuesday with a 220-204 vote, with seven Republicans voting in favor.
It was the third time the House has passed a similar war powers resolution, according to a report from Washington-based news outlet The Hill, but the number of Republicans in support increased from four to seven.
"Iran must be held accountable for killing Americans, supporting terrorism, threatening the Strait of Hormuz, and pursuing nuclear weapons," Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), one of the Republicans who voted in favor, wrote in an X/Twitter post on Wednesday morning.
"Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war," he said.
The House first approved a war powers resolution in June, marking a significant shift in the House, which had previously blocked several war powers resolutions aimed at restricting the administration's authority over the conflict. The House approved a second one in July.
US Republican lawmaker Massie seeks Hegseth's impeachment over Iran war
This latest resolution came as Republican US Representative Thomas Massie filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of abusing his office by executing an order for hostilities against Iran without approval by Congress.
Massie filed his articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday as privileged, meaning the House must take them up within two legislative days.
The impeachment resolution is unlikely to pass, but the maneuver by the Kentucky Republican could force a vote in the chamber that could be difficult for some of his fellow Republicans as they prepare to leave Washington before November's midterm elections.
Massie, an outspoken critic of the war on Iran and aid to Israel, is not up for reelection. He lost his primary in May to a candidate backed by Trump after Massie angered the president by leading a push to release Justice Department files tied to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Massie was defeated by Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL backed by Trump and bolstered by heavy spending by pro-Israel groups.

Israel will ‘finish job’ in Gaza and remove Palestinians: Defence minister
JERUSALEM – Israel’s defence minister said on Sept 16 it was only a matter of time before the country resumes full-scale war in Gaza and moves to force out its two million Palestinians.
Israel Katz, who is known for outspoken remarks, was responding to criticism from another right-wing contender ahead of Oct 27 elections.
Katz said 70 per cent of Gaza had already been emptied of its population in the Israeli offensive launched after the Oct 7, 2023, attack by Hamas.
He said that an October 2025 ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump had “supreme value for all Israelis” by leading to the return of remaining hostages and ensuring “a commitment by the United States” to disarming Hamas.
“We all understand that this is not going to happen – and the IDF is prepared, once given the directive to eliminate Hamas, to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan,” Katz said in a statement, referring to the Israeli military.
He said earlier in September that Israel was ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza by sea and land but was waiting for the United States, which he said was discussing where the two million people would go.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has denied any plan to “displace people out of Gaza against their will”.
Katz had described the migration plan as voluntary, saying most Palestinians wanted to leave.
Nearly all of Gaza’s population has been internally displaced and most of the territory lies in rubble after the war.
The Hamas-led attack of Oct 7, 2023, killed 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on Israeli official figures, the deadliest attack ever against Israel.
Militants also took 251 hostages to Gaza.
Israel’s retaliatory military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 73,700 people, according to the territory’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and does not distinguish between combatants and civilians, and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
While the 11-month-old ceasefire has reduced the level of violence, Israel has still regularly carried out strikes in Gaza.
A total of 1,375 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Hamas said in late July that it was ready to disarm, in what Trump hailed as a breakthrough.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the latest stage of the plan and said there would be no Israeli withdrawal from Gaza until Hamas verifiably decommissions all weapons. AFP

Poland scrambled its aircraft and closed two airports due to Russia's attack on western Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Poland scrambled its military aircraft due to Russia's attack on western Ukraine and closed the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów for several minutes. No threats to the country were detected.
On the morning of September 16, Poland scrambled military aircraft and suspended operations at the airports in Rzeszów and Lublin amid a Russian attack on Ukraine’s western regions. RMF24 reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to Poland’s Operational Command of the Branches of the Armed Forces, military aircraft began operating in the country’s airspace at around 7:00 a.m. Ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems were also placed on alert.
The command noted that these measures were preventive in nature and aimed at ensuring the security of Polish airspace.
Due to the need to ensure freedom of action for military aircraft, operations at the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were temporarily suspended. The restrictions lasted several minutes.
At the same time, Poland’s Government Security Centre (RCB) sent a warning to residents of the Lublin and Subcarpathian voivodeships.
At around 7:30 a.m., it reported that the Russian attack on Ukraine had ended and that there was no threat to Polish territory.

Lithuanian MEP: Europe must stop being afraid to respond – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:15:00 UTC
16:15:00 KST

Russia’s hybrid war against Europe did not begin with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, nor in recent years. The Kremlin intelligence services have been conducting hostile operations across Europe since Vladimir Putin came to power.
For too long, Europe has failed to respond adequately. Some worried that a stronger response would provoke Moscow. But the opposite has happened. The Kremlin interprets hesitation and fear of escalation as weakness, inviting further aggression. Every weak response teaches the Kremlin that it can test the next boundary, create more disruption and chaos inside our societies without facing consequences serious enough to change its behaviour. Putin goes as far as he is allowed to go. Fear of escalation has not prevented escalation: it has further encouraged it.
Europe is a target of Russian hybrid warfare that is becoming increasingly less hybrid. It combines military and non-military tools often designed to remain below the threshold of open armed conflict, including cyber operations, disinformation, economic coercion, sabotage and weaponising migration. The line between hybrid and conventional warfare has blurred. We hear daily about acts of sabotage and sabotage attempts on our infrastructure and drones violating our airspace and even being laden with explosives, like in Leipzig. Around elections, Russian cyberattacks, and disinformation campaigns intensify. GPS jamming and spoofing are everyday occurrences in Europe’s eastern border regions.
Russia remains the primary threat to Europe’s democratic integrity. It targets us through information manipulation and hybrid interference. By deploying hundreds of thousands of fake social media accounts, particularly around elections, it seeks to influence people’s minds, portray Russia as strong and invincible, and amplify narratives and candidates favourable to the Kremlin.
Russia does not act alone: it has partners in authoritarian states such as Belarus, China, Iran and North Korea. Belarus, for example, has weaponised migration at the EU’s borders, with over 36,000 coordinated crossing attempts recorded in 2024. In the Baltic Sea, Chinese-linked vessels have been involved in incidents damaging critical data and electricity cables.
Russia, its allies and its proxies must face real consequences, not just condemnation. We need a common threat picture, stronger tools, greater preparedness, real operational capacity and the will to use them. Any violation of a member state’s sovereignty must be met with effective retaliatory measures.
EU member states have yet to develop a coordinated response to hybrid warfare nationally, at European level and, where relevant, with NATO.
Europe’s eastern flank is its first line of defence, and we need faster implementation of the Eastern Flank Watch, an EU initiative intended to strengthen surveillance and defence along the bloc’s borders with Russia and Belarus.
We must also introduce tougher rules for Russian passport holders entering the EU. The minimum is to ban entry for anyone serving in Russian security and intelligence organisations, including former members who have fought in Ukraine.
The EU must use its economic and diplomatic power to stop the de facto Russian fleet from operating and bypassing sanctions. The owners and operators of these ships must be penalised. Furthermore, the consequences for damaging critical underwater infrastructure (CUI) must be significantly increased to serve as an effective deterrent.
We need better intelligence-sharing, more resources to counter disinformation and stronger protection of our critical infrastructure. But most of all we need sanctions that hit Russia’s economy at the heart.
Since the beginning of Russia’s attack on Ukraine, the EPP Group demanded decisive sanctions, but the Council’s step-by-step approach was slow, and the Russian economy had time to adapt. Kremlin propaganda claims sanctions do not work. This is false. Sanctions do work but require stronger enforcement and bolder measures.
In July, EU adopted 21st package of sanctions against Russia. By the end of the year, Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) will be banned from the EU and pipeline gas imports will be phased out by 30 September 2027. The European parliament strengthened the European Commission’s initial proposal towards a ban on oil and its products, ending long-term contracts sooner than originally proposed.
These are welcome decisions, but more must be done. The European Parliament’s proposals are set out in the report that the plenary adopted on 16 September. Europe can be strong if it wants to. But this resolve is challenged by a huge, lying Russian propaganda machinery.
European leaders must stop fearing the measures needed to defend our security. Today, Ukraine is an example of the will to defend and to win. So are Moldova and Armenia, which have faced massive hybrid attacks using every tool in Moscow’s arsenal, and whose leaders and people have nevertheless stood firm.
Rasa Juknevičienė is an MEP from Lithuania, EP rapporteur on Hybrid warfare

4 Years Since the Discovery of the Izyum Mass Graves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:14:00 UTC
16:14:00 KST

The stink of corpses being exhumed from the pine forest north of Izyum wasn’t particularly strong, but it was everywhere. It smelled somehow a little of skunk, but without the orange overtones. Mostly, it was a faintly sweet smell of decay that lingered in the air.
The woods where Kremlin occupation forces and police buried Ukrainian civilians who died or were murdered in custody during Russia’s eight-month occupation of Izyum are second-growth and cultivated. The trees are straight, their trunks about the thickness of a human arm or leg. The ground is brown sand, soil considered all but useless for farming by Ukrainian standards. Trails used by picknickers, children, and mushroom pickers crisscross the forest. There’s not much underbrush, making it easy to move through the trees in almost any direction.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The graves dug into the floor of the Izyum forest, from which 449 sets of human remains were ultimately recovered, are not arranged in neat rows. Instead they are scattered seemingly at random. Most of the burial sites appear to have been chosen where the trees stood far enough apart to allow a body-sized grave to be squeezed between the pines. Severed roots line the edge of nearly every grave. Some of the dead were laid on their backs, like in a proper cemetery. Others were buried curled into a fetal position. The ground above the graves is lumpy and hillocked, likely because there was neither the space nor the energy to spread the soil evenly. As a result, walking through this part of the forest is not so easy.
Zelensky Says Putin Wants All of Ukraine, Rejects ‘Win-Win’ Peace Concept
Just to the south of the forest is a residential development of individual family homes. Residences are fairly wealthy by eastern Ukrainian standards, including stonework, modern windows, new power transmission lines, and concrete roads. There’s even a bus stop. The graves are about 150 meters (492 feet) away from the nearest houses. People living in the neighborhood (called Pisky due to the sandy soil), during occupation said that the Russians drove into the woods at night, where lights were sometimes seen through the trees, and the noise of vehicles and men moving around in the woods was audible at all hours.
During the occupation, Russian martial law allowed soldiers to kill any civilian during dark hours without warning. So in Pisky village, residents stayed inside. The burials continued night after night, unseen by most non-Russian witnesses.
But, as the Izyum occupation was still in progress, an academic group called the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL) compiled multi-temporal satellite imagery that confirmed about 55,000 square meters (592,015 square feet) of ground in the forest had been excavated between April 5-July 1, 2022.
At least 2 military excavator vehicles and more than 40 military vehicles had been present during the digging, with the layout of the pits closely resembling mass graves, according to researchers.
Later investigations by Ukrainian police found that Russian forces occupying Izyum moved quickly to suppress potential civilian resistance, identifying and detaining residents they believed remained loyal to the Ukrainian government. Occupation authorities initially targeted former Ukrainian service members, government officials, business owners, and professionals, groups the Russians considered most likely to oppose the invasion and subsequent occupation. Thousands of people were taken into custody during the months Russian forces controlled the city. The least fortunate were subjected to violent interrogations and torture. Some died, likely by accident. Others were deliberately murdered.
During the exhumations, workers placed decomposed bodies into white body bags for later examination and identification. A mobile DNA collection laboratory was even set up on site. Forensic investigations conducted over the following six months by Ukrainian and international coroners and investigators concluded that Russian police and military security personnel had committed war crimes, and possibly mass murder, against Izyum’s civilian population. However, the full scale of the crimes remained unclear.
The final count showed that between 414-425 sets of human remains were exhumed from graves in the woods north of Izyum, including about 215 women, 194 men, and five children. A total of 22 were identified as Ukrainian service members, while the rest were civilians.
Most of the remains showed signs of torture or violent death. Around 30 victims had ropes around their necks, bound hands, broken limbs, or gunshot wounds. An unspecified number of male victims had been mutilated, including cases in which the genitals had been removed. Other bodies bore signs of death caused by shelling or airstrikes. While these deaths occurred during Russia’s occupation of the area, they provided less direct evidence of war crimes, mass murder, or the abuse of civilians in occupied territory than cases involving torture, execution-style killings, or other forms of military abuse.
Identified torture victims included Izyum businessman Oleh Salyha. According to his family, Russian police abducted him from a city street, and they never saw him alive again. His remains showed signs of torture with both sharp and blunt instruments before being executed by gunshot.
During the exhumations, even with journalists present, the woods north of Izyum were almost silent. A shovel crunching into soil was audible dozens of meters away. The loudest sound was the DNA lab’s generator. The scuffling step of men carrying another corpse out of the forest was heard, with cameras clicking or whirring in the background.
Four years after paratroopers from Ukraine’s 25th Airborne Brigade and infantrymen from the 80th Air Assault Brigade entered Izyum and first heard residents’ accounts of torture and killings carried out by Russian forces, Ukrainian prosecutors have identified 11 Russian servicemen and two Ukrainian nationals loyal to Russia as complicit in the arrests and murders. The case went to trial in June 2026, with all defendants being tried in absentia.
A separate case involving three Russian servicemen accused of torturing and killing two civilians in Izyum resulted in convictions in July 2026. All three received 15-year prison sentences, though prosecutors are appealing for life imprisonment. Two senior occupation officials, Russian Army Colonels Ahmed Duduyev and Sergey Safonov, remain on Ukrainian and international wanted lists.
In March 2025, the US government terminated funding for the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL). White House officials said the decision reflected concerns that Yale University’s leadership was overly left-leaning and therefore undeserving of federal support. HRL subsequently transferred data collected on Izyum to other institutions and has continued its Ukraine-related research on a reduced scale.
FULL DISCLOSURE: Korshak studied at Yale, however, decades before the HRL’s 2021 founding. He reported from the mass burial site in Izyum on Sept. 23, 2022 and is an eyewitness to the last remains’ removal.

Ukraine govt approves 2027 budget draft: revenue up 8.7%, spending up 13.5%
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
10:13:07 EEST
16:13:07 KST

Ukraine's Cabinet of Ministers has approved a draft law "On the State Budget for 2027," prepared by the Ministry of Finance, which provides for state budget revenues next year of UAH 5.65 trillion, UAH 452.1 billion, or 8.7%, more than the 2026 plan as amended.
Total expenditures will amount to UAH 7.27 trillion, UAH 864.9 billion, or 13.5%, above the current year's figure, according to a statement on the Finance Ministry's website.
According to the statement, the need for international support in 2027 is estimated at $52.6 billion.
The main priority of the draft remains the security and defense sector, to which almost UAH 4.89 trillion (43.8% of GDP) is proposed to be allocated, UAH 517.9 billion more than under the 2026 plan. In particular, UAH 1.79 trillion is earmarked for payroll and related charges (UAH 337.5 billion more than in 2026), almost UAH 2.3 trillion for weapons and military equipment (UAH 1.4 billion more than in 2026), UAH 264.9 billion for a reserve fund (UAH 51.3 billion more), as well as UAH 30 billion for state guarantees for weapons and equipment. Another almost UAH 500 billion is earmarked for other sector expenditures (UAH 127.7 billion more than in 2026).
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky also said on Telegram that there are plans to additionally raise at least UAH 1 trillion from partners next year for these needs.
"We expect this to be at least UAH 1 trillion, and that is even more than this year. However, I want to emphasize that the needs of the defense forces for 2027 are significantly higher. The cost of the war is rising. We are working to complete the precise calculations," he wrote.
As the Finance Ministry said, the 2027 budget also substantially increases funding for the social sector, education, health care, veterans policy and support for the economy. In particular, education spending will increase by UAH 58.8 billion to UAH 328.5 billion, which will make it possible to ensure an average monthly salary of UAH 27,300 for an experienced teacher (65% more than in 2026), as well as to finance meals for all students in grades 1 through 11.
Health care will receive UAH 292.5 billion; in particular, thanks to the expansion of the medical guarantees program, the average salary of a specialized-care physician will be at least UAH 30,000.
According to the press release, UAH 540.3 billion is earmarked for social payments and measures of the Ministry of Social Policy (UAH 72.6 billion more than in 2026). Of this amount, UAH 292.8 billion is a transfer to the Pension Fund to pay pension supplements (UAH 41.5 billion more than in 2026), UAH 66.4 billion is for support for people with disabilities and their social integration and prosthetics (UAH 31.9 billion more than this year), UAH 51.9 billion is for increased benefits for children with disabilities and persons with disabilities (UAH 28.3 billion more than provided for in 2026), UAH 11.5 billion is for providing assistive rehabilitation devices and high-functionality prosthetics (UAH 3.6 billion more), and UAH 4 billion is for providing nationwide social services (UAH 2 billion more than this year).
As for expenditures of social funds, the state budget provides for UAH 1.3 trillion (UAH 218.2 billion more than in 2026), including UAH 1.28 trillion (+UAH 213 billion) for Pension Fund expenditures, UAH 31.6 billion for the Unemployment Fund (UAH 5.3 billion above the 2026 figure), and another UAH 1 billion for the State Social Protection Fund for Persons with Disabilities, the Finance Ministry said.
According to the ministry, support for the economy and business will amount to UAH 96 billion (UAH 11.4 billion, or 13.5%, more than in 2026), including UAH 45 billion earmarked for the eOselia program (UAH 12 billion more), UAH 29 billion for the Affordable Loans 5-7-9% program (UAH 1 billion more), and UAH 10.1 billion for the Innovation Development Fund, including Brave1 defense technologies and robotics (UAH 2.1 billion more than in 2026).
UAH 58.7 billion has been reserved for insuring businesses against war risks (UAH 18.7 billion more than in 2026), with the source of revenue being an increase in value-added tax.
The draft also provides for UAH 7.4 billion to support agricultural producers. Another UAH 116 billion is planned to be allocated to state investment projects and programs.
In addition, the draft provides for the partial (25%) restoration of the State Road Fund in the amount of UAH 52.8 billion, as well as the allocation of UAH 18.2 billion to compensate for tariff differences to support regions and public utilities (UAH 2.2 billion, or 13.8%, more than the UAH 16 billion provided for in 2026). The total volume of local budgets in 2027 will amount to UAH 1 trillion 34.5 billion (UAH 84.5 billion, or 8.9%, more than UAH 950 billion in 2026).

Palestinians in West Bank waive more than $20 million in debts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:12:51 UTC
16:12:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinians in occupied West Bank waive more than $20 million in personal debts
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are struggling under mounting financial pressure, with debt has become a growing source of anxiety, particularly as incomes shrink and economic uncertainty deepens amid Israeli restrictions and abuses.
Against this backdrop, some Palestinians have chosen to ease the burden on those struggling by giving up money owed to them.
The trend followed an individual initiative launched by Palestinian journalist and community activist Alaa al-Rimawi, who called on creditors to forgive debts owed by people unable to repay them.
Speaking to The New Arab, al-Rimawi said he came up with the idea after learning about a Palestinian teacher struggling with debt. He contacted the creditor, who agreed to forgive the amount owed.
Dubbed "Forgive for the Sake of God", the initiative is not backed by a charity, political organisation or institution.
What began as a personal intervention developed after al-Rimawi began sharing stories of debt forgiveness on social media, prompting people across the occupied West Bank to contact him about debts they had waived and outstanding cheques they had cancelled.
"The idea began with the desire to lift people's spirits and ease their burdens," al-Rimawi remarked. "We found that there were people burdened by debt they could not repay, while, on the other hand, there were creditors willing to forgive."
The cases reported to and documented by al-Rimawi now involve more than 65 million shekels (around US$21.7 million) in debts and outstanding cheques that creditors agreed to waive, either fully or partially.
He described the response as unprecedented, particularly because some creditors chose to destroy or "grill" cheques and promissory notes rather than pursue repayment.
"This is the first time in the history of debt forgiveness that we've seen 'grilling cheques'," he said. "We are used to grilling meat, but grilling cheques and promissory notes is a first."
For some creditors, al-Rimawi noted, the value of relieving another person's financial distress had come to outweigh the money they were owed.
"Paper money has lost its significance in Palestine; benefactors and creditors are now donating it, viewing it as nothing compared to the value of relieving someone's distress," he said.
"We want to reach a point where we can say this people is unparalleled in its capacity for forgiveness," he added.
Forgiveness over repayment
Among those taking part is Abu Sobhi, a livestock merchant from Hebron. He decided to waive more than 50,000 shekels (US$16,700) owed to him by several people.
"My decision was not because I did not need the money. I have my own obligations, but I recognised that some debtors simply could not afford to repay," he told TNA. "The economic hardship has affected virtually every section of Palestinian society."
"Merchants themselves are under pressure, workers have lost their sources of income, and employees do not always receive their full salaries. Ultimately, everyone is affected; I felt that if I could lift even a portion of this burden from someone, it was the right thing to do," he added.
In Ramallah, Salama, the owner of a shop selling educational supplies similarly waived more than 25,000 shekels (US$8,300) in outstanding debts.
He told TNA that "debt creates a psychological burden alongside its financial consequences."
"Debt weighs on a person not only financially but also psychologically," he said. "There are people who lie awake at night worrying about how to settle their debts; some have lost their income or struggle to provide for their families' needs."
"I told myself I could afford to forgo this amount. While it might represent a financial loss for me, for the debtor, it could mean relief from the immense pressure that haunts them daily," he added.
He stressed that debt forgiveness should not be viewed as an obligation for every creditor, but rather as an option for those who can afford it.
"Everyone knows their own means and circumstances," he said. "I am not saying everyone must waive what is owed to them, but those who can should not hesitate to do so."
Burden lifted
For some debtors, the decision to forgive has brought relief they had not expected.
In Nablus, Abu Mohammed learned that a clothing merchant had decided to forgive the debts of everyone who owed him money. He was among them.
"I was surprised to learn that the merchant had announced the forgiveness of all debts, and upon realising I was among those forgiven, I felt a great sense of relief […] I never expected him to waive his right in such a manner," he told TNA.
The debt had been a constant source of anxiety.
"I was always thinking about how to repay the amount, especially given the current economic conditions," he said. "When a person is in debt and doesn't know where the funds will come from, the matter weighs heavily on their mind constantly."
He said the merchant's decision was particularly meaningful because he knew the money had been legitimately owed.
"I know the money was rightfully his and that he has his own obligations, which is why his decision came as such a surprise to me," Abu Mohammed said. "This act of forgiveness lifted both a financial and a psychological burden from my shoulders."
For him, the initiative illustrates the importance of solidarity at a time when many Palestinians are struggling to meet basic expenses.
"People need one another today. You might not be able to give someone cash, but if you are owed money and choose to forgive the debt, you are helping them immensely," he said.
He argues that cancelling debts will not resolve the occupied West Bank's wider economic crisis, but said it can give struggling families room to recover.
"The problem goes beyond the debt itself; yet, when you absolve someone of a sum they were unable to pay, you give them a chance to get their life back in order anew," he added.
Economic pressure deepens across West Bank
The initiative comes as the West Bank faces a prolonged economic crisis driven by Israeli restrictions, declining employment opportunities and the Palestinian Authority's financial difficulties.
The crisis predates Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, but has intensified since October 2023 as movement restrictions increased and tens of thousands of Palestinian workers were prevented from reaching jobs inside Israel.
Clearance revenues, consisting largely of taxes and customs duties collected by Israel on behalf of the Palestinian Authority, have also been a recurring source of financial pressure. Delays and withholding of portions of the funds have weakened the Authority's ability to meet its salary obligations.
Meanwhile, restrictions on movement and trade have affected merchants and small businesses, while rising living costs have further reduced household purchasing power.
According to Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics data, the West Bank economy contracted by eight per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, while per capita GDP declined by about 9 per cent.
Unemployment also remained high, reaching around 28 per cent in 2025, according to World Bank data, down from approximately 35 per cent at the beginning of the war.

EU-China trade deficit has hit ‘tipping point,’ warns von der Leyen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:12:03 UTC
16:12:03 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivers a speech during the International Space Summit at the Grand Palais in Paris on Sept. 10, 2026. | Aurelien Morissard/AFP via Getty Images
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will use her State of the Union speech on Wednesday to reiterate her warning over the EU’s ballooning trade deficit with China, as Brussels steps up negotiations with Beijing ahead of a key October deadline.
“Our trade deficit with China is now €1 billion euro — a day. It has reached a tipping point,” she was due to tell lawmakers in Strasbourg, according to her prepared remarks obtained in advance by POLITICO.
“Some say the second China shock is looming. But it’s already here. It shows in our communities and factories across our Union. It leads to de-industrialisation in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable,” she said.
Advertisement
“This is why we are engaged in a dialogue with China to rebalance our trade,” von der Leyen added. “But this dialogue must now lead to results. China’s weaker domestic demand means it also needs our European market. So, it is in both our interests to work together to find solutions.”
The Commission president’s speech gave no detail, however, on the actual steps Brussels was prepared to take to protect European industry from what it sees as unfair competition.
Brussels and Beijing are engaged in an intensifying sequence of talks, with the EU's trade chief speaking with his Chinese counterpart on Thursday, and a team of senior trade officials expected in Beijing next week. Brussels is under pressure to deliver results in time for an October summit of EU leaders, including on trade defense instruments against subsidised Chinese exports.
“Let me be clear: we will use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship. Words are good. But deeds are better,“ said the Commission president.

US Congress will investigate Russian oligarch who financed Donald Trump Jr's wedding, says Reuters
Democrats in the US Congress have launched an investigation following reports that a Russian oligarch paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the wedding celebrations of Donald Trump Jr.
Source: European Pravda, citing Reuters
Details: The Democrats' move follows a ProPublica investigation revealing that Umar Kremlev, a wealthy Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association (IBA), paid for Trump Jr's wedding celebrations in the Bahamas in May.
The investigation uncovered that Kremlev may have provided hundreds of thousands of dollars to cover the costs of Trump Jr's wedding.
It also highlighted Kremlev's close ties to the Russian government.
"Why is a Russian oligarch and friend of Vladimir Putin financially supporting the President's son? What does Umar Kremlev expect in return for funding this three-day wedding in the Bahamas?" said Congressman Robert Garcia.
Garcia currently serves as the top Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and would take over as chairman if his party wins control of the House in November's midterm elections.
The US president's son declined to comment, while his wife Bettina stated in an Instagram post on Monday 14 September that Kremlev is a friend who made an "extraordinarily generous wedding gift", emphasising that he paid for two after-parties rather than the wedding itself.
Trump himself, who did not attend his son's wedding, stated that he does not know Kremlev and that the controversy surrounding the wedding is "not a big deal".
Garcia and other leading House Democrats have been preparing investigations into Trump, his family and ethics questions that have arisen since the start of the president's second term in January 2025.
On Tuesday 15 September, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York described the wedding arrangements as "so corrupt, so venal, so endangering our national security".
"You are dealing with a Russian oligarch, not just a cousin who's giving you a gift... sometimes a wedding gift is a bribe from a foreign autocrat," he stressed.
In this context, it is also worth noting that on 7 August, the US Senate passed a Russia sanctions bill by 86 votes in favour. This piece of legislation was co-authored by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham and Democrat Senator Richard Blumenthal.
On 14 September, the bill cleared the House Rules Committee, after which it passed another procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives, paving the way for a floor vote as early as Wednesday.

Hosni Nedim and Ikram Kouachi
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
At least 14 Palestinians, including five children, were killed Wednesday when a residential building housing displaced people that had been damaged during Israel’s genocidal war collapsed in western Gaza City, according to Palestinian sources.
 
A medical source told Anadolu that the bodies of 14 Palestinians, including five children, and 25 injured people were taken to hospitals in Gaza City after the collapse of the Al-Saada building in the city's Al-Sinaa area.
 
Palestinian Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said during a news conference at the scene that the building had previously been targeted by Israeli bombardment during the war before collapsing early Wednesday.
 
Bassal said around 100 people remained missing under the rubble.
 
He warned that around 2,000 damaged buildings at risk of collapse remain occupied by residents and displaced Palestinians across the Gaza Strip.
 
Bassal called on the international community to provide the equipment and machinery needed to enable rescue teams to recover those missing.
 
Gaza Mayor Yahya al-Sarraj said during the news conference that the building's collapse “warns of the danger of more damaged residential buildings collapsing.”
 
He stressed the need to allow mobile homes to enter Gaza before winter to provide alternatives for residents and displaced people.
 
In remarks to Anadolu, Gaza Municipality spokesman Hosni Muhanna said that displaced families had been living inside the collapsed building after fleeing the harsh conditions in tent camps.
 
He also warned of the risk of further collapses of damaged and cracked residential buildings across Gaza, calling for the urgent entry of heavy and specialized equipment needed for rescue operations and rubble removal.
 
Anadolu's correspondent reported that official institutions in Gaza had resorted to using equipment from private-sector companies due to shortages of heavy machinery and equipment.
 
According to the latest figures from Gaza’s Health Ministry, 1,375 Palestinians have been killed and 4,686 injured in Israeli attacks since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025.
 
The figures bring the Palestinian death toll from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, to nearly 74,000, with more than 174,000 others injured, according to the Health Ministry.

Iranian missile and drone attacks caused widespread damage to US military positions across the Middle East, including buildings, vehicles and aircraft, according to newly obtained photographs reported by CBS News on Tuesday.
The images, provided to CBS News by active-duty service members on condition of anonymity because of military media restrictions, show damage at several US positions in the region.
“This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public,” one deployed service member told the network. “We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”
At Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, one photograph shows what CBS News described as a direct hit on the rear section of a Boeing E-3 Sentry aircraft, with its tail severed from its charred fuselage.
Other images from the base show heavily damaged buildings and barracks alongside concrete “T-wall” barriers, which are designed primarily to provide protection against threats such as grenades and mortar fire.
‘We're just watching them’
Photos from Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a major staging area for US Army personnel, armoured vehicles and some aircraft, also showed extensive damage, according to the report.
The images emerged as the US defence department's inspector general released a report estimating equipment losses from the war on Iran at up to $3.7 billion, including nearly 60 aircraft.
In a mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general said US Central Command reported Iranian strikes on US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon did not respond to CBS News' request for comment.
“These are not ‘squirters’ getting through,” the service member said, referring to terminology used by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a March 1 attack on Kuwait's Port of Shuaiba that killed six US troops.
“We're not defending these bases. We're just watching them get destroyed,” the service member reportedly added.

Rail sabotage: farm activists suspected as police investigate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:10:30 UTC
16:10:30 KST

Rail sabotage: farm activists suspected as police investigate
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Police and the security service AIVD are investigating the widespread sabotage on train tracks throughout the centre and east of the Netherlands on Tuesday, which brought train services to a standstill for much of the day, amid reports that radical farmers’ protest groups were responsible.
Further disruptions on Tuesday evening continued after certain tracks, that had already been cleared, were again targeted, according to infrastructure company ProRail.
Sources told broadcaster NOS they had seen farmer groups discussing taking direct action on Prinsjesdag, including by fixing metal pipes to train lines. Doing this fools the system into thinking a train is already on the track and turns signals red.
A photo of a pipe fixed to a rail also circulated in online farmers’ groups, although it is not clear who took it or where, NOS reported. No arrests have been made and no group has claimed responsibility so far.
Justice minister David van Weel pledged to catch the culprits on Wednesday morning.
Farmers’ organisations have condemned the actions and said they had nothing to do with it. The Farmers Defence Force, responsible for recent motorway disruptions, said it was not responsible but that “wild actions” by individual farmers were expected on budget day in reaction to the government plans on nitrogen and livestock numbers.
Farming lobby LTO Nederland said the actions crossed a line. “Sabotage has nothing to do with the right to protest,” a spokesman told NOS. “Whoever is behind this should ask themselves seriously what interest is served by it.”
Farm protesters also set hay bales, tyres and pallets alight beside motorways including the A2 and A28, and police arrested 7 people near Breukelen. It is not known whether the same people were involved in the rail sabotage.
Police and intelligence officials have not yet commented on who they suspect is behind the actions, but sources did confirm to NOS that farmer protest groups were one scenario being considered.
Prime minister Rob Jetten said what happened went beyond all limits and created dangerous situations.
The disruptions coincided with Prinsjesdag, the state opening of parliament in the The Hague and the annual budget announcements.
Bart Schuurman, professor of terrorism and political violence at Leiden University, told NOS he expects public prosecutors to pursue serious charges. Deliberately endangering rail traffic carries a maximum sentence of 15 years, and potentially more if a court finds a terrorist motive. “Even if they were not consciously out to kill or injure anyone, they took the risk that trains would derail or collide,” he said.

Former Kosovo president Thaçi sentenced to 25 years in prison

Thaçi had denied all charges.

Back to Thaçi’s sentencing in The Hague, here is our senior international correspondent Peter Baumont’s take on today’s events.
“Known by the nom de guerre of Commander Snake during the war, Thaçi stood out among the KLA leadership as an intelligent and articulate figure who would later charm diplomats – most notably the US secretary of state Madeleine Albright – at the negotiations in Rambouillet that ended the conflict.
But behind the self-assured image he projected as a senior political figure, he was long dogged by allegations of a darker and more ruthless side from his time as a wartime commander.
Thaçi’s defence partly rested on the notion that while serious abuses did occur, the KLA was a not a strictly centralised organisation, claiming that Thaçi’s senior position in the rebel group did not indicate culpability for crimes committed by local units.
“Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaçi told judges in February.
The trial was opposed by many in Kosovo. Outside the court, Kosovo foreign minister, Glauk Konjufca, told the media: “A terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war. It is a sad, unjust, undeserved decision.”

These convictions give hope to thousands of victims of the Kosovo war who have waited for more than two decades to get justice for the horrific crimes committed against them and to know the fate of their loved ones.

Thaçi and co-defendants 'criminally responsible' for war crimes of detention, cruel treatment, torture, murder, ruling says
We are now getting a bit more on the findings against Thaçi and his three co-defendants.
Here is from the Kosovo Specialist Chambers & Specialist Prosecutor’s Office:
“The Trial Panel found that all four Accused were criminally responsible for the war crimes of arbitrary detention against 385 individuals,cruel treatment against 49 individuals, torture against 303 individuals, and murder against 96 individuals.
The Trial Panel found the accused not guilty of crimes against humanity because the Specialist Prosecutor failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that there was a widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population. The accused were also found not guilty in connection with a number of specific incidents of war crimes.
The judges found that during the Kosovo conflict Mr. Thaçi, Mr. Veseli, Mr. Selimi and Mr. Krasniqi contributed significantly to the common criminal purpose of targeting perceived opponents of the Kosovo Liberation Army’s political and military goals, including Kosovo Albanians associated with other political or military forces, like the LDK and FARK; individuals alleged to be associated with the FRY/Serbian authorities; and certain members of ethnic minorities, including a number of Roma and Serbs.
The targeting of such opponents took the form of killings; arrests and detention without due process; physical and psychological mistreatment; as well as other forms of abuse, intimidation and harassment.
With limited exceptions, the Trial Panel found no evidence that any of the victims had engaged in any criminal activity, taken an active part in hostilities or presented any other legitimate security concern for the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA).”
And here is a bit more detail on Thaçi himself:
“In the case of Hashim Thaçi, the Trial Panel found that as a member of the General Staff of the KLA and in his capacity as the head of the Political Directorate, he was a key member in formulating and implementing the common purpose that entailed setting up detention facilities; identifying individuals perceived as opposing the KLA; arresting and detaining them; and, if necessary, killing them.
This included the targeting of alleged “collaborators”, the setting up of a structure, competent bodies and regulations to do so, and the deployment of “special warfare” against Opponents, including through the publication of communiques and political declarations and other public statements expressing tolerance and encouragement for the commission of crimes against opponents.
The Trial Panel further found that Hashim Thaçi also personally participated in crimes, including the arrest, arbitrary detention and interrogation of 13 parliamentarians and the arrest, detention, transfer and murder of Behajdin Allaqi.
He further disseminated false information about detainees and victims of the crimes committed by KLA members, gave false assurances of compliance with international humanitarian law on behalf of the KLA, and contributed to a policy of impunity in respect of perpetrators of crimes against opponents.”

'Current system is reaching its end,' NR's Bardella says in response to von der Leyen
The European parliament is still discussing von der Leyen’s address.
In sharp contrast with von der Leyen’s comments, the far-right National Rally president Jordan Bardella criticised her for constantly “glorifying what you have done,” while, in fact, “the [current] system is reaching an end.”
“We have the Europe of those who write the rules; the bureaucrats who write waste public money and make up taxes for tomorrow … and then there’s the Europe that has to pay, the second Europe: those who have to pay €2.5 for a litre of petrol … they have to pay for heating, they have to pay increasing bills.

“Let’s look at the world around us: the war in Ukraine, war in the Middle East, Islamist terrorism, food insecurity, energy insecurity. The US is investing, China is investing, and we continue to regulate even more.
We’re regulating things that we no longer produce. We’re taxing things that we no longer know how to make. And we’re also taxing things that we’ve banned the production of in Europe. That is the major paradox in Europe. And that’s why we need to change.”
He called that “when the money is European, the jobs need to be in Europe; when the money is French, the jobs need to be in France” and urged the commission to “get ride of red tape, these absurd and useless rules.”
I’m bringing you these quotes as Bardella’s National Rally could find itself in a very strong position in France after next year’s presidential election, with Marine Le Pen leading in the polls.

He is scheduled to speak 11:30 local time (10:30 UK) tomorrow.
Von der Leyen's offer to Canada 'cannot be overestimated in political and trade significance' - snap analysis
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
Ursula von der Leyen’s dramatic offer to open the gate to Canada to become the EU’s first ever associate member (9:54) cannot be overestimated in political and trade significance.
It, at once, aligns what Canadian prime minister Mark Carney called the “middle powers” in his Davos speech in January but creates an opening for a speedy enhanced trade deal particularly on critical raw materials and rare earths.
It also sets Canada apart from the UK which could, once upon a time, have some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean break Brexit.
Two points of realpolitik make it possible that the long winding road that typifies third country’s relationships with the EU could turn into a high speed motorway.
Canada has something the EU desperately needs: rich supplies of CRM and rare earths in a bid to diversify from China which has a stranglehold on both.
And Europe has something Canada urgently wants: new market for products it can no longer sell into the US in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.
Looking at the bigger picture a new enhanced trade deal between the EU and Canada could leave the UK somewhat scrambling in a two speed race.
Keir Starmer talked about forging a CRM and rare earths deal with Canada but it never materialised.
If political energy in Brussels is now focused on Canada that could be bad news for Andy Burnham.

Revolut applies for a banking licence in Switzerland

Unknown Publisher

Revolut applies for a banking licence in Switzerland
The British ‘neobank’ Revolut, whose services are already used by over a million Swiss residents, is now applying for a Swiss banking licence.
The online bank plans to invest more than CHF150 million in the Swiss market over the next five years.
The granting of a licence by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) would pave the way for a full range of banking services in Switzerland, Revolut stated in a press release on Wednesday. The application is currently being reviewed by FINMA.
Revolut is already regarded as the largest “neobank” in Switzerland. According to its own figures, it already has 1.3 million customers in the country. In the 2025 financial year alone, the customer base grew by around 240,000 people. This means the British fintech company significantly outstrips its nearest competitors in Switzerland – the finance app Yuh has around 400,000 customers and Neon around 250,000.
Despite its expanded range of services, many Swiss residents still primarily use Revolut as a low-cost “travel payment app”. With a Swiss banking licence, Revolut now aims to offer local customers “full-featured” salary accounts with Swiss IBAN numbers and Swiss deposit protection. The future range of services is also set to include payment processing for merchants, whilst pension pillar 3a products and a Twint service are currently under review.
More
Are neobanks the answer for the Swiss Abroad?
Revolut plans to invest more than CHF150 million in setting up the Swiss bank and expanding its presence in the local market. The funds are to be channelled into the development of new products as well as the creation of local jobs. In addition, there will be expansion at board and management level, it is reported. The neobank already employs around 30 staff in Zurich; this figure is likely to rise significantly once it secures a banking licence.
The London-based fintech company is now one of Europe’s largest banks, with over 80 million customers, and is experiencing rapid growth. The company already holds banking licences in the UK, Lithuania and France. In the US, Revolut recently received conditional authorisation from the OCC, the banking regulator.

US used dozens of interceptors against Iranian attack on Jordan: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:06:45 UTC
16:06:45 KST

The US military fired as many as 70 Patriot interceptors and more than a dozen THAAD missiles to counter a recent Iranian ballistic missile attack on Jordan, highlighting growing pressure on Washington’s air-defence arsenal, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.
US forces used between 60 and 70 Patriot interceptors against an Iranian barrage involving about 20 ballistic missiles, while more than a dozen Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors were also launched, according to US and regional officials cited by the Journal.
The expenditure was roughly equivalent to the number of interceptors US forces had used over an entire week at other points in the conflict, the report said.
Iranian missiles reportedly used warheads that separated into multiple projectiles as they approached their targets, making them more difficult to intercept.
Some missiles also reached Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, damaging fighter jets and other aircraft, although no US personnel were killed in the latest attack, according to the Journal.
Iran adapts missile tactics
US officials told the Journal that Iranian attacks have become increasingly sophisticated, combining different missile types, trajectories, maneuvers and warhead designs in attempts to penetrate American defences.
The latest attack adds to the heavy use of US missile defences during the conflict.
By mid-July, US forces had fired about 1,700 Patriot and more than 200 THAAD interceptors, while US Navy ships had launched roughly 150 Standard Missile interceptors against Iranian missiles and drones, according to officials cited by the Journal.
The high expenditure has raised concerns about Washington's ability to replenish stocks quickly, as well as its capacity to respond to potential threats in other regions, including Europe and the Indo-Pacific.
The Defense Department's inspector general has also warned of “strategic inventory shortfalls” and bottlenecks in the US industrial base that could hinder munitions resupply.
Pentagon rejects shortage claims
The Pentagon has rejected suggestions that US interceptor stocks are depleted.
“Reports suggesting that the United States’ munitions are depleted are completely false,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said, adding that the US military remains capable of responding to threats.
President Donald Trump has likewise said the US maintains large stocks of interceptors and is increasing production.
Lockheed Martin, which manufactures Patriot interceptors, produced 620 in 2025 and is seeking to raise annual production to about 2,000, according to the Journal.
Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command, also said separately that he was not concerned about interceptor shortages and that American forces remained prepared for potential contingencies.
The pressure is nevertheless being felt across the region.
Gulf states have sought additional air-defence munitions following months of Iranian missile and drone attacks, while the demand for interceptors has also affected the availability of systems for Ukraine as it defends against Russian strikes.

Danish companies using AI are hiring fewer young and highly educated workers, analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:05:33 UTC
16:05:33 KST

Danish companies that adopt artificial intelligence tend to hire fewer new employees afterward, with younger and highly educated workers seeing the biggest impact, according to a new analysis from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank.
The analysis found that employment grows more slowly at companies that use AI compared with similar companies that do not.
However, there are so far no signs that the growing use of AI has reduced overall employment in Denmark.
Signe Krogstrup, a director at Danmarks Nationalbank, said this could mean that people who are no longer hired by companies using AI are finding jobs elsewhere in the labor market.
“In Denmark, we have a flexible labor market and widespread digitalization, and that puts us in a good position to benefit from AI,” she said in a press release.
The analysis also found no signs that increased use of artificial intelligence has affected wages.
Concern over junior jobs
Djøf, a Danish trade union and professional association, said the effect on younger and highly educated workers should be taken seriously.
“Employers must be careful not to saw off the branch they are sitting on. In the short term, it may look attractive to cut junior positions when AI can perform more tasks,” Djøf Chair Sara Vergo said in a written comment.
“But tomorrow’s experienced specialists and managers can only emerge if companies hire, train and give responsibility to recent graduates today.”
AI use is particularly high in the real estate and rental sector and in information and communication, according to the analysis.
Krogstrup said it remains unclear how the technology will affect employment in Denmark in the longer term.
“It cannot be ruled out that employment could fall in the longer term, but on the other hand, it could also be that AI supports the creation of new companies and job functions to such an extent that employment actually increases,” she said.
Danish companies among heavy AI users
The analysis combined Statistics Denmark data on companies’ use of AI with information including employment and wages.
This allowed researchers to identify patterns at the individual company level, something Danmarks Nationalbank said had not previously been possible to the same extent in Denmark or abroad.
The analysis also found that Danish companies have adopted AI widely.
The technology is used particularly by the largest companies, while Danish businesses use AI more than companies in many other European countries.

====================================================================================================

Court rules in favor of local residents in Nursipalu Training Area expansion dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

Court rules in favor of local residents in Nursipalu Training Area expansion dispute
Tallinn Administrative Court upheld complaints filed by nonprofit organizations and local residents seeking to annul government orders expanding the Estonian Defense Forces' Nursipalu training area.
The court emphasized that annulling the orders does not mean that expanding the Nursipalu Training Area is impermissible in principle. The court had no doubts about the state's threat assessment, the resulting need to expand the training area or the legality of the choice of location. However, it found flaws in both orders.
The court found it unlawful that the 2023 order made a decision in principle to expand the training area at a time when the state did not have sufficient information to make an informed decision that took into account the impact on both the natural environment and local residents' living environment.
The environmental impact of the project had been described only superficially, no noise study had been conducted and only a preliminary Natura assessment had been carried out. Moreover, some potential impacts had been unlawfully excluded from that assessment.
Regarding the later order, the court identified shortcomings in two areas. First, some impacts on Natura 2000 sites near the training area had still not been assessed by 2024.
The Natura assessment is inadequate with regard to the impact on more sensitive bird species that are among the conservation objectives of the Karula Special Protection Area, as well as the impact on the Kubija Lake Special Area of Conservation.
Second, no effective environmental measures have been established to mitigate noise disturbance for residents living around the training area. According to the court, the state had acknowledged that, particularly during large-scale exercises, noise levels at the nearest homes exceed recommended limits for military noise. However, the court found that the mitigation measures introduced were general in nature and did not include specific restrictions or safeguards.
The Administrative Court found that the measures should either ensure compliance with noise limits at all homes or, alternatively, provide local residents who would be exposed to noise exceeding the limits with an effective means of avoiding such exposure. "It should also be kept in mind that the noise assessment was based on the assumption that there would be no firing at night, but in practice that assumption has proved incorrect. Nighttime noise limits are lower than daytime limits," the court said.
The court explained that activities with a significant environmental impact must be tolerated when they are necessary for reasons of overriding public interest, there is no reasonable alternative and the necessary measures have been taken to reduce their impact. However, before such a decision can be made, the impacts must first be identified and effective mitigation measures must also be developed.
If the shortcomings identified by the court are remedied, the state may be able to issue a new order that is largely the same in substance, with the necessary additions.
The court dismissed some of the complainants' claims because they lacked standing. Most were individuals who lived more than 10 kilometers from the expanded training area. One company also filed a complaint, but the court found that the interference with its freedom to conduct business was not sufficient to give it standing.
The ruling has not yet entered into force. It may be appealed to Tallinn Circuit Court within 30 days.
