Heating tariffs in Latvia could be on average 5–15% higher this heating season than during the previous one, Climate and Energy Minister Jānis Vitenbergs (NA) said in an interview with TV3’s programme “900 sekundes” on Wednesday.
“For most companies, the increase will be moderate,” Vitenbergs said.

As previously reported by LETA, the Ministry of Climate and Energy (KEM) plans to propose increasing the housing benefit and expanding the number of households eligible for it during the upcoming heating season, while also maintaining monthly support for protected electricity users.
For the upcoming heating season,
the ministry proposes expanding the range of support recipients to include low-income families,
families with children and senior citizens. KEM proposes allocating ten million euros for this purpose.
KEM also proposes increasing the coefficients used to calculate housing benefits during the heating season. This would increase support for existing recipients while allowing a wider range of households to qualify for the benefit.
At the same time, the ministry proposes increasing the state’s co-financing share for municipalities to 50%, thereby reducing the additional burden on municipal budgets.
Around 31,000 households currently receive housing benefits. Together with the Ministry of Welfare, a proposal has therefore been prepared to expand the scheme, reserving up to ten million euros for this purpose.
The proposed changes are expected to allow an additional 28,000 to 38,000 households to qualify for support
and increase assistance by 40 to 70 euros per month per household member.

This would allow various groups of households to continue receiving the existing monthly discount of 20 to 25 euros on their electricity bills until the end of the year.
KEM stresses that ahead of the 2026/2027 heating season, natural gas reserves are sufficient, while the availability of wood chips and pellets has improved following high demand during the summer. Meanwhile, the average increase in district heating tariffs across Latvia remained below 5% in September.

The 'silent waste' of Greek seas: Thousands of concrete blocks lifted from seabed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:02:08 UTC
16:02:08 KST

Reducing them is the goal of the 'Fishing For Litter' programme, which has recovered more than 6,000 concrete blocks from the seabed since 2019.
More than 6,000 concrete blocks and thousands of synthetic ropes, which are used illegally by traditional Mediterranean fishing vessels and then abandoned at sea, have been recovered from Greek waters in recent years.
Abandoned fishing gear makes up a significant share of the waste that ends up on the seabed. Its removal is at the heart of the Fishing For Litter programme, run by the Athanasios C. Laskaridis Public Benefit Foundation, in partnership with the environmental organisation iSea.
According to iSea's Communications Manager, Anastasia Charitou, since 2019, when the programme began, 6,278 concrete blocks and around 11,700 ropes linked to fishing boat activity have been recovered and recorded.
"The biggest problem is found in the Euboean Gulf, followed by the Thracian Sea and the Thermaic Gulf," says Charitou.
Since 2019, fishers taking part in the programme have removed more than 360 tonnes of waste from deep waters. Over 83 per cent of it is plastic, while 34 per cent consists of abandoned fishing gear.
The programme is continuing this year across Greece, with the participation of 67 fishing vessels and an expanded geographical reach.
How do concrete blocks end up on the seabed?
The problem is linked, among other things, to a practice used during night-time fishing with gri-gri, traditional Mediterranean fishing boats.
After the fish have been located, fish-aggregating light devices known as 'robots' are deployed. These are small floating boats equipped with lamps, which are lowered into the water near the fishing vessel in order to attract and concentrate the shoals.
As iSea notes in its report titled 'The silent waste of fishing – How synthetic ropes and concrete blocks pollute the seas', the fish are attracted by the light source, which simulates moonlight.
To keep the light devices stable, they need to be anchored. The General Port Regulations stipulate that 'robots' must be deployed with appropriate anchors and lifted out of the water once the fishing activity is finished.
In theory, special small anchors are connected to the devices by chains. At the end of the process, the 'lampsman', the crew member who monitors the fish around the lights, gradually hauls in the equipment, steering the shoal towards the main vessel at the same time.
However, according to iSea, because the prescribed procedure is more time-consuming, in some cases it is replaced by an improvised and illegal practice.
Instead of anchors, concrete blocks are used, usually two for each light device, which are attached with polypropylene ropes, the so-called 'gri-gri ropes'.
When the time comes to recover the light devices, the ropes are cut. The 'robots' quickly return to the vessel, but the concrete blocks and severed ropes remain on the seabed.
In this way, a practice that saves time for the crew turns into a permanent source of waste on the sea floor.
Thousands of kilos of solid waste on the seabed
"The concrete blocks are passively fished by the fishers. They get tangled in their nets and are thus removed from great depths. Those that are recovered and recorded in the programme weigh around four to five kilos each," Charitou explains.
On the basis of the 6,278 concrete blocks recorded to date alone, this amounts to dozens of tonnes of solid material that had been abandoned at sea.
The problem, however, is not limited to the volume of waste.
Synthetic ropes and concrete blocks accumulate on the seabed and put pressure on benthic ecosystems, affecting organisms and habitats that are in direct contact with the sea floor.
At the same time, polypropylene ropes, because of their low weight, can hang in the water column and wrap around the propellers of other vessels, causing mechanical damage, as well as entangling marine life and breaking down into toxic microplastics that fish ingest.
Similarly, when concrete blocks get caught in fishing nets, they can damage the equipment and destroy part of the catch.
Impacts on biodiversity and fishing
For iSea, this practice is not simply a matter of marine pollution. Leaving these materials on the seabed harms ecosystems, creates risks for other vessels and adds yet another stress factor in marine areas that are already under pressure from overfishing and the accumulation of waste.
The organisation stresses that tackling the phenomenon requires stricter and more systematic inspections to ensure the existing legislation is applied, as well as the imposition of the penalties provided for.
Among the measures proposed are beefing up on-the-spot checks at sea, and inspections when fishing vessels leave and return to port.
At the same time, according to iSea, a clearer description of the gri-gri fishing gear in legislation is needed, especially with regard to the auxiliary fish-aggregating light devices and their anchoring equipment.
The aim is to fully clarify what constitutes the correct and lawful way of using them, so that a practice which today leaves thousands of "silent waste" items on the seabed can be effectively curbed.

‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa

16:00:14 KST

The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.
When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.
Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.
On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.
“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data.
For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.
However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.
The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”
South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.
“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.
Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”
Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.
Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.
Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.
“When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.
“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”
The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.
Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.
“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.
“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”
Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.
She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

Caught between the US and China, can Switzerland stay neutral in the AI race?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Caught between the US and China, can Switzerland stay neutral in the AI race?
The debate over neutrality is particularly heated in Switzerland ahead of a vote on the issue on September 27. But what does it mean to be neutral in a world where artificial intelligence, cloud services and digital infrastructure increasingly depend on the United States and China?
For more than two centuries, Swiss neutrality has defined Switzerland’s position in armed conflicts. On September 27, Swiss voters will decide whether to enshrine a more restrictive interpretation of neutrality in the Constitution limiting the country’s ability to impose sanctions on belligerent states outside those decided by the United Nations Security Council.
Whatever the outcome of the vote, the question of how to remain neutral in a world in which artificial intelligence (AI) and other strategically important technologies are controlled by two rival powers – the United States and China – is as pressing as ever. This issue is particularly sensitive for Switzerland, which depends heavily on technologies developed by both countries.
“If you are in the middle, you get caught in the crossfire,” says Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy.
Driven by economic competition and geopolitical tensions, the US and China are accelerating the development of increasingly powerful AI systems, even “at the expense of security,” Rickli says. The rise of advanced, autonomous agentic AI models is an example.
“With agents, you have new entities that are potentially able to develop and carry out their own plan, including staging their own attack without human intervention, in order to reach their assigned goal. And this is something completely new,” Rickli says. In this environment, he believes the danger of mistakes or escalation is becoming more tangible.
Maxime Stauffer, co-founder and CEO of the Simon Institute for Longterm Governance, a Geneva-based think tank, believes that advances in frontier AI are changing the cyberspace threat landscape.
“Day to day, various states and non-state actors launch cyberattacks on each other. That’s known and almost routine. But there used to be an equilibrium between offense and defence capabilities, which AI is now disrupting,” he says.
The growing US-China rivalry over AI has even prompted comparisons with a new “Cold War”, although the analogy remains contestedExternal link.
Despite the calls, neither Washington nor BeijingExternal link appears willing to slow down the AI race. “We’re leading China in AI (…) and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” US President Donald Trump said recentlyExternal link. China, for its part, has dismissed calls to slow down the development of AI, calling them “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook”.
Both countries use access to their technology, sanctions and industrial dependencies for geopolitical leverage. In this context, remaining equidistant between Washington and Beijing is becoming “increasingly difficult,” Rickli says, “because you have to choose a side, in order to avoid potential sanctions”.
According to the Swiss State Secretariat for Security Policy (SEPOS), US and Chinese companies’ growing influence over countries’ economic and military capabilities and the conduct of warfare is “jeopardising strategic stability”.
>>Here is everything you need to know about the upcoming neutrality on September 27:
More
How the neutrality initiative could affect Swiss policy
The law of neutrality also applies in cyberspace
Does this mean Swiss neutrality has become irrelevant in the digital world?
From the perspective of international law, the answer is no. “The fact that the law of neutrality was codified before the advent of cyberspace and artificial intelligence does not mean that it does not apply in these areas,” says Marco Roscini, professor of international law at the University of Westminster in London and an expert on neutrality and armed conflict.
Roscini explains that the general rules governing armed conflict – reflected in the United Nations Charter, the Hague Conventions and the Geneva Conventions and Protocols – remain binding regardless of the technology employed. This was established by the International Court of Justice in a 1996 advisory opinionExternal link. What matters, therefore, is how technologies are used as means or methods of warfare.
For Switzerland, this entails both legal protection and obligations. In the event of a war between China and the United States, for example, Bern would have to take feasible measures to stop either side from using cyber infrastructure on Swiss territory to conduct hostilities against the other.
“Cyberspace is not an abstraction. Clouds, cables, satellites, data centres, servers, computers and the people who use them still have a physical location,” Roscini says.
SEPOS notes, however, that the application of international legal norms to new technologies – including in cyberspace and outer space – is in some respects unclear, or that governments prevent such norms from becoming established.
Sovereignty rather than technological neutrality
Much of Switzerland’s technological dilemma, according to the experts interviewed, does not actually concern the law of neutrality. Dependence on US and Chinese software, digital services or AI systems is primarily a question of sovereignty and strategic autonomy.
The law of neutrality, Roscini points out, primarily applies to the state, not private companies. Switzerland has long taken advantage of the absence of general trade restrictions to do business while remaining neutral. During the Second World War, for example, Swiss companies continued trading with belligerent states, especially Nazi Germany, despite the country’s neutral status.
For to Eugenio Benincasa, a senior cybersecurity researcher at the Center for Security Studies of the Swiss federal technology institute ETH Zurich, a similar strategy characterises Switzerland’s relations with China and the United States today. Switzerland maintains substantial economic relations with both, benefiting from each without fully aligning itself with either side. But this technological dependence, while not in itself compromising Swiss neutrality, “limits the country’s room for manoeuvre,” Benincasa says.
The initiative being put to a vote on September 27 could further limit Switzerland’s room for manoeuvre. By severely restricting Bern’s ability to impose sanctions on belligerent states, it could have repercussions for the country’s reputation and economic interests, according to the Swiss governmentExternal link. Switzerland would no longer be able to join numerous sanctions against countries at war, with the exception of those decided by the United Nations Security Council, where the United States, China and Russia each have veto power.
>>Here’s how the Swiss arms industry has capitalised on neutrality:
More
Arms trade: Swiss neutrality as business strategy
To strengthen its digital sovereignty, Benincasa believes Switzerland should seek to reduce dependencies in the most sensitive sectors, such as critical infrastructure, public administration, defence, intelligence and healthcare. And where Swiss alternatives are unavailable, the country should at least rely on European technologies.
In practice, Switzerland already makes different calculations depending on the technology and the supplier, Benincasa says. In the case of Palantir, a US company specialising in data analytics and security technologies, several Swiss public institutions, including the armed forces, have decided against using its software, partly because of concerns over sovereignty and national security. In other sectors, by contrast, Chinese technologies such as Huawei’s cost-competitive telecommunications infrastructure can be particularly difficult to replace.
“Asymmetric assessments are made based on what the two countries can offer,” Benincasa says. “Talking about complete technological independence is a utopia.”
The diplomacy card
There is, however, one area in which Swiss neutrality could be an asset: diplomacy, not least thanks to the presence of intergovernmental organisations based in Geneva. Historically, neutrality has enabled neutral states to help prevent conflicts from escalating and offer good offices, mediation and humanitarian assistance.
Maxime Stauffer of the Simon Institute in Geneva says Switzerland’s status as a neutral state still helps create space for dialogues on AI amid rapid technological developments and geopolitical tensions.
Stauffer mentions possible areas for such dialogue, including maintaining communication channels to reduce the risk of unintended escalation involving autonomous systems and setting boundaries on AI use against critical infrastructure.
The Swiss foreign ministry has not confirmed the existence of any official Swiss mediation between the US and China on artificial intelligence. But if Switzerland’s current approach to neutrality can genuinely help it mitigate the risks of cyberwar between the two technological powers, it may be less outdated than some might think.

From foil to fishing nets: how completely ordinary household items found their role in the war
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
09:59:38 EEST
15:59:38 KST

From foil to fishing nets: how completely ordinary household items found their role in the war
Kyiv • UNN
The military use household items for camouflage, fortifications, and equipment testing. Their availability helps quickly address local needs.
Foil, a bicycle clamp, a fishing net, and an ordinary nut—things that are not usually associated with military technology. However, during wartime, they can acquire a new purpose: helping test equipment, setting up positions, or addressing certain engineering needs. UNN discussed with military experts how completely ordinary household items have become one of the features of modern warfare.
Details
There are things whose purpose seems so obvious that it is difficult to imagine them in another role. Aluminum foil is for baking meat or fish, a fishing net is for fishing, and nuts are for repairs or construction. However, war changes this logic. In a military environment, an item is assessed not so much by what it was created for as by what else can be done with it. In this way, ordinary household items acquire a new purpose—from engineering fortification to use in military development.
Nuts, screws, and bolts for military development
Anton Zemlianyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation, notes that there are actually many examples of ordinary household items being used by the military.
These include ordinary nuts, screws, bolts, and various metal structures, which can be used to equip positions, construct engineering facilities, or in various military developments. An interesting example is fishing nets. Some Northern European countries send Ukraine used fishing nets that are no longer relevant to them. In Ukraine, they can be put to an entirely different use—in particular, for engineering protection and camouflage
According to him, if we look at the issue more broadly, even civilian radio-controlled models were once used for military purposes.
Before the emergence of large ground-based robotic complexes, there were much simpler mechanisms—essentially small remotely controlled machines—that made it possible to perform certain tasks without a person being directly present. Today, ground-based robotic systems can already be used for evacuation, transporting equipment, and carrying out other tasks
Batteries, cells, and small electronics in the military
The list of ordinary items used in military technology is not limited to nuts, screws, and bolts. Particularly many examples of ordinary items being used by the military are related to electronics.
Military expert Mykhailo Zhyrokhov draws attention to this.
Most of the electronics supplied, for example, from China, effectively have a dual purpose. We can talk about rechargeable batteries and batteries—this is probably the most obvious example. The same applies to small electronic components that can be purchased in ordinary stores, including "Aurora," and which could potentially be used for military purposes. However, it is important to understand that the scale is entirely different. If we are talking about the serial production of military equipment, ordinary consumer goods cannot fully replace specialized components
In other words, this does not mean that the defense industry can simply replace all specialized parts with products from the nearest store. It means that available civilian components can meet specific needs where a specialized solution is more complicated, more expensive, or unavailable in the required quantity.
How to use foil in the military
However, sometimes the issue is not only finding an available part for repairs or setting up positions, but also military testing.
Sometimes such adaptation can look particularly unexpected. Anatolii Khrapchynskyi, a defense industry expert and head of a weapons manufacturing company, says that ordinary foil is used to test aerial targets.
For testing aerial targets, for example, and increasing the effective scattering area on our radars, I use food foil or metal plates, attaching them to a drone. Accordingly, the effective scattering area increases, and we can test how the radars operate
According to him, rapid adaptation makes it possible to solve certain problems.
If you look at how much an aviation-grade loop certified to all aviation standards costs, its price starts at £70. So this is also a question of adapting capabilities that allow us to use inexpensive tools to create our own solutions. For example, we used bicycle clamps to attach antennas. In other words, an ordinary bicycle clamp can be used to attach an antenna. There are actually many solutions. The issue is ensuring that equipment is quickly supplied with tools that are available in large quantities. And this is the main problem. Some equipment that can be certified and tested may simply be unavailable in large volumes
The democratization of technology
This is precisely where it becomes clear why availability is sometimes no less important than technological sophistication. If it is difficult to quickly find or order a specialized component in large quantities, an engineer begins looking for an alternative among what is already available on the market. In this sense, an ordinary hardware store, automotive accessories shop, or home-goods store may turn out to be a kind of "catalogue" of potential engineering solutions.
If we are talking about what we can potentially find in an ordinary store such as "Epicentr," it is important to understand that technology is being democratized. Once, powerful computers were needed to calculate a rocket's ballistics or launch a satellite into orbit, and only certain state-owned enterprises, government agencies, or large companies had them. The same thing is now happening with many technologies. FPV drones initially appeared exclusively as a means of entertainment and for air racing. But we turned them into carriers and means of striking targets, and accordingly they became weapons. Therefore, many things we see in everyday life can acquire an entirely different application. From an ordinary loop to a bicycle clamp for attaching an antenna
Expert Anton Zemlianyi added that virtually any civilian product that can be purchased in an ordinary store or on a marketplace could potentially find some military application. However, this does not mean that every such item automatically becomes military technology.
War forces people to look for unconventional solutions using what is available. If we enter a hypothetical "Epicentr" together, we can see a huge number of things that could be useful to the military. These include wires, tools, various materials for equipping positions, and means for constructing fortifications. But it is important to understand that such solutions often arise not because circumstances are favorable. To some extent, this is forced "cottage" or, to put it more mildly, nonstandard production that makes it possible to address specific local needs. At the same time, I would not view this approach exclusively negatively. If some simple civilian component makes it possible to solve a specific military task, it can be a perfectly effective solution. Especially if it is inexpensive, available, and does not require complex logistics
The path from an everyday item to a military solution can be short: identify a property, find a new application, check whether it works, and scale it up if the solution proves effective. It is precisely the ability to move along this path quickly that becomes an important advantage in war.
War forces us to use what is at hand, combine civilian technologies and materials, and look for the simplest possible solutions to specific military needs. And this is precisely where the ingenuity of Ukrainian engineers and developers manifests itself, to a certain extent
Nuts, foil, and fishing nets are not military technologies in themselves. But in the hands of engineers, they can acquire a new purpose and become part of a solution, especially when speed, availability, and the ability to accomplish a specific task are important.

Israel prepares for renewed Gaza ground offensive as Hamas shows no sign of disarming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:59:06 UTC
15:59:06 KST

No matter what the situation on the ground may look like, nerves remain raw during the holiday season nearly three years after October 7. That feeling is shared by IDF troops operating deep inside the Gaza Strip. The operational reality is vastly different from what it was in the past, with Israel now exercising far broader military control in parts of the enclave, but that control brings its own complex challenges. At the same time, the sense of security among residents of Israeli communities near Gaza remains fragile, despite what the military describes as substantial achievements that are continually being tested.
Nearly three years after October 7, and after 472 IDF soldiers were killed since the start of the Gaza ground operation, Hamas remains armed and retains control over significant parts of the Strip. As long as the terrorist organization does not voluntarily disarm under the U.S.-backed framework, Israeli officials say the IDF may ultimately be ordered to do so by force.
“Everyone understands that Hamas will not disarm and destroy all the tunnels, and the IDF is prepared, if given the order to eliminate Hamas, to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday. Katz has previously said plans to facilitate Gazans’ emigration remain under discussion, while acknowledging that other countries have not agreed to receive them.
For now, several kites recently launched toward Israeli communities near Gaza were enough to put the entire sector back on heightened alert. Southern Command has been working to counter the phenomenon, which has since subsided. The situation on the ground is stark: destruction is extensive, while fortified IDF positions known in military terminology as “meteors” are reinforcing Israel’s hold on the terrain and are intended to remain in place.
The IDF is maintaining what officers describe as a high offensive tempo, including targeted strikes and the destruction of weapons depots. Southern Command views those attacks as pressure on Hamas to move toward an agreement that would include disarmament. “If you do not disarm, we will disarm you,” officials in the command say. At the same time, the military’s operational approach inside Gaza is changing.
Reservists from the IDF’s 179th Brigade, who recently completed a deployment in Gaza, operated around Ridge 70 and opposite the south-central part of Gaza City while controlling the northern edge of the central Gaza camps. During the deployment, they dealt with several significant incidents, including the kite launches and an explosive device detonated against a remotely operated “Panda” bulldozer.
The troops are feeling the cumulative strain of repeated deployments. At the same time, there is concern that the transition from the intense maneuver warfare of earlier phases to a forward-defense posture could eventually breed complacency.
Security officials reject the idea that the military is settling into routine. “There is no intention of turning this into routine territorial brigade activity,” they say. “We are constantly initiating attacks and thwarting threats. That creates a tempo and prevents us from being drawn into routine.”
At one IDF position, troops described the complex procedures used when people approach the Yellow Line, the ceasefire boundary behind which Israeli forces are deployed. The IDF began physically marking the line with yellow-painted posts and concrete barriers to provide what it calls “tactical clarity” on the ground.
Contrary to claims sometimes made about Israeli activity near the line, officers say troops do not automatically open fire on every unarmed person who approaches it. According to soldiers and security officials, an unarmed person approaching the boundary is first monitored, warned and tracked. Troops may fire warning shots nearby and, when circumstances allow, attempt an arrest, they say, after assessing the situation.
Officials say the rules are different when troops identify armed people or suspects who pose an immediate threat. The IDF has repeatedly said forces along the Yellow Line will act against threats to soldiers, while Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir has said the military must remain prepared to move rapidly from defense to a broader offensive if ordered.
The issue has taken on additional significance amid international criticism of Israel’s conduct in Gaza and the controversy surrounding NAZA (“collateral damage”), the Israeli documentary that won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival and leveled serious allegations against the IDF’s conduct in the enclave.
Only weeks earlier, however, the military faced criticism from the opposite direction, with claims that troops were being forced to stand exposed and take risks because they were supposedly prohibited from opening fire.
“It is neither one nor the other,” security officials on the ground say. “These are measured rules of engagement.”
Zamir, speaking at an event honoring donors to the Association for the Wellbeing of Israel’s Soldiers, said: “The IDF is the most moral army in the world. Faced with deliberate attacks on our civilians, a barbaric raid deliberately targeting a civilian population and missiles fired at city centers, we adhere to the values of the IDF and international law and do everything in our power to avoid harming innocent people.”
In areas of Gaza outside Israeli control, Hamas is trying to recover and reassert governance. Roughly 600 humanitarian aid trucks enter Gaza each day under the current system, broadly consistent with figures published by Israeli authorities since the ceasefire. According to Israeli security assessments cited by Ynet, Hamas is exploiting the flow of goods by establishing checkpoints and collecting levies that can approach 50% in some cases. Independent reporting has also documented Hamas authorities taxing goods and profiting from parts of Gaza’s wartime economy, though the amounts and mechanisms vary.
Israeli officials say that money helps Hamas maintain elements of local governance even as its operatives remain under continuing military pressure. The situation, they argue, is a product of the continuing deadlock in negotiations: Hamas is adapting to the current reality and attempting to consolidate pockets of authority, while the IDF continues carrying out strikes against its operatives and infrastructure.
The political environment is also complicating any step that could be interpreted inside Israel as rebuilding Gaza before Hamas is disarmed, including improvements to civilian infrastructure or the deployment of international forces. Netanyahu and Katz have publicly said there will be no reconstruction before Hamas is disarmed and the Strip is demilitarized.
Against the backdrop of the Jewish holidays, political tensions and uncertainty over the future Palestinian political system, the IDF is entering another sensitive period. Commanders in the field are trying to prevent any decline in vigilance.
Although the Gaza front remains diplomatically frozen, Southern Command is maintaining a high tempo of strikes. Military officials say the aim is to sustain pressure on Hamas, prevent it from rebuilding its capabilities, continue targeting terrorists involved in the October 7 attack and reinforce among troops the message that Gaza remains an active combat arena.

Israel’s F-35 jets are getting a new precision weapon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:58:59 UTC
15:58:59 KST

- Rafael announced Sept. 15, 2026, that it is integrating its SPICE 1000 precision-guided munition onto the F-35 Adir for the first time.
- The work is a joint project with Lockheed Martin carried out in the United States, building on years of SPICE 1000 use aboard Israeli F-15 and F-16 jets.
Rafael Advanced Defense Systems is integrating its SPICE 1000 precision-guided munition onto the F-35 Adir fighter jet for the first time, the Israeli company announced Sept. 15, 2026, at the AFA Air, Space & Cyber conference.
The work is being carried out jointly with Lockheed Martin at Lockheed’s facilities in the United States.
SPICE 1000 is a 453 kg (1,000-pound) class guidance kit that converts standard bombs into precision, stand-off weapons capable of hitting fixed and high-value targets from more than 120 km (75 miles) away. It uses an electro-optical seeker paired with scene-matching algorithms, letting it lock onto a target by comparing what it sees to stored imagery rather than relying solely on GPS, a feature designed to keep the weapon accurate even in environments where satellite navigation is jammed or unavailable.
The Israeli Air Force has flown SPICE 1000 for years, primarily on its F-15 and F-16 fleets, and the weapon has been a mainstay of the service’s long-range strike missions. Rafael and Lockheed Martin first signed an agreement to jointly market SPICE kits internationally in 2018, and the two companies have said publicly for several years that F-35 integration was on their roadmap. This week’s announcement marks the point where that integration work has moved forward on the F-35 platform specifically.
SPICE is manufactured in three weight classes: SPICE 1000, SPICE 2000, and the smaller SPICE 250, all sharing a stand-off range of up to 120 km. The family has been sold to multiple air forces beyond Israel and has been integrated on other fighter types, including the Saab Gripen. Rafael has said the SPICE program has won Israel’s Defense Prize.
Because the F-35’s internal weapons bays are limited in size and shape, integrating an existing munition onto the jet typically requires software, wiring and structural work to confirm the weapon fits, communicates with the aircraft’s systems and can be released safely, a process distinct from simply mounting a bomb onto an external pylon.
Neither company disclosed a timeline for completing that work on SPICE 1000, nor did they specify whether the integration covers internal carriage, external carriage, or both.

Think tank suggests Taiwan should integrate its unmanned marine systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:58:02 UTC
15:58:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Navy and Coast Guard should coordinate to overcome challenges in asymmetrical warfare, a DSET statement said on Tuesday.
Asymmetrical warfare involves at least one party with vastly superior military size and resources. The weaker forces would use unconventional tactics and weapons to exploit the much stronger opponent's weaknesses.
Author Cathy Fang wrote to the Ocean Affairs Council's International Ocean Information saying that Taiwan should expand its drone fleet. She added it would lower personnel risk, protect high-value ships, and contain threats.
Fang said the Taiwan Strait is less than 130 kilometers at its narrowest, with rough winter seas crowded by commercial ships. She said that Taiwan should opt for flexible deployments so enemy forces would be spread thin.
Fang said that Taiwan can reference other countries' maritime systems and incorporate working aspects into its naval doctrines. She specified three main US maritime developments.
- Extended monitoring, with drone firm Seasats' Lightfish that crossed the strait in May and identified a covert Chinese escort ship
- Enforcement, with Saildrone's surface drone ship Voyager, which patrolled the Great Lakes and the northeast coast
- Global self-driving boats for patrols and surveillance, fleet escort, and swarm tactics
Fang then made four suggestions on how to proceed:
- On procurement, Taiwan should focus on mission-specific needs and schedule frequent exercises to find the best response measures. NATO naval drills and engagements between Russia and Ukraine provide valuable lessons.
- On coordination, Fang said Taiwan should partner with port authorities, energy, and telecommunications firms to develop a shared platform to counter gray-zone activities and wartime coordination. The Navy and Coast Guard should have protocols for conflict escalation and shared duties.
- On sustained operations, Fang said drone systems must remain operational under disruptions such as jammed signals and sabotage. She noted this would require backup drones, internet, and satellite signal relays.
- On the scale of operations, Fang suggested batched purchases such as the navy's 1,320 drone attack ships and the coast guard's 25 surface boats. She added that joint exercises would boost operational efficiency.
DSET is a government-funded research institute. Its full name is Democracy, Society, and Emerging Technology.

Russian drones hit Ukrainian bus and train, killing five, officials say
KYIV, Sept 16 - Russian drones struck a passenger bus and a train in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, killing five people, Ukrainian officials said, as Moscow pressed on with strikes on transport links and infrastructure.
A photo posted on Telegram by a regional governor showed a white vehicle with blown-out windows and a line of what appeared to be blood streaming down its side. Reuters has not verified the image.
"There is no military logic to this, just another act of brutality," Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on social media, urging the U.S. and Europe to press ahead with toughening sanctions against Russia.
ESCALATING STRIKES ON ECONOMIC TARGETS
Moscow and Ukraine have traded escalating strikes in recent months on logistics and other economic targets, aimed at hampering each other's war effort and damaging morale.
With Ukraine's airspace closed since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, buses and trains have become a vital transport link for ordinary Ukrainians and businesses.
The drone attack on the passenger bus near the frontline city of Nikopol killed four men and a woman early on Wednesday, police said.
A further seven people were injured in the attack, said the governor of the surrounding Dnipropetrovsk region, Oleksandr Hanzha, who posted the photo.
There was no immediate comment from Russia on the attack. Both Ukraine and Russia deny deliberately targeting civilians in the war, triggered by Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbour.
ATTACK ON PASSENGER TRAIN
A Russian drone also attacked a passenger train in Ukraine's southern Mykolaiv region, the acting regional governor said.
All 168 passengers and crew were evacuated and no one was injured, Heorhii Reshetilov said on Telegram. The train was attacked twice more after the first strike, he said.
Zelenskiy said that, in addition to the Mykolaiv train attack, a locomotive in Kovel — near the border with Poland — was also struck.
The incidents follow similar attacks recently, including on a train near Ukraine's border with NATO-member Poland on Sunday, shortly after European diplomats and political figures had used the same line.
Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukrainian railways, hitting 120 passenger wagons, 304 locomotives and 43 railway stations so far this year, the state rail operator told Reuters.
The company said that Russia has attacked 1,700 railway facilities in total since the start of the year, up from 1,206 facilities in 2025 and 842 in 2024.
"Russian forces strike passenger trains, locomotives, stations, and railway routes knowing exactly how essential they are for civilians, evacuations, and Ukraine's economy," Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
"This is not collateral damage. It is a systematic hunt for people and an attempt to paralyse civilian life," he said. REUTERS

Lithuanian defence minister says determining drone origin will take time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:57:00 UTC
15:57:00 KST

An investigation into a drone shot down by NATO fighter jets after it entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus will take time as authorities work to identify the aircraft and determine its flight path and possible launch site, Lithuania’s defence minister said Wednesday.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said specialists needed to thoroughly examine the recovered debris before drawing conclusions about the drone’s origin.
“The investigation will take some time, as the recovered debris must be thoroughly analysed,” Kaunas told LRT RADIO. He noted that drones of different types can be made from similar materials, making it necessary to examine their engines and other technical components.
Equipment will also be needed to reconstruct the drone’s flight path and determine where it may have been launched, he said.
“The engine is important, as are other engineering and technical components, so that our specialists can accurately assess all the circumstances,” Kaunas said.
The minister also said Lithuania had agreed to cooperate and exchange information with Poland, which reported finding a crashed drone of unknown origin on its Baltic Sea coast on Monday.
Kaunas declined to confirm speculation that the drone shot down in Lithuania was Russian, saying there was not yet enough evidence to support that conclusion.
“Russia is carrying out provocations in NATO countries,” he said, adding that some countries, including Germany, have publicly attributed provocations on their territory to Russia.
“Once we receive precise data on all incidents, we will state just as clearly who is behind them,” Kaunas said. “We simply do not want to speculate; we want to investigate this very precisely and present all the information backed by evidence.”
The drone entered Lithuania early Tuesday from Belarus and was shot down in the Kaišiadorys district of central Lithuania by Italian fighter jets stationed at the NATO air base in Šiauliai. Lithuanian bomb disposal experts later defused an explosive charge carried by the unmanned aircraft.
Lithuanian authorities have repeatedly issued alerts about potential air threats in recent months as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues. Tuesday’s incident, however, was the first time a drone had been shot down over Lithuanian territory.
NATO fighter jets shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May, marking the first interception of a foreign drone by NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. In June, French fighter jets participating in the mission shot down a drone over Latvia, the first such incident in Latvian airspace.

Ed Sheeran’s tour of North and South America was plunged into chaos Tuesday when four of his supporting acts abruptly quit in solidarity with the rapper Macklemore, who was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments onstage.
Hours after Sheeran posted on social media about Macklemore's ouster and attributed the decision to the tour's promoters, Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, the Danish band Lukas Graham, and Finneas posted on Instagram that they were leaving the tour.

The moves by his fellow artists put enormous pressure on Sheeran, who has tried to avoid politics and taking a side in the Gaza conflict, arguing that his fans don't come to his shows to hear politics.
Rowe and Beoga each cited their country’s history in their statements explaining their decision. “We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be,” Beoga said.

France's ex-culture minister Rachida Dati is to go on trial Wednesday on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan group, just months after her bruising defeat in the Paris mayoral race.
One of the most prominent figures on the French right, Dati, 60, will stand trial with the fugitive Carlos Ghosn, the disgraced former Renault-Nissan chief, who will be tried in absentia.
Dati has been dogged by controversies for much of her political career.
She resigned as culture minister in February to concentrate on the Paris mayoral race, but lost to Socialist rival Emmanuel Grégoire in March.
Read moreFrench mayoral elections: Fractured vote reshapes alliances ahead of runoff
In 2019, she was placed under investigation on suspicion of lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013 when she was a member of the European parliament.
She became an MEP after serving as justice minister between 2007 and 2009 under President Nicolas Sarkozy.
In 2021, she was charged with corruption and influence peddling over her dealings with Ghosn.
She is accused of accepting 900,000 euros (around $1 million) in lawyer's fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan.
Dati, who is still mayor of the French capital's wealthy 7th district, denies the allegations.

"Unfounded allegations of influence peddling in the European Parliament stem from an artificial intellectual construct devised by the prosecution," her lawyers said.
'Rigorous justice'
French prosecutors argue that a legal services contract signed in 2009 between Dati and Ghosn, under which the former minister was paid an annual fee of 300,000 euros, was used to disguise lobbying work.
Investigators obtained the contract in 2019 during a search of Renault's headquarters following Ghosn's arrest in Japan, in a separate case.
Ghosn, the 72-year-old former chairman and chief executive of the Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi alliance, was arrested in Japan in 2018 on suspicion of financial misconduct, before being sacked by Nissan's board.

Two Anduril executives, Jason Levin, senior vice president for air dominance and strike, and Erin Simpson, vice president for strategy for air dominance and strike, told reporters at the Air, Space and Cyber Symposium that the company has already begun integration and fit checks of 227 kg (500-pound) Joint Direct Attack Munitions, 113 kg (250-pound) Small Diameter Bombs, and low-cost cruise missiles on the aircraft. Pods for 7 cm (2.75-inch) guided or unguided rockets have also been fitted to the airframe, according to imagery reviewed by The War Zone.
The Fury, previously designated YFQ-44A during its prototype phase, is one of two aircraft the Air Force selected in April 2024 for the first increment of its Collaborative Combat Aircraft program, alongside General Atomics’ YFQ-42A. The program is meant to pair uncrewed, semi-autonomous fighters with crewed aircraft such as the F-22 and F-35, extending their sensor coverage and weapons capacity without adding more cockpits to the fight. The Air Force has said it could order between 100 and 150 aircraft under the program’s first phase, though it has not disclosed how many, if any, will be FQ-44s specifically versus YFQ-42As.
Anduril’s aircraft traces its design back to Fury, a concept originally developed by Blue Force Technologies, which Anduril acquired in 2023. The YFQ-44A completed ground testing at Beale Air Force Base in 2025 and made its first flight later that year from Southern California Logistics Airport in Victorville, California. The Air Force selected Anduril for the program’s production phase in June 2026, moving Fury from prototype status toward an initial batch of production aircraft intended to support further testing and eventual fielding. The Air Force has not disclosed the value or size of that production order.
The newly shown weapons integration work addresses one of the central questions about the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program: what the drones will actually carry into combat. Until now, most public discussion of CCA aircraft has centered on their role as sensor platforms and force multipliers flying alongside crewed fighters, rather than on their specific strike capabilities. The range of munitions shown on Fury, spanning guided bombs, smaller precision weapons, cruise missiles and rocket pods, suggests the Air Force is testing the aircraft against a broad set of potential strike missions rather than a single narrow role.

SINGAPORE, Sept. 16 (Xinhua) -- Southeast Asia's six largest economies -- Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- are projected to grow by an average of 4.8 percent annually between 2026 and 2035, according to a report released on Wednesday.
Growth will be supported by sustained foreign investment and capital formation, continued industrialization and infrastructure development, and productivity gains from technology adoption, said a report by Bain & Company, DBS Bank and Vriens & Partners.
Resilient domestic consumption and favorable demographics in several major economies are also expected to provide support.
However, growth paths are diverging, with institutional strength, energy security and technological readiness shaping economies' ability to withstand shocks and capture opportunities.
Vietnam is expected to remain the regional growth leader, while Thailand lags its counterparts. Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand face greater exposure in a downside scenario, while Malaysia, Singapore and Vietnam have greater upside under more favorable conditions.
Foreign direct investment has also surged, with shifts in the investor mix reflecting global supply chain realignment.
The report showed Singapore remains the region's most resilient economy, supported by its safe-haven status, deep markets, fiscal buffers and trusted hub credibility. Its position as a regional center for capital also facilitates investment and business opportunities across Southeast Asia. ■

Details

Daughter of former Gaza hostage confronts UN over UNRWA funding despite Hamas ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:47:17 UTC
15:47:17 KST

Neta Heiman Mina, whose elderly mother, Ditza Heiman, was taken hostage by Hamas terrorists on October 7, 2023, and held prisoner in Gaza for nearly two months, spoke at the 63rd Session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland, on Tuesday. She spoke on a panel on human rights education, confronting the UN over its continued funding of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) despite its ongoing ties to Hamas.
UNRWA was founded in 1949 and operates in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, where it is tasked with providing humanitarian aid and education for Palestinians.
Tuesday’s panel, which was held to mark the anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training, included UN ambassadors and representatives from various member states as well as representatives from human rights and UN-affiliated organizations.
For 48 days of her 53-day-long captivity, her mother, who was aged 84 at the time of capture, was held hostage by an UNRWA teacher, Mina said in her 90-second statement on behalf of both the Geneva-based UN Watch and international NGO Ingénieurs du Monde.
'My mother wasn’t the only one'
“An UNRWA teacher, Abed, kept [Heiman] trapped in his attic in terrible conditions with very little food,” Mina said. “I ask the United Nations: how could you place the education of Gaza’s next generation with someone involved in holding an elderly woman hostage?”
“My mother wasn’t the only one,” Mina continued. “We know of other UNRWA employees connected to the massacre and kidnappings of October 7. Why did UNRWA allow Suhail al-Hindi to be in charge of 8,000 teachers in Gaza while he was a member of Hamas?”
In a written press statement, UN Watch noted that the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training explicitly states that human rights education should “contribute to the prevention of human rights violations and abuses and to the combating and eradication of all forms of discrimination, racism, stereotyping and incitement to hatred, and the harmful attitudes and prejudices that underlie them.”
UNRWA overstated progress on institutional changes, preserved terrorism issues
Mina’s statement came on the heels of a scathing report published by UN Watch on Monday, which claimed that UNRWA has substantially overstated its progress on institutional changes, substituting administrative paperwork for actual reform while underlying issues involving terrorism and incitement remain unaddressed.
The investigation, titled the “Report Card on UNRWA Reform,” analyzed the agency’s implementation of 50 recommendations issued by an independent review group led by former French Foreign Minister Catherine Colonna.
The Colonna review was originally commissioned by UN Secretary-General António Guterres in early 2024 to restore donor confidence after devastating revelations surfaced that UNRWA employees had participated in the October 7 massacre, which led 17 donor states to temporarily suspend $450 million in funding.
UNRWA now says it has successfully completed 41 of the 50 recommended reforms, however, UN Watch analysis concludes that this figure is misleading, noting that, at most, only 13 recommendations have been implemented.
“UNRWA has graded its own homework and awarded itself high marks,” UN Watch Executive Director Hillel Neuer said. “But issuing a policy is not the same as enforcing it. Drafting a plan is not the same as implementing it, and closing a recommendation does not mean that the underlying problem has been solved.”
Alex Carson contributed to this report.

====================================================================================================

Fishing waste from as far away as US and Canada washes up on Portuguese beaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
06:46:46 UTC
15:46:46 KST

Lobster-fishing plastics have drifted across the Atlantic and washed up on Faial and Pico islands, over 3,000 km away. The oldest item dates back to 1983.
Since 2010, researchers at the University of the Azores have been monitoring waste brought in from the sea, until they began noticing the same objects appearing again and again.
"We started to realise that these items, which at first we did not know where they came from, had certain numbers on them. And when we started to find quite a lot, we began trying to look up what they actually meant," explains Christopher Pham, researcher and head of the marine litter research group at the University of the Azores.
It turned out that the objects were coming from the lobster fishery, a sector with significant economic weight along the North American Atlantic coast. They also realised that the numbers printed on some of these plastics were mandatory tags that make it possible to identify their origin and date.
That is how a study involving scientists and volunteers began.
"We asked local people and colleagues that if they went to the beach and managed to find these items, they should bring them back," says Christopher Pham. "We had at least ten people who were very interested and kept sending us material every month."
Between 2017 and 2025, they found more than 1,500 items on the beaches of Faial and Pico.
These two islands are part of the Portuguese archipelago of the Azores, located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, about 1,600 km from mainland Europe.
Waste travels more than 3,000 km
These items are objects or fragments of objects that are placed in the sea to catch lobster, such as corners and clips from the pots (cage-like traps), funnels or tags.
The tags with legible inscriptions had their origin in the United States (63%) and Canada (37%). Within the United States, the tags referred mainly to the state of Maine (80%) and Massachusetts (11%). The tags from Canada refer to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
The study, published this summer, says it is an example 'of how an isolated oceanic archipelago is directly exposed to plastic waste from a coastal fishery that operates more than 3,000 km away'.
For waste to make the journey across the ocean from the North American coast to these Atlantic islands is not exactly a surprise to the researchers; it is more a confirmation. This movement of debris had already been suggested by models showing the behaviour of currents, winds and waves.
"We know there is that direct link and it was to be expected that we would receive particles from this part of the Atlantic, because the currents really circulate clockwise, from west to east," says Christopher Pham, explaining that this study validates those models.
And although this study is limited to the islands of Pico and Faial, this waste can travel much further, even all the way to mainland Europe.
"These lobster-fishing items are also quite frequent along the Portuguese coast and even in England and Ireland," adds the researcher.
More than 40 years in nature
The researchers were also able to determine the age of part of this waste because among it there are tags stamped with the year of registration.
Most of the tags are between 7 and 13 years old. The most recent dates from 2023 and the oldest from 1983, meaning it was put into the sea more than 40 years ago. This shows that these plastics can reach the Azores in just two years and then remain in the environment for many decades without breaking up.
"Most of the items entered the sea many years ago. That is also significant because it shows that plastic has enormous persistence in the environment", says Pham.
"It is very likely that, if we keep looking, we will find things that are perhaps even older. Because these tags are made from very high-quality plastic."
Access to this information was possible because this industry in North America requires this material to be tagged, even though the rules differ between the United States and Canada, for example in terms of the information provided and how long the tags remain valid.
More waste on Azores beaches
Lobster fishing is the most economically important fishing activity in the United States and Canada. In 2020, lobster exports from the two countries were worth around 1.74 billion euros.
Estimates suggest that every year three million pots (traps) are deployed off the coast of the United States and two million off Canada to catch these crustaceans.
But lobster fishing is not the only source of pollution on Azores beaches. There is other fishing-related waste on these beaches in the middle of the Atlantic, but it is less common and cannot be traced back to its source.
"We found trawl nets, but a trawl net can be used in Greenland or in Brazil. In those cases we no longer know where it comes from," explains Cristopher Pham.
"Sometimes we manage to find some pots that are typical of octopus fishing, but these traps are used from Spain all the way to Morocco; they are not as specific as in the case of lobster."
Other types of waste also wash up on these beaches, and they can come from anywhere.
"We almost never know the precise geographic location. Sometimes we have Chinese bottles, but we do not know if they come from China. They probably come from a Chinese ship that was offshore and threw the bottle into the sea," says Christopher.
Besides bottles, there are also cigarette butts, shoe soles and lighters. But the most common waste consists of small pieces of plastic, "a 2-centimetre white piece of plastic", fragments of an unrecognisable object.
"All these towns that are dumping huge amounts of plastic into streams," says Christopher Pham. "With sunlight and the action of the sea, it starts to fragment and then you get that soup of fragments that entered the sea many years ago but are no longer recognisable in their original form."
Tackling the problem at source
Only by knowing where these objects come from can we take measures at the source to solve the problem. That is why labelling fishing gear, as happens in the lobster industry, is so important.
The Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO) has issued recommendations that gear used in fishing should be identifiable. The scientists at the University of the Azores stress how important it is to adopt this practice.
The team behind this study also has specific recommendations for the fishing industry in North America. These include better management of gear, incentives to hand in old material and the creation of collection points.
For these researchers, the next step is to carry out a more systematic analysis, in terms of the density and volume of waste from lobster fishing.
"To try to understand whether this is increasing or decreasing and what proportion it represents in the overall picture of plastic pollution – what contribution these items make," explains Christopher Pham.
But they believe the most important work has already been done: alerting the authorities in the United States and Canada, so that they act.
"It is important that you take action to reduce this flow of plastic into the sea, because people who have nothing to do with the pollution are becoming victims," Christopher Pham concludes.
