====================================================================================================

The homes Australians are shunning and the future risk it carries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:47:52 UTC
14:47:52 KST

IN BRIEF
- New home sales fell 10 per cent in August and are now at their lowest level in more than a year.
- Experts say high borrowing and construction costs are making the new homes Australia needs harder to afford.
Buyers appear to be rejecting newly-built homes, sparking concerns Australia's property market slowdown could worsen a chronic housing shortage.
Sales of new homes fell 10 per cent nationally in August and were 19.3 per cent lower in the three months to August compared with the previous quarter, according to new data from the Housing Industry Association (HIA).
Sales have now fallen for four consecutive months to their lowest level in more than a year.
The slowdown was recorded across all five mainland states included in the HIA survey, which tracks sales by large-volume home builders and is considered a leading indicator of future detached home construction.
Victoria recorded the sharpest quarterly decline, with sales down 27 per cent, followed by Queensland at 20.2 per cent, NSW at 17.5 per cent, South Australia at 10.8 per cent and Western Australia at 8.2 per cent.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
HIA chief economist Tim Reardon said the deterioration meant the recovery in new home building seen earlier this year had been interrupted.
"Today's new home sales are tomorrow's housing commencements," he said in a statement.
"The decline in sales through the middle of 2026 will mean fewer homes commencing construction in 2027."
Why are Australians pulling back?
Independent property economist Cameron Kusher told SBS News that a combination of higher borrowing costs and low confidence was making it increasingly difficult to buy a new home. But he warned that if sales continued to decline leading to fewer builds, it could lead to even higher prices in the future.
"We're seeing really weak confidence around the housing market generally at the moment," he told SBS News.
Tim Lawless, the research director at property data firm Cotality, said the slowdown was also evident across the broader property market, although new homes appeared to have been hit harder.
Cotality estimates home sales across the broader market were about 15 per cent lower over winter than a year earlier and 11 per cent below the five-year average.
"It does look like new home sales have been hit a little bit harder," Lawless said, pointing to higher interest rates, weaker confidence, reduced investment and affordability and serviceability constraints.
The slowdown has been particularly pronounced in Sydney, Brisbane and Perth, where Cotality estimates home sales fell by more than 20 per cent over winter compared with the same period last year.
Lawless said Brisbane and Perth were coming off relatively strong levels of activity, while Sydney's decline was more reflective of severe affordability constraints.
Kusher said new homes typically carried a premium compared with established properties, making older homes more desirable as household borrowing capacity comes under pressure.
"Buyers are asking themselves: "Am I prepared to pay the premium for a brand-new home when I can get an older home, an established home, cheaper?"
"I'm not surprised that we're seeing these ongoing falls, but obviously that's really problematic when you need to be building more homes."
The HIA data does not provide a detailed breakdown of the types or price points of detached homes experiencing the greatest decline.
But Kusher said affordability was clearly becoming a bigger constraint.
Higher interest rates mean some prospective buyers simply aren't able to borrow enough to buy the homes they otherwise might have considered.
HIA has also pointed to rising construction costs, taxation and broader economic uncertainty as factors weighing on the sector.
Reardon said builders were reporting fewer people visiting display sites, declining enquiries and preliminary commitments, and rising cancellation rates.
Lawless agreed, telling SBS News that higher material, labour and other construction costs were also making new homes less competitive with established properties.
Why today's sales matter for tomorrow's housing supply
Government figures show there were 244,000 dwellings under construction in the March quarter of 2026, the most since records began in 1984.
The deterioration in sales is unlikely to immediately show up in housing commencements this year.
The problem comes further down the pipeline, with the impact of weaker sales expected to become more apparent in 2027.
Lawless said some projects may have become financially unviable as construction and labour costs increased, while others may not have secured enough pre-sales to trigger financing.
"Typically most developers would need to have a minimum level of pre-sales before a lender is going to be becoming active in the credit supply," he said.
Kusher said most builders sought to secure a buyer before starting construction rather than building homes speculatively and hoping to sell them afterwards.
Financing speculative construction was particularly difficult when both borrowing and construction costs were high, he said.
That means the relationship between weaker sales and fewer future homes is relatively straightforward.
"If people aren't buying homes, you're not likely to get many homes built," Kusher said.
In 2024 the National Housing Accord commenced with an aspirational target of 1.2 million new, well-located homes over the five years to June 2029.
The target was agreed between federal, state and territory governments, local government and industry in an effort to substantially increase housing supply.
Government figures show this is already behind targets and likely won't be met until the end of 2030, and Kusher warns it could get blown out further still.
Australia needs homes — but at what price?
The slowdown creates a difficult contradiction for Australia's housing market.
Demand has not disappeared simply because fewer people can afford to buy a newly built home.
"The thing with the shortage of supply in housing is that price matters," Kusher said.
"We need more houses, but they need to be at a price that people can afford."
Lawless described the construction sector as being caught "between a rock and a hard place".
"A builder or a developer, obviously, they're not going to be building homes if there's no profit to be had, and consumers or households aren't going to be buying new homes if they're too expensive to purchase," he said.
HIA similarly warned the decline in new home sales was occurring without an equivalent decline in Australia's underlying need for housing, pointing to population growth, low unemployment and the existing shortage of homes.
What could turn the market around?
HIA has warned that further interest rate rises would place additional pressure on a new home market already struggling with weaker demand.
"This is not the time for another rate rise," Reardon said.
Kusher, however, said getting inflation under control was ultimately necessary to restore stability to the housing market — even if doing so meant households faced more financial pressure in the short term.
He said longer-term improvement depended on bringing inflation under control, allowing greater certainty to return to the economy and eventually creating scope for borrowing costs to fall.
"Now that means higher interest rates, and that means it's going to be hard for people."
But he said easing inflation could ultimately provide the conditions needed for both property prices and borrowing costs to stabilise, "and that's when you'll start to see things improve."

China opens Pinglu Canal for trade shortcut to Asean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:46:51 UTC
14:46:51 KST

China opened the Pinglu Canal on Wednesday, giving its landlocked southwest a shortcut to the coast and overseas markets, particularly those in Asean, the country's largest trading partner.
Built at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan, the 134.2-kilometre canal runs from Nanning, capital of south Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, to the Beibu Gulf, the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
The canal stretches along the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic trade route connecting China's inland regions with Asean and other global markets.
It is the first river-to-sea canal project planned and coordinated at the national level since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from southwest China to the sea by more than 560 kilometres compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong.
It is expected to reduce overall logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent and save more than five billion yuan in transportation costs each year.
Lu Xinning, vice chairwoman of the regional government of Guangxi, said the canal creates a new link between China's market of 1.4 billion people and Asean's nearly 700 million consumers.
Its impact, she said, could extend beyond the movement of goods, spurring new cross-border investment and deepening regional supply-chain integration.
The canal took over four years to build. 
Most of it was created by widening, deepening and straightening existing waterways, while a small section had to be excavated through dry land and mountainous terrain.
One of the biggest engineering challenges was a 65-metre difference in water level, roughly the height of a 20-plus-storey building. 
Three navigation hubs, all featuring twin-line ship locks, were built to raise and lower vessels along the canal.
Environmental protection was another priority during construction.
More than 98 percent of the roughly 315 million cubic metres of earth and rock excavated during construction was reused.
The canal also includes a fish passage more than 480 metres long and a dedicated wildlife crossing for land animals including leopard cats and squirrels.
The canal opens in the first year of the country's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), as the world's second-largest economy seeks to promote more coordinated regional development and further expand high-standard opening up – priorities outlined in the plan.
The new artery carries particular significance for China's southwest, which has long lagged behind the more prosperous eastern coast and faced higher costs getting goods to seaports. 
Coal, ore, grain, new-energy materials and auto parts from the region can now take a more direct route to overseas markets.
China's trade with Asean exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time last year. 
In the first seven months of 2026, total trade between the two sides reached US$744.41 billion, an increase of 24.7 percent year on year, accounting for 21.8 percent of China's total foreign trade during this period. (Xinhua)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin’s goal in the war extends far beyond seizing additional Ukrainian territory, adding that Moscow ultimately wants Ukraine to become part of Russia.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are ready for this,” Zelensky said, referring to a potential halt in fighting along the existing front line.
He said negotiations could then continue with the mediation of international partners, adding that a ceasefire without conditions would be preferable to continued fighting.
Zelensky rejects ‘win-win’ concept
Zelensky also rejected the idea that there could be a “win-win” outcome for Russia and Ukraine after the losses caused by the war.
“There is no win-win in this war,” he said, adding that the war ceased to be a situation in which both sides could benefit from the moment it began and caused human casualties.
Zelensky added the most important victory would be to end the war and protect human lives, rather than for either Ukraine or Russia to claim victory.

ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 15, 2026
Zelensky said the envoys had asked Ukrainian officials not to publicly discuss some of their proposals while the two sides examined them in greater detail. He added that Ukraine was preparing for a meeting with US President Donald Trump in New York expected later in September.
‘He needs Ukraine’
The Ukrainian president pushed back against the idea that Putin could be satisfied by obtaining a specific portion of Ukrainian territory.
Asked about Kushner’s comments that territory remained a key sticking point and that Putin had outlined the territorial line he wanted, Zelensky said the issue was not simply about “some kilometers” of land.
“The problem is that we have to change Putin’s mind,” Zelensky said.
He argued that it made little sense to suggest Putin needed only a particular part of Ukraine, given that Russia already controls vast territory elsewhere.
“He needs Ukraine,” Zelensky said. “He needs Ukraine [to] be a part of Russia.”
Zelensky said this was why Ukraine could not simply accept a territorial concession as the basis for a lasting settlement.
He also addressed the prospect of meeting Putin directly, saying he was willing to sit across from his adversary if doing so could bring the parties closer to peace.
He acknowledged that such a meeting was not something he personally wanted, saying he would rather spend the time with his family.
“But he is an enemy, of course,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky said he would nevertheless meet Putin if negotiations could produce meaningful progress toward peace. He argued that he understood Putin’s objective and believed the Russian leader would continue trying to occupy Ukraine unless Ukraine remained strong and received credible security guarantees.
“He will not change his goal,” Zelensky said.
For Ukraine, he added, security guarantees would need to ensure that Russia could not simply resume its attempt to occupy the country after a ceasefire or peace agreement.

SpaceX prepares for first orbital flight of Starship rocket

The SpaceX logo is displayed on a building, May 26, 2020, at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Fla. (AP Photo)
SpaceX announced on Sept.16 it was planning to send its flagship rocket Starship into orbit, a key step in its project to one day reach the Moon or Mars.
The space company co-founded by Elon Musk said the rocket’s first orbital flight will happen next week, with liftoff scheduled from Texas at 7:15 am local time (1215 GMT) on Sept. 22.
During this test flight, the 14th conducted with Starship, SpaceX will also seek to deliver 26 Starlink satellites.
The company said the orbital flight would mark an “exciting new phase” for Starship, its largest and most powerful rocket.
“Flight tests until this point have intentionally flown passively safe suborbital trajectories to maximize public safety,” SpaceX said on its website.
“By going to orbit, the next phase of developing Starship to be fully and rapidly reusable can begin.”
Several Starship test flights have not gone as planned, with the rockets exploding into fireballs -- or as Musk describes it, “rapid unscheduled disassembly.”
Its most recent test flight in July, however, was largely a success, and the first since the company posted the largest initial public offering in history.
Along with orbital flight, Starship has yet to successfully demonstrate several milestones — such as refueling in space — before it can be used for commercial flights, or for travel to the Moon or Mars.

US House votes to end Iran war, 7 Republicans join in favour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:36:53 UTC
14:36:53 KST

US House votes to end Iran war, 7 Republicans join in favour
For a third time, the US House approved a war powers resolution, halting Trump’s ability to continue military action.
For a third time, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt President Donald Trump’s ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The roll call late Tuesday, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict.
Seven House Republicans backed the resolution, including three voting in favour for the first time.
Iowa congressman Zach Nunn, a Republican, explained his vote saying that “with the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization.”
“I will not support another open-ended war,” Nunn said.
None of the resolutions has made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.
Republican Representative Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat.
Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending” – the decades of hostilities from Iran.
“They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States,” Mast said. “Enough is enough.”
The run-up to the midterms
The action is likely to be the last House vote on the Iran war ahead of the midterm elections, where the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns. The war that Trump launched on February 28 has dragged on, with on-again, off-again deadly missile strikes being exchanged and causing havoc in the region for nearly seven months.
Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with fewer than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress as Democrats try to wrest power from Republicans.
US war on Iran
The US war on Iran is worsening inflation and straining the country’s munitions stockpiles, a report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found.
The report, released on Tuesday, found that the cost of the six-month war has reached $38bn and is expected to rise by $3bn per month. The war is projected to increase inflation by 0.5 percentage points in the first three months of 2027.
Trump himself had promised not to involve the US in foreign wars when he won a second term in the White House, and his actions against Iran are weighing on the Republican Party that controls the House and Senate.
Most Americans say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, according to an AP-NORC poll in July.
Previous war resolutions
Congress has tried repeatedly to alter the trajectory of the war against Iran, but efforts to limit the Trump administration’s military action remain a long shot so long as the president can fend off or veto the measures.
The House first approved a war powers resolution in June, and followed up with another one in July, both seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but Republican senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch.
While the Constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also gives the president authority as the commander-in-chief to engage in some military actions. The War Powers Act, created after the Vietnam conflict, sought to impose a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days.

LONDON, September 16. /TASS/. The number of ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to a minimum on Tuesday, with only two entering and two exiting, Reuters reported, citing the Kpler analytics firm.
According to analysts, none of the ships were supertankers with oil or tankers transporting liquefied natural gas.
Before the Middle East conflict began, about 125 large commercial vessels, including bulk carriers, container ships, oil tankers, and LNG carriers, typically passed through the strait each day, transporting about 20% of the world’s daily oil and LNG shipments.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran, with Islamabad acting as mediator, signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.

Jaan Tallinn tops Äripäev rich list with €10.3bn net worth
Tech entrepreneur Jaan Tallinn tops this year's Äripäev rich list with an estimated net worth of €10.3 billion.
There are three billionaires on the list, while all top 10 richest are men.
Tallinn, who co-founded Skype in 2003 and is now a leading figure in AI development, is joined in an unchanged top five by Wise co-founders Kristo Käärmann and Taavet Hinrikus, Bolt founder Markus Villig and media and entertainment mogul Margus Linnamäe.
Äripäev says the Top 500 as a whole also saw strong growth, with the wealth of Estonia's richest people rising by about a third on the year, to €41.4 billion.
The top 10 in the Äripäev 2026 Estonian rich list, with their net worths, are:
- Jaan Tallinn (Metaplanet Holdings, Ambient Sound Investments): €10.318 billion
- Kristo Käärmann (Wise): €1.933 billion
- Taavet Hinrikus (Skaala Investments, Wise): €1.476 billion
- Markus Villig (Bolt): €960.8 million
- Margus Linnamäe (MM Grupp): €686.9 million
- Raul Kirjanen (AS Graanul): €559.2 million
- Oleg Ossinovski (Skinest Grupp): €551.1 million
- Anders Anderson: €497.3 million
- Oliver Leisalu (Bolt): €461.2 million
- Fjodor Berman (BLRT Grupp): €394.8 million
The first woman to appear on the list is Kristi Veeber, one of the owners of holding company Giga, who ranks 46th with €131.3 million.
Journalist: Bulk of Jaan Tallinn wealth derives from shares in Anthropic
Most of Jaan Tallinn's €10.3 billion fortune comes from AI, Äripäev journalist Ken Rohelaan said, with the businessman's stake in Anthropic — the US AI company behind the Claude chatbot — alone valued at nearly €9.8 billion.
This represented a large leap forward in his estimated net worth, Rohelaan said, telling "Terevisioon": "We already suspected a year or two ago that his wealth could be greater than what we had seen or perceived so far, but for the figure to now come in at more than €10 billion was certainly a surprise".
Tallinn got an early start on the AI boom, he noted. "His investments have mainly been focused on artificial intelligence. We may have known about AI for only a few years, but Jaan Tallinn got involved much earlier, and this early entry into the right field is essentially the main reason that helped him get this far," Rohelaan said.
Rohelaan also highlighted Berman's rise to 10th place as the year's biggest change, driven by a buyout of minority shareholders.

Seoul court orders North Korea to pay $32.5m for blowing up office
Pyongyang blew up the Inter-Korean Liaison Office building in June 2020 after days of rising tensions.
A court in Seoul has ordered Pyongyang to pay roughly $32.5m for blowing up an office in North Korea in 2020 that was intended to foster better relations between the two neighbours.
“The court has ruled the North should pay the South Korean government 44.6 billion won in damages,” a spokeswoman for the Seoul Central District Court told the AFP news agency on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi drone headed for Mecca
- list 2 of 3Trump administration plans $2.8bn sale of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel
- list 3 of 3China’s defence chief warns against coercion, avoids US, Japan mention
The lawsuit over the destruction of the Inter-Korean Liaison Office marks the first time the South Korean government has sought damages directly from the North Korean state, media reports said.
The office building was constructed in the dormant Kaesong Industrial Complex, where South Korean companies once employed North Korean workers.
However, Pyongyang blew up the building in June 2020 after days of rising tensions when activists in the South sent balloons carrying anti-Pyongyang leaflets across the border, with the North denouncing the office as “useless”.
South Korea said it would “review the necessary follow-up measures”, though experts consider it unlikely that Pyongyang would ever pay damages over the demolition of the building in the North Korean city of Kaesong.
The case was filed in 2023 under the government of then-South Korean leader Yoon Suk-yeol, who took a hard line on North Korea before he was ousted following his disastrous martial law declaration.
The office opened in September 2018, days before then-South Korean President Moon Jae-in travelled to Pyongyang for his third summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
About 20 officials from each side were stationed at the office in the following months until operations were suspended in January 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
Inter-Korean relations reached a high point in 2018, when Moon and Kim held three summits. But ties deteriorated after a meeting between Kim and United States President Donald Trump in Hanoi, Vietnam, collapsed in February 2019.

A New Gathering in Valparaíso, Chile, Brings Together Master Builders to Safeguard Traditional Trades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

From October 9 to 11, "Oficios en obra" (Trades at Work) will take place at the Parque Cultural de Valparaíso in Chile, a learning and collaboration event centered on the city's traditional construction trades. Organized by the Municipality, the gathering seeks to highlight and preserve work techniques historically tied to the construction of Valparaíso, promoting their recognition and helping ensure their continuity among new generations through activities that are open and free to the public. Once the most important port on the South Pacific, Valparaíso's architecture bears witness to diverse applications of structural timber, rammed earth, and industrial technologies imported during the 19th century. This makes it a subject of study for traditional trades and construction techniques that are being revalued in contemporary contexts of climate and economic crisis, serving as an alternative path forward.
The main objective of "Oficios en obra" is to create a space for exchange, learning, and collaboration around the city's tangible and intangible heritage. Over three days, the event will bring together master tradespeople, practitioners, training institutions, sector businesses, heritage-related organizations, and the community, through trade stands, workshops, and city routes. The program, which includes two days of music, features dialogue panels, keynote talks, hands-on workshops, live demonstrations, knowledge-sharing sessions, heritage routes, and stands, organized around five thematic areas addressing contemporary challenges facing these traditional forms of knowledge.
As the first event of its kind in the region, it sets out to explore the relationship between tradition and innovation, considering the incorporation of new technologies into heritage construction (commonly understood as construction that incorporates traditional methods or local materials). Next, and as the gathering's core objective, comes the concern for safeguarding and passing on knowledge, examining the relationship between practitioners, restorers, and companies, the role of specialized master tradespeople, the development of trade schools, and the identification of trades at risk of disappearing.
A third thematic area involves putting traditional knowledge to use in promoting more sustainable construction practices, tied to the use of local materials, efficient resource management, and heritage conservation from an environmentally responsible perspective. From an even more timely angle, the event's fourth thematic area addresses the visibility of the gaps, barriers, and challenges faced by women and gender-diverse individuals in a historically male-dominated sector, bringing a gender lens to the study of heritage trades.
Finally, the last thematic area of "Oficios en obra" focuses specifically on the city of Valparaíso and the material, regulatory, and economic challenges involved in conserving and maintaining its built heritage. In 2003, UNESCO inscribed the historic quarter of Valparaíso on the World Heritage List for its outstanding universal value, one that transcends borders and generations. The decision was based on criterion (iii), "an outstanding testimony to the early phase of globalization at the end of the 19th century, when it became the leading merchant port on the sea routes of the Pacific coast of South America." The event proposes to examine management challenges tied to the implementation of the World Heritage Site's Management Plan, the restoration of heritage housing, disaster and risk management, and the recovery of public space as a common good.
This first edition joins other local initiatives driven by historical conservation, understood not only as built form, but also as a way of doing things and sustaining them over time. Over the past three years, the Municipality of Valparaíso itself has established a Heritage Trades School offering free courses open to the community through an application system. The training cycles include courses in carpentry, mold-making, rammed-earth construction, and public statuary restoration, focused on the techniques and materials found in the city's buildings and public spaces. As with 'Oficios en obra,' the purpose is to foster the joint generation of knowledge about construction trades, as well as to provide citizens with more tools to understand and develop heritage restoration projects.
Other recent news about heritage preservation worldwide includes a new workspace project in London by the art, architecture, and design collective Assemble, transforming a Grade II*-listed building into a new creative and light industrial workspace. Since its founding in 2010, the studio has built a community around craft and making by providing creative and light industrial spaces resilient to market forces, working as a platform for ecologically and socially engaged work. In early August, the Getty Foundation's Conserving Black Modernism program, dedicated to preserving the architectural contributions of African American architects in the Modernist movement across the United States, announced five new grantee sites, while the UNESCO World Heritage Committee announced 25 new inscriptions to the World Heritage List during its 48th session, including 19 cultural properties, five natural sites, and one mixed property.

Markets on edge as US Fed meets to tackle high inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:29:56 UTC
14:29:56 KST

The spike in oil energy costs caused by the Middle East crisis has put pressure on central banks to temper global inflation. (AFP Photo)
Government borrowing costs have climbed to multiyear highs across major economies as rising oil prices fuel inflation concerns and expectations of further interest rate increases, putting pressure on businesses and households seeking credit.
The benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.04 percent on Sept. 15, its highest since July 2007. The 30-year yield touched 5.4 percent, also its highest since 2007.
Japan’s 10-year yield reached a three-decade high above 3 percent. Germany’s benchmark hovered near its highest since 2009, while French yields approached an 18-year peak. In Australia, 10-year yields climbed to about 5.39 percent, their highest in 15 years.
Treasuries provide a benchmark for dollar borrowing worldwide.
Governments and companies typically pay a premium above U.S. yields, so a rise in that benchmark can make new debt more expensive even if the premium investors demand for credit risk remains unchanged.
In the United States, higher Treasury yields feed into mortgage rates and corporate financing costs. They also increase the appeal of government bonds relative to stocks, raising the returns investors expect for taking greater risk.
“There’s been no catalyst to reverse the current momentum that we’ve seen in bond yields,” Jim Barnes, director of fixed income at Bryn Mawr Trust, told Reuters.
Oil supply disruptions have added to inflation concerns. Brent crude eased to $107.82 a barrel in early trading on Sept. 16 after gaining more than $3 in the previous session.
An attack forced Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline offline, disrupting a route that carries crude to the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Oil loadings at the kingdom’s Yanbu port were also suspended, according to media reports.
Ahead of the Fed’s Sept. 16 decision, markets had priced in a more than 90 percent chance of an increase of at least 25 basis points, according to CME FedWatch.
Large budget deficits and growing corporate borrowing needs are also weighing on debt markets. Shriya Samarth of StoneX cited artificial intelligence spending and concerns about public debt as factors complicating the outlook.
Washington must issue bonds to finance budget shortfalls and refinance maturing obligations, while companies are borrowing to fund major AI projects.
The increased supply can put further upward pressure on yields as borrowers compete for investors’ funds.
Higher refinancing costs gradually add to governments’ interest bills, leaving less room for other spending.
For energy-importing economies, more expensive fuel also raises import costs and complicates efforts to bring inflation down.
Bank of America U.S. economist Aditya Bhave said moving quickly to raise rates would give the Fed “a better chance of quelling inflation and keeping a lid on long-end rates.”

What’s the Pinglu Canal, China’s new gateway to Southeast Asia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:24:50 UTC
14:24:50 KST

What’s the Pinglu Canal, China’s new gateway to Southeast Asia?
China’s first modern river-to-sea canal could significantly cut down time and costs of trade to Southeast Asia.
Beijing, China – China is opening its first modern river-to-sea canal for navigation on Wednesday, a project that aims to dramatically cut down shipping distances between the country’s southern hinterland and Southeast Asia, a region that serves as a critical trade partner.
The Pinglu Canal is located entirely in Guangxi, the region in China’s far south bordering Vietnam and overlooking the South China Sea.
This 134km (83-mile) waterway links the Xijiang River with the Beibu Gulf, the northwestern arm of the Gulf of Tonkin stretching between southern China and northern Vietnam. It gives vast areas of southwest China, including provinces such as Yunnan and Guizhou, a shorter route to the sea and to Asian markets.
The first such canal built by communist China, Pinglu is a part of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor: A project involving southern Chinese provinces aimed at linking areas in western and southwestern China with Southeast Asian countries and global markets. The land-sea trade corridor is itself a part of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative, a web of highways, ports and railroads seeking to connect China with Europe and Africa.
The real gain: Savings in distance and cost
According to local authorities in Guangxi, the canal will shorten the shipping distance between inland areas of southwest China and Southeast Asian countries by about 560km (350 miles) and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent.
Estimates by Zhang Zhiwen, deputy secretary-general of the Guangxi government, indicate that transport costs alone will come down by more than 5 billion yuan annually, or about $700m.
The region’s vice chairwoman, Lu Xinning, describes these returns as “tangible gains” that reduce operating costs and boost domestic and foreign trade.
The canal will allow the passage of ships with a capacity of 5,000 tonnes. Its estimated cost is about 72.7 billion yuan, equivalent to about $10.8bn.
This means cities and industrial areas far from the coast in southwest China will become closer to maritime trade routes. The new trade corridor does not serve Guangxi alone; it is connected to a broader network extending to Chongqing in southwest China, Chengdu in Sichuan province, Guizhou and Yunnan, before goods reach the ports of the Beibu Gulf and, from there, overseas markets.
These changes come at a time when trade between China and Southeast Asia is growing rapidly. According to China’s General Administration of Customs, bilateral trade in the first half of 2026 reached about 4.34 trillion yuan, or about $640bn, an increase of 18.2 percent year on year.
At the southern end of the canal, container-handling capacity at Beibu Gulf Port rose from 2.28 million TEUs in 2017 to 10.06 million TEUs in 2025, with a shipping network covering major Southeast Asian ports.
From waterway to industrial hub
Guangxi is also working to build what it calls the “Pinglu Canal Economic Belt”, with the aim of attracting industries and spreading them out along the new corridor, while linking them to ports, transport networks and supply chains.
The targeted sectors include non-ferrous metals and critical minerals, modern green chemicals, as well as artificial intelligence and information technology. Industrial zones are also being developed near ports, reducing the distance between production sites and shipping centres.
The process of organising and directing shipping sources has already begun to generate new commercial activity. A train loaded with sodium bisulfate recently arrived from Chongqing, the major industrial and transport hub in southwest China, at the port of Nanning, the capital of Guangxi province. After the canal opens, direct commercial sailings are scheduled to begin to the port of Can Tho in southern Vietnam.
On the operational front, Guangxi has adopted a tiered transit-fee system that gives operators a grace period before imposing nominal charges.
Until December 31, 2026, commercial vessels will pass through the three water gates along the canal completely free of charge. Starting January 1, 2027, a fee of one yuan, about $0.14, will be charged for each tonne of a vessel’s capacity every time it passes through these gates. This trial rate will remain in effect until September 2031.
River vessels can sail directly to the berths of Qinzhou seaport without needing to transfer their cargo to other ships, enabling a seamless transition from river to sea.
Resettlement: Another side of the canal project
Building a canal of this scale would not have been possible without addressing a sensitive human dimension: Relocating thousands of families from their land. According to official sources, the resettlement process involved 2,764 households comprising 11,228 people across four counties and county-level cities in Guangxi. In Hengzhou alone, evacuation agreements were signed for 368 homes, which were completely demolished over a total area of 84,200 square metres (906,321 square feet), with 1,221 people temporarily resettled.
The process was not managed solely through financial compensation. Instead, 21 different housing models were designed in accordance with residents’ customs: The orientation of reception rooms, crop-drying areas, poultry enclosures and storage rooms for agricultural chemicals. In Shaping, the largest town in the resettlement project, residents were given four-storey homes covering 420sq metres (4,520sq ft), some with commercial storefronts facing the street.
Still, there is a sense of loss among many, even if mitigated by hope for the future.
In Xinfu, where the village of Fenghuangping once stood, one resident who was forced to leave said: “There is no longer a village called Fenghuangping, but with the Pinglu Canal, tomorrow will be better.”
Some families moved seven-century-old trees to the new site of their homes, including a 217-year-old camphor tree.
The resettlement process was carried out within 39 days, but it was linked to promises of jobs at the construction site and vocational training for residents of the relocated areas.
How geography is reshaping trade security
Straits and maritime corridors have long been the arteries of power in the global economy, but they are also among its most sensitive points of weakness.
The Hormuz crisis embodies this paradox: The passageway through which about one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow can, when threatened, become a factor that paralyses trade and redraws its routes.
Faced with that backdrop, countries around the world are trying to develop alternative routes and supply chains – pipelines, storage facilities and transport corridors that reduce the dependence of nations on just one or two routes.
The Pinglu Canal is China’s latest endeavour to do just that: Build an alternative, shorter and faster route to a critical market.

Family visas for foreign students targeted in migration crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:17:59 UTC
14:17:59 KST

International students to be effectively barred from bringing family to Australia
In short:
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is on the verge of unveiling changes designed to ensure Labor meets its migration targets.
International students are expected to be barred from bringing family members to Australia under the crackdown.
What's next?
Mr Burke will outline the full policy at the National Press Club tomorrow, six weeks after being forced to postpone the address.
International students would effectively be banned from bringing family members to Australia under a long-awaited overhaul of the immigration system to be unveiled by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke tomorrow.
In a speech entitled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Mr Burke will outline changes to try to ensure the government meets its target of reducing net overseas migration (NOM) from 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028.
Mr Burke had planned to announce the policy six weeks ago but was forced to abruptly postpone the National Press Club (NPC) address because of a disagreement between ministers weighing competing priorities.
The ABC understands the reworked plan was endorsed by Cabinet's Expenditure Review Committee this week ahead of the rescheduled NPC address on Thursday.
The government plans to bring down the NOM by cutting the number of temporary visas, which has risen to three million, ensure migrants leave Australia once their visas have expired to prevent so-called "visa hopping", and curb their ability to claim protection.
While international student numbers are expected to be left untouched, the ABC has been told they will effectively lose the ability to bring their families to Australia under the crackdown.
Last financial year 337,427 student visas were granted, and of those, 45,991 were secondary applicants, classed as dependents or family.
Labor's plan has some similarities to One Nation's migration policy, released this week, which included a crackdown on family visas for both students and skilled migrants.
It is unclear whether the government will also target the families of skilled migrants, but Mr Burke recently used his powers to dramatically slow down the processing of skilled and family visas lodged by applicants offshore.
Ahead of the announcement on Thursday, Mr Burke told Question Time he would like to implement Labor's planned overhaul via legislation but will pursue other "levers" if he could not get parliamentary support.
"Since the Hawke and Howard years a whole lot of our immigration system has been demand-driven, and processing speeds is one of the only things, with planning levels, we currently have available," Mr Burke told Question Time today.
"The more tools that are available the better we can target the system.
"The best form of outcome there will be, if we are able to sort our way through, [is] for a legislative option.
"In the absence of that there are still more levers the government will be able to use, and I'll be making those announcements tomorrow."
Changes expected to bridging visas
To address a blowout in bridging visas the government has also been considering removing the work rights of temporary migrants whose claims for protection have been rejected by Home Affairs.
An average of 1,580 claims for protection are being lodged onshore every month, mostly by people from China, India and Malaysia who have come to Australia on a student or visitor visa.
About 90 per cent of those claims are rejected, but applicants have the right to appeal the rulings through the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) and the Federal Court, a process that regularly takes up to eight years.
During that time a person is placed on a bridging visa allowing them to stay in the community and work, prompting government concerns some are simply "gaming the system".
Labor had also been considering changing the favourable treatment of British backpackers to make the scheme less attractive before the prime minister intervened and ruled out any move that could breach the Free Trade Agreement between the two countries.
Under pressure to bring down overseas arrivals, Mr Burke has already made sweeping changes to the migration system, pausing or slowing down the processing of working holiday maker visas in July and reprioritising the processing of skilled visas.
The changes, under Ministerial Direction 119, mean any worker applying for a skilled visa from overseas is now at the back of the queue, pushing visa wait times from days to over a year in some cases.

Where have all the British backpackers gone?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
05:04:22 UTC
14:04:22 KST

Australia's British backpacker boom is taking a different path
For generations of young Britons, Australia came with an unwritten itinerary.
Arrive in Sydney. Find a hostel. Then head north, picking fruit, pulling beers or waiting tables, to clock up the 88 days of specified work needed to extend a working holiday visa.
That deal changed in July 2024.
Under the Australia-UK free trade agreement, British backpackers no longer have to complete specified work to get a second or third working holiday visa. The age limit was also raised from 30 to 35.
And they are coming in record numbers.
More than 79,000 working holiday visas were granted to British citizens in 2024–25, up almost 70 per cent on the previous year.
But the old journey north is disappearing.
Dan McConnell knows it from both sides. The British-born general manager of Mad Monkey Backpackers arrived in Australia on a working holiday visa in 2015.
He travelled the east coast, became a tour guide, found an employer willing to sponsor him and moved to Cairns to secure permanent residency.
Now, he said, British backpackers had far less reason to make the same journey.
His hostels hosted about 8,000 British guests during the post-COVID tourism boom.
This year, with the busy season almost over in Cairns, that figure is closer to 5,300.
He said the change was being felt beyond the number of beds occupied.
"The British people were the ones that were spending a lot of money on our bars, while they were working towards extending their visas," Mr McConnell said.
"The nightlife has drastically dropped off over the past 18 months in Cairns."
Mr McConnell said demand was stronger at the company's Sydney properties, where many working holiday makers were finding jobs and accommodation and choosing to stay put.
"Why would you give up your accommodation, whether that's in a hostel or a share house, to come up to Cairns and run the risk of not being able to find work?" he said.
The working holiday scheme has become part of a much bigger argument over Australia's migration numbers.
The federal government has been considering ways to reduce temporary migration, including whether British backpackers should once again have to undertake regional work to extend their visas.
But in August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ruled that out, saying Australia would honour its free trade agreement with Britain.
On North Queensland farms, growers say British backpackers were once a familiar part of the seasonal workforce.
Now they are increasingly difficult to find.
"There's been a massive drop-off in the Brits,"
"Having the UK workers available did make a difference. It's increased the pressure of finding workers."
Workers from countries including France, Italy and Taiwan have largely filled the gap.
But the disappearance of the British backpacker from regional Australia points to a broader change in the way the working holiday visa is being used.
From adventure to career
Australian National University Migration Hub director Alan Gamlen said the working holiday scheme had gradually changed from a vehicle for travel and exploration into something more closely resembling an international career break.
"It's evolved over time away from this voyage of self-discovery and exploration to more of a targeted career-building exercise,"
"There is more of a move to the big cities."
He said Australia was no longer simply a place to travel through and the working holiday visa could also be a pathway towards a longer-term future.
"Three years of successive visas almost gets them to permanent residence eligibility, so the working holiday visa is seen by some as a first step towards permanent settlement," he said.
Britain was Australia's fourth-largest source of permanent migrants in 2024–25, with 10,205 places granted to UK citizens. Employer-sponsored migration accounted for 4,650 of those places.
Department of Home Affairs figures show 321,116 working holiday maker visas were granted across all nationalities in 2024–25, up almost 37 per cent from 234,556 the previous year.

Former spy chief says media failed to report widely on antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-16
04:56:52 UTC
13:56:52 KST

Former ASIO boss Dennis Richardson says media dropped the ball on antisemitism post October 7
In short:
A former leader of Australia's intelligence service says the media dropped the ball when it came to coverage of antisemitic incidents after the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel.
Dennis Richardson says pretending the issue does not exist plays into the hands of Neo-Nazis.
What's next?
Mr Richardson says an open discussion about the role of extremist Islamists is needed, but warned against targeting the Australian Muslim community more broadly.
Former spy boss Dennis Richardson has criticised the media's handling of "blatant antisemitism" in Australia after the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel and has called for an "open discussion" about extremist Islamists without targeting the broader Australian Muslim community.
Mr Richardson, the former head of Australia's domestic intelligence service ASIO, also took a swipe at public servants, saying they often "hid behind their own cowardice" and engaged in self-censorship.
He said some media decisions not to cover antisemitic preaching may have been "well-intentioned" but were ultimately misguided.
"I tend to agree with those who argue that following 7 October we dropped the ball and failed to draw a line," he said in a speech at the Lowy Institute media award last night.
"I'm not implying a straight-line connection to the Bondi terrorist attack, as the ingredients that gave rise to that terrible incident are more complex.
"I do believe however, that a more forceful and consistent response to the blatant antisemitism we saw in the immediate aftermath of 7th of October may well have set a different tone and drawn a clearer line between the acceptable and the unacceptable."
Hamas took more than 250 hostages and killed 1,200 people on October 7, 2023. Palestinian health authorities say the ensuing military campaign from Israel has killed more than 73,000 people.
At Bondi beach in December last year, father and son Sajid and Naveed Akram killed 15 people at a Hanukkah event.
Mr Richardson said the lack of media coverage of antisemitic incidents was partly "because of a misguided concern that it might inflame social tensions, as opposed to putting the spotlight on the conduct which deserved to be highlighted and condemned".
For example, he highlighted that comments made by an Islamic preacher — without naming him as Wissam Haddad — in November 2023 were not widely reported by the media until 2025, when a federal court judge found those remarks were "fundamentally racist and antisemitic" and "devastatingly offensive and insulting".
Mr Richardson said the sources of antisemitism needed to be addressed in a mature way, "including open discussion about extremist Islamists, without Australian Muslims as a whole feeling targeted".
"Mainstream Muslim leaders should be at the centre of any such discussion," he said.
"Pretending the issue is not there simply leads to conspiracy theories and plays into the hands of extremists at the other end of the spectrum."
Elaborating on Radio National Breakfast on Wednesday, he said: "You play into the hands of Neo-Nazis, you play into the hands of people who want to pretend that Muslims per se are an issue, when of course they're not."
"When you have a discussion about extremist Islamists, you have a real risk that Muslims as a whole feel under pressure."
Calling out public service 'cowards'
Mr Richardson, a retired public servant himself, said he suspected many senior public servants gave frank advice behind closed doors, but he feared those in the "so-called senior executive service" practised "self-censorship".
"They hide behind their own cowardice,"
"[They] will talk endlessly about how difficult it is to give frank advice, but they wouldn't know what it was if they fell over it."
He said the fact that some Jewish children needed security to attend their schools and sporting events was a stain on Australia's social cohesion.
"I still do not understand why it took a royal commission to bring into the public consciousness the fact that some Australian kids have to experience their schooling, sporting, and religious life behind the sort of security you would expect to find in a strife-torn country," he said.
In March, Mr Richardson resigned as a special adviser to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion in the wake of the Bondi terrorist attack.
After the Bondi attack, Mr Richardson had initially been appointed by the prime minister to undertake a review into intelligence and policing agencies, but that was then folded into the broader royal commission.
Upon his resignation he said he feared he would have little influence over the commission's recommendations and said he had been treated as a "highly paid researcher".

Turkey steps up efforts to reach agreement on Black Sea — Fidan
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said this at a joint press conference with Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov in Baku, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
"Our work is currently underway, with particular attention being paid to the Black Sea. We are negotiating with the parties on this issue and have proposals. We have received the parties' responses and are working to reconcile them so that, on this basis, a mutually acceptable approach can be developed," Hakan Fidan said.
According to him, Turkey believes that, given the necessary political will and goodwill of the parties, a basis for compromise can be found.
"Recently, we have stepped up our efforts to reach an agreement. We hope that the necessary initiatives will allow us to bring this process to completion. As our president has emphasized from the very beginning, even the worst peace is better than war itself. Turkey will continue to make every possible effort for peace," the Turkish foreign minister said.
Fidan also drew attention to the growing number of attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea. According to him, since the beginning of the war, Turkey has made significant efforts to prevent the hostilities from spreading to the Black Sea, including through strict adherence to the Montreux Convention and the implementation of the Black Sea Grain Initiative.
He also stressed that the spread of the war to the Black Sea, as well as threats to the lives of Turkish citizens and the operations of Turkish companies, are unacceptable.
The Turkish foreign minister also said that over the past year, the nature of the Russian-Ukrainian war has changed and that it has effectively shifted from a "war of attrition" to a "war of destruction."
"Over the past year, the war has effectively transformed from a war of attrition into a war of destruction. There are now practically no targets left that are not being targeted… We are also seeing an increasing number of civilian casualties," Fidan said.

The offer was previously available to customers of Arbejdernes Landsbank. Following the merger of Arbejdernes Landsbank, Vestjysk Bank and Sydbank, it will now be extended to all customers of the new bank, AL Sydbank.

“That is the promise we are fulfilling now, and it applies both to our existing customers who do not yet have those terms, and then of course the new customers who hopefully will join,” he said.
Randers said the bank hopes the offer will attract new customers and encourage existing customers to stay.
“And then of course we hope that in the longer term, it means that those customers will want to do more business with us when they eventually buy a home or car or save up for retirement or something else entirely,” he said.
The change comes after AL Sydbank told customers this summer that several fees would change following the merger.
According to a Mybanker analysis for TV 2, fees increased for between 55 and 60 percent of the bank’s services, depending on which bank a person previously used. Between 25 and 35 percent of fees decreased.
Customers must have their NemKonto, the bank account used for payments from Danish public authorities, with AL Sydbank to qualify for the free account.
The bank has not yet decided which debit card will be included.

Nearly six in 10 Danish companies with more than 10 employees now use artificial intelligence, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark. That’s almost four times the share recorded three years ago.
In 2026, 59 percent of these companies use AI, up from 15 percent in 2023. The share was 42 percent in 2025.
The uses of AI include analyzing text, converting spoken language into machine-readable code, generating images and videos, and automating work processes.
Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, said it has seen AI move from being mainly a topic of discussion to a tool used in daily business.
“Companies’ use of artificial intelligence is here to stay, and we can see that the large companies are the furthest ahead,” Frederikke Saabye, industry director at Dansk Erhverv, said.
According to the business organisation, companies see greater efficiency as the main benefit of using AI. A lack of employee skills, knowledge and time are the biggest barriers to making greater use of the technology.
IT-Branchen, an industry association representing technology companies in Denmark, said the wider use of AI also increases the need to consider issues such as quality, transparency and data security.
“The more the technology spreads, the more important issues of quality, transparency, data security, and not least human judgment become,” IT-Branchen’s CEO Natasha Friis Saxberg said, adding that the development makes broader AI knowledge and training more important, including upskilling and continuing education for employees.
The Danish government plans to charge tourists 20 DKK per overnight stay in Copenhagen and Aarhus and introduce a levy on cruise ships, according to government sources and a memo obtained by Børsen.
The previously undisclosed measures would help fund tax cuts that the minority government will seek support for this autumn. The plans require backing from other parties, expected to come from the center-right opposition.
The government wants to abolish the 7.5% intermediate tax on annual income between 641,200 DKK and 777,900 DKK. It also plans to remove the top-top tax on income exceeding 2,592,700 DKK.
Corporate tax would fall from 22% to 19% over three years. The ceiling for share savings accounts would rise to 500,000 DKK over the same period, and taxes on shares would be reduced.
Planned funding measures include keeping the duty on chocolate and sweets, reducing the research and development deduction for companies and raising taxes on dividends received by major shareholders.
The government also wants to limit interest deductions to 150,000 DKK for individuals and 300,000 DKK for couples. Estates worth more than 10 million DKK would face a tax rate 15 percentage points higher than today.
The tax cuts are not fully covered by higher taxes and duties. The government plans to use about 1.5 billion DKK from available public funds in 2027, rising to about 2 billion DKK in 2029.
Denmark’s government consists of the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Moderates and Social Liberals. It does not have a parliamentary majority.
Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.
Denmark has rejected Russia’s claim that a Danish military helicopter acted “provocatively” before a Russian frigate fired two flares toward it Monday.
Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Danish helicopters had repeatedly performed “dangerous maneuvers” near Russian warships.
“The latest incident shows that the communication problems are not on the Russian navy’s side, but on the Danish side,” Barbin wrote to the Danish news agency Ritzau.
Denmark’s Armed Forces said the frigate fired two signal or distress flares toward an Air Force Fennec helicopter in international waters off Gedser. The helicopter was conducting routine photographic monitoring of the ship.

Denmark has summoned Barbin to the Foreign Ministry for talks about Monday’s incident.
The Danish government will require police to register all potential crimes as criminal cases and end the practice of shelving reports without a proper investigation.
The Justice Ministry announced Tuesday that it would implement all recommendations from the National Audit Office, Denmark’s independent public spending watchdog. The disputed police practice is known as “washing cases.”
“Citizens must naturally be able to have confidence that the police handle their case properly and correctly, regardless of where in the country you live,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said.
“In the future, all potential criminal cases must be registered as actual criminal cases,” he added.
The Public Accounts Committee, a parliamentary oversight body, strongly criticized police in May after receiving a National Audit Office report on the practice. Cases were reportedly shelved partly to save resources.
The new government reshuffled senior police leadership in June. Top positions in the National Police and PET, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, changed hands.
Several justice spokespersons in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, said they had no confidence in National Police Commissioner Thorkild Fogde after he said he did not know about the practice. Fogde was later removed from the position.
The ministry did not say whether police would receive additional funding. Wammen previously said he was open to providing more money and noted that a multiyear agreement had already increased funding and training.
The National Police and Director of Public Prosecutions must regularly report on future developments to the political parties behind that agreement.
Two earlier State Prosecutor reports were not used because the National Audit Office identified issues they had missed, Wammen said.
Train services between Fredericia, Odense and Copenhagen returned to their normal schedule at 10 a.m. Tuesday after damaged overhead wires near Sorø were repaired.
Trains between Copenhagen Airport and Slagelse also resumed normal operations, Banedanmark, which manages Denmark’s rail infrastructure, and passenger rail operator DSB said on X.
Banedanmark warned that some delays could occur while services restart. It advised passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public journey-planning service, before traveling.
The damage had caused cancellations and delays since noon Monday. Repair work covered the section between Ringsted and Slagelse.
Banedanmark described the repairs as “extensive” and “very complex.” A support cable had fallen, and the equipment holding it had also been damaged.
“These are just some of the damages we see on our traction power system,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Sigsgaard said Monday.
Banedanmark received the first report of the problem at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train traffic was then stopped completely while workers identified the cause.
DSB and Banedanmark said passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes could use DSB’s travel time guarantee.
DSB paid 67 million DKK in passenger compensation during the first six months of 2026, more than twice as much as during the same period in 2025.
A delay of at least 30 minutes provides a new ticket for the same route or a refund of 50 percent of the ticket price. Passengers delayed by an hour can receive 75 percent and claim up to 75 DKK for food and drinks.
Delays exceeding 90 minutes qualify for a full ticket refund.

The hearing will begin at 1 p.m. at Copenhagen City Court, the Copenhagen Police prosecution service said Tuesday. A formal indictment has not yet been filed.
The man is suspected of punching the 32-year-old Swede hard in the jaw or neck. The case falls under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence.
The incident happened June 30 during a public screening at Islands Brygge of the World Cup match between Norway and Ivory Coast.
The Swedish man fell after being struck, hit his head and later died from his injuries. He worked for the Swedish police but attended the event as a private citizen.

The 24-year-old Danish citizen is suspected of stomping on the Swedish man while he was lying down and hitting another Swedish citizen.
The 29-year-old, a Somali citizen, is suspected of kicking the second Swedish man. Police have notified him of the charge by telephone and through his defense lawyer because they have not located him.
Police have said the three cases will be handled separately because there is no evidence that the men acted together. Court dates for the other two men have not been announced.

A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.
Russian frigate fires flares near Danish military helicopter in international waters
A Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, Denmark’s Armed Forces said.
The Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the ship when the flares were fired. One passed close to the aircraft, according to a military statement.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea. No personnel were injured, and the helicopter was not damaged.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats called the incident serious and described Russia’s actions as “very unprofessional seamanship.”
“It is serious. It is an expression of the boundaries having been moved regarding the willingness to take risks from the Russian side,” Bruus said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen will summon the Russian ambassador to discuss the incident, though the date of the meeting has not been announced. Bruus said he did not expect further action beyond that meeting.
The defense minister said the incident would not change Denmark’s monitoring operations.
“We view it seriously, but it is not the case that we will change our behavior, understood in the sense that we have a completely legitimate task in monitoring what is going on,” Bruus said.
Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party, said the incident showed that Russian provocations had reached Denmark.
She called for NATO unity and continued support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
“It is therefore crucial that NATO stands united, and that we continue to support Ukraine,” Støjberg said. She added that she expected a briefing from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.
